It is my view that the matter to be investigated is the forgery of a Palace command, which is beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, and that both of us should report it upward and neither of us should touch it further." He hands over the account, still tacky. "That is written there in those words, so that neither of us can be blamed for the other."

Kessel reads it, and grunts, and something between them settles that will make your fortnight easier. "Room," he says. "You'll have the strongroom under the weigh-house for your sacks, and I'll take the key and the Office can pay me a shilling to make it lawful. — Madam Harrow." The hat goes back on. "The Corn Exchange hall's yours if you want it; it's the only house in Achterhalt and my brother-in-law holds the keys, and he'll ask you eighteen and take twelve." A beat. "And you'll be careful. The last company that played this town had bills cried by that same bellman and the leading man ran off with a farrier's wife, so we're not sentimental here."

He goes, constables trailing. The square exhales. Vane, who has been standing three feet behind you throughout in his plum coat with his hat off, being magnificently silent, now says, "*Twelve*," in the voice of a man in love. "Harrow. The bank, and then the ironmonger, and then I shall haggle with a bailiff's brother-in-law, and it will be the happiest day of my life."

The bank first, as asked — front door, hat on, my arm not offered because he doesn't need it, whatever his face thinks. I watch nine years come off Odalric Vane at a marble counter: the fifth-year business closed square, the take banked like any dull man's money, and a receipt he holds a half-second too long before it goes into the breast pocket where the old notice lives. Then the ironmonger's, where I say only: "Choose me a sky." And I stand back and watch a big man walk a wall of hanging metal with his eyes shut, flicking each sheet with one fingernail, listening.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The clerk at the Farriers' and Merchants' is young, and calls him *sir*, and has never heard of him, which is the kindest thing that has happened to Odalric Vane in a decade. The fifth-year business takes eleven minutes; the ledger is fetched, the coin draw found, the marginal note read out — *paid in coin to bearer, Vane, O., on account of Brandt, H.* — and a copy made for you at twopence. The take goes in. The receipt comes out. He holds it, and then puts it away over the amber notice, and says nothing at all on the steps, which from him is a psalm.

The ironmonger's is a cave of hanging metal, and the ironmonger himself is delighted to be ignored. Vane goes down the wall with his eyes shut, one fingernail, tick — tick — tick, head tilted. A galvanised sheet: "Biscuit." A thin bright one: "Rain on a hat. Useful, not a sky." A great black plate at the end, longer than a man: he flicks it and the whole shop hums, and he stands there with his hand flat on it until it stops.

"That," he says. "It has a *floor* in it, Harrow. Listen — " he flicks it again, low, and the sound arrives under your ribs the way the old one used to before it split. "Twenty-two shillings," the ironmonger says. Vane opens his mouth to haggle, catches your eye, and instead says, with enormous dignity, "Twenty-two shillings, and a shilling to your boy to carry it, and I shall *not* round it, madam, look at me not rounding it."

It goes into the wagon in felt, on the boards, next to nothing else.

At the Corn Exchange he gets the hall for thirteen and considers it a defeat and is happy. And that evening, in the empty hall with the trestles stacked and one lamp lit, while you chalk your plot on the flags because there's no board, Falk comes in and stands over the new sheet in its felt, and says: "Harrow. Ilse from the Rose. Boyle told me a woman spoke to you in the square." He doesn't ask. He waits, exactly as you wait, having learned it from you.

I set the chalk down and give it to him the way I gave the first one — exact, nothing added, nothing softened. "Her name is Ilse Bacher. Ilse of the Rose, in service there at fifteen. She's well — married to a good butter man, a boy of ten named Fenner who can read. She sat down on a kerb in front of people when she saw that bill, because she knew the phrase through a scullery door twenty years ago. She says the fault was never yours to carry — it was hers. She opened the door." I hold his eye for the last of it. "And she sent you this, word for word: his voice is still the loudest thing that ever came through a scullery door. He'll know what I mean. He shouted at Odalric Vane for laughing." And then I wait, exactly as taught.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Falk stands with his hand on the felt over the new sheet and doesn't move for a long moment, and then he laughs — one short surprised bark, up in the rafters of the Corn Exchange, and it hangs there.

"I did," he says. "I did shout at him. He laughed when the boy asked *is that the finish*, and I shouted at him across the table and called him a — " he stops, and looks almost young — "well, I called him a great deal of things and one of them was in Latin. And I have remembered that room every night for twenty years and I never once remembered *that*, that I got angry, that somebody in that room said no. It has been nine men and a bottle and a wager in my head all this time." He takes his hand off the felt. "Ilse of the Rose. Fifteen years old, carrying bread. She opened the door for a child with nowhere to go, and she has been paying interest on that for twenty years, same as Odalric on his four hundred and twelve." He shakes his head slowly. "*Not mine.* She meant the wager. She thought I'd be carrying the wager."

He picks up your chalk and holds it out to you, handle-first, like a sword being returned.

"Finish your plot, harbor. I shall go and sit with the trunk, and I find I want to tell you something and I would rather say it standing here than in three weeks' time." His voice is quite steady. "When the capital is done and the debts are paid and the company is safe, I am going to ask you to help me finish it. Properly. Stage, gas, house, all four acts and the matter following. Once, and correctly, with everyone who chooses to be there and nobody who doesn't." He nods at the felt. "Not yet. Not tonight. But you are the only stage manager in the world who would say *our left*, and I have waited twenty years for someone to say it, and I did not want to die with the asking still in my mouth."

He goes out to the yard. Your chalk plot is half done on the flags, one lamp, the new sky in its felt, and out through the open door the tarpaulin under the lamp with a big man settling onto the tailboard beside it.
messages.speaker: Emeran Falk

messages.body: I take the chalk back the way you take a returned sword — by the handle, with respect for both ends. "Then it goes in the book, Emeran. The standing page, not the crowded one: Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp. Answer owed when the capital is done and this company is safe." And because he'd want the shape of my yes known in advance: "If it's ever yes, it wears these clothes: everyone who chooses, and they choose after hearing Katterau entire — no wagers, no bottles, nobody who signs the small print of nothing unread. And a boy named Fenner Bacher stays home. Whatever house. Whatever date." I finish the plot on the flags, strike the day, and carry the lamp out to the tailboard — some askings deserve company after, and the watch was mine anyway.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He hears the terms out with his head down, and at *no wagers, no bottles* he makes a sound that is nearly a laugh, and at *a boy named Fenner Bacher stays home* he says, "Yes. That first, and the rest after."

You sit on the tailboard with the lamp between you. The trunk under the tarpaulin does nothing at all, and goes on doing nothing, which is how the good nights go. The Achterhalt watch cries eleven; a cat kills something in the yard next door; Boyle comes out at midnight with his pipe unlit and takes over without a word and Falk lets him, which is new.

Achterhalt gives you two nights. *Ilsabet* to a hall of corn merchants who laugh in the wrong places and buy every seat. Prewick's new thunder gets its debut, and the black sheet has a floor in it, and when the storm comes in low the whole Corn Exchange holds its breath, and afterwards Vane cries and says the *Advertiser* never heard a sky like it. Frau Loewe forwards no word from Katterau, because you asked for none.

Then the toll road, and a hundred and ten miles of it, and the empire getting flatter and busier and less kind. Eleven days ahead of the 3rd, the capital comes up out of its own smoke: a wall, a river with real ships, four bridges, and a mass of roofs that goes on being roofs long after you expect it to stop.

At the Northgate customs post a clerk in a green coat reads Prewick's papers, then the company list, then the company list again. He looks up.

"Vermilion Players. You're expected." He stamps twice. "You'll go to the Baraque Theatre in the fourth ward, not the Palace — the command's at the Palace on the 3rd, but you rehearse and lodge at the Baraque, and there's a gentleman been waiting on you there since Tuesday." He hands the papers back. "And madam — the stage manager's wanted at the Office of Public Morals tomorrow morning, ten o'clock, Room Fourteen. Not the clerk. You."

Through the gate with my questions in march order. To Prewick, first, quiet: "Room Fourteen. What is it, who sits in it, and what do they drink?" To the column: "The Baraque, load-in tonight, and the trunk stays wagon-bound — city yard, double watch, Boyle and Toby splitting till I've walked the ground." And to the gatekeeping clerk, mild as milk: "Tell Room Fourteen the stage manager keeps clean books and keeps appointments the same way." Then we roll for the fourth ward — and whoever has been waiting at the Baraque since Tuesday gets met by me, before anyone so much as unpacks a slipper.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The green-coated clerk writes *told* against your name and waves you through, and the capital swallows the wagons whole.

Prewick answers as you go, sitting bolt upright with the noise of the city going over him. "Room Fourteen is the second floor, east corridor. It is Assessment. Not Enforcement, madam — Enforcement is Nine. Fourteen is where they *read*." He wets his lips. "Herr Undersecretary Lenz sits in it. No relation to Toby, I assure you. He is the man who put those two anonymous folios into the Index, or rather his predecessor was, and Lenz has kept the entry unchanged for nineteen years and refused four applications to strike either of them out. I know this because I copied the refusals in my first month and I remember them because they were the only interesting thing I have ever copied." A pause. "He drinks nothing. He is famous for it. He offers tea and does not have any himself, and the tea is very good, and it is a great deal like being weighed."

The Baraque is a real theatre with a bad roof in a poor ward: sixty years old, nine hundred seats, gas throughout, a stage door onto a cobbled yard with a gate that locks — and a man sitting on a mounting block just inside it in a bottle-green coat, with a portmanteau at his feet and a book on his knees, who stands as the wagons come in and takes his hat off, and who is not anyone you have met.

He is about forty. Ink on his right hand. And when he sees you drop from the board and come at him first, before anyone, he says — with something like relief and something like fear —

"You'd be the stage manager. Good." He holds out his hand. "Anselm Krug. I kept that book before you did, and I left Katterau in the night without my boots, and I have been waiting since Tuesday to find out whether Odalric will let me back or have me thrown in the river."

"Bell Harrow." One shake, dry hand. "You keep a decent margin note, Herr Krug — your tin-only line spared a farmer his second concussion." Then the truth of the yard, fast, because wheels are turning in behind me: "It's not my river and it's not my door. But here's how it plays. You stand where you stand; I announce nobody; Odalric sees you when he sees you. And whatever you came to say gets said whole — to his face first, then to the company at supper, Katterau and all. We're past half-told things in this troupe." And I stay planted beside him as the first wagon rounds the gate — a stage manager stands where the scene is about to happen.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The first wagon comes in with Boyle swearing at the arch, and the second, and Falk's last, and the yard fills with the noise of arrival — and then Vane comes round the tailboard with his hat off, mid-sentence about the roof, and stops.

Nobody says anything. Toby freezes with a hamper. Dessa Krul puts down the slippers.

"Anselm," Vane says.

"Odalric."

Vane crosses the cobbles. You do not step in, because you said you wouldn't, and because the big man's hands are open at his sides. He stops in front of Krug, looks at him — at the bottle-green coat, at the portmanteau — and then does the thing you did not predict: he sinks down onto the mounting block, in his good coat, on wet stone, and puts his face in his hands, and says, muffled: "I told them you took the takings. In Katterau. I told the company you'd gone off with the Wednesday take, because I could not — " he stops, and lifts his head, and it is the worst thing you have seen on him — "because I could not say why you went. It was seven pounds and I made it a theft to save myself an explanation, and I have known where you were for two years and said nothing."

Krug stands very still. "I know," he says. "I've had it from three companies who wouldn't have me." A pause. "That's what I came about. Not the river."

Falk has come round the wagon and stopped dead with the rug over his arm. From the archway, Mirelle — who has not moved and whose voice cuts the yard clean in half — says: "Then he'll say it in front of us tonight, at supper, and unsay it in the same breath. Won't you, Odalric." Not a question. "Harrow's already ruled it. Nothing half-told."

And Vane, on the mounting block, in the wet, nods, and gets out, "Yes. Yes. All of it," and then, hopelessly, out of pure habit: "Harrow — ask me for a thing."

"Then here it is. Before supper: three letters, in ink, unrounded — to the three companies that wouldn't have him. The theft unsaid, the fault named as yours, your signature large enough to cost you something. Toby runs them to the evening post before the soup's on." And to Krug, because a yard should know its own weather: "You eat with us tonight. Whatever else gets decided, nobody in my company interviews a man hungry." Then, over my shoulder, the day going on because days do: "Load-in continues. Dessa — the slippers were down four seconds, that's three too many."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"Three letters," Vane says, from the mounting block, "in ink," and gets up, and goes into the theatre in search of a table like a man walking to his own second act.

Dessa Krul picks up the slippers and says, "Four seconds is my *whole* opinion of a man, madam," and carries them in.

Load-in goes. The Baraque is a proper old barn — nine hundred seats, three levels, a rake so steep the pit is a well, and a gas board with a brass wheel worn smooth by sixty years of thumbs. The roof leaks over the O.P. side, and you post a notice about it before you take your coat off, and Prewick reads it.

Krug is useful within nine minutes and does not once say *when I kept the book*: he knows where the Baraque's counterweights bind, and he knows the gasman's name, and he shows Toby a trick with a lashing that Toby will do for the rest of his life. Twice you catch him looking at your prompt corner — at the chalk, the nail, the shape you've made of it — and looking away.

Vane writes three letters at the props table with his hat off. Toby runs them. The soup comes on at nine and the company sits down on flats and hampers in the O.P. wing, and Vane stands up with his glass and does it — says it whole, no rhetoric, the theft unsaid, the fault named, the seven pounds paid out of the float onto the table in front of everybody. Krug looks at the coins and doesn't take them.

"Keep it," he says. "I want the other thing." He turns, not to Vane, but to you. "Madam Harrow. You've got the book and I don't want it back; you're better at it than I was and I've watched your notices go up. What I came for is this." He sets a small parcel on the hamper beside your plate — brown paper, tied, thin.

"Nine pages," Krug says. "I cut ten out of that book and I burned nine of them, and the tenth came back, and I ran. That's the lie I've been living: I never burned any. I couldn't. They're all here." He puts both hands flat on his knees. "And I have read every one of them, madam, which nobody else in this company has done, and I know what's in the ones that haven't happened yet."

I don't touch the parcel. Custody first: "Tonight that goes into Emeran's lining with its kin — after you and I count them into the book together. Nine, numbered as found." Then I open the one lawful door for what he carries: "And you'll give this table what you know, Herr Krug — but as report. Your words. Plain summary, dates where you hold them. Nothing recited, nothing quoted — the play does not speak at my suppers, even secondhand." I look round the flats and hampers, at every face that chose this table. "Anyone stays who wants to stay; anyone may go and no note made of it. This is Katterau's account, the pending column." I nod to Krug. "Begin with what hasn't happened yet."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Nobody goes. Toby's ears go red with the effort of not being sent out; Dessa Krul folds her arms; Prewick puts his notebook away, closed, in his coat, and folds his hands on top of it, which is the most eloquent thing he has ever done.

Krug does it well. He is a stage manager, so he does it as a plot.

"Summary, then. Nine pages. Numbered as they came, and they came in order, which frightened me more than anything." He counts them on his fingers, not touching the parcel. "One and two came at Vessendal two springs ago, and they've happened: a horse lame on a hill road, and a wagon and a printer's line — I never understood the second one till I saw a bill in a bailiff's hand this afternoon and Boyle told me the rest.

"Three, four and five have happened on this tour, and Madam Harrow has all three of them in some form. A door at a bank. A funeral for a small drowned thing. A man in a fourth row." He glances up. "That one has a number in it. Twenty. It's Falk's, and I'll say no more of it at a supper table.

"Six has not happened. It's a boy at a theatre, brought by a woman who doesn't go in." Ilse's face; you say nothing. "Seven has not happened. There's a room in it with fourteen on the door, and a man who does not drink, and a question asked three times.

"Eight has not happened, and it is the one I ran from, and I'll give you its whole substance in five words and no more: *a stage manager rings the bell.*" He looks at you steadily. "That's your page, madam. It's been sitting in my portmanteau in a rooming house in the fourth ward for two years waiting for whoever took my job, and that is the true reason I did not burn them and the true reason I came.

"Nine has not happened and I cannot summarise it, because it isn't a scene. It's a cast list. Twelve names, blank where the names go, and at the bottom, in the copyist's hand: *and the house, entire.*"

The gas hisses. Somewhere out in the nine hundred empty seats the roof drips onto the O.P. side, exactly where your notice says it does.
messages.speaker: Anselm Krug

messages.body: "Then the book gets three new lines tonight." To Krug, first: "You kept it after all, Herr Krug — one page of it, two years, for a stranger you'd never met. That's the job description entire." The procedure follows: after supper he and I count nine pages into the book, numbered as found; the parcel goes to Emeran's lining with its kin — "except page eight. That one comes to me. My name is in the work, and my coat is already load-bearing." Then tomorrow, plainly, so nobody frets in private: "Room Fourteen owes me tea now. If a man who doesn't drink asks me one question three times, he will get the same true answer three times. Clean books read identically on every audit — that is what clean means. Herr Prewick, you'll walk me to the door, wait outside with your watch running, and if I'm longer than an hour, fetch nobody and note the time." I stand, and the flats become a bedroom wall again. "Sleep, all of you. We're eleven days early, and I intend to spend them like a rich woman."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
They sleep, more or less: bodies on flats, Dessa Krul in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under her head, Boyle and Toby splitting the yard, Krug on a hamper in the O.P. wing because he will not take a bed until he is told he belongs. The counting is done at the props table by one candle — nine pages, face-down, numbered aloud, entered by you and initialled by him. Falk's coat takes eight of them; the seam whispers.

Page eight goes into your coat. You do not read it. That takes more than you expected.

Ten o'clock. The Office of Public Morals is a great grey building with a courtyard full of bicycles and a smell of paste and coal. Prewick delivers you to the second floor, east corridor, brass **14** on frosted glass, and takes out his watch and starts it and stands against the wall with his hat in his hands, and does not wish you luck, because he has learned better.

Room Fourteen has one window, two chairs, four presses of ledgers, and a tea tray already laid for one.

Undersecretary Lenz is sixty, dry, small, and unremarkable in a way that is clearly a career. He does not stand. He pours the tea, which is very good, and sets it in front of you, and takes nothing himself, and opens a plain folder.

"Madam Harrow. Nineteen days in post." He turns a page. "You have posted eleven safety notices, buried a sheet of tin with a hymn, stopped a bill in Achterhalt, paid a nine-year storage debt on a stranger's box, ruled out Katterau, and brought this company into the capital eleven days early, which no company has ever done." He looks up, and his eyes are perfectly mild. "First question. Do you know what is in Odalric Vane's iron trunk?"

I drink some of the tea first, because it's good and because refusing it would be a performance. "I have seen inside it once — in a passage in Grevenholt, at night: a ream of blank paper, corners squared. That is the whole of my certified knowledge." Cup down, level. "What I believe is in it I hold as hearsay from men I trust — entered in my book as heard, and marked uncertified. And I notice, Herr Undersecretary, that your own Index stamps a certain entry not to be described aloud in the making of any report. I keep other people's rules when they are better than mine. Ask me what I have seen, and you will get all of it — the same answer every time, three times if you like. Clean books read identically on every audit."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz does not smile. But he sets his pen down, which for him may be the same thing.

"Not to be described aloud," he repeats. "Yes. My predecessor wrote that in the ninth year, and I have declined four applications to strike it, and I have been passed over twice for doing so." He closes the folder. "You may keep your hearsay. I have plenty of my own; the Office is a great warehouse of it. What I want from you is *seen*, as you say. So."

He asks the same question three times, and it is not the one you expected.

"First: has any part of that text been spoken aloud, on a stage or off it, in your hearing, since you took post?" You answer: one line, in Vessendal, in a broken-sky emergency, by Falk, in the wings — upstage — and that you have ruled company law against it since. He writes it. "Second: has any part of that text been spoken aloud, on a stage or off it, in your hearing, since you took post?" Same answer, same words. He writes it again and compares the two lines with a fingertip. "Third." The third time he does not look at the paper at all; he looks at you. Same answer. Same words.

Lenz sits back. "Good. Then I shall tell you what my office is actually for, and you will not repeat it outside this room, and if you do I shall deny it and you will be believed less than I am."

He turns the tea tray a quarter turn, tidying it.

"Twenty-nine of the thirty-one proscribed works are proscribed because somebody was offended. Two are proscribed because they *work*. The Office cannot read a trunk, madam — as your clerk has no doubt told you, with the pleasure of a young man discovering a loophole. So the Office does not chase the object. It counts the *speakings*." He taps the folder. "Every recorded instance for two hundred years, in this press, in that ledger. There have been fourteen. The fourteenth was Katterau, three and a half acts, nine men, and it cost this office four years of clearing up."

Then, mildly: "The fifteenth is scheduled. The Palace command of the 3rd of Frost was not requested by the Palace. It was requested *of* the Palace, in writing, by a private party, and granted, and I have seen the requisition and the hand it is written in, and it is a very good hand." He pushes a single sheet across the desk to you, face-down. "That is a copy of the play list attached to the command. Turn it over. You are the stage manager; you will be the person expected to call it."
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: I set my cup well aside first, so nothing drips on what I'm about to be responsible for. Then I turn it over the way I turn everything now — one motion, both eyes, once, my face doing bookkeeping and nothing else.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
One sheet, ruled, Palace paper, and the printing is beautiful.

**BY COMMAND — THE 3rd OF FROST — THE VERMILION PLAYERS**
*Part the First:* ILSABET'S RANSOM, in four acts.
*Interval.*
*Part the Second:* — and here the line is left blank, ruled but empty, and under it, in the same beautiful hand, in the space where a title goes: **as the company shall determine, being four acts and a matter following.**

At the foot, the requisition endorsement, and a signature, and the signature is not Skarke's.

*Requested: A. Krug, of the fourth ward, in the capital.*
*Granted: by order.*

You read it twice, which you have promised yourself you would not do with pages, and this is not a page, and you do it anyway.

Lenz watches you with his hands folded. "He filed it two years ago, madam, six weeks after he left your company at Katterau — a private subject may request a command performance; it costs a fee and it is almost never granted. This one was granted because the fee was paid by a third party of considerable standing, and because my office was asked for an opinion and my office —" the smallest pause of a man who has been waiting nineteen years for someone to ask him a question in the right order — "my office said yes."

Outside in the corridor, faintly, Prewick's watch is going, and Prewick with it.

"Then I'll spend mine in the right order too." I square the sheet between us. "One. Your ledger of fourteen: what does a speaking cost the house? Not the readers — the audience. Two hundred years of your own records: what happened to the people watching?" I let him reach for the press if he wants it. "Two. The third party of considerable standing. We can both spell it, but I want it said in this room, where things are deniable." A breath. "Three. Your office said yes. So give me Assessment's honest opinion, the one you've been passed over twice for holding: can a fifteenth speaking be done so that it ends the account — finished, once, correctly — or does your ledger say there is no such thing as correctly?" And when he's done: "After which I'm going back to my theatre to discuss with a man in a bottle-green coat the difference between a report and a confession."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz answers the first question by getting up, which takes him a while, and pulling a ledger from the second press. He sets it down open at a ribbon.

"Fourteen speakings. Audience present at eight of them; the other six were readings among players, like Katterau." His finger goes down a column of dates. "The Office's honest finding, madam, and it is the finding that has made me unpopular: *the audience is not harmed.* In two hundred years, not one recorded instance of harm to a person who only watched." He closes the ledger. "The rhyming comes for the ones who *make* it. Speakers, principally. Then whoever provided the room, the money, the paper. Anna Sorel kept the accounts and she is in this ledger. Your Herr Krug cut pages and did not speak a word and he is in this ledger too, in pencil, which is how we mark the ones we are not sure of." He looks at the tea you have not finished. "The house comes to no harm. But the house is *required*. Six readings without an audience did nothing at all, and the Office does not know why, and I have written *appetite* in a margin once and been told to strike it."

"Two." He sits. "Marius Skarke, of the Skarke bank, whose father lodged thirty pages as security against a loan to a wool factor in the fifth year. He paid the requisition fee. He has never asked to speak a line; he asks only to be in the room. I have his letter. It is the most careful letter I have ever received from a rich man."

"Three." Lenz folds his hands, and for a moment something moves in the dry face. "Assessment's honest opinion, which I have held for nineteen years and been passed over twice for holding. Yes. Once. Correctly. Whole. In a house that knows what it is watching, with a text complete and no wagers and no bottles, called by someone competent and stopped by nobody." He puts one finger on the play list. "There has never been a *fifteenth* that finished, madam, because in fourteen tries someone has always been brave and interrupted it. And in every one of those fourteen cases the arranging afterwards was worse than the play." He pushes the sheet the last inch toward you. "You asked whether *correctly* exists. My ledger says: it has never been tried. That is not the same as *no*."

He rings a small bell on his desk — a real one; it makes a real, ordinary sound — and a clerk opens the door for you.

"Madam Harrow. Part the Second is blank because a command cannot name a proscribed work. If the company determines nothing, you will play *Ilsabet* and go home and the fee is forfeit and nobody in this office will trouble you." The mildness does not change at all. "And there is one thing I will not put in a ledger and shall say at my own door instead: your name is now in the requisition file, and files are read. If you mean to refuse, refuse loudly and early, and refuse *in writing to me*, and I will make it the Office's refusal and take the weight of it. That offer expires on the 2nd."

Prewick's watch says fifty-one minutes when the frosted door shuts behind you.
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: "Fifty-one minutes, and none of them wasted — walk with me." Down the grey stairs, past the bicycles. "On the way I'll sort what's tellable from what I drank with the tea. Tonight, after rehearsal: a company hearing. The full kind — benches, soup, everyone; the biggest determination this company will ever sit for." And through the Baraque's gate, before my coat is even off: "Herr Krug. Props table. Now, please. And bring the difference between a report and a confession — I know it's in that portmanteau, because I've just seen your handwriting on Palace paper."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Prewick keeps up with the shorthand of it — *audience unharmed; the house is required; the requisition was Krug's; Skarke paid the fee; the Office's refusal is on offer until the 2nd* — and by the courtyard gate he has gone the colour of his collar and said only, "Then I am the wrong rank for the next fortnight and I shall have to be the right one anyway."

Krug comes to the props table at once. He looks at your face and does not sit down.

"Two years ago," he says, before you can ask. "Six weeks after Katterau, in a rooming house in the fourth ward, with page eight in my pocket and no company that would have me." He puts both hands on the table. "I filed it because I thought that if the thing was going to arrange me anyway, I would rather choose the room. I picked the Palace because the Palace has a fire watch and a gasman and eight exits and a house of nine hundred that would be there because they were *told* to be, not because they'd wagered a bottle. I paid two shillings I couldn't spare. I never expected it to be granted — a private subject's requisition is granted about once a decade, madam, and I know that because I read the pamphlet nineteen times waiting in the corridor."

He swallows. "Then two years went by and nothing came, and I got work as a bill-poster, and I stopped being afraid every morning, and I began to want my life. And then in the spring a letter came saying *granted*, and I have been sitting in a rooming house six streets from here ever since, waiting for you people to arrive so I could tell somebody before the 3rd." He looks down at his hands. "So: report or confession. I don't know which it is. I know I did it and I know why and I know I'd have done it differently now, and I've come to say so before you find out from a man with a folder. Which," he says, reading your face, "I see I've missed by about an hour."

Out in the house the gasman is testing the board, and the lights come up on nine hundred empty seats, all at once, brighter than anyone needs.

"Sit down, Anselm Krug." Full name; the register of rulings. "Last night was a report. This, just now, was a confession. And the thing you filed two years ago is neither — it's a design, and it's the best-built thing anyone has brought me on this tour. Fire watch. Gasman. Eight exits. A house present by order, not by wager. You thought like a stage manager thinking twenty years ahead of his book." I let that stand a breath. "So here's what it buys. Tonight, at the hearing, you give this company the design brief — why the Palace, room by room, exit by exit — and you answer questions till the candle dies. Belonging is theirs to vote on. The cot by the props table is mine to give, and it's yours as of now."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Krug sits. Then he puts his face in his hands, briefly, the way Vane does, and comes out of it dry-eyed and business-like, which is a stage manager's version of weeping.

"Design brief. Room by room." He nods. "I'll need paper and I'll want to walk the Palace stage before I open my mouth — they'll let us in on the 1st for a technical, and if they won't, I'll get in with a bill-poster's ladder and beg pardon after." A pause. "Madam. Thank you for *design*. I've been calling it a betrayal for two years and it's been sitting in me like a stone."

The day goes: gasman, fly rail, nine hundred seats swept by Toby for the price of a bun. Falk walks the Baraque stage twice, once at each end of the afternoon, saying nothing. Mirelle does not come out of the wardrobe cage until four, and when she does she has her gloves on and a small hard look, and she says only, "Harrow, whatever's tonight, I want to speak last."

At nine the benches go up in the O.P. wing, and the soup goes on, and twelve people sit down: Vane, Falk, Mirelle, Prewick, Dessa Krul, Boyle, Toby Lenz, Ottmar Boyle's brother-in-law who has appeared from nowhere and is called Wenzel and plays soldiers, the gasman Hebel who has asked to stay and been allowed, Krug, and you, and the candle Krug has stuck in a bottle in the middle of the trestle.

Vane stands, and for once does not speak. He looks at you and sits down again.

Which leaves the hearing yours to open, twelve faces in the gaslight and a blank line on a Palace play list.

I stand with the book shut, because this part I know by heart. "Company hearing. The matter: a blank line on a Palace play list that reads — as the company shall determine. Hear the whole account before anyone leans." I give it in order, flat as figures. "The door out: real, and open. We play Ilsabet on the 3rd, determine nothing, go home free; the Office will even put its own name on the refusal until the 2nd. Nobody at this table gets to call that cowardice — it's a clean page and I'll rule for it gladly if it's ruled." Then the other column. "The account against: the thing in our yard has never once been finished — fourteen speakings in two hundred years, every one interrupted by somebody brave, and every interruption billed the makers worse than the play. The Office's own ledger says the audience is never harmed — not once — but the house is required. The makers pay: speakers first, then whoever gives the room, the money, the paper. Sit in that arithmetic before you speak." I lay my two pages face-down on the trestle. "Full disclosure, as ruled: page eight says a stage manager rings the bell. Page nine is a cast list — twelve names, blank, and the house entire. There are twelve of us on these benches tonight. Count yourselves." A breath. "Any yes this company determines wears clothes I've already cut: whole, once, correctly; everyone who makes it chooses knowing Katterau entire; a house that knows what it's watching; no wagers, no bottles; a boy named Fenner Bacher stays home — and nobody in the building brave. Herr Krug speaks first: the design, room by room. Then every voice here. Frau Sorel has asked to speak last, and will. I rule after, and not before." I sit. "Anselm. The Palace."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Krug stands and gives it like a plot call, and his hands stop shaking on the third sentence.

"The Palace Theatre Royal. Nine hundred and forty seats, four levels, three staircases from the pit, eight exits and every one of them a legal one — I've counted them from the street and I'll count them from inside on the 1st. Fire watch of two men on duty by statute whenever the gas is lit, one downstage prompt side, one on the fly floor; that's a Palace rule and no company can wave it. Gasman is the house's, not ours, and the board's out of the wings where no actor can reach it. Iron curtain that drops in eleven seconds — I timed it from the gods at a pantomime in the spring." He looks round the benches. "Why the Palace and not a barn: because in a barn, when it gets bad, someone runs, and running is interrupting. In the Palace the doors stand open, the exits are lit, the house has been *told* to be there, and any soul who wants out walks out and the play does not stop. Nobody has to be brave. That's the whole design. It's built so that bravery isn't required."

He sits. Then the table goes round.

Boyle: "Twenty-two mile wrong way I'd have walked. This is nought mile. I'm in, if Wenzel's out — one of us stops with the horses." Wenzel, hastily: "I'll stop with the horses." Dessa Krul, thimble on: "Somebody's got to dress it and I'm not having a stranger in my cage. In. And I want the twelve names read out slow before anybody signs anything."

Hebel the gasman, quietly: "I light gas for a living, madam. I'll light this. But I'll want it in writing that the board's mine and no one else touches the wheel." Toby Lenz, cracking upward: "I'm in—" and Dessa says, "You're seventeen," and Toby says, "I'm *nineteen*," and Dessa says "you're seventeen," and the table laughs, and it is the only laugh of the night.

Prewick stands, because he cannot say anything sitting. "I am the wrong rank. I have said so twice today." He grips his notebook. "My seal makes a performance lawful. If Part the Second is played, either I certify a proscribed text — which is a crime and would end me — or I certify nothing, and it goes up uncertified, which makes every one of you liable and me a witness." He is white. "Undersecretary Lenz can certify it, madam. Assessment can. I intend to write and ask him to come and do it in person, and stand where I can see his hands, and if he refuses I shall certify it myself and be ruined honestly." He sits down hard.

Falk does not stand. "In," he says. "You know why, and I've said it to Harrow already, and I'll not spend the candle repeating it. One condition: I speak the lead and no one else does. It has had my voice once. It doesn't get a new one."

Vane stands last of the men, hat in his hands, and does not quote a single notice. "I gave the room and the money and the paper at Katterau. I'm in the ledger already." His voice is enormous and quiet. "I'll go where Harrow points. But I want it minuted that I asked for the door — the clean page — and if she rules for it I'll drive us home tomorrow and be grateful all my life."

Then the candle has burned an inch, and everyone at the trestle turns, and Mirelle Sorel puts down her spoon.
I let the benches go quiet the way a house goes quiet — on their own, all at once. "Last voice before the ruling. Frau Sorel."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Mirelle stands. She never stands to speak, and the change alone makes Toby sit up.

"You've all been kind enough for ten years not to ask my name, so I'll give it to you and then we can stop being polite." She has her gloves off; the mended one is on the trestle in front of her. "My sister was Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year, and who deposited a sealed box in the Vessendal registry the week before she died, and whose name is in the Office's ledger for a play she never spoke a word of. She kept accounts. That's all she did. And the thing rhymed her a fever in a good bed at the hour a scene falls."

She looks down the table, at each face, unhurried.

"Ten years ago I was billed in this city under a name I'd already stopped owning, and there was a matter with a magistrate's date on it, and I left between an evening performance and a morning summons, and I have never told any of you what it concerned and I am not going to tonight. A page came to me on the road out of Halbern. It said a woman crosses a border twice: once running, once summoned, and the second crossing is by invitation and the invitation is kind." She puts one finger on the glove. "I have carried it in my glove since. I did not need the Office's ledger to know who pays; I've had a receipt in my hand since Vessendal."

A pause; the candle gutters and steadies.

"So. I am *in*." She says it without any weight at all, which is how you know. "Not for Emeran's twenty years, and not for Odalric's debts, and not because it's brave — Harrow's ruled bravery out and quite right. For this: my sister has been in that ledger nine years for the pages she totted up, and the account has never once been closed, and I would rather stand in a lit house with eight exits and Hebel's hand on the wheel and end the thing than spend the rest of my life being rhymed at in strange towns by a play nobody will finish."

She sits, and picks up her spoon, and adds, in her ordinary voice: "One condition, and it's for Harrow and not for the vote. If it goes, I want the Vessendal box left shut and paid for out of the fee. Anna built the one shelf that thing can't read. Let her keep it."

Eleven faces turn to you. The candle has three-quarters of an inch left.
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: "Then hear the ruling while the candle lasts." I stand with the book shut; this one goes in after, fair-copied, because it will be read for years. "The company determines: Part the Second plays. Once. Whole. Correctly. On conditions entered now as law. Emeran speaks the lead and no other voice touches it. Hebel holds the wheel, in writing, and no hand but his. Dessa dresses it and gets her slow reading — and here is when: on the morning of the 2nd, cold, no soup, no candle, every name re-asked and every yes re-given, because a vote by candlelight has to survive a grey morning before I'll spend it. Anyone's no on the 2nd is a no, private, unminuted, and drives home with Odalric's gratitude and mine. Herr Prewick writes his letter to Room Fourteen tonight and I countersign it. Frau Sorel's condition binds: Anna's box stays shut, its storage endowed for fifty years before any other shilling moves. Toby serves the house, not the stage — programmes, rows, doors; the house's people are not makers and they stay that way. Odalric's ask for the clean page is minuted, honoured, and overruled." A breath, and the last of it: "Page nine keeps its twelfth line blank. We are eleven, and Wenzel has the horses. Nobody recruits a twelfth — if the thing wants one more maker, it can apply to the management in daylight, like the rest of this town." I pinch the candle out with two fingers. "Rulings end in smoke, not wind. Bed, all of you. Rehearsal at ten — Ilsabet doesn't care what else we're planning."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Nobody moves for a moment. Then Boyle says, "Aye," the way a man says it at the end of a service, and the benches empty in ordinary noise: hampers dragged, plates stacked, Toby aggrieved about programmes and secretly delighted, Dessa Krul telling Wenzel he's got the best job in the building.

Prewick writes his letter at the props table by the light of the gas pilot, in his best hand, and hands it to you to countersign, and reads it aloud once before he seals it, and it is four sentences and it costs him everything.

Falk stops beside you on his way out. "Ten conditions," he says, "and the ninth is that the play may apply to the management in daylight." He almost laughs. "Harrow, I have known great managers and none of them would have thought to make it queue."

Mirelle takes her glove off the trestle, and — you see her do it, and she means you to — she takes the page out of it, folds it once more, and puts it in her pocket instead, and puts the glove on bare. Then she goes to sleep in the wardrobe cage.

Vane is last, in the dark by the pass door, holding his hat. "Minuted, honoured, and overruled," he says. "You could have let me off it, Harrow. You gave me the asking *and* the ruling, and I find I can carry the pair of them." He blows his nose like a voluntary. "Ten o'clock. *Ilsabet.* I shall be punctual, which as you know is a thing I only am in emergencies."

Then the theatre goes quiet, nine hundred seats in the dark. Your chalk is on the flags; your watch is on its nail; the smoke of the candle is still in the air. And out in the yard, past the propped stage door, Boyle's lantern is up on the tailboard — and the tarpaulin is thrown back, and Boyle is standing well clear of it with his pipe out of his mouth, looking at the iron trunk, whose lid is up.

"Stand where you are, Boyle — you're doing it right." I take his lantern, cross the cobbles alone, and hold the light over the open iron at arm's length. One look. Once. My face on bookkeeping duty, whatever the trunk has filed tonight.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The lantern shows you the inside of the trunk, and it is not blank paper.

It is a full folio. Two hundred pages and more, stacked square, the copyist's small upright hand in even columns, and lying on top of the stack — placed, deliberately, the way a stage manager leaves a note on a prompt desk — a single sheet in that same hand.

You do not read the folio. You look at the top sheet, once, at arm's length, and it is not a scene and not a number. It is a heading, and a list beginning, and the list is your own.

*THE VERMILION PLAYERS, AT THE PALACE, THE THIRD OF FROST*
*Part the Second — as the company shall determine.*
*Falk. Sorel. Vane. Krul. Boyle. Lenz. Hebel. Krug. Prewick. Harrow.*
*and* — the eleventh line, in the same ink, and then the twelfth line ruled and empty —
*and the house, entire.*

Ten names. Not eleven. Wenzel is not on it, and Wenzel took the horses. And the eleventh line, where the eleventh name should be, has been struck through with one clean stroke of the pen, the way you strike a day off a chalk board.

Boyle, from the gate, keeping his distance because you told him to and because he is not a fool: "Madam. Is it a cast list?"

"It's a cast list," I tell him, straight, because half-told things died at a fire outside Halbern. "Mostly ours. Ten names, one struck, one blank — and it can keep its own files; I keep mine." I don't touch the sheet. The lid I close with both hands, the way I'd close any company property at night, and Boyle ropes it while I hold the lantern. "Your watch has company till two — fetch my coat and the coffee that's left." And tomorrow's first item files itself in my head as the ropes creak: the ink wrote Lenz, and this building holds two of those — a boy who serves the house, and an Undersecretary who's been asked to come and certify. Before Ilsabet at ten, the company hears its casting. And the Office hears my question about which Lenz it lent to the ink.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Boyle brings the coat and the coffee and ropes the lid, and then, because his hands need a job, ropes it again a different way.

"Ten names and one struck," he says, at last, into the dark. "Madam, I've been the one that carried it, the one that ropes it, the one on the tailboard. Twenty-two years with this company. I'd rather be *on* a list than off it, and I'd rather know than not." He puts the pipe back in his mouth unlit. "Wenzel's off it and Wenzel's got the horses, and that's your ruling doing its work — that's what I'll tell him. He'll like that better than being spared."

Two o'clock. The city makes its city noises. You get four hours on a flat with your coat over you.

At half past eight the O.P. wing gets its casting, cold and grey and no soup, exactly as it will be on the 2nd: the ten names read out flat, Wenzel's absence explained as ruling and not as favour — Wenzel makes a joke about horses that lands better than it should — and Toby Lenz standing very still while the word *Lenz* sits in the air with nowhere to go.

"That's not me," Toby says. "Is it? Madam. Programmes and rows and doors. You *ruled* it. That's the house, that's not the stage." His voice goes up. "So it's not me. Is it the man from the Office?"

Prewick, gone the colour of paste: "Madam Stage Manager. My letter went last night. I asked him to come. I asked him *in writing*, and I countersigned by you, and if his name was in that trunk before I asked—"

"It was," Krug says, from the props table, quietly. "Or after. There's no telling with the dates. That's the whole horror of it."

And at nine, before you've settled a thing, the stage door bangs and a Palace footman in Palace livery is standing in the yard with a sealed letter and no idea why eleven people are looking at him like that.

"Good morning. You've found the Vermilion Players and nobody's going to bite." I cross the yard with my hand already out and my company behind me pretending to work. "Who is it directed to?" — and whoever it names, I read the direction aloud so the yard hears it before imaginations do, tip the man his shilling from the float, and let him escape with his livery intact.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The footman hands it over with visible relief. Heavy cream paper, Palace seal, and the direction in a clerk's flawless hand.

"*To the Stage Manager, the Vermilion Players, at the Baraque Theatre, fourth ward,*" you read out, and the yard breathes. Not Prewick. Not Lenz. Not Falk. The shilling goes over, the footman goes off at speed, and Boyle shuts the gate behind him.

You open it standing where everyone can see you open it.

*Madam — The Lord Chamberlain's Office presents its compliments and confirms the command performance of the 3rd of Frost, Theatre Royal, at seven o'clock.*

*A technical inspection of the stage is granted on the 1st, from eight in the morning until noon. The house's fire watch, gasman, and iron curtain are at your disposal for the trial thereof; the house's men are not, however, at your disposal for Part the Second, and you are advised that the Chamberlain's Office does not undertake to know what Part the Second is.*

*Part the Second remains blank on the play list. It cannot be printed. It may be announced from the stage on the night by the company, once, before the interval curtain, and not otherwise.*

*You are further advised: the requisition file is closed to the public but has been read this week by two parties. One was a Clerk Third Class of the Office of Public Morals, seconded, whose enquiry was regular. The other was not regular and left no name, and the Chamberlain's Office is not obliged to inform you of this and does so at the personal discretion of the undersigned, who was once a call-boy at the Baraque and has not forgotten what a stage manager is for.*

*— by order, R. Halm, Deputy Comptroller.*

At the bottom, added in a different, older, tireder hand: *Madam, the man who came was left-handed and wrote in a little book. He is not from the Palace and he is not from the Office. I have had the file moved. R.H.*

I read the whole of it aloud to the wing, postscript included — the law is the law, and this house hears its own weather. Then the day gets its orders: "Anselm — the 1st is yours to plot, eight to noon, every exit timed twice, the iron dropped till you trust it. Toby — programmes and rows and doors, and the word Lenz means the Office man until ink says otherwise; you have my ruling and my ruling doesn't blink." Then I sit down opposite Falk with the letter still in my hand. "Emeran. Twenty years ago the thing took the boy Grelle. Took — how? Because a left-handed man with a little book has been reading our file this week, and he asked Ilse Bacher only one question in Katterau: how far did they get. Before I hunt him through the fourth ward, I need to know whether I'm looking for a victim, a scholar, or the eleventh line."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Falk sits down slowly and puts both hands flat on the props table.

"Grelle," he says. "Yes. All right." He looks at the letter, not at you. "Ansel Grelle was our second boy at Katterau. Fifteen, sixteen. He wasn't in the green room; boys weren't. He was in the *passage* with the trays." A pause. "He heard it. Three and a half acts through a door, same as Ilse. And he stayed with the company two more years after, and he got taller and quieter, and in the seventh year he left us at Merrow with his box and a good character, and I gave him three shillings and Odalric gave him a speech." His hand closes. "Took. I said *took* because in the eighth year a letter came to Odalric from a landlady in this city saying a young man had died in her room owing four weeks, and would the Vermilion Players pay it, and Odalric paid it and cried and we all said the play had taken him. I never saw a body. I never saw the letter after Odalric had it."

He looks up. "He was left-handed, harbor. He kept the property list for me at Merrow and I remember it because I could not read his crossings-out."

Behind you at the pass door, Vane — who has come in halfway and heard the whole of it — says, in a voice with nothing performed in it at all: "I never paid it." He is holding his hat. "Harrow, I never paid the landlady. I meant to. It was seven pounds and I hadn't got it, and Anselm had just — " he stops dead, hearing what he is about to say, "—and I told the company I'd paid it, and I have said so at suppers for eleven years."

Krug, at the fly rail, has gone perfectly still with a rope in his hand.

"Say it, Anselm — ropes don't need that much holding." And while he finds his voice: "Odalric. The landlady's letter — name, street, whatever your grief kept of it. And hear my ruling on Ansel Grelle before anybody's feet move: if he's alive, he is not prey, and he is not a line on anything's list. He is owed seven pounds, four weeks' lodging, and eleven years of being mourned wrong. We do not hunt a frightened man through a city he knows better than us." I turn to our bill-poster. "We advertise. Tonight, one small bill, in the places where a man who reads everything reads: WANTED — A PROPERTY LIST KEPT AT MERROW IN THE SEVENTH YEAR. THE VERMILION PLAYERS PAY THEIR DEBTS. ASK AT THE BARAQUE STAGE DOOR FOR THE STAGE MANAGER. ANY HOUR."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Krug lets the rope go and belays it before he speaks, because he is what he is.

"Seven pounds," he says. "Katterau's Wednesday take was seven pounds. That's why the number went in my ear when Odalric said it just now." He comes down off the rail. "And here's mine, and I've never said it out loud. In the seventh year, before I kept your book, I was a bill-poster in this city for four months — this ward. And there was a young fellow pasting the north side who was left-handed and had been on the road with a company, and we never swapped names because bill-posters don't. And when I came back to this trade two years ago I went to the same firm and they said the north-side man had gone off years back, owing nothing, and left an address for letters." He rubs his mouth. "I never followed it up. Why would I. Madam, I can go and ask them tonight."

Vane has sat down on a hamper with the hat in his lap. "Frau — Hensch. Or Hentsch. Rasselgasse, off the meat market, third or fourth house, brown door. I remember it because I walked past it twice in the ninth year and did not go in." He looks up, wretched and steady. "The seven pounds. Out of the fee, Harrow, before anything — after Anna's box. Put it above my own boots on the list."

And the bill goes up that night. Krug pastes it himself in eleven places — the labour exchange, two coffee-houses, the paste-up boards on the north side, the wall by the newspaper offices, the tram shelter, the pawnbroker's window — and does the last one at midnight in the rain.

At four in the morning somebody knocks at the Baraque stage door. Three knocks. Unhurried. Official-sounding, almost — the knock of a man who has been practising it in his head all the way across the city.
messages.speaker: Anselm Krug

messages.body: The advertised words were mine, so the door is mine. Boyle gets my flat hand and stays put. I take the lamp down low — light on the floorboards, not in anybody's face — and open the door its whole width, because nothing arrives half at this address. "Stage door of the Baraque," I say, ordinary as bread. "You're asked-for, not expected, which is the better way to arrive. Harrow — stage manager. The kettle's not long off the gas, there's one chair in this building that doesn't wobble, and nobody else is awake." And I step back and give the doorway all its width.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He comes in the way a man comes in who has been outside a long time in the rain: sideways, so as not to bring the weather with him.

Thirty-five perhaps, in a bill-poster's coat with paste dried white along the cuffs. Tall, and thin, and quiet in the shoulders, and left-handed on the doorframe. He looks at your lamp on the floorboards and something in him settles slightly, because you have not looked at his face.

"Ansel Grelle," he says. "I pasted your bill." A small, terrible pause. "I pasted it at the labour exchange at nine o'clock and then I stood and read it eleven times, and then I went and looked at the other ten, and I have been walking about since." He takes his hat off. "Madam, I have four questions and I have got them in the wrong order all night, so I shall just say them. Is Emeran Falk alive. Is it true you're playing it at the Palace. Does Odalric Vane know I'm not dead." And then, with the first crack in the quiet: "And is it seven pounds you mean, or seven pounds *and* the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch died in the tenth year and there's nobody to pay, and I have been carrying it as though there were."

Behind you in the dark of the wing, a floorboard shifts. Falk has come out of nowhere, in his shirtsleeves with the rug over his shoulders, and has stopped dead six feet back, out of the lamplight, saying nothing at all — because you have taught this company to wait.
messages.speaker: Ansel Grelle

messages.body: "In your order, then." I keep my voice at floor-level, like the lamp. "One: alive. Sober, on watch most nights, gruff as a harbour. And nearer than you think — six feet behind me, in his shirtsleeves, stopped dead the moment you knocked, waiting on your leave. Nobody in this company gets seen before they're ready; it's a law. Two: true. The 3rd, at the Palace. Once, whole, correctly, by choice — with a house that knows what it's watching. You'll read every condition we've cut before you decide anything about anything. Three: since ten o'clock tonight — he learned you weren't dead standing beside the fact that he never paid Frau Hentsch, and his next sentence was: put Grelle's seven pounds above my own boots. Four: both. Seven and the four weeks. A dead landlady doesn't cancel a debt — it re-addresses it, to the man who carried it eleven years." I move to the gas ring. "So. Tea first, or Falk first. Your call entirely, and no wrong answer exists."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The rug slides half off Falk's shoulder and he doesn't notice.

"Falk first," Grelle says, and turns to the dark.

Falk comes forward into the lamp very slowly, and he is enormous and he is not acting, and he stops at arm's length and looks at the man's face for a long moment.

"Ansel," he says. "You've got taller and you're still standing wrong. Put your weight on both feet." And then his voice goes to pieces and he says, "*Boy* — " and stops, and puts one hand on Grelle's shoulder, and stands there gripping it and unable to do anything else.

Grelle says, "I did try to write. In the ninth year. I got as far as *Dear Herr Falk* and then I couldn't say what I wanted, because what I wanted was to ask how far you got, and every time I put it on paper it looked like a threat." His mouth twists. "So I asked everybody else instead. For eleven years. I've a little book with sixty-one pages of it — every soul I could find who was within a wall of that room, and what they heard, and how far. Ilse at the Rose. The ostler at Katterau. Two of your old carpenters. The printer's boy who set a bill in Achterhalt in the fifth year." He looks at you. "I read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's this week. I gave no name because I've had no name to give since the tenth year. Madam, if that makes me your left-handed man, I'd rather be told so straight and put out of this door than sat down with tea under a lie."

Out in the yard the four o'clock rain gets heavier on the tarpaulin. Falk still has not let go of his shoulder.

"Straight, then. You're my left-handed man." I let it land whole. "And here's what that makes you, Ansel Grelle: the only soul in this empire who has spent eleven years doing Assessment's work with clean hands and no office. Your sixty-one pages are the census this company needs before any curtain rises — who is exposed, who must be told, who stays home behind a bolted door. On paper alone, that's a threat. Beside a stage manager's book, it's a guest list done right." Then the rulings, counted plain: "The seven-and-four-weeks pays at dawn, from the float, receipted, above Odalric's boots. The second cot by the props table is yours. And hear this before anything: the cast list in that trunk has its eleventh line struck through by somebody's pen, and it will not be you. On the night, you stand house-side, on the doors, with Toby — you've been on the wrong side of a door for twenty years, Herr Grelle. Come stand on the right side of ours." The kettle sings behind me. "And the tea was never a lie here."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Grelle looks at the kettle rather than at either of you, which is how men that thin in the shoulders keep their faces private, and says, "House-side," and then, "On the doors," and then nothing at all for a while.

Falk lets go of his shoulder at last and turns him round by it, gently, like a man moving furniture he loves. "Sit in the chair that doesn't wobble," he says. "It's the one with the rope round the leg. She'll pour."

Tea happens at four in the morning in a nine-hundred-seat theatre with one lamp on the floor. Grelle drinks it with both hands round the cup and answers every question you put to him about the sixty-one pages in the flat exhausted voice of a man handing over a load he's carried up too many stairs: names, wards, dates, who's dead, who's frightened, who never knew what they'd heard. Twice he stops and says, "This is what it's *for*, then," half to himself, and goes on.

The gaslight comes up grey in the O.P. side windows around six. The company wakes into the news in ones and twos, which is the best way news ever arrives; Dessa Krul takes one look at Grelle and puts a plate in front of him without a word.

Vane comes in last, hair everywhere, and stops in the doorway. He does not perform. He crosses the wing, counts seven pounds and four weeks' lodging out of the float onto the props table, coin by coin, aloud, unrounded, and pushes it across — and then stands there with nothing in his hands and says, "Ansel. I have been telling people at suppers for eleven years that I paid it."

And it's Grelle who says, without looking up from the plate, "I know. I heard you say it at Merrow in the ninth year. I was pasting bills across the road."

The wing goes very quiet. Somewhere above, the roof drips into the bucket you posted the notice about. And Prewick — who has been standing in the pass door for a full minute with an unopened letter in his hand and his hat still on — says, "Madam Stage Manager. From Room Fourteen. It is addressed to *both* of us, jointly, which is not a thing the Office does."

"Jointly addressed, jointly opened." I cross to him and hold the envelope flat while he breaks the seal — his letter bought this answer; his voice can carry it. "Read it out, Herr Prewick. To both of us, and to the room, because I suspect Room Fourteen knows exactly how large this room is."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Prewick breaks the seal, holds it at his regulation reading distance, and reads it out in a voice that starts formal and stops being formal by the fourth sentence.

"*To Clerk Third Class C. Prewick, seconded, and to Madam B. Harrow, Stage Manager, jointly —*

*Your letter of yesterday's date is received, and is the first application in nineteen years to be made in the correct order: that is, by the person who will be blamed, on behalf of the persons who will be harmed, before the event rather than after.*

*I shall attend the Theatre Royal on the 3rd of Frost and certify Part the Second in person, at the prompt desk, from the copy the company uses, under my own seal and my own name. Clerk Prewick's seal will not be employed and Clerk Prewick's report will record that he was overruled by Assessment, which is true, and which will protect him.*

*I require three things. First: the text in advance — the whole of it, in my hands, in this room, and not out of them, by six o'clock on the 2nd. Second: that the company's determination be minuted with every name and every condition, signed, and lodged with me; your ten conditions were recited to me this morning by a footman's cousin and I would rather have them in ink. Third: that the eleventh line be left alone. I have read Krug's file. Do not fill it, do not strike it again, and do not permit anyone to volunteer.*

*You may tell your company that I have wanted for nineteen years to see one of these accounts closed and have never once had a company that would let bravery be ruled out of the building. I am sixty-one and I do not drink and I have no family, which are three qualifications for the prompt desk.*

*— Lenz, Undersecretary, Assessment.*

*P.S. Madam — the ink that named a Lenz did not consult me. I intend to be there anyway. It is not the same thing, and I would be obliged if you would say so to the boy.*"

Prewick lowers the letter. His hands are shaking so hard the paper rattles, and he is grinning like a boy who has been given the sea.

Toby Lenz, from the back of the wing, with his ears scarlet: "Madam — did he mean *me*? The postscript. Did the Undersecretary of Assessment write a postscript about *me*?"
messages.speaker: Casimir Prewick

messages.body: "He means you, Toby Lenz. And he means the difference that keeps this whole house standing, so hear it properly: ink casts. Men choose. The play wrote a Lenz on its list; the Undersecretary chooses to stand at my prompt desk anyway, on his own two feet — which unwrites nothing, and outranks everything. Learn that by heart. It's the best line in the building and it isn't in any play." Then the day gets its orders. "Herr Prewick — the determination, minuted fair: every name, every condition, signed by every hand, lodged with Room Fourteen. Yours is the best hand we have and it's just stopped shaking. Anselm, Emeran — with me in the yard after breakfast. The Office wants the text itself, whole, in Room Fourteen by six tomorrow — which means the folio comes out of that trunk and crosses this city in daylight, and I want three opinions on how such a thing is carried. And company law, addendum, effective now: nobody — nobody — volunteers for line eleven."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"Signed by every hand," Prewick repeats, and sits straight down at the props table with his own pen and starts ruling columns, and Dessa Krul moves his plate to his elbow without being asked.

The yard after breakfast: thin sun, wet cobbles, the tarpaulin thrown half back, three of you standing well clear of it.

Krug goes first, because he thinks in plots. "It doesn't cross the city in the trunk. The trunk is a *thing people watch* — Skarke's man has looked at it, the bailiff's constable has looked at it, and if a left-handed man could read the Chamberlain's file, somebody could read a yard. So: the folio goes in something dull. A hamper of Ilsabet's costumes, and Dessa on top of it, and Boyle driving, and it goes at nine in the morning in the general traffic to the Office's *courtyard* — not the front steps, madam; the courtyard's full of bicycles and clerks and nobody looks at a laundry hamper in a courtyard." He nods at the trunk. "And the trunk stays roped in this yard with the lid shut, and Wenzel sits on it, and if anyone's watching, nothing has happened today."

Falk, slower. "Two hundred pages, harbor. Somebody has to lift it out and carry it fifteen feet and put it in the hamper, and I will tell you now that it should not be me, because I know what it is and my hands know it too. Nor Odalric — he lodged it once already." He looks at the cobbles. "It should be someone with no line in it. Wenzel. Or the boy Toby, and I'd rather not, and you've ruled the house-side people off making anyway." A pause. "Or you. And you're the tenth name."

"And Grelle," Krug says, "who has been within a wall of it for twenty years and never inside the room. Madam, you gave him the doors so he'd stop being the man outside them. Don't make him the porter."

The trunk sits in the sun and does nothing at all. From inside the theatre, faintly, Prewick's voice reading a condition aloud to Boyle for spelling.
messages.speaker: Anselm Krug

messages.body: "It's mine." Flat, before the debate can breed. "The worst fifteen feet in this company belong to the stage manager by job description — on the night I stand at Lenz's elbow with the prompt copy regardless; my hands were always cast. And I will not ask the one grown man the ink spared to come and introduce himself for our convenience." The plot stands as Krug drew it: hamper, Dessa on top and told the whole of what she's sitting on — law's law — Boyle driving, the courtyard at nine, the trunk roped with Wenzel seated on it doing an excellent impression of nothing happening. "Emeran, you'll stand at the yard gate with your back to me while I lift; if the thing wants a witness it can make do with the rug. And I wear my gloves doubled — not superstition. Bookkeeping. Nine o'clock tomorrow."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"With my back to you," Falk says. "Yes. I can do that." He does not thank you; he does something better, which is to take the rug off his shoulders and hand it to Krug, and go and stand at the gate at once, out of habit, six hours early, and be sent away by Boyle for cluttering the arch.

The rest of the day is the ordinary miracle: *Ilsabet* at ten in a nine-hundred-seat house with the pit stalls unbolted so the sound behaves, and Mirelle finding a new pause in the second act that makes the cleaners stop sweeping. Prewick's minute goes round the wing at four and is signed by every hand, Hebel with a wheel-shaped smudge, Toby laboriously and twice because he blotted it, Wenzel with a cross and his name written after by Dessa. Grelle sleeps for nine hours on the second cot and wakes up asking for a broom.

The 2nd, nine o'clock. Cold, bright. Dessa Krul is told exactly what is going in her hamper and says, "Then I'll sit on it and I'll sit *still*, madam, which is more than most of this company manages." Wenzel takes his place on the roped trunk with a nosebag and a look of enormous unimportance. Boyle brings the cart round. Falk walks to the gate and turns his back and puts his hands in his pockets.

Krug opens the hamper and stands away.

The trunk's lid comes up easy — it's been unlocked since Grevenholt, and nobody has ever mentioned that. Inside: the folio, squared, two hundred pages and more, the copyist's hand in even columns, and on top of it the cast list with its struck line, which you have already seen once and do not need to see again.

Fifteen feet. Doubled gloves. And the strangest part is how completely ordinary it is: paper is heavy, that's all, and cold, and it slides the way big stacks slide, and your arms know exactly what to do because arms always do.

The cast list stays where it lay — it isn't text, it's the play's own paperwork, and I don't deliver another author's memos. Folio into the hamper, costumes folded over, lid strapped; Dessa up and sitting still as advertised; Wenzel achieving nothing on the trunk with real dedication. We roll into the morning traffic like laundry with opinions. At the Office courtyard — bicycles, clerks, paste and coal — I carry it up the east stair myself, both arms, doubled gloves, and put it into Undersecretary Lenz's own hands in Room Fourteen and not one step short of it. "The whole of it, as required." And then, because I am what I am: "I'll want a receipt."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz stands up when you come in, which Prewick will not believe.

He takes it in both arms — he is small and sixty-one and he takes it properly, from underneath, the way a man takes something he has thought about for nineteen years — and carries it four steps to his own desk and sets it down and squares the stack with two hands. Then he sits, and rings his small ordinary bell, and says to the clerk who opens the door: "Nobody at all, until I say. Not the Comptroller."

He writes the receipt in full, slowly, out loud as he goes, which you understand is a courtesy to a woman who keeps clean books.

"*Received into the custody of Assessment, this second day of Frost, from the hands of B. Harrow, Stage Manager, one folio in manuscript, unbound, two hundred and*—" he counts the block by thumbing the edge, and gets it in one — "*two hundred and eleven leaves, copyist's hand, no title, four acts and a matter following. To be returned into the same hands before seven o'clock on the third day of Frost, and to be out of this room in no other manner.*" He signs it, blots it, and pushes it across. "There. And this — " a second sheet, already written, waiting — "is the Office's certificate of the *company's determination*, sealed this morning. It will not save any of you from the arranging. It will save every one of you from a magistrate, which is the only thing paper is any good for."

Then he takes off his spectacles and looks at you with his bare, tired, unremarkable eyes.

"Madam. Thirty-one hours. I shall read it all today and all tonight, and I shall be at your prompt desk at six tomorrow with a page turned down where I think a company will want a caution." A pause. "May I ask you one thing not in the correct order? You have the eleventh line struck in a trunk in a yard and a whole company obeying you and a text you have never read a word of." His hand rests flat on the folio. "How do you intend to call a play you do not know?"
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: "The way I called Ilsabet my first night in Grevenholt — off the stage, not off the page." I fold the receipt into my book. "A play tells you what it needs next if you watch the actors' weight; that's the trade. And this one has been telling people what comes next for two hundred years — it is the most over-rehearsed script in the empire. The words are the one part that was never mine to know, and my hands stay clean of them to the end: Emeran Falk carries it whole in the curse of his memory, and he will build me a plot with no text in it — machinery, not words: gas up at the third knock, iron ready on the last speech of the fourth act, a chalk mark where the matter follows. You'll turn down your caution page. And then I'll do the job as it has always actually been done, Herr Undersecretary." I stand and settle my coat. "You don't call what's written. You call what's happening."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz sits with that for a moment, and then does something with his mouth which after nineteen years in Assessment is a smile.

"*You call what's happening.*" He picks up his pen and writes it down — not in the folder, in a small private notebook that comes out of his own waistcoat — and puts it away again. "My predecessor's file on Katterau says the reading failed to finish because a stage manager was not present. I have always taken that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours." He puts his spectacles back on and the folio has already got his whole attention; you are, courteously, gone.

The courtyard, the bicycles, the cart. Dessa Krul sits on an empty hamper all the way back and says only, "Lighter going home, madam," and looks at you sideways, and that is the whole conversation.

Then the 2nd does what you built it to do. Cold, grey, no soup, no candle, the O.P. wing at four in the afternoon: every name re-asked and every yes re-given, aloud, one at a time. Falk. Sorel. Vane. Krul — "In, and slow reading now, if you please." Boyle. Hebel: "Board's mine? Then in." Krug. Prewick, overruled and present. Toby, house-side, glowing. Grelle on the doors. Ten yesses in the grey with nothing warm to help.

And Dessa gets her slow reading: the ten names read out one by one, and the struck eleventh, and the blank twelfth, and *and the house, entire*.

Then it's the 3rd of Frost. Six o'clock.
