The Theatre Royal: gas up, eight exits lit and standing open, iron tested twice at eleven seconds, Hebel's hand on the wheel, the fire watch downstage prompt side and on the fly floor, Grelle and Toby on the doors with programmes, a house of nine hundred and forty coming in under orders and out of curiosity, and at your prompt desk a small dry man of sixty-one in a plain coat with the folio squared in front of him and one page turned down.

Your watch is on its nail. Falk, in the wings, in his own clothes, waiting to be told.

"Then be told." I stop in front of him with the watch already warm in my fist. "Weight on both feet. You are not paying tonight, Emeran — you are being paid: twenty years of interest, collected in one house, in your own voice, to the end. When the matter comes, look to the corner if you need to: you'll find two people who know every word — and me, who knows you, which is better." I straighten nothing on him, because nothing needs it. "Beginners in fifteen. I'm going to walk my house." And I go out through the pass door to walk it — exits, aisles, doors, programmes, and one look, unhurried, at the fourth row, centre.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The Theatre Royal at a quarter to seven is a great warm animal. Nine hundred and forty seats going full: officers with their collars undone, a bishop's household, three rows of the Chamberlain's clerks, drovers up in the gods who got in for eightpence because a Palace command still sells cheap seats, and children — more than you'd like, four or five of them, and none of them named Bacher, and you check.

The exits stand open. Eight of them, lit, with the night coming in cold at each; Grelle has propped every one and stationed himself at the pit doors where he can see six. Toby is doing programmes with the ferocity of a boy who has been given the house to hold, and getting the fourth row right by instinct.

And the fourth row centre is occupied. Marius Skarke, in a good plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, programme unopened on his knee. He has paid at the door like a Christian; Toby will tell you so twice. He does not look for you, and when you pass at hat-distance he says, without turning his head, exactly as he did in Vessendal:

"On the hour, madam. I'll not move from this seat, and I'll not say one word of it aloud. I've written that down and given it to your man on the door." A pause; his hands are shaking slightly on his knees, and he lets you see it. "It's a lovely house."

Behind you, back through the pass door, the wings are filling with the particular silence of a company that has already voted twice. Lenz has his page turned down. Hebel has the wheel. Falk stands with his weight on both feet.

Toby, at your elbow, breathless, at four minutes to: "Madam. House is set. Doors open, all eight, and Herr Grelle says to tell you the count — nine hundred and thirty-nine in, and one seat empty."

"Which seat, Toby?" — and whatever the answer does to the back of my neck, it goes in the book, entered as heard. "Keep a programme on it. Nobody's moved into it, nobody's moved out of it; it gets service like any sold thing in my house." Then the watch comes off its nail into my palm, and the oldest words in the trade do their work: "Places, please. Part the First." And I call Ilsabet's Ransom in the Palace the way I called it in a corn hall full of merchants — clean, cue by chalked cue, a woman doing her job while her job is still simple.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"Row eleven," Toby says. "Seat one. End of the row, prompt side, by the exit." He is already turning to go do it. "It sold, madam — it's on the plan as sold. Nobody's in it."

*Entered as heard.* He puts a programme on it and comes back and stands at the pit door where Grelle can see him.

Then: places, and the animal quiets, and for two hours you get to be a stage manager and nothing else, and it is the last easy thing that will happen tonight.

*Ilsabet* in a Palace is a revelation. The house is enormous and it comes with you; Mirelle takes the first scene and nine hundred and thirty-nine people give up their coughing by her fourth line. Falk's entrance stage left brings a roar that stops the show for eleven seconds and he stands in it and gives them nothing extra. Vane weeps at the top of act three, on cue, and means it. Hebel's gas is the best you have ever worked with. The new black sheet comes in low in act four with a floor in it, and the Theatre Royal holds its breath the way the Corn Exchange did, only nine hundred and forty times over.

Curtain. The house stands. Three calls; Falk gets a fourth alone. Toby, at your elbow, hoarse: "Nobody's gone out, madam. Interval's on and *nobody's gone out* — they're all just sitting there talking."

And then the wings go quiet, and Vane comes to your corner in his plum coat with his hat off, and Krug is at the fly rail, and Lenz has both hands flat on the closed folio, and every face in the O.P. wing turns to you — because the Chamberlain's letter said it plainly: *Part the Second may be announced from the stage by the company, once, before the interval curtain, and not otherwise.*

Someone has to walk out in front of nine hundred and thirty-nine people and tell them what they are about to be part of, and it cannot be a lie, and it cannot be a performance.

I hand Toby my watch, because a stage manager doesn't carry her corner onto a stage. Then I walk out in front of the interval curtain in my working clothes, chalk dust and all, and I stand where the light is and wait for nine hundred and thirty-nine conversations to notice, which takes eleven seconds, and I give it to them the way I'd give a call. "My name is Bell Harrow. I'm the stage manager of this company, and what I'm for is making sure everyone in a house knows what happens next. So: Part the Second is not printed in your programme, and it has no title I can give you, because it has no title at all. It is a play of four acts and a matter following, two hundred years old, and it has never once been finished — every company that tried was interrupted by somebody brave. The people who made it and carried it and speak it tonight are the ones who bear its weight — in two hundred years of careful records, no soul who only watched has ever taken harm, and you have an actuary's word on that, and he is sitting at my prompt desk. What we ask of you is the oldest thing a theatre asks: witness. Stay, if you choose. Leave, if you choose — now, or at any moment; the exits are lit, all eight, and this play will not stop for a leaver, and nobody in this building is required to be brave tonight. Any child here sits by an open door, and any child who'd rather have the foyer and a bun has my note for both. If anyone comes in late, by any door, the house will know them — we keep count here. One seat in row eleven is sold and empty and stays so; let it be. That's everything I know how to tell you honestly, and it's all of it." I look once around the whole house, gallery to pit, the way you check a rig. "The Vermilion Players will finish it tonight. Those who stay — thank you for your witness."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Silence, and then a house doing something you will remember for the rest of your life: nobody applauds. Nine hundred and thirty-nine people sit and look at you, and then a great deal of quiet movement begins.

Twenty-odd get up. An officer takes his wife out by the pit door and she is arguing and he is not. Two of the Chamberlain's clerks go, decently, without hurry. A woman in the second circle collects three children and a bag and Grelle has the door for her before she reaches it and says something that makes her nod. One drover comes *down* from the gods and takes a seat in the empty front row, closer, which is not what you expected. The bishop's household stays entire. Skarke does not move a muscle.

The rest — nine hundred-odd — settle, and it is not the settling of an audience. It's the settling of a jury.

You come off. Toby hands your watch back with both hands, wordless. Lenz has stood up at the prompt desk and does not sit down again; he says, quietly, "That was the correct order, madam," and turns his marked page over so it is face-down.

Falk is standing at the entrance with his weight on both feet. Mirelle beside him with her hands still. Vane behind them, hat off, in the plum coat gone shiny at the cuffs. Hebel's palm on the wheel. Krug on the rail; Boyle at the pin; Dessa in the wing with her thimble on; Grelle and Toby out at the doors; Prewick standing where he can see everyone's hands and no longer pretending to be anything but a member of this company.

Ninety seconds. Falk turns his head, and asks you for it, the way he has asked all tour.

"What am I in, harbor?"

"The one with the ending." I give it to him whole. "Four acts and a matter following, played to the finish for the first time in two hundred years. And you're not in it alone — count the wings." The watch settles into my palm as if it grew there. "Places, please. Part the Second." And then my first call of the fifteenth speaking, low, to Hebel at his wheel: "House to half. Stage to warm. Slow as a sunrise, Herr Hebel — we have all night, and it's ours."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Hebel takes the wheel with both hands.

The house goes to half slower than any house has ever gone, and the stage warms the way a stove warms, and Toby out in the aisle actually stops breathing. Somewhere in the pit a man clears his throat and is shushed by his own neighbour. Nine hundred-odd faces go from gold to amber to shadow.

Falk walks on into the warm.

He does not announce anything. He stands in the middle of the Theatre Royal's stage in his own clothes, and lets the house arrive at him, and then Emeran Falk opens his mouth and begins the play he has carried in his memory for twenty years, and the first line goes out over nine hundred people, and — this is the thing you will never be able to explain afterwards — it is only a line. A man says words. Good ones. Nothing in the wings goes cold. The gas doesn't flutter. The fire watch downstage prompt side shifts his feet and settles.

At your desk, Lenz's hand comes down flat on the closed folio and stays there. Beside you Krug's lips move, silently, four words behind: he is following it from memory too, from nine pages and eleven years. Mirelle waits on your left, hands still, for an entrance she has never rehearsed.

The first act runs eighteen minutes and is a play about a house waiting for someone. It is *good*. That's the horror and the mercy of it, and you have both hands full of a job so you don't have time to be frightened by it, which is exactly why the job exists.

And then Falk turns upstage, and Mirelle steps past you into the light without being told, and behind you — very quietly, at the prompt desk, in a voice meant only for you — Undersecretary Lenz says: "Madam. The knock is in ninety seconds, and it is not written as a sound. It is written as *a knock, three times, from outside the theatre.*"

"Then we answer it." Ninety seconds is a luxury; I've cued storms on four. Toby goes at a walk, not a run, with my exact words: Boyle takes the stage door — the wrong door, the one no audience uses. On the third knock, not before, he opens it wide, lamp held low, light on the boards and not in the face, and whoever stands there hears this house's own liturgy: you're asked-for, not expected. A grown man comes to my corner. A boy — Toby walks him down himself, programme in hand, to row eleven, seat one, the sold seat by the lit exit, and stays within arm's reach all night on my authority. Nobody is turned away, and nobody is unknown. The house knows its latecomers — that is the whole doctrine of this management." And to Lenz, flat, eyes on the stage: "Keep reading me the shapes as they come, Herr Undersecretary. You're the best flyman I've ever had."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz says, "Yes," and turns the folio's page, and does not look up again.

Toby goes at a walk. You watch him the length of the pit — the walk of a boy carrying somebody's exact words like a full cup — and Boyle takes the stage door on the wrong side of the building, out of sight of every soul in the house.

On stage, Mirelle Sorel is standing in a doorway in a play she has never rehearsed, and speaking as though she wrote it, and the house is with her. Falk waits, upstage, weight on both feet.

The knock comes.

It comes from outside the theatre, and it comes into the auditorium — not through the boards, not through the flats: through the walls, the way weather does, the way a cart in the street does. Nine hundred heads do not turn, because they are watching a play, and the play has a knock in it.

One.

The fire watch on the fly floor looks down at you. Krug's hand is on the pin rail, not on a rope, just on the wood.

Two.

Mirelle finishes her line into it and holds — she is *using* it, God help her, she has found the pause — and Falk turns his head an inch toward the wrong door, twenty years of it in one inch.

Three.

Boyle opens the stage door wide, and the cold of the yard comes in along the boards, and his lamp goes low.

And in the doorway, out of the dark, with paste dried white on his cuffs and no hat, stands a man nobody in this company has ever seen, and behind him, holding his hand, a boy of about ten in a good coat, who says clearly into the warm — because children speak at the volume of their own house, not yours —

"*Is this the finish?*"

I am three steps from my corner, and I take them. Low, backstage-sized, level as a fact, looking at the boy and not over his head: "Yes. This is the finish. And you're in time for it." Then the doctrine, whole: "You're asked-for, not expected — the both of you. This house knows its latecomers." My hand tells Toby: programme, row eleven, seat one, arm's reach, all night. My eyes tell the man with paste on his cuffs: my corner, and your name can wait for the act's end. And I am back at my desk inside eight seconds, because the other half of the vow is that the play does not stop — "Herr Hebel. Nothing changes on the wheel."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"Nothing changes," Hebel says, and it doesn't.

Toby does it exactly. He takes the boy's other hand without hurry, gives him the programme, says something quiet that makes the child look up at him, and walks him down the prompt-side aisle to row eleven, seat one, by the lit exit — the sold, empty, serviced seat — and puts him in it, and sits on the aisle step beside him within arm's reach, and does not once look at the stage.

The man with paste on his cuffs comes to your corner and stands where you point, out of Lenz's light. He watches the stage with his mouth open. He does not say a word.

On stage, Falk crosses to the wrong door in his own play and speaks the line he has not spoken in twenty years, and the house takes it, and nothing in the wings goes cold.

Act two runs. Act three. It is a great play, which nobody warned you about — a house, a debt, a creditor come late, a woman who lies kindly, and a boy in a passage who asks a question and is answered. In act three the boy in the play is answered. You feel nine hundred people understand something at once, the way a house does, and up in row eleven a real child of about ten sits with a programme on his knees and watches a thing that has been waiting two hundred years to be told properly.

Act four. Lenz's turned-down page. He puts one finger on it and says, without looking up: "Here. The caution. The matter following begins with a bell, madam, and the folio does not say who rings it — the copyist left the line blank, and it has been blank in every copy since." He does look up then, sixty-one years old and perfectly steady. "Page eight of Krug's said *a stage manager rings the bell.* There is a bell on your desk. There has always been a bell on every desk in the world."

Falk turns downstage on the last speech of act four. Krug's hand goes to the iron's release and stops there, ready and not used. The house is absolutely silent.

The last speech of act four ends the way the great ones end — on a held breath instead of a full stop. And there is a small ordinary bell on my desk, because there has always been a bell on every desk in the world. I look at my stage once, the way I'd check any rig: Falk's weight on both feet. Mirelle's hands still. The wings full of people who chose twice, cold and warm. A house witnessing, entire. A boy in row eleven with a programme on his knees, in arm's reach of a friend. Everything is where I set it. So I do the job the two hundred years were waiting for: I take up the bell and ring it once, clear, the way you call an act — and then I answer it myself, out loud, because in my house nothing rings unanswered. "Beginners, please. The matter following."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The bell goes out into nine hundred and forty seats — small, ordinary, bright, the sound of every prompt desk in the world.

And nothing answers it. Not for one whole second. And in that second you understand, with a completeness that will stay with you for the rest of your life, what has been the matter with this play for two hundred years: it wasn't a curse. It was a bell rung in an empty house, fourteen times, and nobody once on duty to say *heard*.

"Beginners, please," you say. "The matter following."

*Heard,* the house says — not in words. Nine hundred people breathe in together, which is a sound, and it is the sound of a house answering.

On stage, Falk lifts his head. Mirelle moves to him without being cued. Vane comes on from the O.P. side in the plum coat with his hat in his hand — he has an entrance in the matter following; nobody told him; he takes it — and Dessa Krul, who dresses it and does not act, stands in the wing where the boy in row eleven can see her thimble catch the light.

And the matter following is not a scene. Falk says nine lines. Mirelle says four. Vane says one, and it is a number, and he does not round it. Then all three of them stand still and let the house look at them, which is what the copyist wrote, and which is why it has never worked in a green room for a wager: *and the house, entire.*

Then the play stops being a play. There is no curtain line. Falk simply lowers his head, and Lenz's hand comes off the folio and he says, quite loudly, in the voice of the Office of Public Morals: "Certified."

Krug drops the iron. Eleven seconds.

And in the wings, the O.P. side, the P.S. side, the fly floor, the pit doors — nobody moves, and nobody cheers, and out beyond the iron nine hundred people are getting to their feet and making a noise you have never heard a house make before, which is not applause, and Grelle is standing at the pit door with both hands over his face, and Toby has the boy's hand, and your watch says twenty-two minutes past ten.

"House out slow and warm — all eight doors, Grelle; Toby, the boy stays with you till somebody claims him properly, and nobody claims him improperly." The machine runs; my people run it. Then, and only then, I turn to the man at my corner with the paste dried white on his cuffs, who has watched the whole of it with his mouth open and said not one word, exactly as the house's law prefers. "Now, then. The act's ended, and I'm owed a name. Who are you — and whose boy did you bring to my wrong door?"
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He takes a while to come back from wherever the last hour put him, and when he does he wipes his eyes with the paste-white cuff and looks at it in surprise.

"Fennimore," he says. "Fenn Halloran. I paste bills on the north side — the other half of Grelle's beat, madam, we split the wall by the newspaper offices." He gets his breath. "He's not mine. He's — " he turns and finds the boy down at row eleven with Toby, and something in his face collapses with relief at seeing him still there. "He was on the Baraque's step this afternoon. Alone. A woman brought him in a cab and put him out and said she'd be back and told him to be good and *didn't go in*, and she never came back, and the stage door was shut and there was nobody in the yard but a man on a trunk who wouldn't move off it and said to fetch you and he couldn't leave his post. So I took the child to my room and gave him bread and he wouldn't eat it, and he said he'd been told he was expected at the theatre tonight." He swallows. "And your man Ansel had pasted your bills all over my wall this week, madam, and I've read every one of them eleven times, same as him. *Ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour.* So I came to the wrong door and I knocked three times, because it was the door I knew, and — that's all. That's all I did. I only knocked."

Down the aisle, the house going out slow and warm around him, the boy has stood up on the seat to see better and is asking Toby something, and Toby is answering.

"He says his name's Fenner," Halloran says. "Fenner Bacher. He can read."
messages.speaker: Fenn Halloran

messages.body: "Fenn Halloran. You did every part of it right — the bread, the coming here, the knocking. In my books that's three debts, and this company pays its debts; you'll eat with us tonight and be walked home by a man with a lantern." Then the machine turns, quiet and fast. "The boy: soup, warmth, Dessa's corner of the wing — he stays in our keeping tonight, Toby on the cot beside him, and nobody asks him anything past his supper except one question, put kindly: where does his mother think he is." And the wire, before anything else in this city sleeps: "Herr Prewick — Room Fourteen's channel or the Comptroller's, whichever wakes faster. To Bailiff Kessel of Achterhalt, tonight, constable to the Bacher farm by morning: FENNER SAFE, IN THE VERMILION PLAYERS' KEEPING, CAPITAL, UNHURT. COME BY FIRST COACH. FARE PAID AT THE DOOR. — HARROW."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
"Room Fourteen's channel," Prewick says, already moving. "The Office keeps a night telegraph for enforcement matters and I am about to discover whether Assessment may use it." Lenz, from the prompt desk, without looking up from squaring the folio: "It may. Say Assessment, and say my name, and if the operator refuses tell him Room Fourteen will read his file in the morning."

It goes at twenty to eleven.

Soup happens in the O.P. wing of the Theatre Royal, which has never had soup in it before. Dessa Krul makes a nest of the queen's cloaks and does not once fuss over the boy, which is why he stops being frightened; Fenner Bacher eats two bowls, and asks Toby whether the black sheet is the thunder, and is shown it, and is allowed to shake it low.

And when the kind question is put, over the second bowl, he says: "At the theatre. She said I was expected." He looks up. "It was a lady in the cab. Not Mam. Mam's at home with the bolt on — she said stay in, and then the lady came Tuesday and talked to her outside for a long time, and Mam cried, and then Mam said I was to go and be good and she'd fetch me after." He wipes his mouth. "The lady had gloves on and she gave me a bun and she said the stage manager would know my name." A pause. "She did know it."

Across the wing, Mirelle Sorel is standing perfectly still with a cloak half over her arm, and she has gone the colour of paper, and she has not moved since the word *Tuesday*.

Behind you, in the doorway from the corridor, a Palace footman coughs and says, "Madam. There's a gentleman at the front of house won't come in and won't go away. Small man in black. He says to tell you he's still in row four and he'll wait till you're free."

I pick up the other half of the cloak she's holding and fold it with her, shoulder to shoulder, both of us facing the wing wall — the oldest privacy in theatre. "Tuesday," I say, quiet. "The word did something to you. So: tell me what you know about a lady with gloves who hands out buns and knows my name — or tell me you can't say yet, and I'll hold the ground either way, same as always. But if your kind invitation and his bun came out of the same reticule, Mirelle, I need it in the book tonight, because tomorrow I answer to two mothers."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Mirelle folds her half of the cloak with you, and her hands are shaking so slightly that only someone folding with her would know.

"I can say it," she says. "I've been trying to find the hour since Halbern."

She squares a corner. "On Tuesday, at the Baraque, a woman came to the wardrobe cage and gave her name as Frau Dietz and said she came from a house in the capital that had followed my career with great affection. She had gloves on. She gave me a letter. It was on good paper and it was extremely kind." A breath. "It said the matter of ten years ago is understood to have been a misunderstanding; that a certain family would be glad to receive me; and that the child who was placed out in the fifth year has been well brought up, and is ten this winter, and might be brought to see me if I wished it. And it said I should not speak of it to anyone, out of delicacy."

She turns the cloak over. "I have been sitting on that for two days deciding whether to burn it or bring it to you, and while I sat on it a woman with gloves went to Achterhalt and stood outside a farmhouse and made Ilse Bacher cry."

She looks at you for the first time.

"Harrow. My child is ten this winter. Ilse Bacher's boy is ten this winter. And somebody with good paper and a cab has just spent a week making certain that a boy of ten arrived at a theatre door tonight brought by a woman who didn't go in." Her voice does not rise at all. "It is not Fenner. It cannot be Fenner; Ilse bore him and I know when I bore mine and I know what I signed. Which means somebody used that child as a *sentence*." She sets the folded cloak down. "Put it in the book. All of it. And then ask your small man in black what a bank knows about placements in the fifth year, because he has been buying clerks for twenty years and I am done being delicate."
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: I go out through the pass door into the half-lit, emptied house. Skarke sits where he swore to sit, hands on his knees, face like a man who has been somewhere and come back the long way. I take my seat one away — hat-distance, our custom by now — and give him a moment of the quiet he paid for. "It finished," I say, because he above everyone is owed the word. Then: "And now I need the bank in you, not the boy. The fifth year: a child was placed out of the capital — placements move money. Nurse fees, school fees, a quiet annuity, somebody's discretion bought annually on good paper. A gloved woman calling herself Frau Dietz runs kind errands for a certain family, and this week she moved two mothers like furniture. Mirelle Sorel is done being delicate, Herr Skarke, and so am I. What does a bank know?"
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Skarke does not look at you. He looks at the iron curtain, which is down, with the whole finished thing behind it.

"It finished," he repeats. Then he closes his eyes for a moment, and when he opens them the boy is gone out of them and something older and much more useful is there instead.

"A bank knows the fees," he says. "That's all a placement is, madam: a standing order that never varies and never gets queried, and they are the easiest thing in the world to find if you know they exist, because they are the only entries in a great house's accounts that are the same to the penny for eighteen years." He puts his hands flat on his knees again. "The name Dietz I don't know. The *pattern* I know. There is a firm of solicitors in the Kanzelgasse who do nothing but that work for four families, and they use women — always women, always gloved, always called something plain — and the fee for a placement discreetly managed is paid quarterly out of an account that also pays the family's florist, because nobody audits flowers."

He turns his head at last. "You want to know if I can find who has been paying for a child placed out of this city in the fifth year. Yes. I can find it in three days, or four, and I will need a Christian name, or a date, or the ward the mother sang in. And madam —" the first hardness you've heard from him — "I will do it and I will not want anything for it, and you are going to have to let me not want anything, which I understand is the hardest favour a company like yours ever has to accept."

Then, quietly: "There's a second thing, and you'll not like it. The requisition fee for tonight was paid by a third party of considerable standing. That was me — but I paid it *through* the Kanzelgasse, because that is how a man of my sort pays for things he does not want traced." His mouth goes flat. "Which means the same clerks who know a placement in the fifth year have known for two years that the Vermilion Players were coming to the Palace on the 3rd of Frost, and which of them, and with what."

Out in the foyer, a door bangs and Grelle's voice says, "Madam Harrow's inside — sir, *sir*, you can't—" and there are footsteps on the aisle carpet, quick and light, and someone is coming down toward the fourth row who has not been announced.
messages.speaker: M. Skarke

messages.body: I'm on my feet and into the aisle before the footsteps resolve — square between whoever this is and the pass door, because a boy is asleep behind it. "The house is closed," I say into the half-light, level as a sill. "But I'm the stage manager, and if you've come this far past a man on a door, the stage manager is exactly who you want. Name and business. In that order."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The footsteps stop three rows short. In the half-light it is a woman: a good travelling coat, hat askew, gloves — and then she takes the gloves off, which is the first thing she does, and holds them in one fist like a woman who has been told about gloves.

"Ilse Bacher," she says. "Of Achterhalt. I've come off the ten o'clock goods train in a horse-box and I've walked from the yards, and a man on your door told me my son was inside and *safe*, and then he said I couldn't come in, and I'm sorry for him, madam, I moved him." Her voice cracks straight down the middle. "Where's Fenner?"

Grelle arrives at the top of the aisle at a run, dishevelled, mortified, and stops when you lift your hand.

"A lady came Tuesday," Ilse says, all in a rush now, "and she knew about the Rose and she knew about the door I opened and she said there'd been a bill in Achterhalt with my name near it and there hadn't, and she said the only way to keep him out of it was to let him be *seen* somewhere respectable and *counted*, at a theatre, in the capital, with a programme, and then his name would be in the right ledger instead of the wrong one — and she said it in my own kitchen with the bolt on the door and I *believed* her, and I put him in her cab, and she was gone by four and left me a five-pound note on the table." She holds it out; it is real and it is crumpled to cloth. "And I've been carrying that since Tuesday and every hour of it wrong. Then your wire came to Kessel and Kessel's constable was at my gate at eight and I was on the goods train by nine." She looks past you at the pass door. "Is he hurt?"

Behind you, through the pass door, very faintly, Toby's voice saying something and a child laughing at it.
messages.speaker: Ilse Bacher

messages.body: "Unhurt. Fed twice. Currently laughing at my props boy, which you can hear for yourself." I step out of her road as it lands, and take the crumpled note from her hand by one corner as she passes — "Exhibit, not money. It stops owning you the moment it's evidence; it goes in the book with the rest of what that woman touched." Then I hold the pass door its whole width, the way this house opens doors, and say the only other thing she needs: "Through here, Frau Bacher. Mind the third board — it sings."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She goes past you on the sides of her feet without being told, the way people do when they can hear a child.

The third board sings anyway. Fenner's head comes round the wardrobe cloaks at the sound of it, and then the boy is off the nest and across the wing at full speed, and Ilse Bacher goes down onto her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal and takes the whole of him against her coat, and neither of them says anything intelligible for some time.

Dessa Krul puts down her thimble, gets up, and goes to boil water without a word, which is the entire vocabulary of her affection. Toby retreats to the pin rail and stands there looking hard at a rope. Prewick, in the corridor doorway, removes his hat.

Ilse's voice, eventually, into the boy's hair, thick and shaking: "You *bolt* the door and they come in a cab —" and then, looking up over his head at the wing full of your company, at Dessa, at Boyle, at Falk who has come as far as the wardrobe cage and no further: "Emeran Falk."

"Ilse of the Rose," Falk says, and does not take a step closer, and puts his hand over his own mouth for a second like a man at a graveside. "Twenty years."

And into the middle of it, quietly, at your elbow — Skarke, who has followed you in and who is standing where a man of considerable standing has no business standing, holding his hat: "Madam. The five-pound note. May I see it, without touching it?" He looks at it in your hand, at the crumple, at the black stamp along the top edge, and goes very still. "That's not a bank note out of a purse. That's from a sealed hundred — the Kanzelgasse draws them for the families, ten notes to a wrapper, and they're numbered in sequence." His voice is barely there. "I can find out which family drew that wrapper, and when. Tomorrow. Before noon."

"Tomorrow, before noon, then. Thank you — and I'll let you not want anything for it, which we both know is the price." Then the night gets struck like a set. "Beds where bodies drop: Ilse and Fenner keep the nest, together. Halloran gets walked home behind a lantern by Boyle. Grelle — the door you couldn't hold was my mother-shaped door; it's forgiven twice over; stand down. And somebody take a lamp across town to Wenzel — he's been sitting six hours on a finished thing and doesn't know either fact. Relieve him gently; he'll argue." Last, at the prompt desk, where a small dry man is squaring two hundred and eleven leaves: "Herr Lenz. Your receipt says the folio returns into these hands, and it's past that hour. So say what Assessment wants done with a finished thing — because my hands would like to know what they're for now."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz has the stack squared and his own hands flat on top of it, and he has been waiting for you to come to him, and he does not stand up this time.

"What Assessment wants," he says, "and what Assessment can *do*, are two entries." He taps the folio once. "This is proscribed. Nothing tonight changes that; my seal certified a performance, not a text. In law it goes back into your Herr Vane's trunk, and the trunk goes back on the road, and the Index entry stands, and my office minds the two of them for another nineteen years." A pause. "That is what will happen if you and I do nothing clever."

He looks up.

"Here is what may happen instead, and it is the reason I did not sleep last night. There is a procedure — dusty, and nobody has used it since the eleventh year — for the *retirement* of a proscribed work: the Office may certify a text as *accounted closed* and lodge it, sealed, in the Depository under the Hall of Records, where it cannot be performed, cannot be copied, and cannot be sold, and where the entry in the Index is annotated rather than struck." He says it flatly, like a man reading a weight. "It requires three things. A certified performance, whole, with the audience noted — I have that, in my hand, tonight. The consent of every person named in the company's determination — I have that in Clerk Prewick's minute, signed, and it will hold. And the *entire* text, madam. Every copy known to the Office, lodged together." The dry finger comes off the stack. "There are thirty pages in a strongbox in the Skarke bank. There are nine pages in Emeran Falk's coat lining. There is one in your coat which you have not read, and I have not asked you about it, and I am asking you now."

He folds his hands.

"Bring me the halves and the loose leaves, all of it, before the 6th, and I will retire it. And then, Madam Harrow, your hands are for what they were always for: a company, a book, a bucket under a leak." A beat. "And the trunk will be a trunk."
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: "Before the 6th, you'll have the whole of it. On one condition of manner: each piece is given, not collected. Every holder of those pages has paid rent on them in years of their lives — they surrender by their own hand at your desk or not at all, and I stand at each surrendering." Then the inventory, aloud, because that's what a yes sounds like from me: "The strongbox thirty — Skarke, tomorrow noon; it will cost him more than anything he's bought in twenty years, and he'll pay it. The lining — Emeran's, ten and some odd, in the morning, with the rug on. Sorel's one — hers to carry to this desk herself, nobody's errand. The cupboard parcel of thirty — mine to give, and here." I lay it on the folio. "And my last two. The milestone's page — there. And page eight —" I take it out and set it face-down on the stack, my hand flat on it one second, no more — "which I never read, and now never will. Enter it exactly so: surrendered unread. Some accounts close by paying, Herr Undersecretary. That one closes by declining to collect."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz enters it exactly so — he takes up his pen there and then, on the corner of the prompt desk, and writes the whole inventory in that unremarkable hand while you watch, and reads it back aloud as he goes, which is by now the way the two of you do business.

"*Cupboard parcel, thirty leaves, surrendered by B. Harrow, this date. Milestone leaf, surrendered by B. Harrow, this date. One leaf, endorsed by A. Krug as page the eighth, surrendered by B. Harrow unread.*" He pauses over the last one. "I have written *unread* and I have underlined it. In nineteen years I have never had a document lodged with that word on it, and my successor will think it a clerical error and I intend to leave a note forbidding him to correct it."

He blots it, and squares the whole stack again, and then he does stand up.

"By your manner of giving, then. I shall sit in this room from nine o'clock every day until the 6th and receive them one at a time, and stand up for each." He picks up his hat. "Madam. Nine hundred and thirty-nine people went home tonight and will not know for the rest of their lives what they were part of. Two hundred years and one bell." He puts the hat on. "I am going to walk home. I have never once wanted to walk home."

He goes. Behind you the Theatre Royal is going out lamp by lamp under Hebel's hand; the O.P. wing has a woman and a child asleep in a nest of queen's cloaks with Dessa Krul on a stool beside them; Boyle's lantern is somewhere out in the fourth ward walking a bill-poster home; Falk is sitting on the settle from *Ilsabet* with the rug over his knees and his eyes shut and his hands quite steady.

And Vane comes to your corner at last, hat in hand, in the plum coat gone shiny at the cuffs, and stands there like a man waiting to be told what he is in.

Your watch is on its nail. There is chalk on your hands. The house is empty and warm and yours.
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: "You're in a solvent company, Odalric Vane. With a certified miracle behind it, no man's debt on it, and chalk on its stage manager." I let him have the whole of it, because he's earned the unrounded version. "And you're in a booking. The 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, one night only — by command. The bill exists; I impounded two hundred of them at Achterhalt, but the words on it belong to us now. So we honour it, on our own terms: Ilsabet, front doors standing wide, the tour's last night played for nothing but joy. Loewe's house. Perlmann on Bettina's arm. Ilse and Fenner through the front door this time, in the good seats. And the company's dead toasted at the interval — Hessel, Anna, Frau Hentsch, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house." I take my watch off its nail, last thing, like every night. "By command: ours. Now go to bed — you're driving me to a bank at noon."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Vane opens his mouth to weep, and then, visibly, decides against it, which is the single most impressive thing he has done all tour.

"*By command: ours,*" he says. "I shall have that printed. In Hessler's own case, with a note that the man was blameless in his own ink." He turns his hat round once. "Fourteenth of Frost. Loewe will let us the house for thirteen and call it eleven and I shall pay her fifteen and *not round it down*, and there will be no bills cried by any bellman anywhere, and Toby may hold the doors, and Grelle may hold the doors, and Wenzel may hold the horses and be told to his face that it is the best job in the building."

He gets as far as the pass door. Then he stops, and does not turn round, and says to the doorframe: "Harrow. Nineteen days. I hired you in ten minutes because the last one left in the night at Katterau and I would rather have died than tell you why." A breath. "You may put it in the book that I have said why."

Then he goes, and the Theatre Royal gives you its last lamp: Hebel bringing the board down to the pilot, so that the whole enormous house goes to a single blue tooth of flame and the smell of nine hundred and forty people cooling.

Chalk on your hands. Watch in your palm. Down in the wing a child turns over in the queen's cloaks and Dessa Krul says *sssh* to nobody. And out through the propped stage door, in the yard, under a sky going grey at one edge, the iron trunk sits roped on the tailboard with a man asleep against it — Wenzel, who argued, and lost — and its lid shut, and rain beading on it, though there is nothing overhead but morning.
messages.speaker: Odalric Vane

messages.body: Morning does what mornings do after miracles: porridge, and a props list. Ilse and Fenner go home on the midday coach, fares paid, a hamper from Dessa, and a promise extracted in return — the 14th, the Athenaeum, the front door, the good seats, Bacher the butter man included. Grelle walks them to the coach office himself, on the theory that a man should get to be on the right side of a departure for once. Then noon: Vane drives me through the fourth ward with his hat brushed, and I walk into the Skarke bank with my book under my arm to be told what a sealed wrapper knows about a certain family.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The Skarke bank has a marble hall and a lift with a boy in it, and the lift boy calls Vane *sir*, and Vane very nearly bursts.

Skarke does not keep you waiting. He has three things laid out on the desk when you come in: the strongbox — open, with thirty pages in it — and a wrapper of five-pound notes with two gone from the sequence, and a single slip of paper.

"The wrapper first, because you'll want it." He turns the slip round for you. "Drawn on the 9th of Reap, out of the account of the Kanzelgasse firm Behn & Sonder, against fees for one client. Ten notes; two spent; the note in your book is number six. Behn & Sonder have four clients." He puts one finger on the last line, which is a name.

"The Vorn family," he says. "House at the Bittersee, and a district officer of Public Order in the provinces, and — madam — a *Hessel Vorn*, who signed a notice at Katterau in the fifth year with a stamp struck twice, *SEEN, NOT APPROVED*." He sits back. "It's the same family. They are the ones who have been paying a placement out of this city since the fifth year, and they are the ones who sent a gloved woman to two kitchens this week, and I have not the smallest idea why yet, and I will have it in three days."

Then he stands and lifts the thirty pages out of the strongbox himself and holds them out to you — and stops, and takes them back an inch. "No. You told Lenz *given, not collected*." He puts on his coat. "I'll come with you. I'd like to put them on his desk with my own hand."

Out in the marble hall, Vane has got into conversation with the lift boy about the acoustics of the Corn Exchange, and is being listened to.
messages.speaker: M. Skarke

messages.body: Room Fourteen at half past twelve. I stand at the surrendering as I promised I'd stand at every one — one step back, book shut, witness and nothing else — while a small bald man carries thirty pages his father lodged before he was born across a government carpet. Whatever he says over them is his to say; I keep only the entry: given, not collected. And when it's done and the receipt read aloud, I put my hand out to him — the second time ever — and then take my name-shaped news home to the Baraque, because a woman there hears the word Vorn from me before any office in this city learns that I hold it.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz stands up for it, as sworn. Skarke sets the thirty pages down beside the folio, and what he says over them is: "My father lodged these against seven pounds and a wool factor's kindness, and I have wanted them for twenty years, and they are not mine and they never were." He puts his hat back on before his face can do anything, and Lenz reads the receipt aloud — *thirty leaves, surrendered by M. Skarke, this date, given not collected* — and the handshake happens over the desk of the Office of Public Morals, which is where they usually don't.

Then the fourth ward at one o'clock, and the Baraque's yard, and Mirelle in the wardrobe cage with her sleeves rolled, mending the hem she tore in the second act of a play she had never read.

You tell her. *Behn & Sonder. Note number six. The Vorn family, of the house at the Bittersee — and a Hessel Vorn, district officer, who stamped a notice at Katterau in the fifth year.*

The needle stops. She sits for a long moment with the hem in her lap.

"Vorn," she says. "Well." And then, in the flattest voice you have ever heard from her: "Harrow, the matter of ten years ago concerned a young man of that house, and a magistrate's summons that was to be served on me on a Tuesday morning, and a child born in the fifth year, five years before that — and I have spent ten years assuming those were two griefs and not one." She looks up. "They have been paying for him since the fifth year. Which means they *kept* him. Which means the kind invitation on good paper is not a family being generous to a woman they wronged. It's a family that has just discovered their placement is ten this winter and their name is about to be read out in a Palace by a company of players." Her hands come back to the hem, quite steady. "Sit down. Take out your book. I'll give you the whole of it now, from the beginning, and then you'll tell me what a stage manager does with it — because I have never in my life had anyone to hand a thing to."

I sit on the hamper across from her, take out the book, and sharpen nothing — the pencil's ready, like it's been ready for weeks. "From the beginning, then. Entered as heard. Kept as mine. Spent only as you rule it — that's the whole contract, and it doesn't expire." And I write while she talks, the way I'd hold a ladder while somebody climbs.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She gives it to you in order, the way she gives a cue: names, dates, no adjectives.

Her own name, which you write and will not repeat. A ward in the capital and a house at the Bittersee, and a young man called Rupert Vorn who came four nights running to a theatre in the second year and was charming and nineteen and lied about nothing in particular. A child born in the fifth year, in a lying-in house in the eighth ward, and papers signed by a woman of twenty-three with no money and no advice, and a fee paid, and a promise that the child would be *placed* and that she would be told the ward. She was never told the ward.

Then the tenth year: Rupert Vorn dead in a shooting accident in the mountains, and the family's lawyers finding letters, and a summons for a Tuesday morning on a charge of extortion — *extortion*, she says, and the needle goes through the hem hard — because she had written twice asking where the boy had gone.

"So I went over the mountains on a Monday night with a passport that spells a Kessarine town, and Odalric hired me in a yard at Merrow and never asked one question, and I have mended this company's gloves for ten years." She bites the thread. "And every page that has come to me has had a ten in it, and I have known exactly what the arranging was for, and I have never once been able to say the words *my son* out loud until this minute."

The needle goes still.

"Now. What does a stage manager do with it."
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: "First — you just said it out loud. My son. Say it as often as you like from now on; this cage has good acoustics." I let that sit exactly one breath, then I do my trade. "What a stage manager does with it is what I did with a two-hundred-year-old play: rule bravery out of the building, light every exit, and make the house answer when the bell rings. In order. One: no mother meets her son with a summons standing — the paper dies first, in writing, withdrawn and expunged, before any meeting is so much as discussed. They're frightened; frightened people sign quickly; Skarke's lawyers and a Comptroller who remembers what stage managers are for will draft it by Thursday. Two: the boy's keeping gets verified by someone you name — Skarke can audit a nursery out of a florist's ledger. Three: the meeting, if you want it, happens as a house of ours: your date, your ground, your witness, gloves off at the door, the child's own pace ruling everything inside — he's ten, and he chooses like anyone else in my buildings. And four, the payment that costs us nothing: their name, never spoken by this company — their discretion bought with the one coin we mint honestly. Kindness answered with terms, Mirelle. That's what the book does with it." I turn the pencil round and hold it out to her. "You rule. I call."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes the pencil.

She holds it for a moment, and then she does something you did not expect and will remember for years: she writes in your book. In her own clean businesslike hand, on the page under your notes, four lines.

*1. Paper dies first. Withdrawn, expunged, in writing, before any meeting is spoken of.*
*2. Keeping verified. Auditor: M. Skarke. Report to me, not to them.*
*3. Meeting only if the child is asked and says yes. My ground. Harrow present. His pace rules.*
*4. Their name never spoken by this company. Ever. Written here once and not again.*

Then she signs it — with the name she gave you an hour ago, in full, the first time it has been on paper in ten years — and blots it with her thumb, and gives you back the pencil.

"Ruled," she says. "Call it."

And then Mirelle Sorel puts her face in her hands and cries the way people cry who have been carrying something in a glove for a decade, and lets you sit there while she does it, which from her is the largest compliment in the world.

Outside the cage the Baraque goes on: Boyle whistling four notes and finishing the fifth for the first time in a fortnight, Toby dragging a hamper, Falk's voice somewhere out on the stage saying to Krug, "*Our* left, you see. She said *our left*—" and Grelle laughing at something, out loud, in a theatre, which nobody in this company has heard him do before.
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: The days between do what ruled days do: they comply. Thursday, the paper dies — Behn & Sonder sign quickly, as frightened firms sign; withdrawn, expunged, in writing, with a Comptroller's wording and a banker's witnesses, and clause four paid in the only coin we mint. The surrenders go one at a time to Room Fourteen, Lenz standing for each as sworn: Emeran goes with the rug on and gives up the lining — ten leaves and some odd, twenty years of ballast — and walks out visibly lighter than the arithmetic allows. Mirelle carries her one page alone, and comes back with her gloves folded in her pocket instead of on her hands. And on the morning of the 6th I put on my better coat and go down with Lenz to the Depository under the Hall of Records, book under my arm, to see a two-hundred-year account closed — and to spend the one question I've been saving since a lamplit yard: who struck the eleventh line?
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The Depository is three floors under the Hall of Records and smells of cold stone and paraffin. There is a keeper with a ring of keys the size of a horse-collar, and a hundred yards of iron shelving, and a great many sealed boxes with dates on them going back four hundred years, and it is so quiet you can hear the paraffin in the lamp.

Lenz does it himself. The whole of it — folio, thirty, thirty, ten and some odd, two, one unread — goes into a lead-lined case; he squares the stack one last time and then does not touch it again. The keeper solders the seam, which takes eleven minutes and smells sharply of hot metal; Lenz stamps the seal twice, straight both times, and writes on the label in his unremarkable hand: *ACCOUNTED CLOSED. Four acts and a matter following. Certified performance, the 3rd of Frost. Audience: nine hundred and thirty-nine, and one seat sold and empty. No harm recorded.* And then, on a separate slip pasted beside it: *One leaf lodged unread. This is not an error. Do not correct it. — Lenz, Assessment.*

Shelf, row nine. The keeper's key. The iron door.

Walking back up, Lenz answers your question on the second landing, without being asked twice.

"I have thought about nothing else for four days." He stops on the stair. "Madam, I have read every leaf of it now, twice, which nobody else alive can say. There is no eleventh part. There never was. Four acts, a matter following, ten speaking figures and the house. The cast list in that trunk had ten names because ten is what it wanted, and then an eleventh line, and then that line struck." He goes up two more steps and stops again. "The only hand in this business that has been striking things out for two hundred years is the copyist's — *cut, cut, cut* in pencil, on the leaf you fished out of a bucket. And a copyist strikes a line when a line is not needed."

He looks back down at you.

"My finding, for what an old clerk's finding is worth: it wrote an eleventh line because it expected one more maker. And somebody had already ruled that nobody could volunteer." A pause; the paraffin hisses. "You struck it, madam. Nine days before it was written."
messages.speaker: Undersecretary Lenz

messages.body: "Then enter my correction, for the file's sake: I didn't strike a line. I posted a notice — and the copyist read it and did his job. Cut what isn't needed." I put my hand out on the landing, because some partings are transactions and this one is a pleasure. "Best colleague I never met, Herr Undersecretary. The tea's owed in the other direction now — the Baraque's is terrible, and you'll drink none of it with us any time you like." Then the walk home through the grey, and the yard gate, and I stop where I stopped the first night in Grevenholt — and I look at the trunk, roped on the tailboard, under a sky that can't decide about rain, to see what the iron does now that the account is closed.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Lenz takes your hand and shakes it once, briskly, and says, "Terrible tea and a bucket under a leak. I shall come on the 9th," and goes off up the stairs into the Hall of Records with his hat on straight.

The walk home through the grey. The fourth ward, the coal smoke, the Baraque's arch.

And in the yard, roped on the tailboard, the iron trunk sits with the tarpaulin thrown back and the morning on it. Wenzel is asleep against the wheel, off duty, nobody having told him he could be. Boyle is oiling a hinge. And the rain starts while you stand there — real rain, the ordinary kind that comes on out of a grey sky — and it lands on the trunk and it does what rain has never once done to that trunk in nineteen days.

It sits, and pools in the chalk-scarred dent on the lid, and runs off the near corner in a thin brown stream onto the cobbles, and beads on the ropes, and the whole thing goes dark and wet and blotched and completely, insultingly ordinary — a box, in a yard, in the rain, wanting paint.

Boyle looks up, and looks at it, and looks at you.

"Madam," he says slowly, "that's *leaking*."

"Then it gets what every leaking thing in my house gets." I write the notice where I stand and Boyle holds out his hand for it, grinning like his hinge. "And after the bucket: paint. Dessa chooses — vermilion, if the ironmonger stocks honesty — and when it's dry, it carries the thunder. The sheet rides in a box that's learned to hold its tongue." Then the week gets its plot: "The 9th, tea for an Undersecretary — somebody find the pot without the chip. The 11th we roll for Vessendal, all wagons. Skarke's standing invitation goes in writing today: row four, any house of ours, any night, paying at the door like a Christian. And wake Wenzel gently — he's been off duty three days and deserves to hear it sitting down."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Boyle takes the notice and pins it to the trunk itself, on the wet iron, at trunk height, and the paper immediately goes limp and unreadable, and he leaves it there anyway, because it's the principle.

Dessa Krul chooses vermilion, and the ironmonger stocks it, and it takes two coats and Toby's whole Thursday and comes out the colour of a stage's idea of blood. Falk stands over it for a long time while it dries and finally says, "It's vulgar," in a tone of enormous approval, and puts the felt with the black sheet in it inside, and shuts the lid, and it stays shut like a box.

The 9th: tea in the O.P. wing out of the pot without the chip, an Undersecretary of Assessment on a hamper being read Prewick's fair copy of the minute, and Prewick himself so upright he nearly hums. Lenz drinks two cups and says the tea is terrible and has a third.

Wenzel is woken gently and told sitting down, and says, "Well, someone had to be off it," and then, after a moment: "Was it a good one? The play." And Krug says, "It was a great one," and Wenzel nods and goes back to sleep.

The 11th. Grey, cold, all wagons. Boyle on the box of the first; Krug up beside Falk on the second because they have found they can talk; Grelle on the third with the doors of the world in front of him instead of behind. Skarke's letter went Tuesday and his answer came Wednesday, four words and a signature: *Row four. Any night.*

Vane climbs up and settles his coat and takes the reins, and looks down at you standing in the arch with your book under your arm and chalk on your cuff.

"Vessendal," he says. "The 14th of Frost. By command." He grins like a boy. "Harrow — ask me for a thing."

"Then here it is, and it's overdue: pay me." I hold out my hand flat, in the arch, in front of everybody. "Nineteen days, stage manager's wages, in coin, on this spot, unrounded. The last open account in this company's book is mine, Odalric Vane, and I close my books before I travel." And because his face is doing several expensive things at once: "And when you've counted it into my palm — drive for Vessendal, and sing something vulgar going out the arch."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The yard goes quiet in the way it does when everyone decides at once to watch and not to help.

Vane comes down off the box. He takes out the float purse and hands it to Boyle to hold, and then out of his own breast pocket — over the amber notice, under the bank receipt — he takes a folded paper he has evidently been carrying since the 4th, and he counts, into your flat palm, in coin, aloud, nineteen days of a stage manager's wages at a figure that is not the one he mumbled in a dark theatre in Grevenholt but rather two shillings a day more.

"Nineteen days," he says, "at four and six. Four pounds, five shillings and sixpence." A pause. He looks at the coins in your hand and then at you, and for once he says the number twice on purpose. "Four pounds, five shillings and sixpence. And *that* is unrounded, Harrow, because it was three shillings a day when I hired you and I have been paying you at four and six in my head since Achterhalt and I could not think how to tell you without weeping."

He weeps. Then he blows his nose like a voluntary, climbs back up, takes the reins, and hauls the first wagon out under the arch singing something about a farrier's wife that Dessa Krul joins in on and Prewick pretends with all his soul not to know the words to.

The wagons go out one by one into the fourth ward: Boyle, Vane, Falk and Krug, Grelle, Wenzel and the horses, Mirelle with her hatbox and her gloves in her pocket, Toby hanging off the tailboard with the vermilion trunk beside him, gleaming wet in the drizzle and doing absolutely nothing at all.

The arch is yours for one more second. Book under your arm, chalk on your cuff, four pounds five and six in your fist, and a hundred and ten miles of road to Vessendal with your name at the top of the call-list.
messages.speaker: Odalric Vane

messages.body: The road north does what roads do when nobody owes anything on them: it's just weather and miles. Achterhalt on the second evening — Kessel waves us through his square like old custom, and Hessler prints the new bill in his own case with his own hands: THE VERMILION PLAYERS — ILSABET'S RANSOM — THE ATHENAEUM, ONE NIGHT ONLY — BY COMMAND: OURS — and under it, in the old standing type he re-set himself because printers are magpies twice over: the 14th of Frost, at seven. He takes no money and asks to keep one for the shop wall. And when we roll out at dawn there's a butter cart in the column — Ilse, Bacher the butter man, and Fenner riding up beside Toby, bound for the front door of a theatre by invitation that has nothing kind about it, only true. Vessendal by dusk on the 13th, and Frau Loewe on the Athenaeum steps with her arms folded, counting wagons.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Frau Loewe counts the wagons twice, and then counts them again because of the butter cart, and says, "Madam Harrow. You've come back with more than you left with, which nobody does."

The nine shillings and the gas tap are ancient history; she lets you the house for thirteen and Vane pays her fifteen and refuses to be argued down, which offends her so deeply she has to go and stand in the box office for a while. Perlmann is sent for, and comes on Bettina's arm at ten the next morning to walk the stage he has never seen, and is put in a chair in the middle of it and told where everything is, and says, "It is smaller than it sounds," which is the truest note anybody gives all tour.

The 14th, at seven. Front doors standing wide, and no bellman, and no bills but Hessler's. The house fills with drovers and wool men and Loewe's own people and half the market, because it is free and because word has gone round that something happened to this company in the capital and nobody knows what.

Row four, centre, is empty and sold — Skarke's letter said *any night*, and he has not come, and Toby lays a programme on it anyway.

Fenner Bacher comes through the front door with his mother on one side and the butter man on the other, in good seats, third row, and reads his programme all the way down, including the small print about the gas.

At the interval, Vane goes out in front of the curtain with his hat off and toasts the dead by name — Hessel Brandt, wool factor; Anna Sorel, who kept the accounts; Frau Hentsch of the Rasselgasse, who was owed four weeks — and then says, "And every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house," and nine hundred people in a provincial theatre drink to a trade they have never once thought about, and Falk in the wings puts his hand over his eyes.

And in the prompt corner, with the second half about to go and your watch in your palm, Mirelle appears at your elbow in her second-act cloak, and says, quietly:

"Harrow. Skarke's audit came this morning, to me and not to them." She has the letter in her hand, unopened. "I've been carrying it about since ten o'clock. I find I can't open it alone and I can't open it in front of Odalric." A pause. "Beginners is in four minutes. Tell me when."

"Not four minutes before an entrance — I don't spend your instrument." I say it like a cue, because that's what it is. "When is tonight, after the iron: the wardrobe cage, the kettle on, the two of us, and you'll open it with the play already given away and nothing in your hands but your own name. And hear the standing law before you go on: whichever way that letter reads, the ruling holds — your ground, his pace, me present. Nothing in an envelope amends my book." I take the letter from her and put it in my coat, where things wait safely for their hour. "Places, Frau Sorel. You have a house to lift."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She goes on and lifts it. Whatever else the road has done to her, the woman can make a house of drovers forget the rain, and tonight she makes them forget it for nothing, which is harder.

Falk comes on stage left through the door Boyle hung, and Vessendal — which is his own worst town, the town he sat in for a night and a day with the gas down four years ago — stands up before he has said a word. He stands in it, and gives them nothing extra, and afterwards Frau Loewe is discovered in her own box office with the door shut.

The storm comes in low out of the vermilion trunk. Perlmann says, audibly, "That's thunder," and Bettina shushes him and half the pit laughs and it does not matter in the least.

Iron down. Three calls. Fenner Bacher on his feet in the third row with his hands over his head, clapping like a man being paid to.

And then the wardrobe cage, and the kettle, and the letter out of your coat into her hands, and Mirelle Sorel breaks Skarke's seal with her thumb and reads it standing up.

Four pages, and she reads them all before she says anything, and then she sits down on the hamper.

"Well," she says. "He's twelve, not ten." Her voice is doing something complicated. "Born in the fifth year in the eighth ward, placed the same month with a family in the Bittersee village — *not* the Vorns; their steward's brother, on a standing order that never varied for twelve years. School fees paid. A doctor's bills paid twice. He is at a school in the Bittersee and his name is Anton, and Skarke has a *report from the schoolmaster*, Harrow, he's got a schoolmaster's report—" She stops, and turns the page round, and hands it to you, and it is three lines about a boy who is good at drawing and cannot spell.

Then she puts her hands over her face and says, from behind them, "*Twelve.* I have had ten in my head for a decade. Every page that came to me had a ten in it and I thought — " She stops. "Harrow. The pages were never counting his age."
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: I read the schoolmaster's three lines twice, because they're not a page and they're the best text this tour has produced, and I hand them back. "Then let the tens retire, Mirelle. You don't need a cipher anymore — you have a schoolmaster." I pour the tea, because kettles exist for exactly this minute. "He's twelve. He draws. He can't spell. He's real, and he's well, and none of those facts expire while you decide the rest. The ruling stands as written in my book by your own hand: he gets asked, and if he says yes — your ground, his pace, me present. There's no hurry left in it; the paper's dead, the family's bought their silence with ours, and a boy who draws will still draw in the spring." Then, because she's still behind her hands: "And whatever the pages were counting — they're in a lead box under the Hall of Records, sealed by a man who stands up for surrenders. Let them do their arithmetic in the dark."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes the cup. She doesn't drink it, but she holds it, which is what the cup is for.

"In the spring," she says, and it steadies her more than the tea would have. "Yes. He's got a term to finish. And I—" a breath, "—I have never once in my life had a thing I was allowed to do *slowly*."

Then she puts the schoolmaster's page inside her hatbox, and the four pages of audit with it, and she sits up and is Mirelle Sorel again, and says, in her flattest, driest voice: "Harrow. I shall want a needle and my own light and about six months, and I shall want you not to ask me about it, and then one day I shall ask you for something enormous and you'll say yes."

"Yes," you say, and it is entirely a business transaction.

Out in the house, the last of Vessendal is going home; you can hear Loewe locking up with her lamp and Perlmann's stick on the boards and Boyle telling Fenner Bacher a lie about horses. Falk is on the stage in his shirtsleeves, sitting on the settle, letting an empty house look at him. Vane is out in the yard counting a take of nothing and enjoying it enormously.

And Toby Lenz comes to the cage door, breathless, holding the box office slate.

"Madam. Row four, centre. It went out full — nine hundred and one bodies for nine hundred seats, and Herr Grelle says the odd one was a man who came in late, by the front door, and paid at the door, and sat in four centre, and left before the calls." He turns the slate round. On it, in someone's blunt pencil, in the box office's own hand: *Row 4 c. — pd. 1s 6d. — no hat.*

"Enter it exactly as the slate has it — paid, one and six, no hat — and post nothing about it. Our patron pays retail now. That's the whole of the miracle, and miracles don't need notices." Then I carry my book out onto the stage, where a tragedian in shirtsleeves is letting an empty house look at him, and I sit down on the other end of Ilsabet's settle with the standing page open between us. "Emeran. There's an entry here that reads: Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp. Answer owed when the capital is done and the company is safe." I turn it toward him. "The capital's done. The company's safe. And the answer went and performed itself before I could give it. So tell me, as one keeper of accounts to another — how does a bookkeeper close a question the world answered first?"
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Falk looks at the page for a long time, at his own asking written in your hand and the pencil answer that never came.

"You don't close it," he says. "You *transfer* it." He takes the book from you — the only time all tour — and holds it on his knee in the empty house. "That is what a company is, harbor. A ledger with legs. The thing I asked you for on a flagstone floor in Achterhalt got paid by nine hundred and thirty-nine strangers and a boy in row eleven and a man who does not drink, and I did not have to be brave once, and I have been trying for a fortnight to find where to put the balance." He hands it back. "Put it where the good notices go. Not the crowded page."

Then he stands up off Ilsabet's settle, and he does it easily, and that is the part you'll remember.

"And then rule me something for the morning, because I have no idea what I am without that question in my mouth, and I should rather be told than guess. What am I in, Bell Harrow?"

Out in the wings, someone drops a hamper. Vane's voice comes up out of the yard, magnificent and unbothered: "*Achterhalt on Thursday*, and I have written to a man in Katterau about the spring, and Harrow will rule on it and I shall drive where she points—" and Dessa Krul telling him to keep his voice down, there's a child asleep in the second wagon.

Your chalk is in your pocket. The house is dark and empty and the gas is at its pilot, and there's a hundred and ten miles of the rest of it in every direction.
messages.speaker: Emeran Falk

messages.body: "You're in the repertory, Emeran Falk." I write the transfer as I say it, where the good notices go. "Ilsabet at Achterhalt on Thursday. The Wolf King whenever Prewick finishes comparing it. Whatever Katterau asks for in the spring — played by daylight, front doors wide, bills by Hessler. You're in things now, instead of carrying them. That's what you bought at the Palace; it cost twenty years, and it's paid, and I keep the receipts." Then, because he asked to be ruled something for the morning: "Tomorrow you teach Fenner Bacher how to stand — weight on both feet, voice up out of the boots. Skills like that should travel by hand, not by page." I strike the standing page clean across, the way you strike a day that ended well, and I shut the book.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He takes that standing in the dark of the Athenaeum, and it does the thing to his face that no notice ever did.

"*In things.*" He tries it out twice. "I have been the thing being carried since I was thirty years old." Then, briskly, because a great ruin can only stand so much: "Weight on both feet, and the voice up out of the boots. Nine o'clock. Tell the child to eat first; nobody learns to stand on an empty stomach." He goes off toward the pass door, and stops, and says without turning round: "The rug is his if he wants it. His hands will be cold on that cart in the morning."

Then he's gone, and the Athenaeum gives you what theatres give: the gas at its pilot, the smell of nine hundred people cooling, the boards going quiet by degrees.

Out in the yard, the wagons are settling for the night. Vane is being shushed. Krug is arguing pleasurably with Boyle about a lashing. Toby has fallen asleep sitting up against the vermilion trunk, which is only a box, in the rain, wanting nothing. Mirelle's light is on in the second wagon with a needle going in it. Grelle is on the gate — first watch, unasked, because a man likes to stand on the right side of a door.

And on the wall by the stage door, where you posted it three weeks ago and nobody took it down, your first notice in this town is still up, gone soft with weather but legible: **BUCKET UNDER PROMPT CORNER LEAK — DO NOT MOVE — B. HARROW, S.M.**

The bucket is still under it. It is empty, and dry, and Krebs's hinge bites the frame on the first try.
messages.speaker: Emeran Falk

messages.body: Winter does what winter does to a company that owes nothing: it is merely cold. Achterhalt on the Thursday plays to Kessel in the second row, chain of office and all. Winter quarters follow in a market town with a dry hall and honest stoves. Prewick's papers come through at midwinter — attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense — and his mother now writes weekly to a theatre and is answered. Krug takes the second book and the advance work, which suits a man who likes arriving first. Lenz comes twice for terrible tea and drinks three cups both times. Skarke's quarterly audit of nothing arrives punctually, with two row-four ticket stubs pinned to it as receipts. And in the first week of spring, on the road to Katterau — daylight, front doors, Hessler's bills ahead of us — Mirelle climbs up beside me on the box, sits the way she sits, and asks her enormous thing, exactly as contracted. I say yes before she finishes the sentence. That was also the contract.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes yes the way she takes a cue — without ceremony, and slightly annoyed at being got ahead of.

"You don't know what it is."

"You'll tell me for twenty miles," you say, and she does.

It comes out in her flattest voice, which is how you know: a house in the Bittersee village, and a school that breaks up in Reap, and a boy called Anton who draws and cannot spell, and Skarke's schoolmaster willing to be written to, and a steward's brother's wife who has kept the standing order for twelve years and — according to three lines of somebody else's report — is a decent woman who never once knew where the money came from.

"So the enormous thing," Mirelle says, and folds her hands. "I want a season's leave from Reap to Frost. I want you to write the letter to the schoolmaster, because you write like an office and I write like a woman with something to hide, and offices are believed. And I want you to come with me the first day, and stand where I can see you, and go away on the second." A pause; the wagon creaks. "And I want a place kept in the repertory, because I intend to come back, and because if I don't say that out loud I shall lose my nerve in a hotel somewhere."

Ahead, the road bends, and Katterau comes up out of the flat: a church, an inn with a scullery door, and a theatre with a stone front that Falk has not looked at yet, and is now, from his box on the second wagon, looking at.

Behind you, the vermilion trunk rides on the tailboard with the black sheet in it and Toby asleep against it in the sun.
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: Katterau by daylight is what every haunted name turns out to be: a town, with washing out. We're billed for seven — ILSABET'S RANSOM, BY COMMAND: OURS, Hessler's type — and the load-in runs itself these days, which leaves the afternoon. Falk finds me at the props table and asks, in the voice he saves for small enormous things, whether I'd walk with him — not to the theatre. To the Rose. He goes in by the front door, upright, and buys bread at the counter like any man with coin, and I stand where he can see me and touch nothing. Whatever he does with the bread and the scullery door is his to do; I keep only the entry, and I keep it in pencil.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The Rose is not haunted either. It is a taproom with a low ceiling and a dog and a girl of about sixteen behind the counter who has never heard of him.

He buys a loaf and pays and doesn't overpay, which for him is a kind of discipline. Then he stands with it in the middle of the room and turns his head slowly, the way a man reads a set: the passage there, the door to the green room there, the scullery there, still on the left. His shoulders come down about an inch.

He goes to the scullery door and does not open it. He puts his hand flat on it for about four seconds. Then he takes the bread through to the yard door and gives it to two children playing in the mud, who take it with enormous suspicion and go away fast, and Falk laughs out loud into an empty inn yard in Katterau.

Coming out, he says only: "It's smaller than it sounds," which is Perlmann's note, and he says it with great satisfaction.

The pencil entry writes itself: *Falk, E. — the Rose, front door, one loaf, given away. Standing on both feet.*

At six the house begins to come in, and Katterau turns out to be a town that has waited twenty years for a company to be brave enough to come back and is not going to make a fuss about it. The mayor arrives and turns out to be a woman now, and says the old mayor's favour died with him but she has her own, and lets you use the town's fire buckets. Grelle and Toby get the doors. Ilse Bacher is not there, because she lives eleven miles off and sent word she'd rather not, and sent butter.
