And at the half, in a prompt corner in Katterau, with your watch coming off its nail, Krug hands you a folded slip that came to the stage door.

"Not a page," he says immediately. "Ordinary paper. It's from the mayor's clerk."

*Madam — one seat sold, row four centre, paid at the door, gentleman declines a programme and asks that you not be told until the half. He says: on the hour.*

"Then he's in time for it." I send four words back with the mayor's clerk — *the house knows him* — and take my watch off its nail into my palm, where it has worn its own bright patch by now. "Places, please." And Katterau gets its play: whole, on the hour, front doors wide, in the town that taught everyone living the price of stopping early.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Krug goes; the slip goes into your coat with the rest of them.

Katterau gets its play. Mirelle takes the first scene and the room forgets its own name. Falk comes on stage left through Boyle's door and this town — this town — stands up, and it takes a while, and he lets it, and then goes on. Hebel isn't with you, but Krug's on the gas and knows what warm means. The storm comes in low out of the vermilion trunk with a floor in it, and somewhere in the third row a farmer says "God almighty" and is not shushed.

You call it clean, cue by chalked cue, the way you called it in a corn hall and a Palace and a house with a leaking roof in Grevenholt nineteen days after you walked in off the rain.

Iron down. Three calls. And in row four, dead centre, Marius Skarke stands up with the rest of Katterau and claps until the house lights come up, and then makes his way out with the drovers, paying nothing, owed nothing, unremarkable, and is gone before the calls have finished settling.

Toby, at your elbow, with the slate: "Row four went out with the house, madam. Full count. Nobody late, nobody left, nobody empty."

And the stage door bangs, and Vane's voice comes booming up from the yard, and he is holding a letter and his hat is on the back of his head: "*Harrow!* There is a man in Vessendal who wants us for a fortnight in Reap, and a fair at Merrow that pays *actual money*, and I have said yes to both because I am solvent and reckless — ask me for a thing!"

"Then here's the thing, and it books ahead of your bookings." I come down into the yard with the slate still in my hand. "A place held open, Reap to Frost. Frau Sorel takes a season's leave — hers by contract with me, her reasons hers to keep, and nobody in this company asks her a question about it, you first of all. She comes back in Frost to a repertory with her name still at the top of it. Book Vessendal, book Merrow, book the moon if it pays actual money — around her, Odalric. Never over her." I hold his eye until the nod is real, and then I let the night have him back. "And yes to Loewe's fortnight regardless. Her counterweights miss us."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Vane takes it exactly right, which after nineteen days and a winter he now reliably does: no speech, no tears, just the hat coming off.

"Held open," he says. "Reap to Frost. Nobody asks her anything." He turns the hat round once. "Harrow, I have never in thirty years managed a company that could afford to lose its leading lady for a season, and I find that I can, and that it is the *proudest* thing—" He stops himself, visibly, and rounds nothing. "Vessendal a fortnight. Merrow's fair. And I shall write to Loewe tonight and tell her her counterweights are missed."

He goes off across the cobbles bellowing for Krug and the datebook.

Mirelle is in the wardrobe cage taking her hair down, and she does not turn round when you come in, and she says to the mirror, "I heard him from here. The whole yard heard him."

"Then it's booked," you say.

"Then it's booked." She puts the pins in the tin one at a time. "Reap to Frost." A pause; the tin closes. "Harrow. When you write to the schoolmaster — don't write like an office after all. Write like a stage manager. Tell him a woman is coming who does not perform for the people she cares about, and that she keeps her promises to the minute, and that if he wants a reference he may write to a Clerk Third Class of the Office of Public Morals who has never once been able to lie."

Out in the dark of the Katterau house, the last gas goes down to its pilot. Somebody has left your chalk on the props table with your book squared beside it, which nobody in this company did nineteen days ago.

The letter goes as she ruled it — a stage manager's hand, not an office's: a woman is coming who does not perform for the people she cares about; she keeps her promises to the minute; references, a clerk who cannot lie. The schoolmaster's answer takes a fortnight and is four lines, and the line that matters says the boy was asked, and thought about it for two days, and then asked whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills, and said yes. So Reap comes, and the Bittersee turns out to be small water and clean light, and on the first day I do exactly what was contracted: I stand at the turn of the lane, where she can see me, and no nearer. And Mirelle Sorel walks the last forty yards alone, not performing, toward a garden wall where a boy who draws is sitting with a paper in his hands. What happens at that wall is theirs. For the first time in my working life, I keep no entry at all.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
You keep none.

The lane holds its light for a long time — small water, clean light, a wall of loose stones and a boy sitting on it with paper on his knees. You watch her cross the last forty yards, and she doesn't perform, and when she is ten feet off the boy stands up on the wall, because that is what children do to be nearer to something, and you see her put a hand out and *not* touch him, and say something short.

Then you stop watching, because it is theirs, and you turn and look at the water instead for about a quarter of an hour, and when you look back they are both sitting on the wall and the paper is between them and she is being shown something.

On the second day you go away, as contracted. There is a coach at seven; she walks you to it and neither of you says much, and at the step she says, "Frost," and you say, "Frost," and that's the whole of the transaction.

And then the road, and Reap, and the Vermilion Players playing a fortnight in Vessendal without their leading lady and getting away with it, because Dessa Krul dresses the girl who steps up and Falk carries the third act and Vane rounds nothing at all. Merrow's fair pays actual money. Prewick's mother sends a cake to a theatre. Krug's advance work means you arrive twice to find the roof already mended.

Frost comes cold and early. And on the fourteenth, in a yard in Achterhalt with the wagons loaded and Hessler's bills going up, the mail cart brings a letter directed in a hand you have not seen since a wardrobe cage — clean, businesslike, nothing like a copyist's.

Your chalk is in your pocket. Boyle is holding the gate. It is one hour to load-out, and nobody in the yard is looking at the trunk.

I open it against the gatepost in the cold, the yard's good noise going on behind me, and I read it twice — it isn't a page; some letters are for savouring. Then I fold it into the book beside the struck standing page, take out my chalk, and do the last job of the day, which is the first job of the season: I chalk the call on the tailboard where the whole company will read it at load-out.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The letter is four lines and a postscript, and the last line is: *Frost, as booked. I shall want a needle, my own light, and my place at the top of the call-list. He can spell "vermilion." I have taught him nothing else.*

The chalk squeaks on the tailboard. You write it the way you write everything: legibly, and where it can't be missed.

**CALL — 14th FROST — ACHTERHALT**
**BEGINNERS 6.45. SOREL, M. — RETURNS THIS DAY. TOP OF LIST.**
**— B. HARROW, S.M.**

Toby reads it first and shouts, which starts the whole yard. Dessa Krul comes out with pins in her mouth to check the spelling and takes the pins out to say something unrepeatable and pleased. Boyle rings the gate bell with the flat of his hand for no reason at all. Vane arrives at a run with his hat off, reads it twice, and puts both hands on the tailboard as though steadying a horse.

And Falk comes across the cobbles and stands beside you looking at your own handwriting for a while, and then says, "*Top of list.* Yes." He puts his hands in his pockets. "Harbor — the boy Fenner's mother sent butter again, and the mayor's coming, and I am in things."

An hour to load-out. Your chalk is worn to a stub. The vermilion trunk sits on the tailboard under your call with the thunder inside it, doing nothing, wanting paint again by spring — and out on the Vessendal road, a coach is coming in the cold with a woman on it who keeps her promises to the minute.

The coach comes in with the cold riding on it, and the yard does not perform its joy — it simply stops working for one whole minute, which from this company is a standing ovation. I meet her at the gate with call-list chalk still on my fingers, and I say the only thing a stage manager says to a returning lead: "Frau Sorel. Beginners at six forty-five. Your light is trimmed, your needle is where you left it, and the third board still sings." And then I take her hatbox, because some things you carry for people whether they allow it or not.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She lets you take it, which from her is an entire speech.

"Harrow," she says. Then she looks past you at the yard — the stopped work, Dessa with the pins out, Toby on the tailboard, Falk standing on both feet, Vane holding his hat in both hands and managing, for once in his life, to say nothing at all — and she looks back at you, and her mouth does something it has not done all tour.

"The third board sings," she repeats. "Good."

She walks into the yard, and the minute ends, and the company goes back to work around her in the way that means everything: Boyle hands her a hamper to carry because there's a hamper to carry; Krug asks her a question about act two; Dessa says the hem's been let down two inches and she'll want fitting before the half. Nobody asks her one question about Reap to Frost. Prewick removes his hat and puts it back on.

You carry the hatbox in yourself and set it in the wardrobe cage under her own light, next to her needle, where she left it — and beside the needle, propped against the mirror where she will find it in about four minutes, somebody has already put a folded sheet of paper.

It is not a page. It is drawn in soft pencil, badly and with great care: a wagon, a horse too small for it, a box on the tailboard coloured in hard with something red, and along the bottom, spelled correctly, the one word he has been taught.

I leave it exactly as propped — some notices post themselves, and this house doesn't move other people's mail. The afternoon does its good ordinary work: Ilse's cart at four with butter and the butter man and Fenner, who marches straight to Falk and demonstrates standing — weight on both feet, voice up out of the boots — and is inspected like a soldier and passed. Kessel sends word he's coming in his chain. Prewick and I count fire buckets out of pure ceremony, nine of nine, no mice. And at the half I knock at the wardrobe cage the way I knocked on iron once — twice, soft — and ask through the door if the hem sits.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The needle stops on the other side of the door.

"The hem sits," Mirelle says. A pause; a small movement of paper. "Harrow — come in a moment."

She has the drawing pinned to the mirror frame at eye height, where an actor sees herself, and she does not mention it and neither do you. She is in the second-act cloak with the pins out of her mouth and the tin closed.

"Beginners in twelve," she says, entirely businesslike, and then, without changing her voice at all: "He spells 'vermilion' and nothing else, and he has begun writing it on things. His schoolmaster wrote to *me* about it. To me." She smooths a fold that doesn't need it. "That's all. I only wanted somebody in the building to know that a schoolmaster wrote to me, and I couldn't say it in the yard."

Then she stands, and shakes the cloak out, and is the leading lady of the Vermilion Players again in the time it takes to breathe.

"Twelve minutes," she says. "Go and call your house, Harrow."

And out beyond the cage the Achterhalt hall is filling: Kessel's chain catching the gaslight in the second row, Ilse Bacher and the butter man and a boy of ten sitting bolt upright with a programme, Grelle propping the doors and counting, Toby at the pit end, Falk somewhere in the dark on the O.P. side with his weight on both feet.

Your watch is on its nail in the prompt corner, three feet from a stub of chalk, on a call you wrote yourself this morning.
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: "Called, then." Places, and the hall settles the way honest halls settle — coughs spent early, Kessel's chain going still in the second row. Krug takes the gas board and knows what warm means; I bring the house to half slow as a sunrise, out of respect for old habits that earned it. And then Ilsabet's Ransom goes up in Achterhalt with a returning lead at the top of the call-list, and I stand in my corner with the watch in my palm and let the first scene rise to meet her.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
It rises. Mirelle Sorel walks on into the warm and Achterhalt — a hall of corn merchants who laugh in the wrong places — goes quiet by the third line, which is one line faster than they managed at midsummer.

You call it the way you have called it forty times now: cue by chalked cue, off the actors' weight rather than off the page, the plot running in your hands like something with its own pulse. Falk's entrance stage left. Vane's tears at the top of act three, on the beat, and meant. The storm in low out of the vermilion trunk with a floor in it, and Fenner Bacher visibly *waiting for it*, and getting it.

Iron down. Three calls; Mirelle gets a fourth she didn't ask for, and takes Falk's hand for it, which she has never done.

Then the hall empties into the cold, and the wing fills with the good noise, and Kessel comes backstage in his chain to say something official and says instead, "That was a fine thing," and shakes hands with the wrong people in the wrong order and doesn't care.

At half eleven the vermilion trunk goes back on the tailboard with the black sheet in it, and Boyle ropes it, and Wenzel sits on it because he likes to.

And in the prompt corner, on the last look round with the gas at its pilot, your watch comes off its nail into your palm — worn bright, warm, entirely yours — and there is chalk on the ledge, and the call-list for tomorrow blank and waiting, and Vane's voice out in the yard already saying, "Vessendal, and then the fair, and after that I have an *idea*, and Harrow will rule on it—"

Soup happens, because soup is the one law older than mine. I let the benches fill — pins, thimble, chain of office departed, a boy of ten allowed up late against all butter-man judgement — and then I rule on the standing offer. "The idea, Odalric. Out loud, to the table, the way ideas get their weight taken." And while he draws breath I open the floor the old way: "And after him, the spring — every voice, youngest last, because the youngest has been rehearsing his and deserves a warmed house." Under the table, Toby Lenz sits up like a rope gone taut. "And somebody write to Hebel this week. A wheel that good shouldn't winter unwritten-to."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Vane stands, and he has to be told twice to sit, and then does the thing he has learned this year, which is to say a plan without a single rounded number in it.

"A second wagon *properly*," he says. "Not Krebs's brother-in-law's cart. And a fit-up: our own flats, our own door — Boyle's door, the very same one, taken off its hinges and carried — so that we do not depend on what a hall keeps in its scene dock, and so that when we come to a town with no theatre we are *the* theatre. Eighty-two pounds, Harrow. Not eighty. Eighty-two, and I have Krug's figures and Loewe's fortnight and the fair, and it can be done by Reap if nobody buys a new coat." He sits. "That is the idea and I have not once said the word miracle."

The table goes round.

Boyle: "That door's my door and I'll carry it." Krug, with the datebook: "Eighty-two's honest. It's the first honest number he's ever given me." Dessa Krul: "Then I want a proper hamper and I'll say no more." Grelle: "There's a fit-up firm in the fourth ward owes me a favour and a ladder." Prewick: "The Office allows a company its own portable proscenium; I have looked it up already, twice, for pleasure." Falk: "In." Mirelle, needle going: "In — and the spring is Katterau again, if they'll have us, in daylight, with the front doors wide, and this time we play *two* nights."

Then, youngest last, into a warmed house: Toby Lenz stands up, ears scarlet, and says, "I want to be second stage manager. Not props. Second on the book, under Madam Harrow, and I'll learn the plot tables and I'll keep the notices and I'll—" his voice cracks upward and he pushes on through it — "and I'm nineteen, and I held the doors at the Palace, and I didn't look at the stage once."

Dessa Krul, without looking up: "He's eighteen."

Toby: "I'm *nineteen*."

Eleven faces turn, as they do, to you.

"The eighty-two: ruled yes." I say it into my book as I write it. "Entered at eighty-two, spent to the penny — and the first plank of that fit-up carries Hessel Brandt's initials somewhere only this company knows to look. A theatre we carry ought to carry him." Then I look at the boy standing in his own scarlet ears. "Toby Lenz. Second on the book — ruled, with terms. You chalk tomorrow's call under my eye. The bucket rounds are yours alone from tonight. You learn the plot tables from Krug, who kept a book before either of us. And in the spring, at Katterau —" I let it land the way he's been waiting two seasons for it to land — "a house of six hundred, and you call the storm. You, on the book, me standing behind you saying nothing." A beat, house-timing. "And you're nineteen the day you call it clean. Until then, Dessa's arithmetic stands."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Toby sits down very suddenly, and then stands up again because he can't stay in the chair, and says, "Yes, madam," in a voice that goes nowhere near where he wants it to.

Dessa Krul says, "Eighteen," with enormous satisfaction, and puts a second bowl in front of him.

Krug takes the datebook and writes it in himself — *T. Lenz, 2nd on book, from 14 Frost* — and turns it round for you to initial, which is the moment the boy actually understands that it happened. Boyle raises his cup. Grelle, who has been on the doors of the world for twenty years, reaches over and shakes the boy's hand as though they were both men in a trade, and that finishes Toby off entirely.

"Hessel Brandt's initials," Vane says, into the noise, "on the first plank." He is not weeping. He looks at his own hands on the table. "H.B. And I shall be the one to cut them, and I cut wood badly, and it will look terrible, and it will be *right*."

Falk lifts his small brandy — the one he still doesn't drink until after — and doesn't propose a toast, because you've all had enough of those, and instead says to the table generally: "Weight on both feet, all of you."

Then the benches break up, and the wing goes down to lamp and stove: Prewick writing to his mother, Mirelle's needle, Wenzel already asleep, Fenner Bacher being carried out to the butter cart insisting he isn't tired.

And Toby Lenz comes to the prompt corner with the chalk in his hand and looks at the blank tailboard and then at you, waiting to be told how a call gets written.

"Then hear the whole church of it, because it's short." I don't take the chalk from him; that's the point. "Legibly, and where it can't be missed — that's half. The beginners time goes first and largest, because the entire day hangs from that one nail. Names before numbers; a call is about people, the arithmetic only serves them. Nothing on the board you haven't checked with your own feet — if the call says the wagon leaves at eight, you have stood in the yard and looked at the wagon. And at the bottom, your name, every time. A call is a promise with a signature on it, Toby Lenz. That's why it works." I step back from the tailboard and put my hands behind me. "Vessendal. Load-out at eight, beginners six forty-five the day after. Write it."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He looks at the tailboard for a long moment, and then he does the thing that tells you the ruling was right: he goes and stands in the yard first, in the cold, and looks at the wagon, and puts his hand on the wheel, and comes back.

Then he writes. The letters are too big at the start and too small at the end and he has to squeeze **HARROW'S** into a corner, and he spells *beginners* with three n's and fixes it with his sleeve, and it takes him nine minutes.

**LOAD-OUT 8. WAGONS IN YARD — CHECKED.**
**VESSENDAL. BEGINNERS 6.45 THE DAY AFTER.**
**SOREL, FALK, VANE, KRUL, BOYLE, KRUG, WENZEL, GRELLE, PREWICK, LENZ.**
**— T. LENZ, 2ND ON BOOK, FOR B. HARROW, S.M.**

He steps back and looks at it and goes red again. "It's crooked, madam."

Behind you, in the doorway with the stove-light on him, Falk reads it over the boy's head and says, "It's legible, and it's got everybody's name on it, and it's signed." He puts the rug over his shoulder. "That's the trade, boy. She'll tell you the rest for the next twenty years."

The yard is quiet. The vermilion trunk sits under the new call with the thunder inside it. Your watch is in your pocket and the chalk is in the boy's hand, and there is nothing at all to keep you up — which, after this year, is the strangest sentence in the world.

There being nothing to keep me up, I stay up anyway — old habit, good stove. Falk is at it with the after-show brandy he finally drinks now, one thimble, slow. I sit on the other stool and hold my hands to the iron, and spend the quiet on the one thing I never bought all year. "Twenty years, you told the boy. He'll get the rest of the trade from me. So here's the one thing I never got from you, Emeran. Harbor. You've called me it since my second night in Grevenholt, and I never once asked."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Falk turns the thimble round on his knee and looks at the stove for a while.

"When I was young and stupid and *the* Falk, I played a season in a port," he says. "Not a good season. And there was a harbor there — a working one, ugly, coal and fish — and I used to walk out on the mole at four in the morning when I couldn't be in a room with myself, and watch the boats come in." He drinks about a third of the thimble, which for him is a great deal. "And they came in bad. Some of them shipping water, some of them with a man hurt, some with nothing in the hold and a crew that had been out too long and knew what they'd be told at the counting-house. Every one of them mattering to somebody. And the harbor took every single one exactly the same. It didn't ask what you'd caught. It didn't ask if you'd been brave. It didn't ask you to be interesting, harbor, that's the whole of it — it just held still and let you tie up."

He sets the thimble down.

"When Odalric hired you in ten minutes and you stepped over the third board without being told twice, I had been drinking at nine in the morning for eleven years so that a play wouldn't surface in me whole, and Anselm had gone in the night, and I had a coat full of pages. And you posted a notice about a bucket." He shrugs, an old man's shrug, enormous and dismissive. "So. Harbor."

The stove ticks. Out in the yard, the tailboard call sits crooked and legible in the dark, with everybody's name on it, and a signature.
messages.speaker: Emeran Falk

messages.body: I take it the way harbors take things: still, and without making it interesting. "Then I'll keep the name." The stove ticks between us once, twice. "And here's your side of the ledger, Emeran, since we're settling: a harbor's pay is getting to be one. Before this company I managed houses — good houses, clean books, and nobody ever once tied up." I stand and bank the stove, last job of the last hour. "Bed. Load-out's at eight, and for the first time in my working life the call has my name on it underneath somebody else's — which I find I like."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He doesn't say anything to that, and doesn't need to; he lifts the thimble an inch, the way he did in a dark theatre in Grevenholt the night you walked in out of the rain, and drinks it off, and gets up and goes to his wagon with the rug over his shoulder and his weight on both feet.

You bank the stove. The wing goes to red and then to nothing much.

Out in the yard the frost is starting on the cobbles and on the ropes and on the crooked call, and the vermilion trunk sits under it with the thunder inside doing absolutely nothing at all, which it will go on doing for years, in twenty-nine towns, wanting paint by every spring.

Eight o'clock will come. Boyle will swear at an arch, and Vane will sing something vulgar going out of it, and a boy of eighteen will stand in the yard with his hand on a wheel before he writes a number down.

For now: the stove ticking down, your watch in your pocket with its bright worn patch, and the last thing left to do tonight, which is to walk out past the tailboard and see whether the frost has taken the chalk — and to find that it hasn't, and that the bottom line is still perfectly legible.

**— T. LENZ, 2ND ON BOOK, FOR B. HARROW, S.M.**

Winter is Vessendal's fortnight, Merrow's fair, and a fit-up growing in Loewe's scene dock: our own flats, our own proscenium, and Boyle's door taken off its hinges and carried like a relic — with H.B. cut into the first plank by Vane's own hand, badly, exactly as promised, and varnished over so it stays badly forever. Hebel writes back that the capital is dull and the Baraque's new gasman is a vandal, and to send for him if we ever play a house worth a wheel. Lenz comes at midwinter, drinks three cups, and inspects the fit-up like a text. Skarke's quarterly audit of nothing arrives with one Katterau stub pinned to it. Drawings come with the post now — the newest is a theatre, and every door in it is drawn standing open. Toby learns plot tables until Krug dreams in them. And when the roads dry, the letters go and come: Katterau, two nights, the mayor's own favour. We roll in the first clean week of spring, the whole book of us, front doors first.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The spring road is dry and loud and full of blossom that gets in the horses' ears.

Katterau by daylight, second time: a town with washing out, a church, an inn with a scullery door, and Hessler's bills already up because Krug went ahead on Wednesday and pasted them himself. The mayor meets you in the square with her own favour, which turns out to be the loan of the town's carpenters and a barrel for the company. The fit-up goes up in five hours and looks — Vane says it aloud, twice — *like a theatre*, and H.B. sits in the first plank badly cut and varnished forever, at ankle height, where only this company knows to look.

Two nights. Six hundred seats each, and both nights out.

The first is yours: *Ilsabet*, called clean, Mirelle at the top of the list, Falk through Boyle's own carried door, the storm in low with a floor in it.

And the second night is Toby's, as ruled two seasons ago in a wing in Achterhalt. He is up at five. He has walked the plot four times, checked the wagon he doesn't need to check, and written the call so straight it looks printed. At the half he is grey.

"Madam," he says. "The storm's on page nine of my book and I've said it to myself all day and now I can't remember what warm means."

Your watch is in your palm and there is chalk on the ledge, and behind you, in the dark of a house that has been waiting twenty years for this company to be ordinary in it, six hundred people are coming in through open front doors.

"Nobody remembers what warm means at the half. I've gone grey at forty halves; the grey is the trade arriving." I turn him by the shoulder to face the stage, not the book. "Warm was never in your pages, Toby. It's out there. You don't call what's written — you call what's happening. Watch Falk's shoulders. Watch Sorel's hands. Watch the house breathe, and the storm will ask you for itself at the only moment it can, same as it's asked me forty times." Then I do the thing I've been saving two seasons: I put my watch — nail-worn, palm-bright, the only one it's ever been — into his hand and close his fingers on it. "Mine. For tonight. It knows the weight of a house; let it teach your hand. You give it back at the iron." And I step into the shadow behind the corner, where saying nothing is the whole of my job.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He looks at the watch in his fist as though you had handed him a live bird, and then he stops shaking. Not gradually. All at once, the way it happens the first time.

"Beginners, please," Toby Lenz says, and his voice goes exactly where he sends it.

He calls it. Not perfectly — he takes the act-two flat cue two seconds late and Krug covers it on the gas so smoothly that nobody in the world but you and Krug will ever know. But he watches Falk's shoulders and holds a pause he wasn't told to hold. He watches Mirelle's hands and brings the light after her, not with her, which is the sort of thing you cannot teach.

And in act four, six hundred people in Katterau lean forward at once, and it is the only moment it can be, and Toby Lenz doesn't look at page nine at all.

"Storm — go."

It comes in low out of the vermilion trunk with a floor in it, and Katterau takes it in the chest, and up in the gods somebody laughs from pure fright and is shushed by half the town.

Iron down. Three calls. Falk gets a fourth and gives it to Mirelle, who gives it to the house.

And in the prompt corner, with the gas going to its pilot and the good noise breaking out behind him, Toby turns round and holds out the watch on his flat palm — bright-worn, warm from an hour in a boy's fist — and cannot say a single word.
messages.speaker: Toby Lenz

messages.body: I take the watch off his palm and weigh it once — same weight, warmer — and put it back on its nail, where it lives. Then I say it at wing volume, because rulings are public or they're nothing: "Two seconds late on the act-two flat, and Herr Krug's wheel will be bought a drink about it. Otherwise: clean. Toby Lenz called Katterau — six hundred, both doors, a storm on its only moment — clean." And I look past his shoulder to the wardrobe doorway, where a woman with pins in her mouth has been watching the whole act, and I wait for the arithmetic to be conceded.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Dessa Krul takes the pins out of her mouth, one at a time, without hurry, and sticks them in her cuff.

"Well," she says. And then, to the whole wing, in the voice she uses for men who put wet chestnuts in slippers: "He's nineteen."

The wing goes up like a house — Boyle bellowing, Grelle's hand on the boy's shoulder, Prewick applauding at regulation volume with his hat off, Wenzel awake and confused and joining in anyway, Vane arriving from nowhere and weeping instantly and magnificently, Falk saying "*Weight on both feet, nineteen,*" and Krug, from the gas board, without turning round: "You owe me a drink and it's a Katterau drink, which is the expensive kind."

Toby Lenz stands in the middle of it and holds it, and does not milk it, which he learned from watching a man come through a door.

Later — much later, benches, soup, the barrel the mayor sent — the noise thins out into the yard, and the wing goes down to stove and lamp. Mirelle mends. Prewick writes to his mother about a boy who is nineteen. Falk sits with his thimble and doesn't drink it yet.

And your call-list for tomorrow is still blank on the tailboard, and the chalk is in the tin, and Toby is out there in the dark with a lantern, standing in the yard with his hand on a wheel, checking a wagon before he writes a number down.
messages.speaker: Dessa Krul

messages.body: The season runs the way solvent seasons run: towns, weather, the fit-up going up in five hours and coming down in four. Reap brings Loewe's fortnight, and the Athenaeum takes us back like a relative — counterweights sound, gas tap repaired, the brick in the passage scrubbed pale where a smear once was. And mid-fortnight, at the corner before the half, Mirelle comes to me with a letter in her hand and her gloves nowhere at all. The schoolmaster's hand. She holds it out and lets me read it whole: term's ended; the boy has asked — asked himself, in his own words, spelled his one word right in the middle of them — whether he might come as far as the door of the theatre where the wagon lives. I fold it back into her hand and give her the only ruling this company has ever really had. "Doors are what we're for. Name the day, and I'll have the front ones standing wide."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes it back and folds it into three, which is exactly how she folded a page in a wet field outside Halbern a year and a half ago, and puts it in her pocket rather than her glove, because she does not wear the gloves for that any more.

"The 20th," she says. "Loewe's last Thursday. He'll come on the coach with the schoolmaster's sister — she's a sensible woman, apparently, and has been briefed." A breath. "As far as the door, Harrow. That's what he asked for. Not a seat, not the house. He wants to see where the wagon lives, and then go away again, and I have decided that is the wisest thing anybody in this business has said in ten years."

The 20th comes grey and bright. Front doors standing wide from four o'clock, which puzzles Frau Loewe until you tell her nothing and she stops asking, because she is that sort of woman.

At five the coach sets down two people at the top of the street: a sensible woman in brown, and a boy of thirteen who is tall now and has a satchel and does not want his hand held.

Anton comes as far as the door. He stops in the doorway of the Athenaeum with the whole warm dark of the house behind you all, and he looks at it for a long time — the gaslight, the boxes, the empty stage — and he says, to nobody in particular, "It's smaller than it sounds."

And in the passage, out of sight of the doorway, Emeran Falk puts his hand flat over his mouth and turns away.
messages.speaker: Mirelle Sorel

messages.body: "It is," I agree, from my side of the threshold, because the truest notes get seconded in this house. "Smaller than it sounds, and bigger than it looks. Most good things run that way." And then I honor the terms of a wise contract to the letter: "The wagon lives through the yard door, off the passage — the red box rides its tailboard, and the horse that pulls it is exactly the wrong size, as somebody's drawing correctly reported. That far is still 'as far as the door,' if you want it. Your pace rules everything inside these walls; it's the law here, and I keep the book." And I step back, and leave the passage to Mirelle and the boy, and go stand where stage managers stand — near enough to be found, far enough to be no part of the scene.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
You stand at the pass door with your hands behind you and the whole business happens twenty feet off and none of it is yours.

He takes the wagon. He walks through the passage — past the pale scrubbed brick, past the ladder whose foot sits flat now — and out into the Athenaeum's yard, and he looks at the vermilion trunk on the tailboard and then at the horse, and he says, "The horse *is* too small," in the tone of a man whose professional judgement has been confirmed after long doubt.

Wenzel, sitting on a bale, says, "She's the right size and the wagon's too big," and the boy considers this with enormous seriousness and writes nothing down and clearly files it forever.

Twenty-five minutes. That's all it is. He does not come into the house. He asks Boyle what the ropes are for, and Boyle tells him properly, at length, with knots. He asks Dessa what's in the hamper and is shown the queen's slippers and does not touch them because he isn't asked to. He looks at Falk from about ten feet, and Falk — who has recovered himself and come out into the yard with the rug over his arm — says, "You're standing wrong. Weight on both feet," and the boy corrects it instantly and looks *pleased*.

And Mirelle stands where she can see him and does not perform for him once.

Then the sensible woman in brown looks at her watch and says the six-forty coach, and the boy says thank you very correctly to about four people in the wrong order, and stops in front of his mother and doesn't hug her, and holds out his hand instead, and she shakes it.

At the top of the street he turns round and shouts back, at full volume, in front of the whole street:

"Vermilion!"

And then he's gone, and the yard is very quiet, and Mirelle Sorel stands in it with her hands at her sides, and Frau Loewe, from the stage door, says gruffly to nobody, "Doors open at half six, and the gas tap's a *disgrace*," and goes inside so as to be no trouble.
messages.speaker: Anton

messages.body: Doors at half six, and the evening does what this company's evenings do now: it simply works. And after the iron, with the good noise gone off to its soup, I sit at the prompt corner and open the book to the end of the old pages, and make the season's last entries before I rule it off. The play: finished, retired, shelf row nine, no harm recorded. The company: solvent, twelve strong, carrying its own theatre and one badly cut set of initials. Sorel, M.: shaken hands with, at the top of a street. Lenz, T.: nineteen, clean, second on the book. Falk, E.: in things. Grelle, Prewick, Krug, Boyle, Krul, Wenzel, Hebel corresponded-with: worth keeping, every one. Harrow, B.: paid, unrounded — and home, which is a thing with wheels. Then I strike the season clean across, hang my watch on its nail, and put the chalk back in its tin — and I leave the last line of the page unwritten, for the house to fill, since it always does anyway.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The chalk goes in the tin. The watch hangs on its nail. The book lies open at a ruled-off season with one blank line at the foot of the page, and the Athenaeum's gas drops to its pilot, and the house does what it has always done and fills the line without asking you.

Out in the passage a bucket gets set down under a leak that doesn't exist yet, because Toby Lenz checks with his own feet now. Boyle's voice in the yard, arguing about a knot with nobody. Vane, further off, magnificent and solvent: "*Merrow*, and then a man in Grevenholt has written about the Corona — the roof, Harrow, the roof is *mended*—" Krul telling him there's a child asleep, and no child anywhere, and Vane lowering his voice anyway. Falk's thimble on wood, once, set down empty. Mirelle's needle. Prewick's pen. Grelle propping a door open because it's what he does now instead of standing outside one.

And on the tailboard in the dark, under the frost that isn't coming yet because it's spring, a crooked call in a boy's hand with everybody's name on it and two signatures at the bottom, and above it a red box with the thunder inside, doing nothing at all — a trunk, in a yard, wanting paint.

Load-out at eight. Beginners the day after. And your bucket, dry and where you left it, holding still and letting the whole thing tie up.

The season's last letters bring the loop round the way good ledgers do: the Corona at Grevenholt, roof mended, a manager's hopeful hand, and Vane's face over the breakfast table doing arithmetic and sentiment at once. I rule yes without being asked twice. So Frost finds the wagons rolling into the town where a wet woman once held up a coaching-inn notice — a year and a half ago, give or take a world — and I go to the stage door first, out of old habit. It's latched. Krebs's hinge has held all this time; the door bites its frame like it means it, exactly as invoiced. So I do the thing the house taught me and knock: three, soft, unhurried — the knock of a woman who has been practising it across two seasons.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Three knocks, soft, on a door that bites its frame.

Footsteps inside — slippers, and slow — and then bolts, two of them, and the door comes open a foot on an old man with a lamp held at the height regulations prefer.

"Aye?"

"Bell Harrow. Stage manager, the Vermilion Players."

He lifts the lamp. Then he lowers it, all the way, so the light lands on the boards and not in your face, which nobody in Grevenholt has ever done before.

"Then you'll be the one that posted the notices," he says. "I'm Krebs. My brother did your hinge." He steps back and pulls the door wide, its whole width, because that is how it opens now. "There's a bucket under your prompt corner, madam. It's been there since Katterau — the *other* Katterau, the one before yours. Nobody's dared move it."

Behind you the wagons are coming in under the arch: Boyle swearing at it, Vane singing something vulgar and being shushed by Krul, Toby standing in the yard with a lantern and his hand on a wheel before he writes a number down.

And inside, in the half-dark of a house with a mended roof, the third board from the pass door waits to sing at you for the second time in your life.
messages.speaker: Krebs the doorkeeper

messages.body: "Then let's hear it." I step in over the threshold and put my weight on the third board on purpose. It sings — same note, held all this time — and I write in my book that some repairs are not wanted and never will be. At the prompt corner I find the bucket exactly where my first notice put it, and I make the ruling Krebs has clearly been waiting a year and a half to witness: "The bucket stands. It's the oldest notice in this company's church, and it's on permanent duty now, dry or not." Then the yard pours in behind me — flats, hampers, the red trunk on Toby's count — and I give the Corona its news like a gift: "Load-in tonight, two nights billed. Ilsabet the first. And the second night, Herr Krebs, this house gets a debut: the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Krebs sets his lamp on the prompt shelf, next to the bucket, and stands looking at the pair of them for a moment with the satisfaction of a man whose long private opinion has been ratified by an authority.

"Permanent duty," he says. "I'll tell the gas boy. He's been trying to fill it with rags since June."

Then the Corona takes you all in, and it is exactly the same house — leaky-shaped even with a mended roof, thirty rows and a gallery, the smell of old gas and older luck — and it is not the same at all, because your own proscenium goes up inside it, and your own door, and H.B. at ankle height where only this company knows to look.

The load-in runs itself. Toby calls it; you stand in the shadow behind the corner and say nothing twice.

*Ilsabet* the first night, to a Grevenholt house that remembers the Vermilion Players as the lot who came through in the wet a year and a half back and had something wrong with their thunder. The storm comes in low with a floor in it and thirty rows of wet coats sit up.

And the second night: Prewick's *Wolf King*, compared line by line, certified, stamped straight, with his seal on the paper and his mother's cake in the wing. He stands at the back of the O.P. side for the whole of act one with his hat off.

Then the last curtain of the season falls in the house where you were hired in ten minutes, and Vane comes to your corner with his hat in his hands and asks you for a thing — and this time, for the first time in two years, you already know what he's going to ask, because Krug's datebook is open on the props table and there are eleven towns in it and none of them empty.

"Then ask it with the book open, Odalric." I turn it round on the props table so the eleven towns face him. "I like my questions documented, and you've never once asked me a small one in this building."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
He puts his hat down on the datebook — on the whole spring, hat over eleven towns — which is a thing he has never done.

"It's not a booking," he says. "Harrow, I am fifty-four, and I have a company that owes nothing and carries its own theatre, and a second on the book who is nineteen and getting better than either of us, and one day I am going to be a man in a chair in a wing." He looks at the eleven towns under the hat. "The name is mine. The wagons are mine. The trunk was mine and now it's just a box with the thunder in it. And when I go — and I *shall* go, I intend to go grandly and probably mid-speech — I want it minuted, in a book, with a signature, that the Vermilion Players go to whoever is keeping the book. Not to a creditor. Not to a nephew. To the stage manager." He gets it out without one tear, which costs him visibly. "So. That's my thing. Will you have them?"

Behind him the wing is doing what it does after a last curtain: Krul packing, Boyle striking your own proscenium down for the winter, Falk sitting with the thimble he'll drink at midnight, Mirelle mending, Grelle propping the doors, Prewick with cake, Toby out in the yard checking a wagon with his hand on the wheel.

Your book is open on the table under his hat, and there is a pencil in your pocket, and the ink is in the box where the ink always is.
messages.speaker: Odalric Vane

messages.body: "Yes." Plain and first, because he asked plainly and it cost him. Then I reach for the ink, because pencil is for opinions. "But I'll have it written better than you asked it, Odalric. Not to Bell Harrow — to the book. The Vermilion Players pass to whoever keeps the company's book: me this year, and in forty years somebody neither of us has ever met, who checks wagons with their own feet and signs what they post. That way you're not leaving them to a woman. You're leaving them to the trade — and the trade doesn't die mid-speech." I clear his hat off the datebook and set the page straight. "Herr Prewick writes it fair, the wing witnesses, you sign it unrounded. And I countersign underneath — where my name likes living these days."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
Vane's mouth opens, and nothing grand comes out of it. He sits down on the hamper instead and says, "*To the book*," and then, quietly, "That's better than mine. That's *much* better than mine," and puts his face in his hands for a moment, and then gets up and hollers for Prewick with his whole chest.

Prewick writes it fair on the props table of the Corona at eleven at night, in his ironed hand, and reads it aloud twice — *The name, the wagons, the properties, the fit-up, the debts if any, and the goodwill of the Vermilion Players pass upon the death or retirement of Odalric Vane to the keeper of the company's book, and thereafter to each keeper in turn* — and it takes two sheets, and he numbers them.

Vane signs it unrounded. You countersign underneath. Then the wing witnesses, because you said the wing would: Falk with a flourish, Mirelle in her clean businesslike hand, Krul with the pins out of her mouth, Boyle, Krug, Grelle, Wenzel's cross with his name written after by Dessa, Prewick as scrivener, and Toby Lenz last, coming in from the yard with cold hands, reading it twice, understanding it on the second read, and signing very carefully — *T. Lenz, 2nd on book* — because one day, and everybody in the room knows it, that will matter.

Then it's done, and it's a piece of paper, and it goes in the book.

The Corona goes down to its pilot light. The bucket stands on permanent duty under the oldest notice in the company's church. Your watch comes off its nail into your palm, worn bright, and the season is ruled off, and out in the yard the wagons are loaded for winter quarters and a boy is chalking a call with everybody's name on it.

And Odalric Vane, in the archway, in the plum coat gone shiny at the cuffs, turns round and says — because he cannot help himself, and because it is the last line of the year and somebody has to say it —

"*Ask me for a thing.*"
messages.speaker: Odalric Vane

messages.body: "Then here's my thing, and it winters well." I close the book over the new minute. "When the notices go up in spring, the first soul who comes in out of the weather answering one is mine to hire. My door, my lamp, my ten minutes. You stood a wet stranger in front of a company once and had her signed inside ten minutes — I want to learn what that costs to do. You may watch from the wings and weep." He accepts on the spot, magnificently. And winter takes us: quarters, stoves, plot tables, Krug's datebook fattening. And in the first wet week of spring, in a market town with a hall and no pit band, I write the notice myself and post it where coaching-inns post things: WANTED — A MUSICIAN, FOR A COMPANY THAT CARRIES ITS OWN THEATRE. APPLY AT THE STAGE DOOR. ASK FOR THE STAGE MANAGER.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The notice goes up on a Tuesday, in the wet, on a board that already carries a horse auction and two lost dogs.

It takes four days. Then, on the Saturday afternoon, with the fit-up half up and Boyle arguing with a beam, the stage door opens without a knock and a woman comes in out of the weather with a fiddle case under her coat, sopping to the shoulders, and stands on the third board and looks around at nine hundred years of other people's chalk marks.

She's about thirty. Her boots are done for. She has the notice in her fist, gone to pulp with rain.

"The door was open," she says. "It shouldn't have been."

Behind you, out of sight in the wing, someone stops breathing — Vane, in the shadows, with his hat off, exactly where you told him he could stand.

The lamp is at your elbow. Your book is under your arm. And ten minutes is precisely as long as it has ever been.
messages.speaker: Rosza Emmerich

messages.body: "It was open on purpose." I come out of the corner into the lamp's spill and turn the lamp down low as I come — light on the boards, not in her face. "We latch it when the house sleeps and we open it when weather's coming. It took this company two seasons to learn which is which. Bell Harrow, stage manager — you're inside my ten minutes, and they started when you stepped on the singing board." I set the book on the props table, open, pencil across it. "So: your name. What the fiddle can do when a house of six hundred leans in. And why a company that carries its own theatre should carry you. Any order you like — and drip all you want, the boards have heard weather before."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She thinks about the order. That's the first good sign; she doesn't just start talking.

"Rosza Emmerich." She sets the case down on the boards where she is standing — not on your table, which is the second good sign — and thumbs the catches without opening it. "What it can do when a house leans in: hold them there. I played four years for a dancing school, which is where you learn that nobody in the room is watching you and the tempo is your entire job. Then two years in a pit band in Kessarine, until the pit band stopped being paid, and then a winter of weddings and one funeral a week, which is where you learn to change a tune when a room changes." She wipes rain off her chin with the back of her wrist. "I can read. I can transpose while playing, which the last man in this trade could not, and I know it because I've asked. I don't drink at work. I can mend a bow and I can't mend anything else."

Then, the third question, and she looks straight at you for it.

"Why you should carry me." A pause; she is deciding whether to lie, and doesn't. "Because I walked eleven miles in this to a hall with no pit band, madam, and I read your notice four times standing in the wet before I came in, and it's the only bill I've ever seen posted by a company that said *ask for the stage manager* instead of *apply within*. Which told me somebody in here keeps a book." She nods at the one on your table. "I'd like to be in a book. I've been paid out of hats for two years."

Out in the wing, in the dark, Vane makes a small sound and gets himself under control.
messages.speaker: Rosza Emmerich

messages.body: I count it back to her on three fingers, the way I watched a man do it once, in this trade's other famous ten minutes. "You thought about the order before you spoke. You set the case on the boards and not on my table. And you told me the truth when a lie stood cheaper." Then the terms, which are short because they're real: "Wages plain, posted on the board, paid to the minute, unrounded — nobody in this company is paid out of a hat. A line in the book today; a bunk in the second wagon; and the church is four sentences long: check with your own feet, sign what you post, nothing sounds on our stage that isn't in a certified copy — your tunes will be, there's a clerk who'll love the work — and when the third board sings, let it." I turn the book to face her and hold out the pencil. "Rosza Emmerich, musician. Sign."
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes the pencil in a hand that is shaking with cold rather than nerves, and reads the line above hers — the whole call-list, every name, and *T. LENZ, 2ND ON BOOK, FOR B. HARROW, S.M.* at the foot of it — and she takes a moment over that. Then she signs, carefully, her whole name, and puts the pencil down across the page exactly where you had it.

"Beginners at what hour?" she says.

Which is when Vane comes out of the wing with his hat over his heart, weeping magnificently, both arms out, saying, "*Madam Emmerich* — eleven miles in the wet — you shall have a *stove*—" and Rosza Emmerich takes a step back onto the singing board and looks at you for a ruling about this large plum-coloured weather that has arrived in her afternoon.

Behind him: Boyle still arguing with the beam, Toby crossing the stage with a lantern and stopping dead at the sight of a new name in the book, Falk somewhere out front saying "*Who's that?*" in a voice designed to be heard, and Mirelle's needle stopping in the wardrobe cage.

The board sings under Rosza's boot. Your lamp is low. Your ten minutes are up with four to spare.
messages.speaker: Rosza Emmerich

messages.body: "Ruling: that's the management," I tell her. "It's harmless before supper, and the stove is real — accept both." Then I give the last order of the day, which has been waiting two seasons for someone to give it to: "But first. The house is empty, the gas is warm, and this company has carried its own theatre a year and a half without one note of music inside it. Play us something, Frau Emmerich. Whatever eleven miles sounds like when it comes out right." And I step back into my corner and hang the watch on its nail — beginners can stand four minutes; we're owed a tune — and I let the doorways fill.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
She takes the fiddle out with wet hands and tunes it against her ear, quickly, badly, then properly. Then she straightens, and puts her weight on both feet without being told, and plays.

It isn't grand. It's a dance tune out of somewhere flat and cold, in a minor she doesn't apologise for, and she plays it at walking speed, the tempo of eleven miles — and the Corona's borrowed cousin of a hall, with your own proscenium half up in it and H.B. at ankle height, does what a house does: it gives it back a little, and the sound gets bigger than the woman making it.

Doorways fill. Boyle stops arguing with the beam and stands in the O.P. entrance with the beam still in his hands. Krul in the wardrobe doorway with pins. Grelle propping the pass door with his shoulder because there is no one to keep out. Toby's lantern lowered to the boards. Prewick, hatless, at the top of the aisle with a cake tin. Krug with the datebook shut. Wenzel from the yard, smelling of horse. Mirelle in the wing, hands still. Vane weeping without a single quotation. And Falk, in the middle of the stalls in his black coat, standing with his weight on both feet and his head tipped back.

She finishes. Nobody claps; this company has learned better than that.

Falk says, into the whole warm empty house: "God almighty. We've had thunder for a year and no *music*."

And your watch is on its nail, and the fit-up is half up, and there is chalk in the tin, and a new name in the book, and the third board waiting to sing at the next soul who comes in out of the weather.
messages.speaker: Rosza Emmerich

messages.body: "Supper," I call into the warm, "and then beginners for the season." And late, when the hall is down to stove and lamp and somebody's fiddle case is drying in the wardrobe cage with the queen's slippers, I make the day's entry, which is the last of my part to tell: Emmerich, R., musician — hired inside ten minutes, four to spare. Eleven miles, walking tempo. Worth keeping. Then the watch on its nail, the chalk in its tin, the lamp down to its blue tooth — and the last line of the page left open for the house, since the house always fills it anyway.
messages.speaker: Bell Harrow

messages.body:
The lamp goes down to its blue tooth and the hall makes its night noises: the stove ticking, Boyle's beam finally beaten and lying where it belongs, Wenzel asleep somewhere he shouldn't be, Krul's pins going into the tin one at a time. In the wardrobe cage the fiddle case steams gently beside the queen's slippers, which Dessa has decided is acceptable and will not be discussing.

Out in the wing, Falk sets his thimble down empty; Prewick's pen scratches to his mother; Mirelle's needle goes on a while longer than anyone's. And on the tailboard in the yard, by lantern, a boy of nineteen who has stood with his hand on the wheel first writes the call for tomorrow with everybody's name on it and two signatures at the foot — and the newest name in the book, spelled right, because he asked her twice.

Your book lies open at a page with one line left blank on it. Somewhere along the passage, the third board sings under a boot nobody has accounted for — and then Rosza Emmerich's voice, low, from the dark, entirely practical: "Madam. Beginners at what hour?"
messages.speaker: Rosza Emmerich

scenes.title: The Vermilion Players Hire a Stage Manager
scenes.summary:
Bell Harrow arrives at the Corona through an open stage door, notice in hand, answering a call for a stage manager with the Vermilion Players. Emeran Falk, drinking brandy, agrees the door shouldn't be open and warns her about a loose board. Odalric Vane tests her with a question about calling a show off an unknown book; prompted by Mirelle Sorel from the fly floor, he hands her the prompt book — thick with others' writing, one page torn out near the back. Harrow accepts, conditionally, and demands plot tables, a daylight walk of the stage, and a bucket for the leaking prompt corner. Vane promises fair pay from Vessendal. Mirelle mentions a bucket under the star trap "since Katterau," and the word stops Falk mid-motion.

Casimir Prewick, a clerk of the Office of Public Morals, arrives, requiring her name spelled correctly. Vane steers her around a chalk-marked iron trunk; Prewick asks if it's hers — it isn't numbered. Falk notes the thunder trough needs repair since a ball struck a farmer at Merrow. Mirelle warns Harrow not to touch the trunk herself. Harrow obeys, then watches Vane move it — too light, then heavy. In the bucket she finds the missing page, prophetic and cryptic, marked "cut. cut. cut." She pockets it.

Prewick shows her an older notice signed by Hessel Vorn of Katterau, oddly stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED — not an Office form, though "everyone here has been there." Harrow copies the name and files it "under found level."

Alone with Falk, she asks about the handwriting. He names Anselm Krug, who vanished from Katterau, and explains the copied pages' history: don't burn, don't return, don't read one twice. She's already broken that rule. She gives him the page; he hides it in his coat lining.

The trunk is later found moved with no footprints but hers. Mirelle asks what the page said; Harrow recites it. Mirelle reveals the pages have predicted true events before, calls her own number ten, and asks that any such page come to her first. They set six o'clock at the ostler's yard and agree to silence.

Harrow writes her lists, knocks on the trunk — "Good night to the house" — no answer. At her lodging, a note addressed to her by a stranger who couldn't have known she existed awaits, unexplained.
scenes.history:
Bell Harrow arrives at the Corona through an open stage door, answering a call for a stage manager with the Vermilion Players. Emeran Falk warns her of a loose board. Odalric Vane tests her, then hands her the prompt book—thick with others' writing, one page torn out. She accepts conditionally, demanding plot tables, a daylight walk, and a bucket for the leaking prompt corner. Mirelle Sorel mentions a bucket "since Katterau," and the word stops Falk cold.

Casimir Prewick, a clerk of Public Morals, arrives; he asks about an unnumbered iron trunk. Mirelle warns Harrow not to touch it. Harrow watches Vane move it—too light, then heavy. In the bucket she finds the missing page, marked "cut. cut. cut," and pockets it. Prewick shows an old notice signed by Hessel Vorn of Katterau, stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED.

Alone with Falk, she learns of Anselm Krug, vanished from Katterau, and rules about the pages: don't burn, don't return, don't read twice. She's already broken that. She gives Falk the page; he hides it in his coat lining.

The trunk moves with no footprints but hers. Mirelle admits the pages predict true events, calls herself number ten, and asks to see any future page first. They set six o'clock and silence.

Harrow knocks on the trunk—no answer. At her lodging, an unexplained note awaits, from a stranger who couldn't have known she existed.

journals.entry: Came in out of the rain by the Corona's stage door — open, which it shouldn't have been — with the notice in my hand. Falk in the dark with a thimble of brandy told me about the third board; I stepped over it and got a tilt of his glass for it. Vane arrived in plum, asked whether I could call a show off a book I'd never seen for actors who lie about their entrances; the woman on the fly floor, Sorel, told me to say yes before he wept. I said yes, if the book is honest and the liars are consistent. Asked for plot tables, a daylight walk, a bucket. Got the prompt book — two hands in it, a page cut out near the back. Prewick, clerk from the Office of Public Morals, wanted my name spelled and noticed the iron trunk wasn't numbered. Vane steered me six wide paces around it. Learned the thunder: trough, iron balls, tin sheet, third joint wanting a nail since Merrow. Sorel warned me not to drag the trunk — ask him and leave. I did, and watched in the tin: he wiped the lid, pressed the chalk, lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox, then shoved it properly, scraping. In the bucket under the star trap, the missing page. Read it twice — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut in pencil. Pocketed it, not the book. Prewick brought an older notice: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED; he says the Office issues no such form, and Katterau is on no itinerary he was given, yet everyone here has been there. I copied the name into my own notebook. Nailed the trough and asked Falk about the upright hand: a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in Vane's trunk; Krug cut nine pages and burned them, the tenth came back, then he was gone without his boots. Don't burn, don't return, don't read twice — too late. I gave Falk the page for his lining. Found the trunk shoved back snug, chalk smeared four feet along the brick, no footprints but mine, Vane out of the house. Told Sorel the page word for word; her lamp dipped at nine years. Pages started at Vessendal two springs ago; they come slantwise and late. Her number is ten, and a ten goes to her first. Six o'clock, the ostler's yard. Set the bucket, trimmed the ghost light, wrote my three lists, knocked twice on the trunk and was annoyed to find I'd been waiting for an answer. At my lodging, a folded paper under the candle-end with my title on it, in a copperplate that isn't Prewick's.

Awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when a girl came in out of the rain with the notice and complained about our open door. Told her about the third board; she stepped over it without needing telling twice, which is more than Krug ever managed. Odalric did his interview, Mirelle told her to say yes, and the thing was done — Bell Harrow, stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had been under the star trap since Katterau and I found my glass difficult to lift for a moment. Offered the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, since Odalric was busy calling a concussion emotion. Later, from the passage, heard him move the trunk alone and remarked that two seasons ago it took four of us and a plank. When the house had emptied I sat on the star trap sill and told her she might ask me anything but one thing while she climbed. She nailed the third joint — two seasons it waited — and asked whose the small upright hand was. So I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, travelling in Odalric's iron trunk, never opened on this tour. Nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, and then no more Krug. Told her not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice, and saw by her colour that she already had. She handed the page over as if it were a badly behaved prop. I put it in my lining with the others and wished her good night. Then the trunk began to move in the passage, and Odalric was nowhere in the house.

A stage manager walked in out of the weather with the notice in her fist — read, came, noticed the open door: three references on three fingers. Bell Harrow. I engaged her on the spot, promised plot tables, a bucket, a fair figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and said of the book only that it is as honest as books are. Steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back; Prewick, curse his level lamp, held light over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. Showed her the thunder — the trough, the balls, the tin — while Falk told the story of the farmer at Merrow as he always does. Then the ladder's foot, and the trunk against it, and she asked me, without turning round, to shift it a hand's breadth left, and went off for her bucket like a good clock. Alone, I wiped the beading from the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say. Lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox — light, wrong, answering — and I set it down and took my hands off it. Then I shoved it properly, a hand's breadth and a little more, and called out that the ladder was served and to note the repair to the credit of the management. After that I did not stay in the house.

Mending a glove on the fly floor by no light when the new one came in out of the rain. Told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears. Mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, and enjoyed what the word did to Falk's glass. Came down the ladder past her ear and gave her the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, it can't have it because of the trunk, don't drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does. She did it exactly, which tells me something. Went out front, came back cloaked with my hatbox to find the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick — he'll say the porters did it; the Corona has no porters. Asked Harrow what the page said and she gave it to me flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut beneath in pencil. Nine years is not my number. I told her what I know and no more: the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first was a joke of Falk's, it described a horse going lame and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow. They come slantwise and late. I told her mine is ten, and that a page with ten in it comes to me first — not to Odalric, not to the boy with the notebook. Six o'clock at the ostler's yard: plot tables for Ilsabet, and no mention of this. Then out into the wet to find my bed.

Reported to Herr Vane that the fire notice by the scene dock had fallen again and found a stranger on the stage: the new stage manager. Gave my name and office and asked for hers, spelled — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring — for the certificate. Held my lamp over the iron trunk in the passage and asked whether it was hers; she said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. It is not numbered. Wrote in my book, under the thunder trough: unsecured iron, height. Re-hung the fire notice level, two taps, and found a second notice behind it — older, worse, concerning the storing of unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, and stamped twice, the first strike crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. I asked whether to bring it; she said bring it, notices are hers now, the reading and the taking-down both. She copied the officer's name into her own notebook and told me to file it under found level. I said what I should not have said aloud: the Office approves, proscribes, or refers. Not approved is what a man writes when he has been told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow. Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, and yet everyone in this company has been there. Then I took my lamp and went to get dry.

scenes.title: Four Acts and a Storm
scenes.summary:
Before the chain came off her door, Bell found a copperplate letter tucked under her candle-end: unsigned, addressed "for Herr M. Skarke, by his hand." It named the Vermilion Players' debt — vacant since the 14th of last month — securing the wagons, canvas, counterweights, horses, and every taking to Vessendal, interest running weekly. She was to present herself at the Corona box office on the third performance's morning for a counting before an agent; no need to tell Vane. One item stood apart: "1 trunk, iron, contents unspecified" — not to be opened, not sold. The landlady mentioned a civil gentleman asking after her room; Bell told her to say the stage manager keeps clean books, then filed the letter behind Vorn's name.

At six, in the ostler's yard, Mirelle gave Bell honest plot tables copied from Krug's, margined "tin only, NOT the trough, in houses under 40 ft" — the Corona's grid ran thirty-two. They fed the old horse an apple and rehearsed Ilsabet; the line "You were not sent for" stopped Prewick cold. His itinerary omitted Katterau and gave the capital date as the 3rd of Frost; Vane's said the 17th. Bell resolved to ask Vane herself before the half; neither she nor Prewick would say Katterau first.

Backstage, Vane granted all three of Bell's requests — Krebs the carpenter, tin only, ten minutes over the book — then bolted when Falk pressed him about the trunk. In the foyer he confessed the fourteen-day lie and Skarke's man in town, begging for books "so clean a man reading them learns nothing he is not owed." Bell took his cream card, noting the house numbers and the trunk, and set a reckoning for after the show.

Fourth row centre stayed empty; a stranger asked about a fifth act. The old tin split in the storm scene; Falk covered it wryly. Afterward, a pencilled note on a torn playbill read: "Nine years' interest, Herr Vane. Vessendal, at the counting." Prewick found two warm seats and no hat; Falk found the iron trunk dragged open — full of blank paper — Vane's hat and one glove beside it, his coat still on its peg. No Vane.
scenes.history: At the Corona, new stage manager Bell Harrow finds a torn, prophetic page marked "cut. cut. cut." hidden in a leaking bucket, tied to vanished Katterau writer Anselm Krug and copied pages with dangerous rules: don't burn, don't return, don't read twice. Emeran Falk, who knew Krug's hand, hides the page in his coat after Bell breaks the rule by rereading it. An old notice from Hessel Vorn of Katterau, stamped SEEN. NOT APPROVED, links Office clerk Casimir Prewick, Vane, and Katterau itself—none will name it first. A chalk-marked iron trunk moves mysteriously, its weight inconsistent, watched over by fly-floor worker Mirelle Sorel, who reveals the pages predict true events and claims "number ten" as her own. An unsigned letter reveals manager Odalric Vane's hidden debt to Vessendal/Skarke, with the trunk's contents "unspecified" and untouchable. Mirelle gives Bell true plot tables restricting thunder effects to tin, not the trough—unlike the Corona's official book. Vane confesses his fourteen-day lie about the debt before vanishing after the performance: a pencilled note demands payment, and his hat, glove, and the trunk—now full of blank paper—are found, but Vane is gone.

journals.entry: Read the folded paper on the step before the chain came off: clerk's copperplate, no name, no address, for Herr M. Skarke. The post empty since the 14th; wagons, canvas, counterweights, two horses, all properties pledged against a capital loan, and every taking between here and Vessendal; interest weekly, travelling ahead of us. Third performance, box office, morning, counted before an agent, and no need to tell Vane. One iron trunk, contents unspecified, valued separately — do not open, do not permit its sale. The candle guttered as I finished. Landlady: a civil gentleman asked which room, and wrote down her refusal. Told her to tell him the stage manager keeps clean books. Filed it after Vorn's name. Six in the ostler's yard: Mirelle gave me honest tables copied off Krug's storm plot — tin only under forty foot; the grid here is thirty-two — and I cued her Ilsabet flat. Prewick's Office itinerary: no Katterau, capital on the 3rd, a Palace date. Ours says the 17th. I'll do the asking; he watches hands; neither of us says Katterau first. Counted nine buckets and found five honest. Got three yeses from a frightened man: Krebs, tin only, ten minutes over the book. He ran. Cornered him at his own poster, wet-haired, no Blue Boar on him, holding Skarke's card. Fourteen days he'd been selling himself. Took the card — 340 seats, two wagons, two horses, and the trunk — and set him a pitiless map after the show. Called four clean scenes; the tin split; Falk covered me; told Prewick he'd held the sky up with his wrists. Then a fifth act in pencil on my own playbill: nine years' interest, Vessendal, at the counting. Sent Prewick front, Falk to the passage. Box office: float counted twice, plum coat on the peg, no Vane. Two warm seats and no hat. Trunk out, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry: Was in the ostler's yard before her, on the mounting block with my cloak under me, and did not say good morning. Gave Harrow my own copy of Krug's plot tables — honest, which the book is not — with the margin on it: tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot. The Corona is thirty-two. Fed the old horse, who is older than any number Odalric says aloud. Made her cue me Ilsabet, act two, from you were not sent for, and told her not to be kind about it; she wasn't, and the yard stopped being a yard. Prewick said "Oh" out loud and was appalled at himself, which I shall keep. Told him to unfold his itinerary and left them to their papers. Going front later I told Harrow that Odalric was awake with his notices and frightened, and that a frightened man says yes, so ask now. Told her: again tonight, before the half. Played the storm; the old tin barked and went to tea tray; Falk put in a line that is not in the book and the house forgave us, so I took the next off him and rode it home. Decent applause. Gloves mended and drying on the sill.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry: Up all night with arithmetic. Came out of the inn hatless with my bundle and found the stage manager and Sorel in the yard, and asked for the itinerary — the real one, if there are two. Then Sorel spoke Ilsabet at somebody who was not there and I said "Oh" aloud, which was not proper. Laid my Office paper on the mounting block against hers: mine has Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance 3rd of Frost. Hers has Katterau and the 17th. The 3rd is a Palace date, not ours. I offered to ask Herr Vane, or to stand where I could see his hands; the stage manager will ask, before the half, and neither of us says Katterau first. Wrote down TIN ONLY with pleasure. Counted the fire buckets with her: nine notionally, five with water, one a solid drum of whiting which I declared a monument, two hiding behind the star trap under bench legs. Discovered that tin shaken low is thunder and shaken high is merely tin, and was told it is in the plot now. Then the sheet split on my only cue and heaven went to a tea tray. She signed me softer and I kept going. I broke the sky. She said I held it up with my wrists while it broke and that the tin will be buried with honours at Vessendal, and I put it in felt. Afterwards, front of house on her order: no hat on the fourth row centre — only the pressed plush where a hat had been. Both seats warm. Nobody passed me at the doors, and I count house; it is the one thing I am for.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry: Sober by morning and carrying a brandy I did not drink. Came up the aisle in time to hear Odalric begin about the properties list being a document of aspiration, and told him plainly it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town — answer her, she nailed the trough. He laughed too big, clapped my arm, and went out the front doors to see about a carpenter, which was her errand. Gave Harrow the brandy for Krebs, who bargains better wet, and sat in the dark of the house to watch the empty stage, which is all I want at that hour. Wings for the show, saying nothing. The old sheet split mid-storm and went up into tin, so I stepped a half-pace into it and said that even the sky is out of coin tonight; the house barked once and forgave us, and Mirelle took the next line off me clean.
