After the curtain I looked out through the pass door at the empty fourth row and the hat set crown-down beside it, and heard myself saying it: a bell is rung, and nothing answers. Told Harrow that whoever wrote her paper has read the page — which means a page she has not shown him — and asked where Odalric was. She sent me to the passage and the scene dock. Found the iron trunk dragged two feet square into the middle of the passage, the scrape fresh, the lid up, and inside a neat stack of blank paper. His hat face down on the flags, and one glove, and no Odalric. Called her once.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry: Woke frightened and did what I do: coffee, the shutter up, and the Vessendal Advertiser on my Lear read aloud to nobody. Harrow came for three things while yes was cheap and had all three — Krebs for a shilling and let him feel he won, tin only because thirty-two feet is thirty-two feet, and ten minutes over the book, standing up. Then Emeran, sober and grey, told her it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town, and said she nailed the trough, so I laughed and went out the front doors for a carpenter I had no intention of finding. Found Skarke's man's card instead, or it found me: counted our seats from the street. Gave her her ten minutes at last, cornered by my own poster with my hat off. Told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd, I have been telling the company the 17th since Merrow, because there is not money for four towns but there is time for three and Katterau, six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. Fourteen days is what I have been selling myself, and I have run out of buyer. Asked her not for dishonesty but for books so clean a man learns nothing he is not owed. She wants the road laid against the 3rd tonight, and the company told if Katterau will not fit. Gave her the card; it went like handing over a bird. Called places in twenty and shut the pass door. After the curtain I counted the float twice, and the second count was smaller than the first, because the first was hopeful.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry: Came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. Showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon.
journals.state: Back over the smithy with a shilling and an empty glass, pleased with a hinge well shown and a bargain he thinks he won.

scenes.title: Ropes at First Light
scenes.summary:
In the wet passage, Harrow inventories by lamplight and states three facts: nobody passed Prewick's doors, the plum coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal. She orders load-out at first light, the trunk roped and in her sight, and demands Falk explain the fifth act. Falk says the pages come blank; the trunk has been clean paper for fourteen years, "and every so often it is not." There is no fifth act—only a thing after the fourth with no name in the folio—and at Katterau they never staged it and it happened anyway. The late man is a creditor from nine years past; the bell rings, nothing answers, then the play "simply arranges." He claims the trunk for his own wagon.

Vane arrives soaked, hatless, with chestnuts. Harrow makes him account: the Blue Boar untouched, a cart hired at eleven shillings, forty minutes not fifteen. Falk confirms nobody passed him. Vane reveals nine years ago he borrowed in Vessendal from a dying friend and repaid him, unsigned; Skarke bought the papers. What comes to the counting is "a signature nobody gave." A passing cart whistles four notes, stopping mid-fifth. Harrow pockets the playbill, promises Vessendal "clean books and a bad surprise," and demands names from that night; Vane promises ink and a notary. Falk reports Prewick still waiting.

Prewick asks what travels in the trunk, from her, not the Office. Harrow tells him everything: the nameless fair copy, pages that reach prompt books, Katterau, fourteen years of blank paper. They trade knowledge; he shows her the Proscribed section, thirty-one titles, two matching her play. His rule: Falk speaks no uncompared line—"He said it upstage tonight. Toward the trunk."

At dawn Harrow calls the roll; Boyle notes a missing name, Krug; Vane deflects. At noon Falk reveals a page with ten written on it. Sorel reads it aloud at a saint's marker—a prophecy of a child and a border crossing—and claims it as her own, refusing Falk's help, hiding it in her glove.

That night, camped at Halbern's crossroads, Skarke's agent appears, demanding inspection terms; Harrow counters with her own three conditions, all accepted. He refuses the fire, citing a page: "the agent comes early and is not admitted."

After soup, the company debates Katterau. Boyle refuses; Krul refuses; Falk reveals its cost—Anna Sorel, Grelle's voice, Vane's nerve. Vane says, "Rule Katterau, and I shall drive where you point." The ruling is left unmade.
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a worn prompt book with a torn-out page. She finds that missing page in a leaking bucket—a cryptic prophecy marked "cut. cut. cut."—and learns of Anselm Krug, a vanished writer from Katterau whose copied pages predict true events and must never be burned, returned, or read twice. Clerk Casimir Prewick investigates discrepancies in official notices and dates. An iron trunk, "contents unspecified," moves mysteriously and ties to a debt owed to Skarke via Vessendal; manager Odalric Vane confesses hidden fourteen-day-old debts. Mirelle Sorel, guardian of true plot tables, claims a personal stake in the prophetic pages. During a performance, Vane vanishes after a creditor's note appears; he returns soaked, with a shaky account, revealing an old unsigned debt now claimed by a mysterious "signature nobody gave." Emeran Falk explains the trunk holds blank paper except when it doesn't, and that a nameless "fifth act" once happened at Katterau, unstaged yet real. Harrow trades knowledge with Prewick, learning of banned plays. At dawn, Krug's name surfaces missing from the roll; Falk finds a page numbered ten, which Sorel claims as prophecy. Camped at a crossroads, Skarke's agent negotiates terms, refusing fire per foretold text. The company argues over "Katterau," revealing deep losses, leaving the decision unresolved.

journals.entry: I took inventory of the passage aloud — hat, glove, lid, blank ream — and gave Falk my three facts: nobody past Prewick's doors, the coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal, so we arrive. Ropes at first light. He told me there is no fifth act: four acts and a thing after them with no name, and the late man is the creditor, and after the bell the play stops telling and arranges. He took the trunk for his own wagon. Then Vane walked in by the mended door with chestnuts, and I made him stand and be looked at, handed him his hat and the pencilled playbill, and got chestnut-plain truth: the Blue Boar, a carter at eleven shillings, forty minutes. And the real number — nine years is a debt he paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. A signature nobody gave. I promised clean books and a bad surprise, and every name from that room. Prewick was still in the fourth row on cold plush, having chosen for the first time not to write. I gave him my whole ledger for his lesson: the Office reads text only, and there are two Proscribed entries — anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Falk is not to speak an uncompared line; he said his line upstage, at the trunk. Roll call at first light; a Krug missing from it. At noon a page with ten in it came onto the felt and I carried it face-down to Sorel and read it beside her: a child of ten, a border crossed twice, a kind invitation. She put it in her glove. At Halbern's I met Skarke's agent on a milestone — clean boots, no name — and traded initials, an instrument, and ten paces hands in pockets; he told me, to deny it later, that Skarke read aloud 'the agent comes early and is not admitted'. Then the hearing: dates unrounded, arithmetic laid bare, every voice heard. Falk said Katterau and what it took. Vane asked me to rule it. I have not ruled.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry: She crouched over the trunk and counted it like a scene, and asked me for the fifth act, so I told her: the pages come blank, that chest has been clean paper fourteen years and every so often it is not, and there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing following with no name in the folio, which at Katterau we did not stage and which happened anyway. The late man is the man who is owed. I shut the lid and gave her the hat rather than keep it, and said the trunk rides in my wagon where I can hear it, since I shall not be sleeping. Then Odalric came in by the wrong door with chestnuts, alive, absurd, and I told her nobody had passed the boy. He said nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I carried my split tin out in felt, told her she held the corner without shouting, and sent her down to Prewick. On the road at noon a page had come to sit on the tin, dry, in the copyist's hand, with a ten in it; she looked at the number and nothing else and would not let me ask. She was gone longer than the soup, so I sang. At the fire I said the name once, in my own voice: Katterau. Nine of us, a green room, a wager and a bottle, read aloud sitting down — three and a half acts. It took four years to arrange, and it took Anna Sorel and the boy Grelle and my voice for a season and Odalric's nerve for good. It has never been finished. Let her rule.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry: Came in wet and pleased with myself — a carpenter found, Krebs's brother-in-law and his cart bought at eleven shillings when I had offered twelve so the man might feel he lost — and there was my trunk dragged into the middle of the passage with the lid shut and Harrow's lamp on it, and Falk against the wall, and I put the chestnuts down on the flags like a fool. She made me stand and be looked at and put my hat in my hands with a torn playbill on top, pencil side up. Nine years. I read it twice. So I told her the thing I have not said aloud: the loan is two seasons old; nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from a man who was dying and my friend, and I paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke has bought his papers. What comes to the counting is a signature nobody gave. She did not weep at me or dismiss me — she gave me a task: every name that was in that room, in ink, in the wagon. There was a notary. There is always a notary. I gave the boy the chestnuts and a story. I slept four hours and called it seven, and answered present at her roll, and did not want to hear Boyle say there used to be a Krug on this list. Mirelle told me the company would hear the road tonight and I said yes. Harrow read the dates out unrounded, all of them, and everyone spoke, and Falk said Katterau and what it cost me. I stood up with my hat in my hands and asked her to rule it. I shall drive where she points.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry: I sat in the fourth row, dead centre, on plush that had gone cold, and waited for the stage manager because I had decided not to write anything down — the first time in my service that I have chosen that. I told her so, and told her what I had: two warm seats and nobody past my doors, the sound going up half an octave when the sky broke, and Herr Falk speaking a line that is in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom. I asked to be told what travels in that trunk, by her, and not too late. She told me everything, entered as heard: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages that arrive in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau, unstaged and happening anyway; fourteen years of clean paper. So I opened the back of my Index, where three pages are sewn in with black thread, and showed her the Proscribed section — thirty-one titles, twenty-nine with authors, and two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following, stamped not to be described aloud in any report. And then I understood the useful, horrible thing: the Office reads only text, so I could certify Vessendal honestly with that trunk twenty feet from the stage door. I do not like being useful in that way. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; she is not to let Falk speak an uncompared line. He said it upstage, toward the trunk. I answered present at the roll with my luggage numbered one to four, item four the Index, riding with me. At the fire I said aloud that if we play Katterau I must lie either way, that I find I am able to, and that I wish to be asked and not simply arrived with.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry: Answered present with my hatbox on my knees and heard Boyle say there used to be a Krug on the list. At noon Harrow came alongside the first wagon holding a page and said there was a ten in it and that she had read the number and nothing else. I told Odalric to stop the wagon and he did it without one question and went to be busy with a strap, which is the best of him. I walked twenty yards to a marker with the saint's face worn off and unfolded it, and then I called her over, because I would rather two of us knew than one: the child is ten this winter and does not know the word mother, having been taught another; a woman crosses a border twice, once running, once summoned, and the second invitation is kind. I let her read it, so it is hers now; I was too tired to be careful. She told me, unasked and without being sworn to silence, that the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. Not Falk's lining — he has enough of other people's endings sewn into him. I put the page inside my mended glove, palm flat against my wrist, and pulled the glove on over it, so it rides where I can feel it. Then I told Odalric the company would sit down and hear the road tonight, unrounded, and he said yes in a small voice. At the fire I gave my one voice: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour and I will go to it; Katterau, no — not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry: Answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers have two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box.

Answered present at the roll — front of house, props, and pit band if there's a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal that will have me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads and came back running without the bucket, because there was a gentleman sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd go to Katterau — six hundred seats, I've never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces and said only if it were ruled.

Answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that there used to be a Krug on this list and he's not here. Fixed a shed wheel-rim in the afternoon with wire and language. At the fire the stage manager asked me first, being soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle holds, three if it don't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us. And the sum nobody had said: Katterau is back. Twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I'll walk it if it's ruled. I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

Came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and waited on the milestone with the case on my knees; the boy for water told me yes, these were the Vermilion Players, and I told him I was early. The stage manager came alone with a lamp and a book and wrote me down as agent, no name given, boots clean, and I let her. Better to deal with one who owns nothing; Herr Vane weeps. I read the three matters in the order of the letter — takings counted before spent, schedule properties not sold or pledged or repaired at expense, and the trunk valued separately and to be inspected, not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never before been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her whether she knew why. She said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't. Her three: daily counting initialled by me — better practice than I am used to and I shall report it so; the nine-year instrument produced — a certified copy only, the strongbox in the room, and she must say the words about a magistrate on Friday; the inspection at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets — agreed, gladly. Then I told her the fourth matter, which I will deny: when Herr Skarke gave me the trunk instruction he had a page before him and read from it aloud without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I did not go to their fire. The road back was quite dry.

Came at first light for the eleven shillings and took the second wagon on with my cart, the axle honest as promised. Six days of road ahead; by mid-morning I was whistling, four notes and stopping in the middle of the fifth, over and over, without noticing.

scenes.title: Behind the Lion
scenes.summary:
At the fire, Bell Harrow rules with the book shut. Katterau will not be settled "this tour, and not for money" — but "not never." Vessendal must give a matinee across three nights; the 3rd stands; Boyle takes the toll road. From tonight, nothing may be spoken on or off stage unless it's in a certified copy — no wagers, no bottles, no lines invented to cover a broken scene. She tells Prewick he has "also arrived with" and orders Vane to drive for Vessendal. Prewick, having only Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll, and Vane's cut of the Wolf King, demands certified copies of everything and vows to sit up comparing. Falk repeats "Not never," touches Bell's head, and leaves muttering toll distances. Vane weeps himself to sleep in his coat. Mirelle reveals that Anna Sorel was her sister, that she kept Vane's accounts that year, and that any signed receipt went into her box.

Bell joins Falk at the roped trunk, where paper turns inside though "it says nothing — it reads." Falk has heard it twice before, near Katterau and Merrow; there are no mice. It stops mid-page; he keeps watch all night. Bell finds a blank sheet outside the ropes and hides it with the tin.

Two days later, Vane pays the toll exactly. At the Athenaeum, Bell pays Frau Loewe's debts, forbidding inspection before Friday. An agent mentions a gentleman from the capital, lodging at the Swan, who doesn't drink. Loewe recalls Falk once hiring the dark house alone, chalking a great plot, and a woman from Katterau later seeking him — Loewe lied that he'd gone south. Falk admits he drew all four acts from memory to bind it to one man: "It wants an audience... it is a play."

Toby delivers a paid, anonymous card for three nights, fourth row centre. At the river they bury the split tin. Mirelle sends Bell to the registry, unable to go herself. There, Vane's names appear in the ledger; Anna Sorel's sealed box remains unreleased, eighteen shillings owed. Bell pays; Prewick certifies the register. The executor, Josias Perlmann, reveals Brandt never signed the receipt — "between friends" — and died before he could. "Say what you want and be quick."
scenes.history: At the Corona, Bell Harrow becomes stage manager for the Vermilion Players under Odalric Vane, inheriting a prompt book with a torn page and a rumor of a bucket "since Katterau." Emeran Falk warns of hazards; Casimir Prewick, a Public Morals clerk, scrutinizes paperwork and an unnumbered iron trunk. Harrow finds the missing page—cryptic, marked "cut"—linked to vanished writer Anselm Krug and forbidden copying rules. Mirelle Sorel reveals the pages predict real events; her sister Anna died connected to Katterau. A copperplate letter exposes Vane's hidden debt to Skarke of Vessendal, secured against the company's goods, including the untouchable trunk. Plot tables show the Corona's grid unsafe for the "trough." Vane confesses his lie; after a performance, he vanishes, later returning soaked, claiming an old unsigned debt now haunts him as "a signature nobody gave." Prewick and Harrow trade secrets; Falk reveals the trunk cycles blank paper except when it doesn't, and hints at a nameless "fifth act." Skarke's agent appears at camp with eerie foreknowledge. The company argues over Katterau's cost; Harrow rules disputes unsettled but enforces strict script discipline. The trunk's paper turns and "reads" itself. In town, Bell pays debts, uncovers Falk's solitary staging of the full play, and learns from executor Perlmann that Brandt's debt to Vane was never signed before his death.

journals.entry:
I ruled it standing with the book shut: Katterau no, not this tour and not for money — but not never. The 3rd stands, a matinee out of Vessendal or a reason, the toll road for Boyle, and company law: nothing spoken on a stage or off it that isn't in a certified copy. Prewick asked to be arrived with; I arrived with him. Vane I pointed at Vessendal. Then Mirelle, glove in her lap: Anna Sorel was her sister, kept Odalric's books that year, and every receipt in the world went into her box.

Falk's lamp was moving under the barn. I gave the night thirty seconds of my own ear and heard paper — page by page, unhurried. "It says nothing. It reads." He's heard it at Katterau after the wager and at Merrow the week Krug cut the ninth. It stopped mid-page, like a man interrupted. Outside the ropes I found one blank sheet; into the felt with the tin, not into my book.

Two days' road, eight shillings unrounded. At the Athenaeum: the agent punctual to the town, Frau Loewe with a letting book and nine shillings owed — paid from my hand, trunk roped in her yard, nothing near her under-stage. Her dates cost me nothing: Falk hired her dark house four years ago for two shillings, chalked a full plot in it, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. The agent gave me a courtesy I did not ask for: the strongbox's gentleman rode ahead and is in this town.

Card at half six — fourth row centre, three nights, paid, no hat wanted, and he did not use the doors. Sold things get service: a programme on the seat, counts only, no staring. We buried the tin in the river and Prewick waded in.

Morning: Vane's names in ink; the registry behind the lion with Prewick's seal for a lamp. Anna's box is there, sealed, nine years unpaid — eighteen shillings paid, clock stopped, register lines certified twice. Kin's proof or a magistrate. The executor is Perlmann, blind, above the saddler's — and someone else has asked after that box twice: "paper, I expect. It usually is." I put Odalric at the door and told him no performance. Perlmann knew his cuff, and told us the receipt was never finished.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry:
She ruled it: Katterau no — and then not never, which is a different sentence entirely, and I found I had a use for the rest of my life after all. I blessed her head like a gatepost and went off counting toll miles in verse.

Then I had the tarpaulin off and stood listening, and she came across the camp on the sides of her feet and asked. I told her the truth: it does not speak, it reads. Twice before — Katterau, the night after the wager; Merrow, the week Krug cut the ninth page. Not mice. It stopped mid-page, the way a man stops when someone comes in, and I put the felt down against it like bedding and sat the night on the box, and once I said a line into the dark and stopped myself. She found a sheet lying outside the ropes; she says it was outside, and I believe her, which is the worst of it.

Two days' road and then the stone front with my name spelled right on the bills. Loewe still holds the house. I could not get down. Harrow came to my wheel and gave me a job instead of sympathy, which is why she is the harbor. So I told her what I chalked on that stage four years ago: the whole thing from memory, four acts and the matter following, alone, to see whether the arranging would come to one man and be done. It would not come. It wants a house. It is a play.

Load-in, and a proper grid, and a thunder run nailed by somebody who cared. At the river I said the sailors' words over the tin and made the clerk put it in, and he did, boots and all, and the wool warehouses gave the words back. Eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly in service.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry:
She ruled, standing, and did not spare me: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, and drive for Vessendal. I wept — I am not ashamed of it — quoted my Lear notice at nobody, and slept in my coat. At the toll gate I paid eight shillings to the penny because she was standing there. Vessendal came up out of the flat and the Athenaeum knows what it has; I went straight to the box office to learn the number of seats sold, which is the only prayer I have.

At breakfast I gave her the names in ink as promised: Hessel Brandt on the Kohlgasse; the notary, Perl or Perlmann, inky fingers and a cold; Anna Sorel; a doctor whose name I never had; a nun; myself; and the one in the passage I never saw and have thought of for nine years. Writing it down was worse than saying it.

Then she took me up a stair that smelled of leather with her clerk behind, set me at the door and said: no performance. Three knocks — the smallest sound I have made in my life. Bettina opened it, and then Josias in the doorway with his white eyes past me, finding my sleeve and rubbing the worn place on my cuff: nine years, and I have not changed my coat. He told them what I have never been able to prove: I came at eleven at night with the whole of it and said God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and he would not sign, between friends, and died on the Tuesday. The receipt was never finished. It is the only unfinished instrument of the old man's life. I stood in the doorway and could not speak.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry:
The ruling came and I was asked and told I had also been arrived with, which I shall remember. I stood up trembling and said what I needed: certified copies of everything. I have Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll and Herr Vane's cut of the Wolf King and nothing else, and the company plays four, and there are no farces. I sat up with a candle and compared to line four hundred and twelve and fell asleep upright with four scripts on my knees, and it is the most work I have ever set myself and I am extremely pleased.

At the river I was fetched from my comparing without knowing why, and Herr Falk said the sailors' words and then handed me the tin and said it was mine. I waded in to the ankle and ruined my boots and pushed it under and it made one last small thunder. I have attended a funeral for an object and it was not ridiculous. I noted it.

This morning, collar and seal and my regulation walk, behind the lion with the stage manager. The counter clerk went from we open at half past to this way, Herr Clerk on the words Office of Public Morals, and I asked for the register itself and not a copy. The lease is there; Brandt's deposits released to an executor with an unreadable scrawl; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. The clerk told me, correctly, that my seal certifies plays and not boxes, and Harrow turned that into work: I copied the three lines word for word and stamped them, crooked, then again clean, and gave her both. The probate roll gave us Perlmann, Josias, notary. Then up a saddler's stair, and an old blind man who could hear my starch.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry:
She gave the ruling standing and shut, and Katterau went into the ground for this tour, and I let out the breath I have been holding since Halbern. Nobody said aye; we don't.

I stayed while she banked the fire, my glove off with the page still in it, and gave her the thing she'll need before Friday: the notary at that deathbed. Odalric will not have the name — he remembers notices, not names. So I said it out loud for the first time in years. Anna Sorel was my sister. She kept his accounts that year, and if there is a receipt anywhere in the world with a signature on it, it went into Anna's box, and her box went where the others go.

Two days of road. I did not look at Vessendal once; I watched the river instead, which is a thing you can do with a town.

Coming up the mud from the tin's burial — nine of us, lanterns, and Falk's sailors' words, which were better than the tin deserved and exactly what it deserved — I told Harrow where to go: the registry behind the lion, eight to noon, and the lease in the fifth year was Vessendal's, so Anna's box came here. I cannot go in. My name is in that building on paper I would rather not stand next to. She can.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry:
Ruling came down and I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling means to me. Toll road, then — eight shilling, and cheaper than a horse, and I said so first. Wired the axle in the morning and it held two days.

Backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard, took first watch on the trunk with a lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. Got relieved twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river and grumbled about it and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said what wanted saying: kettle's no good, kettle's a bell. And then nobody said anything for half a second, which is how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.

She ruled and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. No Katterau. Good.

Swore at a wet stocking in the frost, carried the queen's slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics because that brick is filthy. Went down to the river for the tin and said there'd be new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word. I keep my needle going. I still don't want another warm box.

She ruled no Katterau and I sat down hard, and I don't know if I was sorry or glad, and I'll be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. Boiled the water in the morning without being asked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

Dropped the tailboard first thing in the Athenaeum yard, took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes and ran to catch up for the tin going into the river, and it made one last thunder going under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house and didn't wait and didn't come in by my doors — I was on the doors, I've learned that. She gave me standing orders: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, and count row four in and count it out. Counts only, no staring.

Waited in the Athenaeum doorway from noon with the case on my knees, next to the woman who holds the lease and does not like me. When the wagons came I was looking at the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon, and the stage manager put herself between it and me before the horses had stopped and said today nobody looks at anything of theirs but the stage and the billing. Friday, ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets: I have it written in my instruction book in her words, Herr Skarke will be displeased with me, and it stands. I stepped back from the wagon and said I have eyes and the road is where it is.

Then I gave her a courtesy she had not bought: the strongbox came up from the capital this morning by coach, and the gentleman who should have come up with it rode ahead. He is in the town. I said good afternoon, that I am at the Swan, and that I do not drink. The doorway woman watched me the whole way out.

The agent had been in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I told the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, my ledger is the letting book, and I am the one who gets paid first. Nine shillings from the spring and a repaired gas tap, and Vane might open on that debt but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm on the spot, unrounded, and took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself and swore nothing of theirs would go near my under-stage, and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard and never cross my threshold — it marked my brick once already. I warmed to her by a degree.

Then she asked me to finish a sentence, and wanted it in dates, so she got it. Winter of the fifth year: Emeran Falk came alone, no company, and hired my house for one night at his own cost, two shillings, because he was Falk and I was young enough to be impressed. He never opened it. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; on the second evening he gave back my key and thanked me very kindly. The stage was covered in chalk — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. And a week later a woman came from Katterau asking for him, with a child, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell the same lie again.

Load-in until six. He did not get down off his box for a long while.

Two of them at the door before we opened, and the one in the collar had the Office of Public Morals on his seal, so I took them through — a search only, he said, and the register itself, not a copy, which is how you know a man who has read a register before. The Athenaeum lease, fifth year: there. Brandt, Hessel, wool factor: three items, released to the executor in the sixth year, and the signature a scrawl. Sorel, Anna: one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, nine years' storage unpaid. I told them what I always tell them — depositor, kin with proof, or an officer with a warrant — and that a seal that certifies plays does not certify boxes.

Then the lady put eighteen shillings on my counter and counted it twice, and asked for lawful things in reverse order, so I did lawful work: stopped the clock, wrote out kin's proof in full, fetched the probate roll. Brandt's executor is Perlmann, Josias, notary, above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse — eighty, blind, doesn't practise, daughter takes in sewing. I decided I liked her, so I gave her the other thing: that box has been asked after twice by the same gentleman, not kin, once with money and once with a lawyer's letter, and got nowhere, and the second time he asked me what was in it and I said I don't know, and he said, paper, I expect. It usually is.

Bettina told me there was somebody on my stair. Three soft knocks — not a creditor's knock. Then a voice I have not heard in nine years saying only, It's Vane.

I found his sleeve, and then his cuff, and the worn shiny place on it, and knew it: nine years and he has not changed his coat. I told him what he came for, since he never could say it himself. He came at eleven at night on Hessel Brandt's last evening with a bag of money and counted it onto the counterpane and said this is the whole of it and God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and made me stop writing. I did not finish the receipt. I said sign, Hessel, and he said no, between friends, and on the Tuesday he died. It is the only unfinished instrument of my life and I have thought of it every week since.

There were others on the stair — a woman breathing steadily, and starch, an officer of some kind. I told them to say what they want and be quick. I am old, and I am not deaf, which is worse.

Three strangers on our stair before ten, and I stood in the door with the sewing over my arm and weighed them, as I do. Then my father called out from inside and the one with the hat off said a name, and whatever was coming was not mine to stop, so I stepped back and let him have it. He held my father's hand on his own cuff for a long time.
Not present.
journals.state: Not present.

scenes.title: Unpaid
scenes.summary:
Harrow lays out three asks; Perlmann agrees in order: he will swear his account Thursday at nine before Registrar Braun, with his own clerk and Bettina writing while he marks. Skarke's assignment is good but the debt is dead — a paid debt is paid — though a magistrate wants corroboration, and since the money came in a bank's bag, banks keep counterfoils. Vane names the bank, then corrects himself: no branch here; he drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on his knees. The three executor items were Brandt's wool-loft lease (sold), his marriage certificate, and a sealed packet marked TO THE VERMILION PLAYERS WHEN THEY NEXT COME, AND NOT BEFORE, unopened nine years. Anna Sorel had asked whether a sealed deposit could ever be read by anyone, even the registrar; told no, she wept with relief. Perlmann asks which of them is Sorel — it's only Prewick, who names himself and produces his certified register copy: "It is a record, boy." Bettina brings the tin box; Harrow writes and Perlmann marks a receipt. Perlmann tells Vane to change his coat.

Prewick telegraphs Achterhalt for the counterfoil, paying four shillings himself. At half eleven, nine of the company gather round the tailboard as Harrow opens the packet: a letter, the counterfoil, a copyist's page (unread, given to Falk's lining), and an iron key tagged UNPAID — the Athenaeum green-room cupboard key, Falk says. Vane reads, ashamed: he'd paid the whole loan, but Brandt refused a receipt because the money wasn't his — lent from a fund held for an unnamed party, whose marker was left as security. "He held a play."

In the green room, the cupboard yields an oilcloth parcel: thirty pages, SECURITY LODGED — ONE FOLIO, FOUR ACTS AND A MATTER FOLLOWING. Prewick guesses the Index's two anonymous folios may be halves; Harrow forbids reporting it and hides the parcel.

Boyle announces the agent's visit moved up; counting is now tonight after the show. Skarke, now senior at the Swan, cancels the trunk inspection, demanding delivery against valuation, and sends a letter: he holds thirty pages lodged by his own father; deliver the trunk and all debts are discharged. He reveals he was the child at Katterau whom Falk fed and sent back. Harrow insists the counting proceeds as scheduled.

Between shows, Falk tells Harrow the play only rhymes, not copies, and unfinished in two hundred years is "not a curse... an appetite." Vane bursts in celebrating the take and stops short at their faces.
scenes.history: At the counting, Skarke's terms are set for tonight regardless of celebration. Harrow, holding both her half and the parcel's half of the same folio, weighs whether completing the play could end the debt for good—or feed the "appetite" Falk fears. Vane, still shaken by Brandt's history and his own near-ruin, defers to her judgment. Falk warns that assembling the whole text might not close the account but open it wider, since the thing "reads" rather than merely sits written. Mirelle's claim on any tenth page, Prewick's insistence on certified copies, and Vane's promise to drive wherever Bell points all converge on the same choice: whether to bring the two halves together before Skarke's counting, risking whatever "matter following" means, or keep them apart and let Katterau remain unsettled "not never." The company, worn from Halbern's crossroads through Vessendal and the Athenaeum's revelations, awaits her ruling as the hour approaches, the trunk roped, the tin buried, the key still marked UNPAID, and Skarke — once the child at Katterau — waiting at the Swan for either delivery or refusal.

journals.entry:
I put three asks to Perlmann and got all three. He will swear it Thursday at nine before Braun, who was his clerk; Bettina writes, he makes his mark. The assignment will be good and the debt is dead, but a magistrate wants corroboration, and the corroboration is a bank bag with a counterfoil behind it — Achterhalt branch, Farriers' and Merchants', Vane's own memory of the coach seat. The third executor item was a sealed packet for us, unopened nine years; I wrote the receipt in my own hand and he marked it. He told Vane to change his coat. Prewick's certified register lines went on the table beside my receipt, and the old man felt the stamp and softened. Prewick drafted the telegraph and paid the four shillings out of his own purse.

In the yard I opened the packet on the tailboard with nine of them round it: look first, nobody reads aloud, nobody touches. Letter, counterfoil, a copyist's page I turned face-down with the back of my finger and passed unread into Falk's lining, and a key tagged UNPAID that Falk named as the green-room cupboard. Brandt never held papers; he held thirty pages of a play, lodged as security by a party whose name he never gave. I opened the cupboard with three inside and Prewick at the threshold, and the parcel is thirty pages, not two hundred. It is under my coat and it does not cross the yard.

Then the agent, out of turn and honest about it: counting brought forward to tonight, Skarke in the town, inspection cancelled, the trunk to be delivered to the Swan against valuation and every instrument discharged. He signed himself the child in the passage at Katterau. I told Falk flat because he asked flat. I told the agent the counting stands against my book and the trunk's answer will be spoken at the counting, in front of everyone.

Matinee: half a house, honest laughter, a sky better nailed than most. Mirelle gave me the numbers — nine Odalric's, twenty Falk's, ten hers, ring the bell and she'll come. And Falk gave me the arithmetic I asked for: it rhymes, it has never been finished, it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take, and the gentleman is in the fourth row early, reading his programme.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry:
I let go of his cuff and found my chair, and Bettina put the shawl over me and stayed, which is her right. I took them in order, as one should. My account they may have sworn: Braun sits Thursdays and was my clerk, and I will go on my daughter's arm and make my mark. I told the woman with the book what a magistrate wants — the assignment will be good and the debt will not, and corroboration is the bank's counterfoil, because the money came in a bag with a bank's mark. Vane named the bank before I had finished the sentence, and sounded surprised at himself.

The three items I released as executor: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed in his own hand, to the Players when they next came. They did not next come. Nine years it has sat in the tin box with my mother's rings, unopened, and I gave it to them and required a receipt, being a notary and not dead.

Then Anna Sorel. She asked me whether a thing deposited sealed could ever be read — not by anyone at all, not even by the registrar, after years — and I said no, madam, it is a box, it will sit there, and she wept with relief, and I did not ask what for. I asked which of them was Sorel, because the breathing at the back had stopped moving at her name, and it turned out to be only a clerk with a stamp, who put a certified record on my table. Records are the whole of the defence.

I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed me. I sent them away, and told Vane to change his coat.

I let them in and I stayed. Father found his chair without help; I put the shawl over him and folded my arms and listened to all of it — the swearing on Thursday, which means my arm to lean on and my hand to write it out, and the bank bag, and the three items. When he said the tin box I went up and fetched it and put the packet into the woman's hands, brown paper gone soft as cloth. I set his finger on the receipt where his mark should go. Then he told them to go away, and told Vane to change his coat, which was fair.

I stood very still at the back holding my stamp, and the old man took my breathing for Sorel's. I said my name and rank and put my certified copy of the register lines on his table beside the stage manager's receipt — Sorel, Anna, one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, dated and mine. He felt the stamp with a fingertip and said records are the whole of the defence, and I have written nothing better in my life than that entry.

At the post house I drafted the request for the counterfoil standing up, Achterhalt branch, fifth year, month of Frost, purpose evidence, magistrate's hearing Thursday nine — and added REPLY PAID and paid the four shillings myself, and would not be argued with. Banks love being asked for their own records.

In the yard I saw the packet opened and did not touch anything. At the green room I was put on the threshold with my notebook and told to keep my silence, and I did. Then the arithmetic arrived and went through me: the Index lists two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following, and I have been counting them for years as one entry duplicated in error. Thirty pages in that cupboard and two hundred in the trunk. Two halves. She has forbidden me to put it in any report until she understands what it adds to, and I obeyed, which is a thing I have begun to do on purpose. I sat in the dark of the stalls through load-in with a script on my knee and did not once look at the trunk in the yard.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry:
Perlmann said it all again in front of them, and then said the bag had a bank's mark, and my mouth answered before my head: the Farriers' and Merchants' — and then no, no branch here in the fifth year, I drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on my knees, and I remember that coach seat as I remember my mother. Three items: the loft lease, the certificate, and a packet with my company's name on it that has sat in a tin box for nine years because we never came back. He gave it to Harrow. He told me to change my coat, and he was right, and I did not answer.

On the stair I shook. In the yard she opened it and made me read the letter standing, silently, twice, and I did — and it is worse than being owed. Hessel refused the receipt because the money was never his to lend. He held it out of a fund for another party whose name he never told me, and he took that party's marker as security, and put it in the green-room cupboard, and tagged the key unpaid, and left it for us, and asked God to have mercy. Four hundred and twelve marks, the whole of it, and nine years of me saying so, and all the time the thing behind the debt was not paper. It was the play.

I went into the green room with Harrow and Emeran and saw her lift out thirty pages, which is not a folio. Then the day put its boots on: load-in at ten, and a matinee, and a take so good I came through the pass door shouting about it with the bag in my fist, and stopped when I saw their two faces.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry:
In the yard she opened the merchant's packet and I saw the key before I saw anything else and my own voice went strange: not a registry key — green room, prompt side, the cupboard under the chalk board, where Hessel kept our petty cash the year he bankrolled us, the cupboard I stood in front of four years ago with a stage full of my chalk and no key. The tag turned in the wind and said UNPAID. She gave me the copyist's page face-down and unread and I put it in my lining with the others; they whispered when they met.

Vane read the letter twice standing and told us Hessel had never held papers. He held a play. Thirty pages lodged as security by a party without a name.

I stood in the green-room doorframe with both hands flat on it while she lifted the parcel out, and it was thin, and thin is the whole of the horror: ours is two hundred pages and whole and roped in the yard, and somebody lodged a piece. Then the little man came to the gate and she read his master's letter and I asked her to say the name, and she said it flat: M. Skarke, who was the child in the passage at Katterau, nine years old, and would I remember the door. The scullery door. He stood through the whole reading with his hands behind his back and said is that the finish, and Odalric laughed and said no, boy, that's three and a half, and we gave him bread and sent him back out. He has been arranging for twenty years and he does not want the wagons.

Then I asked what I was in, because there was a call time. Between shows she asked me the other end of the arithmetic and I gave her my twenty years' worth: it does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died of a fever at the hour the passage scene falls; whole, with gas and a house, the rhyme would not stop at nine of us. And it has never been finished. Two hundred years of being interrupted. A play that has never had its ending is not a curse — it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry:
I came last into the yard and stopped six feet off when I saw what was in her hands — brown paper and a merchant's hand. I heard the whole of it from where I stood: Anna asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read and was told no and wept, and Hessel Brandt never held papers, he held a piece of the play. I did not go into the green room. There was a matinee to dress for and I dressed for it.

At the half I found Harrow in the prompt corner with something flat under her coat and told her the only thing I can do for her tonight: he will ask a question with a number in it. Nine is Odalric's. Twenty is Falk's. Ten is mine, and I will answer it myself, and she is not to spare me. Ring the bell and I'll come.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry: Took the watch through the night and woke Toby for his. Stood in the ring round the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel and said nothing, because nothing was wanted. Then the little man with the brass case was at the gate on a Wednesday, asking after her by name, and I went and said so, and she had me open it to talking distance and no farther, which I did. The town clock struck the quarter and got it right, and I said what wanted saying: load-in for the matinee's at ten. Then I swung the gates and it was ten o'clock and the day went on being a day.

Came down into the yard with my thimble on and stood in the circle while she untied the tape. Letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. I caught myself tapping the thimble on my thumbnail while Vane read it twice standing up, and stopped, because the yard was that quiet. Whatever it says, his face went a colour I have not seen on him. Then ten o'clock, and a hem to dress with pins in my mouth, and a matinee, which is what I am for.

Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk, and after that I was in the yard when she opened the packet, and I did not touch anything and did not say anything, which is new for me. Then load-in, and I laid a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights being all three nights. At the half I called the half hour and reported the thing I was put there to report: the gentleman is in the fourth row already, come in early, reading his programme.

I came at nine on a Wednesday and said so first, because my instructions had changed by telegraph and she has been decent with me and deserved daylight. I gave her the reason: Herr Skarke came into the town last night, he is at the Swan, and I am no longer the senior man here. The counting is brought forward — tonight, after the first performance, in the box office, strongbox present — and I waited while she wrote it, as I did on the milestone. Then the second instruction, which I was to give her and not to Vane: the inspection is cancelled and replaced. The trunk to be delivered to the Swan tonight against valuation. I have carried eleven schedules and I have never wanted so badly to lose a client, and I said so. I handed her the letter, which I had read, because I read everything I carry. She read it once in the open. Falk came out of the stage door and stopped dead at my case. She told me the counting stands against her book, witnesses welcome, and that the trunk's answer will come from her mouth at the counting in front of everyone — that is how valuations are done, she said. I touched my hat and went.

Load-in at ten and the counterweights exactly as bad as I warned her they were, and I said so more than once. They had some business in my yard before that with a parcel and a great deal of standing about in silence, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked no questions, having swept that stage once already for a man's madness.

scenes.title: Our Left, and the Man in Row Four
scenes.summary:
At the Athenaeum, Bell Harrow sends Vane to bank the takings with Boyle and sits by Herr Skarke in row four, a small, hungry man who admits he has waited since age nine to sit among such people, has thirty pages of theatrical inheritance and could never buy the rest, and asks nothing tonight. Bell warns him half a play is hungrier than none.

Backstage, Falk shows Bell that their practical door matches the wrong one from Katterau's folio, and offers to enter upstage right instead. Bell rules: "As blocked. As certified." Falk enters stage left; nothing goes wrong. Skarke leaves before curtain calls, leaving his rug with a note: he doesn't want the trunk, the assignment will be produced and withdrawn, Perlmann's evidence unneeded — he's been given "one for eightpence and a seat in the fourth row." He'll return tomorrow, paying properly, and never come nearer than row four. The rug is for Falk, whose hands were cold — Falk notes bitterly that empresses and mayors gave him gifts, but no one ever noticed his hands before.

In the box office, the assignment is endorsed "withdrawn, this date," witnessed by the agent and Frau Loewe, everything initialled. The agent says: "Discharged tonight. Not forgiven" — the pages return to the capital Saturday regardless of Skarke's wishes. Vane, briefly unafraid, asks what they do now; Bell says: learn solvency, two more nights, then Achterhalt, then the capital.

Afterward, Bell shows Mirelle three routes into Anna's box, warning that opening it may undo Anna's work, though it would bar Skarke's lawyers forever. Mirelle reveals her birth name isn't Sorel — it exists in a capital police file, differs again on her passport — and she won't risk registering days before entering the capital. Instead she asks Bell to learn who came from Katterau four years ago asking for Falk.

Frau Loewe recalls: a dark, thin-faced countrywoman, hands like "your Frau Sorel," asking after Falk, with a silent boy of five or six, saying finally: "Then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his." Mirelle recognizes the coat as her mother's — hers, then — and asks for silence.

Falk reflects that in the folio, a woman's lie about paternity is the play's kindest act — "It rhymes." Skarke returns quietly the remaining nights, sending nothing further. At load-out, Vane hands Bell the float bag and says, "Harrow, ask me for a thing."
scenes.history: Bell Harrow joins the Vermilion Players as stage manager under Odalric Vane, receiving a battered prompt book with a torn-out page, found by Emeran Falk and Mirelle Sorel to be tied to strange, prophetic "Katterau" pages that reach prompt books and predict real events. Clerk Casimir Prewick investigates alongside her. An unnumbered iron trunk, tied to vanished writer Anselm Krug and moneylender Skarke of Vessendal, proves central: Vane owes nine years' interest on an unsigned loan from the late Brandt, secretly funding an unnamed party's play-security. Vane vanishes and returns; the trunk yields only blank paper that "reads" itself at night. Harrow enforces strict rules—certified copies only, no invented lines—after learning Katterau's cost: Anna Sorel (Mirelle's sister), Grelle's voice, Vane's nerve. Investigating registries and executors, Harrow, Prewick, and Perlmann uncover Brandt's sealed packet: a counterfoil, an unread copyist's page, and a key to thirty pages of the play's folio, held by Skarke's son—the child Falk once fed at Katterau. Skarke discharges the debt without taking the trunk, keeping distance from row four. Mirelle, hiding her true identity, learns a woman resembling her mother once sought Falk, implying Mirelle's true parentage ties to him. The company moves on, uneasy, toward Achterhalt and the capital.

journals.entry: Sent Vane to bank the bag and walked the centre aisle at the half to look at row four. He is small, thirty at most, black coat, walked-in boots, a rug, and he read the programme to the bottom with his lips moving and then looked at the set the way Prewick looked at a broken tin sheet. He spoke first: better nailed than Katterau. So I sat a hat's distance off and told him half a play is hungrier than none, that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that we do finishes here. He said he is not a wicked man; twenty years, thirty pages, never able to buy the rest; the room is lovely; nine, twenty, ten come from cheap clerks; no questions tonight. Then Falk, grey in the wings: our practical door is stage left, so is Katterau's scullery door, so is the wrong door the creditor comes late by in the folio. I ruled as blocked, as certified — ours-whole beats theirs-half — and he went through it on the hour and it was only a door. Skarke put his face in his hands and went out before the calls, leaving a rug and a pinned note: he withdraws the claim, keeps the counting, needs no Perlmann; got his ending for eightpence and a seat; keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never nearer than row four; back tomorrow, paying at the door. Postscript for Falk's cold hands, and I told him plain. Counting clean and initialled, the assignment endorsed withdrawn, discharged not forgiven, the thirty pages riding to the capital Saturday regardless. Vane owes no man anything and asked what we do now: be solvent, bank Perlmann Thursday anyway, Achterhalt, the capital early. Struck a line through today. On the yard steps Mirelle told me her name has never been Sorel and will not go on any register twelve days before the capital; she chose Odalric's neck over her own and asked me for Loewe's woman instead. Loewe gave me all of it, including it was not his, and a boy nine or ten now. Thursday I banked Perlmann's oath and the Achterhalt counterfoil, and delivered both reports word for word. Saturday, on the steps, Vane handed me the float bag unasked.
journals.state: On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.

journals.entry: I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas — and found the room lovely, which I had not expected. I could not stop counting the joints; the trough is better nailed than Katterau and you can hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke to her without turning, and apologised, and told her the truth: I have wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, and that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that they do finishes here, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked; that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer have bought me nothing; that I found out everything from clerks, because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing. Then the doors went and the drovers came in wet, and I moved my rug onto my own knees, and I watched. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls, because I had had what I came for, and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I do not want the trunk tonight, the claim is withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, and never let me nearer than row four. Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sat where I sit and sent nothing further.
journals.state: Somewhere in Vessendal or on his way back to the capital, plainly dressed, without his rug, briefly and dangerously happy; his thirty pages locked in a strongbox travelling north by his own arrangement, and his wanting not ended.

journals.entry: I saw it two minutes before beginners, dressed and cold sober: our practical door is stage left. At Katterau the scullery door was stage left of the green room and the boy came in by it, and in the folio the creditor enters late by the wrong door, and the wrong door is stage left — and the man himself sitting in the fourth row. I offered to go round upstage right, six extra steps, nobody the wiser, and I gave the ruling to Harrow and swore not to argue it. She said: as blocked, as certified; ours-whole beats theirs-half; that door was hung by Boyle and painted by Krul and it opens onto a play with an ending. Our left. I walked through it on my cue for the six hundredth time and it was a door, and the house found me, and nothing came. Twenty years, and nothing came. I do not know what to do with that; I told her I should want telling at intervals. After the calls she brought me a rug off the fourth row and told me plainly that my hands were cold in the second act and the whole house saw it. An empress gave me jewellery and a mayor gave me a horse and neither of them noticed my hands. I wore the coat to the counting and heard the debt discharged, and did not drink my brandy in the green room, and stood in the rug and let Vane toast Hessel Brandt. Thursday, in the empty wings, Harrow gave me a message four years old from a woman out of Katterau: tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. In the last act of the folio a woman sends exactly that word, and it is a lie, and the lie is the kindest thing in the play. It rhymes. I shall never know which this was.
journals.state: In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.

journals.entry: I played the first scene to wet wool and drovers and had the house by the fourth line, and never knew, until afterwards, that Harrow and Falk had spent the two minutes before beginners on the question of a door. He came on stage left as blocked and the house stood up for him and nothing in the wings went cold. In the green room I let the room say Hessel Brandt and did not lift my glass with them; I said And Anna to Harrow alone, and drank, and pulled my glove straight over the wrist. On the yard steps she laid out the box: a certificate, two ratepayers swearing kinship, or a magistrate's order — and said honestly that nothing says the box ever opens, that opening it might break Anna's one shelf, and that a kin claim once entered keeps Skarke's lawyers off it forever. So I told her what I have told nobody: my name is not Sorel and never was; the name I was born to sits in a police file in the capital under a matter with a date and a magistrate, and my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I will not put my true name on a register twelve days before I walk into the capital by invitation, which is the page, word for word. I want the box shut forever and I want it mine, and I have never been able to have both. Thursday belongs to Odalric's neck, not mine; my eighteen shillings' stopped clock does not care about names. I asked her instead for Loewe's woman from Katterau, and the child's age. She brought it back exact on Thursday: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, stood the way I stand. That is my mother's coat — Anna's, then mine, then someone's. I asked for silence, and the road to Achterhalt to think on it.
journals.state: At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.

journals.entry: She sent me to bank the bag with Boyle at the half and kept the word for the counting, which I obeyed without asking, being a man who has learned that much. Then the house, and Falk through that door on the hour, and the applause coming up out of the stalls over him, and I stood at the back of the wings and wept and told nobody that the Advertiser would not have been generous. Three calls, and a third for Emeran alone that he did not ask for. In the box office with the shutter down I sat with my hat off and my hands flat while the assignment was read out and the second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in Skarke's own hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe, who insisted. Every figure initialled against her book. Discharged tonight, said the agent, not forgiven. And then it was nine o'clock on a Wednesday and I owed no man anything, and I sat on a stool too small for me and could not name what I was feeling, and asked her what in God's name we do now. She said: learn to be solvent, two more nights, Perlmann's oath banked Thursday all the same, then Achterhalt, then the capital early. In the green room I stood with the jug and the wrong hat and toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor of this parish, who would not sign and would not tell and would not open a parcel for nine years, and I did not round the number. Thursday the oath was sworn before Braun and the bank confirmed the draw at Achterhalt in my name. Friday full, Saturday the strongbox gone. At load-out I gave Harrow the float bag without being asked, and asked her to ask me for a thing.
journals.state: In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.

journals.entry: I sat the performance in the stalls with my script and my oilcloth and made no note of the two warm seats, since the occupant was in them and paid for. Falk came on stage left through the practical door exactly as blocked and certified, and I observed that nothing occurred that was not in the book. After the curtain I was in the box office for the counting with the shutter down: assignment produced and read, second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in the creditor's hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe. I copied the whole instrument for the Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it straight the first time. Afterwards I was put on a crate in the green room with a plate of Krul's mutton, and on the third mouthful I discovered that I was happy, which I did not report.
journals.state: In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.

journals.entry: I gave them my house for the evening and it went well enough, though the counterweights are what I said they were and the trough drips. They wanted a witness at their counting in the box office, and I made sure it was me, since I am the one who gets paid first and I signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Then soup in my own green room with two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Later, locking front of house with the lamp low, the stage manager put me one more question between managers: the woman who came from Katterau four years ago. I told her the truth, having finished the key first. A name like Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and said so in the first minute, dark and thin in the face, and she stood with her hands still, the way their Frau Sorel stands. She did not ask if Falk was here; she asked whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The child was a boy, five or six, who sat on my step and did not fidget and thanked me for a bun very correctly, and she never once looked at him while she spoke. And I told her the piece I have never told anybody: when I said he'd gone south, she said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I have wondered whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child. Five or six then; nine or ten now. I saw the stage manager's face do what it did, and said good night, and reminded her the matinee's at two.
journals.state: In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.

journals.entry: Doors and row four, all three nights being all three nights, and the programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opened. Counts only. He came in early again with a rug over his arm, and I ran the beginners call myself and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle — one line, and it's about a door. Then the show, and the house standing up for Herr Falk when he came through the door, and the loudest thing I have ever stood in. Afterwards I did my count and got it wrong and right at once: row four went in one and came out none, and he'd left the rug on the seat with a paper pinned to it, and I said so at her elbow with my voice gone. She made everybody take their bows first. I put the chalk back in its tin, took the watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate, and ate my soup on the tailboard while the lion's bell struck ten and got it right.
journals.state: On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.

journals.entry: Took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it as I was told, no questions. My door held: Falk went through it on his cue, stage left, and it opened like a door and the house came down, and I'll take that. After the curtain I fed the horses, roped the tarpaulin, brought a jug up to the green room and sold Toby the watch till midnight for a penny and a plate. Saturday I checked the ropes twice, because twice is the number, and we loaded out.
journals.state: In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.

journals.entry: Pot on from the second act — mutton, barley, and something I got in the market that nobody needs to hear about. Glared at a baby through a gap in the flats and it quieted. My paint went through that door with Falk on the hour and came back none the worse, and the house stood up. Then the green room full, two candles on the cupboard, Vane on his feet with the jug toasting a wool factor, and Prewick on a crate discovering food. No warm boxes tonight. Good.
journals.state: In the green room over her pot with a plate going round, thimble on, pleased and saying little; wanting the queen's slippers to last to Achterhalt and no more warm boxes.

journals.entry: Twelfth schedule, and the strangest counting of my life. Box office, shutter down, strongbox open between the candles, Vane with his hat off and his hands flat. I produced the assignment and read it out, and then the second sheet, endorsed and signed across in my client's own hand, withdrawn, this date — I witnessed it, and so did the woman who holds the lease, because she insisted on it. Her book against mine, every figure initialled: matinee, evening, the lease-holder's cut, eleven shillings for a cart. The officer copied the whole of it for his Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it true first time, which I have never seen done. Discharged tonight, I told them; not forgiven, and my client knows the difference better than I do. Then my last instruction, given whole: the thirty pages stay in the strongbox, the strongbox goes back to the capital on Saturday's coach whether or not he changes his mind, and he wished her to know he made that arrangement while he was happy. I closed the case and left. Saturday I rode beside the box out of the square.
journals.state: On the capital coach out of Vessendal, brass case on his knees and the strongbox at his side, sober as always and privately relieved; wanting to deliver the pages north before his client's happiness wears off.

journals.entry: Thursday, on my daughter's arm, before Braun who was my clerk. I swore the account: the eleventh hour, the bag on the counterpane, the whole of it counted out, Hessel laughing and refusing to sign between friends, the receipt I never finished, and the Tuesday he died. It was copied and sealed straight, and I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed. Nine years I have thought of that instrument every week, and now it is on a register where a magistrate can find it, whether the creditor wants it or not. Records are the whole of the defence.
journals.state: Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse, in his chair with the shawl over him, spent and lightened; wanting nothing now but to be told, some day, that the paper was enough.

journals.entry: Thursday at nine, as I knew it would be: my arm for him to lean on up the steps, and my hand to write it out, and my finger on the place for his mark. Braun was civil and quick, which I did not expect of a magistrate. They took a copy and sealed it, and I brought my father home and put him in his chair, and he was tired in the good way. That is the whole of my part in it, and it was mine.
journals.state: Back in the rooms above the saddler's with the sewing taken up again, her father resting in his chair; quietly proud and watchful, wanting no more strangers on the stair.

scenes.title: Bills for a Road We Have Stopped Walking
scenes.summary:
On the Athenaeum steps Harrow named her price for the float bag: at Achterhalt Vane must walk her into the Farriers' and Merchants' himself, hat on, and close the fifth-year business he'd owed the town for nine years of avoidance. Vane agreed, admitting they'd once held him four hours in a back room while a boy rode to Vessendal to vouch for him, and promised her a magnificent sky and a rounded-down price. Frau Loewe waved goodbye; Falk lifted Skarke's rug to her; the column rolled.

Twenty miles on, at the Achterhalt milestone, Boyle found dry folded paper under the wet stone. Harrow read it alone: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who doesn't go in, asking in the fourth act "is that the finish" and unanswered — no number this time. She pocketed it, telling Falk it was not his but theirs.

In the market square a bellman cried a fresh bill: THE VERMILION PLAYERS — FOUR ACTS AND A MATTER FOLLOWING — ONE NIGHT ONLY — BY COMMAND. Harrow forbade repeating it, paid the bellman to stop, and gave the criminal matter to Prewick, who impounded nine bills, declared a forged Palace command meant arrest not fines, and that only his seal could inspect a printer's order book. Mirelle noticed the worn type on the bottom line — kept nine years.

At his shut shop, printer Hessler confessed the forme had made itself up on his stone overnight, paid for under a wet proof with no order recorded; the standing line read a date that Vane's false itinerary would have placed them at Katterau.
