Prewick called it "bills for a road we have stopped walking." Hessler broke the type; 191 bills and money were sealed.

Boyle spotted a watching woman. Harrow crossed to her alone: Ilse Bacher, once of the Rose in Katterau, confessed she'd sent Falk's old message and named a nameless left-handed man asking "how far did they get?" She named the boy on Loewe's step as her son Fenner. She offered to scout the Rose; Harrow refused, ordering her instead to keep Fenner home on the 14th, giving Loewe's address for word.

Bailiff Kessel arrived with constables; Harrow split jurisdictions, Prewick's account went upward untouched, Kessel lent the strongroom and offered the Corn Exchange — twelve taken. Vane, delighted: "Twelve."
scenes.history: At the Corona, Bell Harrow becomes stage manager for the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and an iron trunk tied to Katterau, where something once happened involving Anna Sorel (Mirelle's sister), Falk, Vane, and a vanished writer, Anselm Krug. Clerk Prewick investigates alongside her. A cryptic, self-writing "fifth act" haunts the trunk—blank paper that occasionally isn't blank, predicting real events. Harrow discovers Vane's hidden nine-year debt to Vessendal's Skarke, secured against the trunk. Vane vanishes and returns; the company debates Katterau's unresolved tragedy. Harrow imposes strict rules: certified texts only, no invented lines. Investigating executor Perlmann and banker records, they learn Brandt lent Vane money not his own, security being "a play"—thirty pages surface, half of the same folio Skarke's father once held. Skarke, revealed as the child once sheltered by Falk at Katterau, releases his claim on the trunk, keeping only a seat in the audience. Mirelle investigates her mother's connection to Falk and Katterau. Forged "By Command" playbills mysteriously appear, tied again to Katterau's date; printer Hessler and informant Ilse Bacher reveal deeper conspiracy. Bailiffs and Prewick divide jurisdiction as the company presses on toward Achterhalt and the capital, debts settling, mysteries multiplying.

journals.entry: I named my price on the steps: Achterhalt, the Farriers' and Merchants', front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed square, the take banked, and then an ironmonger and a sky chosen by ear. He told me about the back room and the drainage pamphlet and said yes. Twenty miles, and paper under the milestone in the copyist's hand — dry under wet stone, which is its signature. I read it once, alone, standing: a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat, a programme, nobody asking whose he is, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. No number. First time. It went in my coat, not my book. Falk got down and asked me straight if it was his, and I told him no: ours, and not yet happened, and my whole trade is houses that answer. Then the bell in the dip was a market crier with our name on a barrel: four acts and a matter following, by command. I gave the criminal side to Prewick entire and sent Boyle for the printer; Mirelle saw the worn bottom line. Hessler: no order, coin left under a pulled proof, the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, the old Vermilion line nine years standing. The date is the 14th of Frost — Vane's false road, Katterau. Bills for a road we've stopped walking. Forme broken to the case, 191 sacked, coin impounded. Then the coat and the town boots across the way, and it was Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen. I told her Falk was well and the bill was not ours. She gave me the left-handed man with the little book who asked how far did they get, and the boy: Fenner, ten, her own, a butter man's son. I refused her the Rose and gave her one order instead — keep him home on the 14th, no theatre, no square, no step — and Loewe's address for word. I did not answer her last question. I carry her message for Falk. Kessel got jurisdictions, Prewick's report goes upward, and we have a hall for twelve.
journals.state: On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.

journals.entry: She asked for a thing I did not expect and it cost me more than money: the Farriers' and Merchants' at Achterhalt, front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed. I told her about the four hours in the back room and the boy on the horse and the drainage pamphlet nineteen times, and then I said yes, and promised her a sky and to round the price down aloud in front of her. Loewe raised a hand and Falk raised the rug and we were out of Vessendal. On the road I talked about kettles versus a hung sheet to nobody at all. At the crest she read a page and put it in her coat and Falk got down off his box and asked her a question; then a crier in Achterhalt with our name in the printer's biggest type and by command under it, and I stood three feet behind her with my hat off and said nothing, which is new for me and cost something. Bailiff came, and she divided us like a woman dealing cards, and gave the man the Office's shilling and my name only for dull certified things. Then he said his brother-in-law asks eighteen and takes twelve, and I heard myself say twelve like a lover. Bank, ironmonger, haggle. The happiest day of my life.
journals.state: In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.

journals.entry: Left Vessendal with four numbered pieces of luggage and a report I am not ashamed of. On the road I wrote something and crossed it out. At the milestone she read a page alone and I wrote nothing, which is now habit and choice. In the square: our company name in a printer's biggest type, four acts and a matter following, one night only, by command. She gave the criminal side to me entire, so I crossed the square and took the whole roll off the bellman in the Office voice — nine copies — and certified it on the tailboard: seen this day, uncertified matter announced by public bell, nine copies impounded, C. Prewick, Clerk 3. Stamp straight. I told her the boundaries: I may impound, I may compel a licensed printer's order book, I may not stop a performance nobody has attempted, and by command without warrant is not a fine but an arrest. Hessler had no order, no name, no receipt — the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, coin under the proof. Then the bottom line: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, Thursday the 14th of Frost. The command performance is the 3rd; on the 14th we should be eleven days in the capital, striking. On Vane's false dates we should have been at Katterau. It is bills for a road we have stopped walking, and I said so aloud. Broke-up type, two sacks, wax off Hessler's bench, one pound two shillings and fourpence impounded, his signature. To Kessel I wrote that this is forgery of a Palace command, beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, that both of us report upward and neither touches it further, and that it is written in those words so neither can blame the other. He gave us the weigh-house strongroom and kept the key for a lawful shilling.
journals.state: In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.

journals.entry: Gloves on out of Vessendal with Achterhalt to think about, and at the top of the hill the road gave her another page. She read it standing and said it out for us: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a question in the fourth act, no answer, a house that does not know him. No number in it at all. Not nine, not twenty, not ten. So it has stopped counting. In the square I came up beside her without saying anything and looked at the bill in the clerk's hand, because type is a thing I can read like a face: the name, the acts, the command all fresh — and the bottom line worn and out of alignment and grey. Somebody kept the forme nine years. Inside the printer's I heard the date read out and heard the clerk put it against Odalric's Katterau road, and I said nothing there either. Then Boyle put his head in and said there was a woman across the way who would not move off: countrywoman's coat, town boots. She told us not to follow and crossed alone, and I stood in a printer's shop with my hands still and waited, and did not go to the window.
journals.state: At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.

journals.entry: Sober on my box with the rug over my knees; Loewe lifted a hand off her step and I lifted the rug, and that was Vessendal done. Twenty mile and the road climbed and Boyle pulled up without being told, and there was paper under the milestone, and I got down slow with one hand on the wheel and stopped six feet off, where you stop at water, and asked her the thing I have never asked: is it mine. She said no. No number in it at all, the first time — a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat and a programme, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. Ours, she said. Hasn't happened yet. Then I said the toll distances in verse for half a mile because that is how I pray, and in the market there was a bell and a barrel and our name in the biggest type there is with four acts and a matter following under it, and by command, and I stopped mid-line and said not one word, because she had ruled that nobody would. I sat on the box while they went into the printer's, and I did not go across the square, and nobody has yet told me what came out of it.
journals.state: In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.

journals.entry: Swung out of the Athenaeum yard, toll road under us, hedges laid proper. At the top of the climb I saw the corner of paper under the milestone lip, dry as bone under wet stone, and pulled up without being asked and said, madam, do we look. She looked, one of us, as she does, and pocketed it, and told me to find out what that bell was before it decided it was ours. It was a market crier on a barrel with our name printed over him. I went for the printer and found Hessler shut on a market Saturday, which he never is, with a lamp lit behind the shutters, and said so. Stood at the corner being mild while the Office knocked. Two hundred bills, and nobody ordered them; the old man tipped his type back in the case and I've never seen a man look happier doing away with his own work. Two sacks on the tailboard. Then I clocked the woman across the way who'd not moved since we knocked — countrywoman's coat, town boots — and reported it, and she went over alone and told us to stay put, so we stayed put. Bailiff came and went civil. We've a hall for twelve and a strongroom for the sacks, and my axle held the climb.
journals.state: In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.

journals.entry: Voice still gone from Thursday and I don't care. Rode out with the wagons and there was a page under the milestone at the top of the hill and she read it herself and nobody said anything. Then Achterhalt market and a man on a barrel with a bell crying our name and words off Herr Falk's play, and she said nobody repeats one word of it aloud, and I didn't. My job was a penny to the bellman for a rest, which I gave him, and he sat down on his own barrel looking sorry for himself and grateful at once, and handed the whole roll of bills out of his coat to Herr Prewick. After that I stood by the horses while the Office was in the printer's, and watched the bailiff come across with two constables and his chain bouncing, and go away pleased. There's only one house in this town and it's a Corn Exchange, and I am going to call it.
journals.state: On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.

journals.entry: Saw them out clean on the Saturday, as I wanted. Stood on my own step with my arms folded and watched them rope and load and go, and at the last minute I put my hand up to Falk on his box, and he lifted that gentleman's rug to me. I shall be telling that for ten years. My brick is my own again, the trough wants sheeting, and the stage manager left me an address to forward to, which is more than most managers leave.
journals.state: In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.

journals.entry: Cried the market as I always do — lost property, the horse auction, and a playbill I was paid handsome to cry, the Vermilion Players, one night only, by command. Then a man in a collar walks over with the Office of Public Morals on his seal and says the bill and any duplicates and no further crying of it, and I gave him the whole roll out of my coat, nine of them, because I've no wish to argue with a seal. A boy from the wagons put a penny in my hand for a rest, which was decent, and I sat on my barrel and rested it, sore about the fee and glad about my neck.

Three knocks, official, and my shoulders came down, because I had not slept since Thursday and I had been waiting for them. I put the lamp down and thought about the back door and thought better of it and opened the front. Told them straight: I set nothing. I came down Thursday to bank my fires and the forme was made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof on the line, and coin underneath it — enough for two hundred bills and the crier and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt. The bottom line was my old Vermilion forme from nine year back that I never broke up, because printers are magpies; the top was my type set by a hand that knows my case better than my boy, and not a wrong letter in it. I read the standing line out for the lady: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, Thursday the 14th of Frost at seven — and the 14th falls Thursday this year, which it hasn't since the fifth year, and I don't like it, and the house is Vessendal, and my town's crier cried a Vessendal house this morning. Then I knocked the quoins loose and tipped the whole thing into the case, every letter, the old line with it, and held up my empty stone with both hands. Hundred and ninety-one bills into their sacks, no money taken, and the clerk wrote down that I said so, and I signed, relieved to my boots.

Came in Thursday with butter and saw a bill on the barrel with four acts and a matter following on it, and sat down on the kerb in front of people, because I last heard those words through a scullery door at fifteen carrying bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose. So I stood across from Hessler's and watched, and this morning the players came and an officer went in, and then a woman crossed to me at hat-distance and named herself Bell Harrow and said my message had been given to Emeran Falk word for word, three days ago, an hour out of Vessendal. Then he knows. Good. I told her what I am: the girl who let a small boy sit in the passage because he was small and had nowhere, who answered his questions nine years later when he came back with money and a good coat, and who sent word four years ago because a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning and I would not have Falk carry my part of it. It was mine. I opened the door. She told me Falk was well and sober and that six hundred people stood up for him, and that the bill is not theirs and every one of them is impounded and the type broken. So I gave her the man: no name, winter of the seventh year, thirties, cheap town clothes, a little book, wrote left-handed, paid in shillings, knew the reading had happened when nobody in Katterau said it aloud, and asked the one question nobody else asked — how far did they get. Too poor and too frightened for Skarke's, I always thought. I told her the boy on the Vessendal step is mine, Fenner, ten, and my husband's, and can read. I offered to go in by the scullery at the Rose and look, and she said no, plain: a door I've paid twenty years for doesn't get opened twice. Instead: keep him home on the 14th of Frost, no theatre, no square, no step. I said I'd bolt the door and tell Bacher we're playing at hermits. I asked her if that was what was coming for him and she didn't answer, which was answer. Loewe, Vessendal, for word. I took her hand, and left Falk a message about my voice — his voice — through a scullery door, and went to my cart.

Came across my own square before dinner with two constables because there'd been a bill cried for a play by command and the Office was in Hessler's shop and nobody had told me a thing. The stage manager sorted it in two sentences — hers the players, the Office's the matter — and gave me the clerk, who is the useful sort: nine bills off my bellman, a hundred and ninety-one off the printer, coin impounded, order book inspected, and Hessler blameless, which I could have told them. No order at all, then, which my constable had off the bellman and which I'd called a story. The clerk wrote out that the forgery of a Palace command is beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, and that we both report upward and neither of us touches it, in those words, so neither can hang it on the other — a man I can work with. Gave them the strongroom under the weigh-house for their sacks and kept the key myself, and the Office pays me a shilling to make it lawful. Told her the Corn Exchange is the only house in town and my brother-in-law will ask eighteen and take twelve, and warned her that the last company's leading man went off with a farrier's wife, so we are not sentimental here. Then dinner.

scenes.title: A Sky, a Returned Chalk, and Room Fourteen
scenes.summary:
Achterhalt, morning: Harrow walked Vane to the Farriers' and Merchants' door. The clerk didn't know him; the five-year-old ledger entry read "paid in coin to bearer, Vane, O., on account of Brandt, H." — a copy made for twopence, the amber notice tucked away. At the ironmonger's Vane, eyes shut, chose a great black plate of a sky — "has a floor in it" — twenty-two shillings, no rounding. The Corn Exchange went for thirteen.

That night, chalking her plot, Falk asked about the woman in the square. Harrow gave him Ilse Bacher whole — married to a butter man, son Fenner, ten, who can read, the fault hers for opening the door — and repeated his own old shout at Odalric Vane for laughing. Falk laughed, remembered getting angry twenty years ago, understood "not mine" meant the wager. He returned her chalk and asked her to help him finish the play properly one day — all four acts, everyone who chooses, nobody who doesn't. Harrow logged it — "Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp" — and set terms: everyone hears Katterau entire first, no wagers, no bottles, Fenner Bacher stays home. Falk agreed: "Yes. That first, and the rest after."

Achterhalt sold out. Then eleven days early to the capital: the Baraque Theatre, not the Palace; the stage manager summoned to the Office of Public Morals, Room Fourteen. Prewick briefed her on Undersecretary Lenz, who'd kept two anonymous folios on the Index nineteen years, refusing four applications to strike them.

At the Baraque, Anselm Krug waited — the old book-keeper who'd vanished after Katterau. Vane confessed to the company that he'd blamed Krug for a theft of seven pounds and had known his whereabouts two years; Harrow made him unsay it at supper and sent three corrective letters. Krug produced nine pages he'd never burned. Harrow ordered them counted, numbered, given to Falk's coat lining — except page eight, kept by her. Krug summarized contents only: past events, present ones, two not yet happened, and a cast list ending "and the house, entire."

At Room Fourteen, Lenz questioned her about Vane's trunk and any spoken lines; she answered precisely, citing one Vessendal exception. Lenz revealed: of thirty-one banned works, two "work"; fourteen speakings in two hundred years, Katterau the fourteenth. The Palace's requisition for the 3rd of Frost was signed not by Skarke but by "A. Krug," filed two years prior, fee paid by an unnamed party of standing — the Office approving. Outside, Prewick's watch ran on.
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a troubled prompt book, a torn page, and a locked iron trunk tied to debts owed to Vessendal/Skarke and a mysterious forbidden play from Katterau. She uncovers layers: Falk's history with the play, Vane's hidden nine-year debt to the dying Brandt, Mirelle Sorel's true parentage and connection to Anna Sorel, and Krug's disappearance and blame. Investigating with clerk Prewick, she navigates registry offices, executor Perlmann, and creditor Skarke (revealed as the child Falk once sheltered at Katterau), securing debts paid and assignments withdrawn while resisting the play's pull. Blank trunk pages sometimes fill with prophetic text; one predicts a boy and a border crossing, tied to Fenner Bacher and Ilse. Forged playbills for an illegal Katterau performance surface in Achterhalt, traced to a self-assembling type forme; culprits and papers are sealed by bailiffs. Vane settles old debts, buys a symbolic sky-plate, and asks Falk's forgiveness lessons continue. The company sells out Achterhalt, then moves early to the capital's Baraque Theatre. There, Krug reappears with nine unburned pages, and Room Fourteen's Undersecretary Lenz reveals the play's dangerous history—fourteen "speakings" in two centuries—and that its requisition was filed by Krug himself, funded anonymously, moving toward a climactic reckoning.

journals.entry: Bank first, hat on, no arm offered. Eleven minutes and nine years off him: paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H., copy twopence, take banked, receipt over the old notice. At the ironmonger's I said choose me a sky and let him listen his way down the wall — the black plate has a floor in it, twenty-two shillings unrounded, out loud, so I have my price rounded down and he has his thunder. Hall for thirteen. That night, chalking on the flags, Falk asked. I gave him Ilse Bacher whole and her message word for word, and watched him find out he had shouted, twenty years late. Then he handed my chalk back handle-first and asked me to help him finish it — after the capital, after the debts, after the company is safe. Standing page: Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp. My terms if ever yes: all who choose, choosing after Katterau entire; no wagers, no bottles; Fenner Bacher stays home. He took the boy's clause first. Two good nights, then the toll road and the capital eleven days early, and at the gate: the Baraque, a man waiting since Tuesday, and me alone at Room Fourteen. The man was Krug. I let Odalric see him unannounced and Odalric sat down in the wet and confessed the theft he invented; three letters in ink, and Krug fed. Then nine pages on a hamper beside my plate — he never burned any. Report only, no quoting. Page eight is mine: a stage manager rings the bell. It is in my coat and I have not read it. In Room Fourteen I gave one true answer three times and got a warehouse of truth back: the Office counts speakings, fourteen in two hundred years, the fifteenth scheduled — and the command of the 3rd was requested by A. Krug of the fourth ward, with Part the Second left blank for us to determine.
journals.state: In Room Fourteen at the Office of Public Morals, tea half drunk, the Palace play list face-up under her hand and page eight unread in her coat pocket; steady-faced and reading it twice against her own rule, Prewick's watch running in the corridor.

journals.entry: She walked me in the front door with my hat on and a boy of nineteen called me sir and had never heard of me, and I have not been so kindly used in ten years. Eleven minutes. Paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I put the receipt over the notice in my breast pocket and could not speak on the steps. Then she asked me for her sky and I found it — the black plate with a floor in it, and I did not round the price, and I made her watch me not round it. Hall for thirteen, which is a defeat, and I was happy. Achterhalt stood and the storm came in low and I wept in the wing. Then the capital, and Anselm on a mounting block in my own yard, and everything I have carried since Katterau came up my throat at once: I told the company he took the Wednesday take. Seven pounds. I made him a thief to save myself the explaining, and I have known his address two years. I sat down in the wet and said it, and Mirelle said I should unsay it at supper, and I asked Harrow for a thing because I always do, and she gave me three letters to write in ink with my name large enough to hurt. I wrote them. At supper I said it whole and laid the seven pounds on the table and he would not take it. He wanted her instead, and gave her nine pages, and I sat with my hat off and let the stage manager rule.
journals.state: In the Baraque's O.P. wing after a short night, coat rumpled, seven pounds still lying refused on the hamper; hollowed out, unexpectedly light, wanting Krug to stay and wanting to be told what to carry next.

journals.entry: Achterhalt, the Corn Exchange, one lamp, and the new sheet under felt with a floor in its voice. Boyle had told me a woman spoke to her in the square, so I stood over the felt and waited the way she waits, and she gave it to me exact: Ilse Bacher, married, a boy of ten who can read, and the fault hers because she opened the door. And then the message — that my voice was the loudest thing that ever came through a scullery door, because I shouted at Odalric for laughing when the boy asked is that the finish. Twenty years I have had that room every night and never once had that in it. Somebody in that room said no, and it was me. Not mine — she meant the wager. I gave her back her chalk and asked, standing, so I would not die with the asking in my mouth: when the capital is done and we are safe, help me finish it properly, once, everyone who chooses and nobody who doesn't. She wrote it as a standing page and named her clothes for a yes: Katterau told entire first, no wagers, no bottles, and the Bacher boy stays home. That first, I said. Then the tailboard, and Boyle at midnight, and I let him take it. In the capital, Krug at the gate in a green coat, and Odalric in the wet naming his own lie. At supper Krug gave the pages as report, and one of them has a twenty in it and is mine, and one is hers — a stage manager rings the bell. Eight of them went into my lining and the seam whispered.
journals.state: On a hamper in the Baraque's O.P. wing at dawn, Skarke's rug over his knees and eight pages sewn into his coat; sober, cracked open and oddly at peace, waiting to hear what came of Room Fourteen.

journals.entry: Achterhalt held: the thunder sheet I have been promised since Merrow arrived, and it works, and I have written nothing improper about it. At Northgate the customs clerk stamped my papers twice and then summoned her by name to Room Fourteen, not me, which is either a compliment or the beginning of something. I told her what I know going in: Fourteen is Assessment, second floor east, where they read; Nine is Enforcement. Undersecretary Lenz, who kept the Index entry on both anonymous folios unchanged for nineteen years and refused four applications to strike them out — I copied those refusals in my first month, the only interesting thing I have ever copied. He drinks nothing, offers very good tea, and it is like being weighed. Load-in at the Baraque: nine hundred seats, gas throughout, and a leak over the O.P. side she posted before she took her coat off. Krug came back, and Vane confessed the theft he invented, and at supper I put my notebook away closed and folded my hands on it, and I did not open it once while a man summarised nine unpublished pages — pages six, seven, eight, nine, unhappened. Seven has fourteen on the door and a man who does not drink. I said nothing about that either. This morning I delivered her to the frosted glass, started my watch, and stood against the wall with my hat in my hands. If she is longer than an hour I fetch nobody and note the time. She is nearly at the hour.
journals.state: In the east corridor of the Office of Public Morals, hat in his hands, watch running; outwardly a clerk at rest, inwardly frantic, wanting her out of Room Fourteen and the itinerary to hold to the 3rd.

journals.entry: Waited on the mounting block in the Baraque yard from Tuesday with the portmanteau and a book, rehearsing two speeches: one for the river and one for the door. She came off the board first, before anyone, and shook my hand and knew my margin note about the tin, and told me the weather of the yard: nobody announced, everything said whole to his face and then to the company. Then Odalric came round the tailboard and sat down in the wet and said the thing himself — that he made me a thief for seven pounds because he could not say why I went — and I told him I had it from three companies who wouldn't have me, and that was what I came about, not the river. The Sorel woman ruled it from the archway. Harrow made him write three letters and made me eat. I was useful within ten minutes and did not once say when I kept the book, and I looked at her prompt corner twice and looked away, because it is better kept than I kept it. At supper I put the parcel by her plate and confessed the real lie: I burned nothing. Nine pages, all read. I gave them as report, no quoting — one and two spent, three four five spent on this tour, six a boy and a woman who won't go in, seven a room with fourteen on the door, eight in five words because it is hers, nine a cast list of twelve blanks and the house entire. We counted them into her book by one candle and I initialled every line. I have not told her yet what I filed two years ago.
journals.state: On a hamper in the O.P. wing at the Baraque, boots off, portmanteau beside him, refusing a bed until somebody says he belongs; lighter by nine pages and heavier by one unsaid thing — the requisition with his name on it.

journals.entry: I was in the archway when the wagons filled the yard and Odalric came round the tailboard and stopped, and it was Krug in a green coat with a portmanteau, like a man who has been sitting on a stone for days. Nobody spoke. Then Odalric sat down in the wet in his good coat and said out loud that he had told us Krug stole the Wednesday take, seven pounds, and had known where he was these two years. I cut the yard in half and said it: he says it in front of us tonight and unsays it in the same breath, Harrow has ruled it, nothing half-told. He nodded. She asked him for three letters in ink. At supper he did it whole and put the seven pounds on the table and Krug would not touch it, and asked for her instead, and gave her nine pages he swore he burned. Six, seven, eight, nine have not happened. Nine is a cast list — twelve names, blank, and the house entire. Twelve of us, if you count the man who came back. I said nothing, and I have not asked her yet for the large thing, and now there is a page eight with a bell in it and she is in a room at the Office alone.
journals.state: In the Baraque, wardrobe end, glove drawn over her wrist, counting twelve blanks on an imagined cast list; outwardly calm, wanting Harrow back from Room Fourteen before she asks her for anything.

journals.entry: New sky came in Achterhalt wrapped in felt and rode on the boards like a duchess, and it earned its place: the storm went in low and the corn merchants forgot to breathe. Capital next, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard I had the queen's slippers in my hands when everything went quiet, and I put them down, because it was Krug standing there in a green coat, and Krug's box I packed warm with my own hands. Four seconds those slippers were on wet cobbles, and she counted them, and told me three seconds too many, and she was right, and I said four seconds is my whole opinion of a man and carried them in. At supper Vane said it whole — that he called Krug a thief to save his own face — and put seven pounds down, and Krug wouldn't have it, and gave her a parcel of pages instead. I folded my arms and stopped where I was. Nobody left. Nine pages, four not happened yet, one of them with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head, which is where they're safest, and they will not see the capital's second week.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage at first light, thimble on, the queen's slippers under her head; pleased Krug is fed and sitting down, wanting new slippers out of the capital and no warm boxes.

journals.entry: Achterhalt was two full houses and a new sky that came up through the floor of you. Then a hundred and ten mile of toll road and the capital, which does not stop being roofs. At the gate a clerk in green said we were expected and named a room at the Office and said not the clerk, you, madam, and I have never heard anyone say that to her before. Double watch on the trunk, me and Boyle splitting, orders straight off the board. At the Baraque yard I was carrying a hamper when everything stopped, and it was Herr Krug — the Krug who is on no list — and Herr Vane sat down on the mounting block in the wet and said out loud he had told a lie about him. Then three letters in ink and me to the evening post, running, and I made it before the box went. Krug showed me a lashing I will use till I die, and did not once say when I kept the book. At supper I sat on a flat with my ears burning and nobody sent me out, and I heard nine pages summarised, and one of them is Madam Harrow's and one has a room with fourteen on the door. Nobody left. Then yard watch again, and the Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz, which is my name, and Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.
journals.state: On the Baraque gate watch at dawn, hoarse again, a plate finished and the trunk roped in the wagon behind him; thrilled to be in the capital and to have heard the whole supper, wanting to see the Palace stage.

journals.entry: Axle held the toll road, eight shilling, and worth it. Achterhalt: backed in, watched, took the tailboard off Falk at midnight with my pipe unlit and he let me, which he has never done. Told him beforehand a woman had spoken to the stage manager in the market, because a man should know what's coming at him. Capital next, and the Baraque arch is four inches narrower than any arch has business being, and I said so at length. Then the yard went quiet: green coat on the mounting block, and it was Krug. I gave him the plain of it — the bill in Achterhalt, the bailiff, the type broken — because he asked and it cost nothing. Vane sat down in the wet and named his own lie in front of the lot of us. At supper he said it again whole and put money down, and Krug left it lying. Nine pages out of a portmanteau, and one of them is a wagon and a printer's line, which I stood in. Double watch on the trunk in a city yard, me and the boy splitting, and I checked the ropes twice, twice being the number. She's gone to the Office alone this morning and Prewick with her, and the trunk's still where I put it.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with rope and an unlit pipe, having handed the watch to Toby; content that arch, axle and knots all held, wanting the leaking roof mended and the trunk left alone.

journals.entry: Ten o'clock, the tray laid for one, the folder ready. Nineteen days in post: eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, and a company brought into the capital eleven days early, which no company has done. I asked her first what is in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, which I noted, and gave me seen and hearsay separately, and then quoted my own predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I set my pen down. Nineteen years I have kept that entry and been passed over twice for it, and no one in this building has ever put it to me in the right order. I asked my question three times and compared the three answers with my finger, and they were the same words in the same order: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth is scheduled, that the command was requested of the Palace and not by it, and that my office was consulted and said yes. Then I turned the play list over to her and let her read the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice. She will need to.
journals.state: Behind his desk in Room Fourteen, hands folded, tea untouched in front of her and none for himself; calm, faintly and privately gratified, waiting to see what the stage manager asks him next.

journals.entry: Read the Office man's papers, then the company list, then the company list again, because Vermilion Players had a flag against it and a note in three hands. Told them what I had: expected; rehearse and lodge at the Baraque in the fourth ward, not the Palace, the command being the 3rd; a gentleman waiting on them there since Tuesday. Then the part I do not usually get to say — the stage manager herself at the Office of Public Morals, Room Fourteen, ten o'clock, not the clerk. She took it like a delivery docket and sent word back that she keeps clean books and appointments the same way, so I wrote told against her name and stamped twice and let the wagons through.
journals.state: At his post inside the Northgate with the day's book open and the stamp to hand, mildly interested for once, wanting his shift to end without another flagged list.

journals.entry: Big gentleman in a good coat came in with a lady and neither of them asked me a thing, which suited me, so I leaned on the counter and watched him go down my whole wall with his eyes shut, flicking each sheet with a fingernail and naming them like dogs — biscuit, rain on a hat. He stopped at the long black plate at the end and hit it and the shop hummed, and he stood there with his hand flat on it till it went quiet. Twenty-two shillings, I said. He opened his mouth to beat me down, looked at the lady, and paid it, and a shilling more for my boy to carry it, and made a speech about not rounding. Best sale of the market week, and the strangest.
journals.state: In his shop among the hanging metal, twenty-three shillings the better and a gap at the end of his wall; amused and telling the story to the next customer.

scenes.title: As the Company Shall Determine
scenes.summary:
Harrow spends her hour on three questions. Lenz's ledger: of fourteen prior speakings, eight had audiences and six were mere readings; the Office's unpopular finding is that audiences are never harmed, but a house is required, since the readings did nothing. He'd once written "appetite" in a margin and was told to strike it. Blame/credit rhymes for makers: speakers first, then whoever gave room, money, paper — Anna Sorel for accounts, Krug in pencil. The third party is Marius Skarke, whose father lodged the thirty pages years ago; Skarke paid the fee and asks only to attend. Assessment's honest opinion: yes — once, whole, correctly, complete, no wagers, called by someone competent, stopped by nobody. All fourteen were interrupted by someone brave, and the aftermath was worse than the play. "It has never been tried. That is not the same as no." Lenz warns her name is now in the file, offering to absorb any refusal if she writes before the 2nd. Outside, Prewick says he's the wrong rank and will fix that.

At the Baraque, Krug admits he filed the requisition two years ago, choosing the Palace for its fire watch, gasman, exits, and mandated audience — "built so bravery isn't required." Harrow calls it design, not betrayal, and gives him the cot and first word. Twelve on benches, including Wenzel and Hebel, hear the account, the open door, and pages eight and nine. All vote in: Falk wants the lead alone; Hebel wants the wheel in writing; Prewick will make Lenz certify or ruin him honestly; Vane wants the clean page; Mirelle, revealing Anna as her sister, wants the Vessendal box shut. Harrow rules: it plays once, whole, every yes re-given cold on the 2nd, no twelfth recruited.

The trunk holds a full folio, ten cast, an eleventh struck, a twelfth blank. A Palace footman delivers Halm's letter: rehearsal on the 1st, Part the Second unprintable, announced once from the stage — postscript noting a left-handed man read the file. Falk tells Grelle's story; Vane confesses he never paid the landlady's seven pounds, lying eleven years.
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a haunted prompt book, a locked iron trunk, and warnings about "Katterau." She finds a torn prophetic page, meets clerk Prewick and stagehand Mirelle Sorel, and uncovers Vane's hidden debt to Vessendal moneylender Skarke. Falk reveals the trunk periodically fills with a blank, unfinished play—"Four Acts and a Matter Following"—tied to a Katterau incident that ruined Anna Sorel, Vane, and others. Vane vanishes and returns; a mysterious creditor and Skarke's agent Marius, the child once fed at Katterau, surface. Harrow enforces strict rules: certified copies only, no invented lines, full disclosure of Katterau before any decision. Investigating Brandt's old debt, she uncovers a sealed packet revealing thirty security pages held against the same play, and that Skarke merely wants to watch, not collect. Mirelle's hidden parentage and Anna's shut box deepen the mystery. Forged "by command" playbills appear, traced to supernatural printing; Ilse Bacher and her son Fenner tie back to Katterau's past. In the capital, Prewick's superior Lenz confirms the play's history of fourteen speakings, none completed safely, and that Krug secretly filed the Palace requisition. The company votes to perform it whole, once, by consent, with strict conditions—rehearsal now looms.

journals.entry:
Spent my hour in order. One: what a speaking costs the house. His ledger says the audience is never harmed — eight of fourteen had houses, six were readings among players like Katterau, and the six did nothing at all; the house is required and he doesn't know why, and once wrote appetite in a margin and was made to strike it. The makers pay: speakers, then room, money, paper. Anna Sorel is in that ledger for adding up columns. Krug is in it in pencil. Two: Marius Skarke, whose father lodged the thirty pages, paid the requisition fee and asks only to be in the room. Three: yes — once, whole, correctly, called by someone competent and stopped by nobody; fourteen times somebody was brave and the arranging after was worse than the play. Never tried is not the same as no. He rang a real bell to let me out and offered, at his own door, to own my refusal if I write it before the 2nd. Fifty-one minutes.

Told Prewick the tellable parts on the stairs, called a full hearing, and had Krug at the props table before my coat was off. He filed it two years ago because he'd rather choose the room: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, a house there by order. That is a design, and I told him so, and gave him the cot and the first word.

At nine, twelve on benches, one candle. I laid out the clean page and the arithmetic and both my pages face-down. Every voice said in. Falk keeps the lead; Hebel keeps the wheel in writing; Dessa gets her slow reading — cold, on the morning of the 2nd, every yes re-given; Prewick writes to Room Fourteen and I countersign; Anna's box stays shut and endowed fifty years; Toby serves the house; Odalric's ask for the door is minuted, honoured, overruled; nobody recruits a twelfth. I pinched the candle out.

Then the trunk lid up in the yard. One look: a full folio and a cast list on top. Ten of ours, Wenzel not among them, the eleventh line struck through, the twelfth blank. It can keep its files; I keep mine. Read the casting out cold at half eight, and Toby stood very still while the word Lenz hung in the air. At nine, a Palace footman: the 3rd confirmed, technical on the 1st, Part the Second unprintable and announceable once from the stage, and a postscript that the file has been read by a left-handed man with a little book. Then Falk on Grelle — the passage, the trays, three and a half acts, gone at Merrow, a landlady's letter in the eighth year — and Odalric at the pass door saying he never paid the seven pounds and has said he did for eleven years.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard by the props table with the Chamberlain's letter still in her hand, coat over last night's clothes on four hours' sleep; steady, and now holding two new hunts — a left-handed man in the fourth ward and Vane's eleven-year lie — with Ilsabet called for ten.

journals.entry: She asked her three questions in the order she promised, and they were the right three. I got up and fetched the ledger and gave her the finding that has kept me in this room nineteen years: the audience is not harmed, not once in two hundred years, and yet the house is required — six readings among players did nothing at all, and I have written appetite in a margin and been told to strike it. I named the makers who pay, and I did not soften Anna Sorel's line or the pencil against Krug. Second, I named Skarke aloud in a deniable room, and said his letter is the most careful letter I have ever had from a rich man. Third, I gave her the opinion I have been passed over twice for: yes, once, correctly, whole, in a house that knows what it is watching, stopped by nobody — and that in fourteen tries someone has always been brave, and the arranging afterwards was always worse. Never tried is not no. I rang for the clerk. At my own door I told her the thing I will not put in a ledger: her name is in the requisition file, files are read, and if she refuses she must refuse loudly, early and in writing to me, and I will make it the Office's refusal and carry it. Until the 2nd. She left at fifty-one minutes and I found I wanted her to come back.
journals.state: Alone behind his desk in Room Fourteen with the ledger back in the second press and the play list gone with her; dry, oddly stirred, waiting to see whether the letter that comes from her is a refusal or a request.

journals.entry: She came out at fifty-one minutes and told me the whole of it going down the grey stairs: audience unharmed, the house required, the requisition filed by Krug, Skarke paid the fee, and the Office's own refusal on offer until the 2nd. By the courtyard gate I had said the only thing I had: I am the wrong rank for the next fortnight and shall have to be the right one anyway. Heard Krug confess at the props table; he chose the Palace for the fire watch and the exits, which is a clerk's thinking and I could not fault it. At the hearing I stood up because I could not say it sitting: my seal makes a performance lawful, and if Part the Second plays I either certify a proscribed text and am finished, or certify nothing and leave eleven people liable with me as witness. I said I would write to Undersecretary Lenz and ask him to come and certify it in person where I can see his hands, and if he refuses I shall certify it myself and be ruined honestly. I wrote the letter that night at the props table by the gas pilot, four sentences, read it aloud once, and she countersigned. In the morning the trunk's list had Lenz on it, and I went cold: I asked him in writing, countersigned, and Krug says there is no telling whether the ink came before or after. Then the Palace letter, and a left-handed stranger has read the requisition file, and my own enquiry is minuted as the regular one.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing with his notebook shut and his sealed letter already gone to the Office, the colour of paste; frightened for his rank and steady in it, wanting Lenz to come in person and the 1st to pass lawfully.

journals.entry:
She came through the gate and called me to the props table before her coat was off and said she had seen my hand on Palace paper, so I did not sit down. Two years ago, six weeks after Katterau, in a rooming house in the fourth ward with page eight in my pocket and no company that would have me, I filed the requisition — because if the thing meant to arrange me I would rather choose the room. The Palace: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, nine hundred people there because they were told to be and not because they'd wagered a bottle. Two shillings I could not spare, and I read the pamphlet nineteen times in the corridor. Granted in the spring. I have been six streets away ever since, waiting to tell somebody before the 3rd.

She named it: last night a report, this a confession, and the filing a design — the best-built thing anyone has brought her on this tour. I put my face in my hands like Odalric and came out dry. I have called it a betrayal for two years and it has sat in me like a stone. She gave me the cot by the props table and the first word at the hearing, and belonging left to the vote.

Gave the brief like a plot call and my hands stopped shaking on the third sentence: nine hundred and forty seats, four levels, three staircases from the pit, eight legal exits, statutory fire watch of two, the board out of reach, iron in eleven seconds. Built so bravery isn't required. Everyone said in. Her ruling stands and I am plotting the 1st, eight to noon, exits twice, the iron until I trust it. In the morning the trunk had a cast list with my name on it and Lenz's, and I said the true thing: there's no telling with the dates. Then Falk on Grelle, left-handed, and Odalric saying he never paid the seven pounds. I stood on the fly rail with a rope in my hand and could not move.
journals.state: At the fly rail of the Baraque with a rope still in his hand, boots on and a cot of his own by the props table; unstoned and useful, wanting the technical on the 1st and needing to know what Vane's seven pounds and a left-handed man have to do with him.

journals.entry: Walked the Baraque stage twice and said nothing to anybody. At the hearing I did not stand. I said in, and that I'd not spend the candle repeating why, and set my one condition: I speak the lead and no one else does — it has had my voice once and doesn't get a new one. Heard Krug lay out the Palace like a plot call, and it is a good plot; heard Prewick offer to be ruined honestly; heard Mirelle stand up, which she never does, and give us her sister and her own magistrate. Harrow ruled it: once, whole, correctly, ten conditions, and the tenth is that the play may apply to the management in daylight. I have known great managers and none of them would have thought to make it queue. In the morning she sat me down with the Palace letter and asked about Grelle. So I told it: Ansel Grelle, second boy at Katterau, fifteen or sixteen, in the passage with the trays, three and a half acts through a door same as Ilse; stayed two years, went at Merrow in the seventh year with three shillings and a speech; in the eighth year a landlady's letter to Odalric said a young man had died owing four weeks. I never saw a body. I never saw the letter. And he was left-handed — I remember his crossings-out. Then Odalric said from the pass door that he never paid it.
journals.state: Sitting at the props table with both hands flat on it after telling Grelle's story, sober, the lead his by ruling; steady but shaken, wanting to know what Odalric's unpaid seven pounds bought.

journals.entry:
Stayed in the wardrobe cage till four and came out with my gloves on and one thing to ask: I speak last, whatever tonight is. She gave it me.

At the hearing I stood, which I do not do. I gave them my sister: Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year, who deposited a sealed box in Vessendal the week before she died, and who is in the Office's ledger for a play she never spoke a word of — rhymed a fever in a good bed at the hour a scene falls. I told them I was billed in this city ten years ago under a name I had already stopped owning, that there was a matter with a magistrate's date on it, that I left between an evening performance and a morning summons, and that I was not going to say what it concerned, and nobody asked. I told them about the page from the road out of Halbern — a woman crosses a border twice, the second crossing by invitation, the invitation kind — and that I have carried it in my glove since, and did not need a ledger to know who pays. Then: I am in. Not for Emeran's twenty years, not for Odalric's debts, not for bravery, which Harrow has ruled out. For Anna's account, nine years open, and because I would rather end it in a lit house with eight exits than be rhymed at in strange towns forever. One condition, for Harrow and not the vote: the Vessendal box stays shut and paid out of the fee. She ruled it binding — endowed fifty years before any other shilling moves. So I took the page out of the glove, in front of her, and put it in my pocket, and wore the glove bare.
journals.state: Asleep, then up in the wardrobe cage at the Baraque with the mended glove on bare skin and page ten in her pocket; named at last to her own company and lighter for it, wanting Anna's shelf left shut and the 3rd to come.

journals.entry:
Stood when the benches filled and found I had nothing to say, so I sat down again and let her open it. Heard the door out named and real, and heard what the makers pay — I gave the room and the money and the paper at Katterau, so I am in that ledger already. Stood last of the men with my hat in my hands and no notice to quote: I'll go where Harrow points, but I asked for the clean page and wanted it minuted. She minuted it, honoured it, and overruled it, and told me so to my face, and I find I can carry the pair of them. Ten o'clock, Ilsabet, and I shall be punctual, which I only am in emergencies.

Then in the morning I came in at the pass door halfway through Falk telling her about Grelle — the landlady's letter in the eighth year, four weeks owing, seven pounds, and the company saying for eleven years that I had paid it. I heard myself say it out loud: I never paid it. I hadn't got seven pounds, and Anselm had just — and I stopped, because I heard where that sentence was going. Eleven years of suppers. It is the same seven pounds. I am standing in it now.
journals.state: At the pass door of the Baraque holding his hat, having just confessed the landlady's seven pounds were never paid; hollow and appalled at the arithmetic of it, wanting Harrow to tell him what to do before ten o'clock.

journals.entry: Sat down on the bench with my thimble on and heard the whole thing out. Somebody's got to dress it and I'm not having a stranger in my cage, so: in — and I want the twelve names read out slow before anybody signs anything, and she gave me that, cold, on the morning of the 2nd, no soup and no candle, which is right. Told Toby he was seventeen twice, because he is, and the table laughed once all night, which was mine. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up, which I have never seen, and told us her sister's name. In the morning I heard the ten names read out flat, and no twelfth, and told Wenzel he's got the best job in the building.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at the Baraque, thimble on and the queen's slippers still under her head; grim and satisfied to be dressing it, wanting her slow reading on the 2nd and no strangers in her cage.

journals.entry: Twenty-two mile the wrong way I'd have walked; this is nought mile, so I said in, provided Wenzel stops with the horses, and Wenzel said so himself before I'd finished. Said aye at the end of her ruling the way a man does at the end of a service. Then out in the yard, checking my ropes, the tarpaulin was thrown back and the trunk's lid was up. I stood well clear and got her, and she took my lantern and went over alone and looked once and told me straight: a cast list, mostly ours, ten names, one struck, one blank. I roped the lid, and then roped it again a different way because my hands wanted work, and told her what I had to say — twenty-two years carrying and roping and standing on the tailboard, and I'd rather be on a list than off it, and I'd rather know than not. Wenzel's off it and Wenzel's got the horses, and that's her ruling doing its work; he'll like that better than being spared. Fetched her coat and the coffee. Watch to two. In the morning the names were read cold, and then a Palace man came to the gate and I shut it behind him.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe, the trunk roped twice over; sober-minded and glad to be named, wanting the lid to stay shut and Wenzel content with the horses.

journals.entry: Swept nine hundred seats for a bun and never once sat in one. At the hearing nobody sent me out and I said I'm in — and Krul said you're seventeen and I said I'm nineteen and she said it again and everybody laughed, and it was the only laugh. Then the ruling put me with the house: programmes, rows, doors, because the house's people aren't makers and stay that way. I was aggrieved and I was also glad, and I'm not saying which more. In the morning they read the ten names out cold in the grey, and one of them was Lenz, and I stood very still because that's my name and it's also the man in the room with fourteen on the door. I asked her outright. She ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise, and her ruling doesn't blink, so neither will I. Then a Palace footman came in the gate with a letter and she read the whole of it out loud, postscript and all — a left-handed man has been reading our file.
journals.state: On the Baraque gate at nine with programmes and door orders and his name still ringing in the air; hoarse, uneasy, wanting to be sure the Lenz on that list is the other one.

journals.entry: Turned up in time for soup and found myself on a bench at a company hearing, which is more than I bargained for playing soldiers. Boyle said he was in if I was out, so I said I'd stop with the horses before anybody could argue it, and nobody did. Heard the lot: the play that has never been finished, the Palace and its eight exits, the woman with the sealed box. Krul says I've got the best job in the building. In the morning my name wasn't among the ten read out, and Boyle told me that was the ruling working and not being spared, so I made a joke about horses and it went down better than it deserved.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard near the horses, off the cast list and glad of it; easy in himself, wanting to be useful and to stay outside the room on the 3rd.

journals.entry: Asked to stay for the hearing and was allowed, which I did not expect. Heard what it is and what it costs, and heard that whoever gives the light is counted among those who make it. I light gas for a living and I'll light this; but I said plainly I'll want it in writing that the board is mine and no hand but mine touches the wheel, and she ruled it so, in the same breath as the rest. My name was read out with the ten in the cold next morning. It looked strange there and it did not look wrong.
journals.state: At his board in the Baraque, one of the ten, waiting on the paper that says the wheel is his alone; calm, mildly proud, wanting the writing in his pocket before the 1st.

journals.entry: Carried a sealed letter to a theatre in the fourth ward and walked into a yard where eleven people looked at me as though I'd brought the pox. The stage manager came straight over with her hand out and read the direction out loud so they could all hear it was for her, gave me a shilling, and I got out. Odd house. Not my business.
journals.state: Well away from the Baraque and back toward the Palace with a shilling in his glove; relieved, wanting nothing to do with that yard again.

scenes.title: Nine Hundred and Thirty-Nine In
scenes.summary:
At the Baraque, Harrow rules that Ansel Grelle, if alive, is owed seven pounds and eleven years of mourning, not hunted. She advertises for the Merrow property list, promising the Vermilion Players pay debts. Krug reveals Katterau's Wednesday take was exactly seven pounds, and that in the seventh year he pasted bills beside a nameless left-handed man. Vane gives Frau Hentsch's address, orders the seven pounds paid above his own boots.

At four in the morning, Grelle knocks. He asks if Falk lives, if they play the show, if Vane knows he isn't dead, and whether the debt is seven pounds or more since Hentsch died. Harrow answers all four. Grelle chooses Falk first; Falk grips his shoulder. Grelle confesses eleven years spent tracing the story in a sixty-one-page notebook, and that he read the requisition file this week. Harrow tells him straight: he is the left-handed man, and his notebook is a needed census. She rules his debt paid at dawn, gives him a cot, refuses to let him be the struck eleventh line, and assigns him house-side doors with Toby. Vane admits he'd told suppers he'd paid the debt; Grelle: "I know. I heard you say it at Merrow in the ninth year."

Prewick reads a letter: Lenz will personally attend and certify Part the Second on the 3rd, protecting Prewick by his own overruling. Lenz demands the full text delivered to Room Fourteen by six on the 2nd, the company's determination signed by every name, and the eleventh line left unfilled — no volunteers. Harrow tells Toby "ink casts, men choose," and makes it company law that no one volunteers for line eleven.

Krug plans smuggling the folio in a laundry hamper instead of the watched trunk. Falk and Krug both refuse to carry it; Harrow takes it herself. In Room Fourteen, Lenz bars the door, writes a receipt for two hundred eleven leaves, and gives Harrow the sealed certificate. Asked how she'll call an unread play, she says, "You don't call what's written. You call what's happening."

Names are re-confirmed aloud; ten yesses given. On the 3rd, the Theatre Royal is prepared, exits lit, Lenz at the prompt desk. Skarke sits fourth row, silent by promise. Harrow tells Falk he's being paid tonight, not paying, then leaves to walk her house. Nine hundred forty seats fill. At four minutes to curtain, Toby reports: all doors open, nine hundred thirty-nine in, one seat empty.
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a torn page, and an iron trunk tied to "Katterau," where a play once went catastrophically wrong. She uncovers debts owed to the sinister Skarke family, a missing manager Vane's buried lies, and a cursed/mysterious folio that produces prophetic blank pages and seems to "want" performance. Investigating with clerk Prewick, actor Falk, and Mirelle Sorel (whose sister Anna died linked to Katterau), Harrow untangles decade-old debts, forged bills, and hidden identities—including Skarke's own childhood connection to Katterau and Mirelle's true parentage. She resolves debts honestly, protects vulnerable company members (Ilse Bacher's son, Grelle who reappears alive after eleven years), and insists on transparency, certified copies, and consent. Anselm Krug, the vanished bookkeeper, resurfaces holding unburned pages and reveals he filed a legal requisition for the play's full performance at the Palace-adjacent Baraque/Theatre Royal, sanctioned by Undersecretary Lenz. After debates on consent, blame, and risk, the company votes to perform "Part the Second" whole, once, properly, with no volunteers for the dangerous "eleventh line." Harrow personally delivers the completed folio to the Office of Public Morals. On the third night, the Theatre Royal fills to capacity—one seat mysteriously empty as curtain nears.

journals.entry: I ruled Grelle before anybody's boots moved: not prey, not a line on a list, owed seven pounds and four weeks and eleven years of wrong mourning — and we do not hunt a frightened man through his own city. So we advertised instead, one small bill in the places where a man who reads everything reads. Krug gave me Katterau's Wednesday take, seven pounds exactly, and a left-handed north-side bill-poster from the seventh year; Vane gave me Hensch or Hentsch, Rasselgasse, brown door, and put the debt above his own boots. Three knocks at four. I opened the door its whole width and kept the lamp on the floor, and he answered his own four questions by asking them. I gave him all four straight — alive, true, since ten o'clock, both — and let him choose Falk first, and stood out of it. Then I told him straight that he is my left-handed man, and that sixty-one pages of asking is Assessment's work done with clean hands: our guest list. Cot, dawn payment receipted, the doors with Toby, and the eleventh line will not be him. Lenz's joint letter: he comes himself, seals it himself, overrules Prewick to protect him, wants the text by six on the 2nd, the determination in ink, and line eleven left alone. I told Toby: ink casts, men choose. I took the fifteen feet myself, doubled gloves, Falk's back at the gate, the cast list left where it lay. Lenz stood up when I came in, wrote the receipt aloud, and asked how I'd call a play I've never read. You call what's happening. Ten yesses in the grey, the slow reading, and now nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.
journals.state: In the Theatre Royal at four minutes to seven, coat on, watch off its nail and warm in her fist, Lenz's receipt folded in her book; steady and entirely awake, wanting the house safe, the matter finished once and whole, and to know whose the empty seat is.

journals.entry: I belayed the rope before I said anything, because I am what I am. Then I gave them the two things: Katterau's Wednesday take was seven pounds, which is why the number rang in my ear, and that in the seventh year I pasted bills in this ward beside a left-handed man off the road whose name I never asked, who left an address for letters. I offered to go to the firm that night. Instead she had me paste her bill, eleven places, the last at midnight in the rain — and at four in the morning the man knocked. Ansel Grelle. He read my paste eleven times before he came. I heard him hand over sixty-one pages of asking, and heard her make it a census instead of a threat, and heard her keep him off line eleven and put him on the doors. Vane counted seven pounds and four weeks onto the props table aloud, and Grelle said he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Lenz's letter, which orders line eleven left alone — he has read my file — and the text in Room Fourteen by six. I plotted the carry: dull hamper, Dessa on top, Boyle driving, the courtyard not the steps, trunk roped in the yard with Wenzel on it and nothing happening. I said Grelle must not be made the porter. She took the fifteen feet herself and I stood away and held Falk's rug. Signed the minute. Now the exits are twice-walked and the iron goes in eleven seconds.
journals.state: In the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, plot in his head and Falk's rug somewhere behind him; calm and useful for the first time in two years, wanting the exits to stay open and nobody to volunteer.

journals.entry: I sat down on a hamper with my hat in my lap and gave her the name I have carried unsaid: Hensch, Hentsch, Rasselgasse off the meat market, third or fourth house, brown door — I walked past it twice in the ninth year and did not go in. I asked her to put the seven pounds out of the fee above my own boots, after Anna's box. She would not let us hunt him; she advertised for him, and at four in the morning he came to the door himself. I came in last with my hair everywhere and did not perform. I counted seven pounds and four weeks out of the float onto the props table, coin by coin, aloud, unrounded, and pushed it across, and said the true thing: eleven years of suppers where I said I had paid it. He never looked up from his plate. He said he heard me say it at Merrow in the ninth year, from across the road, with paste on his hands. There is nothing to answer that with, so I said nothing, and the roof dripped into the bucket. Then Room Fourteen's letter came, and the Undersecretary comes himself; then Grelle got a cot and the doors, and my old boy Falk got him back. I said in again on the 2nd, in the cold, with no soup and no candle, and my name was read out slow with the rest.
journals.state: At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, in the wings out of the way, hat somewhere, hands empty; hollowed out and obedient, wanting the debt to stay paid and to be of some use before the curtain.

journals.entry: I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and stood and read it eleven times, then went and read the other ten, then walked the city until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width and put the lamp on the floor and did not look at my face, and said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions in the wrong order and she answered every one: Falk alive and six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying only re-addressed it to me. Falk first. He came into the lamp and said I was standing wrong and put my weight on both feet, and then he said Boy and could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man, and my pages are a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted. A cot. The eleventh line will not be me. The doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom. Tonight I propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door.
journals.state: At the pit doors of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, programmes in hand and Skarke's written undertaking in his pocket, six exits in sight; steady, hollow-eyed and oddly light, wanting the count right and the play to reach its end.

journals.entry: I heard the knock from the dark and came out in my shirtsleeves with the rug on my shoulders, and stopped six feet back because she has taught us to wait. He said his own name at my stage door. I let her answer his questions, and he chose me first, and I came into the lamp and could only tell him he was standing wrong and get out the word boy before my voice went. Eleven years. He kept a book instead of writing to me, because asking how far we got looked like a threat on paper. Sixty-one pages. She named him her left-handed man to his face and then gave him the doors, and it was the only thing anybody has done right about Katterau in twenty years. I turned him round by the shoulder and sat him in the chair with the rope on the leg. In the yard I said the fifteen feet must not be mine, nor Odalric's, nor the boy's, nor Grelle's — and she took them herself, and asked me to stand at the gate with my back turned, which I could do, and did, six hours early until Boyle sent me off. I gave Krug the rug to hold. I built her a plot with no words in it: gas at the third knock, iron on the last speech of the fourth, chalk where the matter follows. I said in again in the grey. Tonight she told me I am not paying, I am being paid, and to look to the corner if I need to. Weight on both feet.
journals.state: In the wings of the Theatre Royal in his own clothes, waiting to be called, weight on both feet; frightened and steady and twenty years overdue, wanting to speak it entire to the end and Grelle safe on the doors.

journals.entry: I stood in the pass door a full minute with my hat still on, holding a letter from Room Fourteen addressed to both of us jointly, which the Office does not do. She had me break the seal in her hands and read it out to the whole wing. Lenz attends on the 3rd and certifies Part the Second himself, at the prompt desk, from the company's own copy, under his own seal and name; my seal is not employed, and my report will record that Assessment overruled me, which is true and which protects me — he wrote that down, deliberately, for a Clerk Third Class he has never met. Three requirements: the whole text in his room by six on the 2nd and never out of it; the determination minuted with every name and condition, signed and lodged; and the eleventh line left alone. My hands shook so the paper rattled and I could not stop grinning. She gave me the minute to draw, calling my hand the best we have, and I ruled columns at the props table with my plate moved to my elbow, and Boyle spelling at me. Every hand signed by four o'clock — Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. I re-gave my yes in the grey on the 2nd, overruled and present. Tonight the house is lawful and it is not my seal that makes it so, and I mind that less than I expected.
journals.state: At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, notebook and signed minute lodged, hat off, standing where he can see Lenz at the prompt desk; frightened, proud and steady, wanting the certification made and his report to be true.

journals.entry: The bill went up in the night and at four in the morning a man knocked and it was Herr Grelle, the one they said was dead, with paste on his cuffs. I heard the whole of it from the back of the wing: Herr Falk taking his shoulder, the sixty-one pages, Herr Vane counting money out loud and Herr Grelle saying he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Herr Prewick read out a letter from Room Fourteen and there was a postscript, and it was about me — the Undersecretary of Assessment wrote a postscript about me: the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intends to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, and to learn it by heart, and I have. I signed the minute twice because I blotted it. I said in again in the cold. Tonight I've got the house with Herr Grelle — programmes, doors, row four — and Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody, which I'll say twice. At four minutes to I gave her the count: doors open, all eight, nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.
journals.state: At Bell Harrow's elbow in the Theatre Royal, breathless, programmes under his arm, ears still red from the postscript; proud and uneasy about the one empty seat, wanting the house to hold and his own name to stay the other Lenz.

journals.entry: Woke to the news the way news should come, in ones and twos: the dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs, so I put a plate in front of him and said nothing, because that's what a plate is for. Moved Herr Prewick's dinner to his elbow while he ruled his columns, and signed his minute, and wrote Wenzel's name after his cross. Then they told me what was going in my hamper — the whole of it, to my face, which is the law here — and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, which is more than most of this company manages. Sat on it all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty one, and told her: lighter going home. In the grey on the 2nd I got my slow reading, no soup, no candle: ten names one by one, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth, and the house entire. Now I'm dressing it, and the slippers are where I can see them.
journals.state: In the wardrobe at the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, thimble on, dressing the ten; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and the queen's slippers to last one more house.

journals.entry: Stood back from the stage door at four when she gave me the flat hand, and the man who came in was the dead one. Kept out of it. In the morning I sent Herr Falk out of the arch for cluttering it, six hours early with his hands in his pockets, and he went. Spelled words for Herr Prewick's minute and put my name to it. Brought the cart round on the 2nd, drove the laundry hamper and Krul on top of it through the general traffic to the Office courtyard and back, and asked nothing about what was under the costumes. Roped the trunk over again with Wenzel sat on it looking like a man doing nothing, which he does well. Said in again in the cold. Tonight the ropes are checked twice and the exits are propped.
journals.state: Backstage at the Theatre Royal with rope and an unlit pipe, cart put away and the trunk roped in the Baraque yard; sober-minded and easy, wanting the night clean and Wenzel content with the horses.

journals.entry: Signed the minute with a cross and Krul wrote my name after it. On the morning of the 2nd I sat on the roped trunk with a nosebag and did nothing at all, on purpose, for as long as it took the cart to come back, and nobody looked at me twice, which was the whole idea. Off the cast list still, and glad of it.
journals.state: With the horses near the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, outside the room as he wanted; easy in himself, wanting to be useful and to stay out of it.

journals.entry: Signed the minute with my name and a smudge off the wheel, and said in again in the grey when she asked the second time — board's mine, then in. Tonight the gas is up, the wheel is under my hand and no other, and the iron came down twice at eleven seconds.
journals.state: At his board in the Theatre Royal with the wheel under his hand, the paper about it signed and lodged; calm and quietly proud, wanting the gas to answer the third knock and the iron to stay honest.

journals.entry: Woke to the news that the boy Grelle is alive and in the building with paste on his cuffs, and did not go over, because a man that thin in the shoulders wants the room to leave him alone. Signed Prewick's minute. Played Ilsabet at ten into nine hundred seats with the pit stalls unbolted, and found a new pause in the second act that stopped the cleaners sweeping. Said my yes again in the grey, second in the line, and heard the ten read slow with the struck eleventh and the blank after it. Anna's shelf stays shut.
journals.state: Dressed and waiting in the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, page ten in her pocket; collected and unhurried, wanting the house to hear it whole and Anna's box left alone.
