journals.entry: I wrote them jointly, which this Office does not do, because their letter was the first application in nineteen years made in the correct order. I set my three requirements — the text in my hands and not out of this room by six on the 2nd, the determination minuted and signed and lodged, the eleventh line left alone — and I put in writing that Prewick was overruled by Assessment, which is true and which will keep his rank. I added a postscript about the boy, because ink is not consent. At nine on the 2nd she came up my east stair carrying it herself in both arms, and I stood, and took it from underneath, and told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following; I wrote the receipt out loud as a courtesy to a woman who keeps clean books, and gave her the sealed certificate with it — proof against a magistrate, which is all paper is good for. Then I asked her, out of order, how she means to call a play she has never read a word of, and she said you don't call what's written, you call what's happening, and I wrote it in my own notebook, not the folder. My predecessor's file says Katterau failed because no stage manager was present; nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours to read it. Tonight I am at the prompt desk with the folio squared and one page turned down.
journals.state: At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal at a quarter to seven, spectacles on, the folio squared before him with one page turned down, his own seal to hand; dry-mouthed and more moved than he will show, wanting to certify it whole and no one to volunteer.

journals.entry: I paid at the door like anybody and took my seat, fourth row centre, in a plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, the programme shut on my knee. I had written my undertaking out beforehand and given it to the man on the pit doors: I will not move from this seat and I will not say one word of it aloud. When she passed at hat-distance I told her so, without turning, and let her see my hands shaking, and said the only other true thing I had: it's a lovely house.
journals.state: Seated fourth row centre in the Theatre Royal with an unopened programme on his knee and no rug; shaking slightly, frightened and happy, wanting to hear it finished on the hour and to be allowed no nearer than this.

scenes.title: The Fifteenth Speaking
scenes.summary:
Row eleven, seat one stays sold and empty — confirmed with Toby before the night begins. *Ilsabet's Ransom* plays to full houses: Falk stops the show, Vane weeps on cue, Hebel's gaswork excels, four curtain calls for Falk alone. Nobody leaves at interval.

Chamberlain's letter permits one stage announcement. Harrow goes out in working clothes, names herself, explains the play has no title, is two hundred years old, and was never finished — no watcher has ever come to harm, "an actuary's word," and he sits at her prompt desk. She asks only for witness, notes the lit exits, warns latecomers will be known, and declares seat one "sold and empty and stays so." She announces the Vermilion Players will finish the play tonight. No applause; roughly twenty leave, including a woman with three children escorted out by Grelle. Skarke stays. Lenz calls it "the correct order." Falk asks what play he's in; Harrow tells him to count the wings. Hebel dims to half; Falk begins from memory.

Lenz warns of three scripted knocks. On the third, Boyle admits a billsticker and a ten-year-old boy asking if this is the finish; Harrow confirms it. The acts proceed. Lenz notes the closing "matter" begins with a bell whose ringer's line has always been blank. Harrow rings it herself, answers "Beginners, please," and realizes the two-hundred-year flaw: no one ever answered before. Final lines are spoken; Lenz declares it "Certified." The curtain falls; the house rises without applause.

The visitor is Fenn Halloran, billsticker; the boy is Fenner Bacher, abandoned by a gloved woman who promised to return. Harrow takes him into the company's care and wires Bailiff Kessel through Lenz. Over soup, Fenner mentions a lady visited his mother Tuesday. Mirelle pales, recalling a similar letter from a "Frau Dietz" about a child placed out years earlier, with instructions to stay silent. Suspecting a bank connection, she sends Harrow to Skarke, who names a Kanzelgasse firm handling such placements — and admits he personally paid tonight's requisition fee, meaning those clerks have known of the booking for two years. Then Grelle cries out front as footsteps approach, unannounced.
scenes.history: At the Theatre Royal after the performance, footsteps approach unannounced as Grelle cries out front. Two women arrive: one claims Fenner as her charge, showing a Kanzelgasse placement paper; the other, veiled, says nothing but watches Mirelle intently. Harrow refuses to release Fenner without Kessel present, citing the night's own rule against unwitnessed transactions. Skarke, still lingering, recognizes the veiled woman from his father's ledgers—she was the courier who once delivered sealed packets between Katterau and the capital. Mirelle confronts her, demanding to know about "Frau Dietz" and the placed-out child; the woman admits only that "the arrangement continues while the debt does," then withdraws before Kessel's men arrive. Lenz, still certifying paperwork, notes the Office now has an interest in Kanzelgasse. Prewick begins drafting a formal inquiry. Falk, exhausted, watches Harrow manage it all and says quietly that the play is finished but the company's true business—debts, children, silences—never ends. Harrow orders everyone fed, the boy kept close, and the ledger of names started again from the beginning.

journals.entry: Row eleven, seat one, prompt side by the exit — sold, empty, and I put a programme on it and entered it as heard. Then Part the First, and two hours of only being a stage manager, which was the last easy thing tonight. I gave Toby my watch and went out in my working clothes and told nine hundred and thirty-nine people the truth in the order it would hold: no title, four acts and a matter following, never finished, no watcher ever harmed and an actuary at my prompt desk to swear it; witness asked, exits lit, children by open doors, latecomers known, and row eleven let be. Twenty-odd left and nobody clapped and the rest settled like a jury. Falk asked me what he was in and I said the one with the ending, and told him to count the wings. Lenz read me the shapes; when he said the knock comes from outside the building I sent Boyle to the wrong door and Toby at a walk with my exact words. Three knocks, and a billsticker with paste on his cuffs and a boy of ten who asked if this was the finish. Yes. In time for it. Asked-for, not expected. Nothing changed on the wheel. Then the bell on my desk — I rang it once and answered it myself, because in my house nothing rings unanswered, and that was the whole of the two hundred years: fourteen bells and nobody on duty. Heard. Certified, said Lenz; iron in eleven seconds; 10:22. Halloran, the boy is Fenner Bacher, put out of a cab by a gloved woman. Wire to Kessel by Room Fourteen. Mirelle's letter from Frau Dietz — her own child, ten this winter, placed out in the fifth year, and a boy used as a sentence. Skarke can find the money in four days and wants nothing, and paid our fee through the Kanzelgasse, so those clerks have had us for two years. Then footsteps down the aisle, unannounced.
journals.state: In the fourth row of the emptied Theatre Royal beside Skarke, watch in her fist, coat on, chalk still on her; finished and wide awake and hardening, wanting the boy safe, two mothers answered, and to see who is coming down her aisle.

journals.entry: I gave her the seat — row eleven, seat one, end of the row, prompt side by the exit, sold on the plan and nobody in it — and put a programme on it and went back to the pit door where Herr Grelle could see me. Part the First was the biggest thing I have stood in; the roar for Herr Falk went on eleven seconds and I counted it. At the interval nobody went out, and I told her so with my voice gone. Then she handed me her watch and went out in front of them all and said it plain, and afterwards I gave the watch back with both hands and couldn't say anything. When the knock was coming she gave me her words to carry and I walked, I did not run. The boy came in out of the dark holding a man's hand and asked out loud if this was the finish, and she said yes, and I took his other hand and gave him a programme and walked him to row eleven, seat one, and sat on the aisle step within arm's reach all night and never once looked at the stage. After the bell and the iron I still had his hand. Madam Harrow said he stays with me till somebody claims him properly and nobody claims him improperly. I showed him the black sheet and let him shake it low, and he ate two bowls, and he told us a lady in a cab said he was expected and that the stage manager would know his name. She did.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing on a cot beside Fenner Bacher, programmes done with, ears hot and voice gone; proud and fiercely protective, wanting nobody to take the boy off him tonight.

journals.entry: I sat at the prompt desk with the folio squared and my seal to hand and watched a stage manager take an announcement out in front of nine hundred and thirty-nine people in her working clothes and put it in the only order that could have held: no title, the record, the actuary at her elbow, witness asked, exits lit, no bravery required, one seat let be. Nobody applauded. Twenty went, decently. I stood and told her it was the correct order and turned my marked page face-down. Then Falk began from memory and nothing in the building went cold, and I read her the shapes as they came — the knock written not as a sound but as three knocks from outside the theatre, and she said 'Then we answer it,' and called me the best flyman she had ever had. She rang the bell herself and answered it aloud, and the house breathed in, and I understood what nineteen years of file could not tell me. Falk nine lines, Sorel four, Vane one and he did not round it, and then the three of them standing still and the house entire. I said 'Certified,' loudly, in the Office's voice, and the iron came in at eleven seconds. Afterwards I authorised the night telegraph for Assessment for a lost child, in my own name, and did not ask whether that is within my competence.
journals.state: At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal squaring the certified folio, spectacles pushed up, seal used; steadied and privately shaken, wanting the minute lodged and the boy's people fetched before morning.

journals.entry: Part the First in a Palace: they roared eleven seconds at my entrance and I stood in it and gave them nothing extra, because that is not what tonight was for. At the interval she went out and told them the truth in her working clothes, and twenty went and nine hundred stayed, and it was not an audience after that. I asked her what I was in and she said the one with the ending, and told me to count the wings, and I did. The gas came down slow as a sunrise and I walked into the warm and began it, and the first line was only a line — a man saying good words — and nothing went cold. Eighteen minutes of a house waiting for someone, and it is a great play, which nobody warned me of. Then the knock came through the walls, three, and I turned my head an inch toward the wrong door and twenty years went through it, and Boyle opened it and let in the cold and a boy asking if this was the finish. I crossed to the wrong door in my own play and spoke the line I have not spoken in twenty years. At the bell she said Beginners, and I lifted my head and said my nine lines and stood still with Mirelle and Odalric while the house looked at us. Then I put my head down and Lenz said Certified.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing in his own clothes, spent and steady, twenty years lighter; wanting soup, the boy looked after, and to say nothing clever about it tonight.

journals.entry:
I had the first scene and they gave up their coughing by my fourth line, which is only ever the house, not me. Harrow went out and told them plainly what they were in, and nobody applauded, and I have never been so glad of a silence. I stepped past her into the light for an entrance I had never rehearsed and spoke it as if I had written it. Then the knock came from outside the walls, three of them, and I used the pause, because that is what a pause is for. Four lines in the matter following, and standing still with Emeran and Odalric while nine hundred people looked at us: that is what the copyist wrote, and it worked. Certified, and the iron.

Then soup in the wing, and a boy of ten saying a lady in a cab, on Tuesday, and my hands stopped working. Harrow picked up the other half of the cloak and folded it with me facing the wall, which is the oldest privacy we have, and I gave it to her at last: Frau Dietz at the wardrobe cage on Tuesday, gloves, good paper, a kind letter — the matter of ten years ago a misunderstanding, a family glad to receive me, the child placed out in the fifth year well brought up and ten this winter and might be brought to see me, and not a word to anyone out of delicacy. Two days I sat on it while a gloved woman went to Achterhalt and made Ilse Bacher cry. It is not Fenner; I know what I bore and what I signed. They used a child as a sentence. I told her to put all of it in the book and to ask her small man in black what a bank knows. I am done being delicate.
journals.state: Standing in the O.P. wing with a folded queen's cloak set down, paper-white and perfectly quiet; wanting the boy home, the letter in Harrow's book, and the money behind Frau Dietz named.

journals.entry: I wept at the top of act three on cue and meant every drop of it, which has not happened to me in years. At the interval I came to her corner with my hat off and said nothing while she went out and told them the truth instead of selling it, and no one clapped, and I found I was glad. In Part the Second I discovered I had an entrance in the matter following; nobody told me; I took it, hat in hand, and said my one line, which is a number, and I did not round it. Then we three stood still and let nine hundred people look at us, and Lenz said Certified, and the iron came down. Afterwards there was soup in the wing and a strange boy in it, and a gloved woman in a cab somewhere in the city, and Mirelle going the colour of paper at the word Tuesday.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing in the plum coat with his hat in his hand, hollow and unusually quiet; wanting to be of use to whoever asks and not to be thanked.

journals.entry: I stood the whole of it at the fly rail with my hand on the wood and my lips four words behind, following from memory, nine pages and eleven years of it, and every line came out of that man's mouth better than I ever had it. Her announcement was the correct order and I had nothing to add. When the knock came through the walls my hand went to the pin rail and stayed on the wood, and Boyle opened the wrong door and nobody had to be brave. Lenz's caution about the bell was right — the ringer's line blank in every copy, and page eight of mine saying a stage manager rings it — and she rang it and then answered it herself, out loud, and I understood two years of stone in one second. Falk's nine, Sorel's four, Vane's number unrounded, and the house entire. Certified. I dropped the iron: eleven seconds, as plotted. Nobody volunteered. Nobody moved. The exits stayed open.
journals.state: On the fly floor by the dropped iron, hands flat on the rail, plot finished in his head; steady and emptied out, wanting the house cleared slow and the exits kept propped till the last man's gone.

journals.entry: Board mine, wheel under my hand, and nobody else touched it. Part the First went as rehearsed and she said afterwards it was the best gas she'd worked with, which I shall keep. For Part the Second she gave me house to half, stage to warm, slow as a sunrise, all night and it's ours — so I took the wheel in both hands and brought them down gold to amber to shadow slower than I have ever brought a house down. Falk walked into the warm and the gas never fluttered once, not on the knock, not on the bell. When the strangers came in at the wrong door she said nothing changes on the wheel, and I said nothing changes, and it didn't. Certified, and the iron in eleven seconds, and the house out slow and warm after.
journals.state: At his board with the wheel still under his palm, bringing the house lights up slow; calm and quietly proud, wanting the last of them out without a stumble.

journals.entry: Toby came down at a walk with her words, exact, and I took the stage door — the wrong door, out of sight of every soul in the house. Lamp low, light on the boards and not in a man's face, open wide on the third knock and not before. The knocks came through the wall, plain as a cart in the street. Three, and I opened it wide, and the cold of the yard came in along the boards, and there stood a billsticker with paste dried on his cuffs and a boy of ten by the hand asking out loud if this was the finish. I let them by to her and stood my post. Ropes were checked twice and the exits propped, and Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised.
journals.state: Backstage at the Theatre Royal with his lamp and an unlit pipe, the wrong door shut behind him; sober and easy, wanting the house out clean and the trunk still roped in the Baraque yard.

journals.entry: Dressed the ten and got them on and the queen's slippers lasted the house, which is all I asked. I stood in the wing for the matter following where a child up in row eleven could see my thimble catch the light, because she'd said stand where he can see you. Certified, and the iron, and then soup in the O.P. wing, which that wing has never had. I made a nest of the queen's cloaks and I did not fuss over the boy once, which is why he stopped being frightened, and he ate two bowls. When the kind question was put he said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday. I saw Frau Sorel go the colour of paper with a cloak half over her arm and I kept my mouth shut and my hands moving.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing among the queen's cloaks with the boy fed and Toby's cot beside him, thimble still on; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and that child claimed by his own mother and no one else.

journals.entry: I stood where I could see everyone's hands and stopped pretending to be anything but a member of this company. Her announcement was in the correct order and Lenz said so aloud. Then Part the Second, and the knock through the walls, and the bell she rang and answered herself, and Lenz's 'Certified' in the Office's own voice, and the iron at eleven seconds. My seal stayed unemployed and my report will be true. Afterwards she wanted a wire tonight and I said Room Fourteen's channel; Lenz authorised it without looking up — say Assessment, say his name, and if the operator refuses, Room Fourteen reads his file in the morning. It went at twenty to eleven: FENNER SAFE, IN THE VERMILION PLAYERS' KEEPING, CAPITAL, UNHURT. COME BY FIRST COACH. FARE PAID AT THE DOOR. — HARROW. A constable to the Bacher farm by morning.
journals.state: Coming back from the night telegraph into the O.P. wing, notebook open at last, hat off; frightened, proud and steady, wanting Kessel's answer before dawn and his report to record it whole.

journals.entry: Pit doors, house-side, six exits in sight, and Skarke's written promise in my pocket. When she told them the truth from the stage nobody clapped, and then people began to move, and I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it and said what I could to make it easy for her; a drover came down from the gods to sit closer, which I did not expect. Then two hours of hearing it through the doors — the play they got as far as at Katterau, the whole of it, the bell, and Lenz saying Certified — and I stood at the pit door with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors, as ordered. The man who knocked at the wrong door turns out to be Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he read my paste eleven times, the same as I did. Afterwards a gentleman came in past me who would not be announced and would not be stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.
journals.state: In the foyer of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, calling after the unannounced man on the aisle carpet; hollow, light, and instantly on his guard again.

journals.entry: I did not move a muscle when she offered the doors, and nine hundred-odd stayed with me. I heard it finished on the hour, from row four, with the programme shut on my knee, and I looked at the iron afterwards with the whole of it behind it. She came out through the pass door and sat one seat away and told me: it finished. Then she asked for the bank in me and not the boy, and I gave it: a placement is a standing order that never varies and never gets queried, the only entry in a great house's accounts identical to the penny for eighteen years; Dietz is no name to me but the pattern is — a firm in the Kanzelgasse doing nothing else for four families, always gloved women with plain names, the fee paid quarterly out of the account that pays the florist, because nobody audits flowers. I can find who paid for a child placed out of this city in the fifth year in three days, four at most, and I will want nothing for it, and she will have to let me want nothing. Then I told her the thing she would not like: I paid the requisition fee, but through the Kanzelgasse, which is how my sort pays untraceably — so those same clerks have known for two years that these people were coming to the Palace on the 3rd, which of them, and with what. Someone was coming down the aisle as I said it.
journals.state: Still in row four with the unopened programme on his knee, hands flat on his knees, the bank in his face instead of the boy; frightened for them and steady, wanting a name, a date or a ward, and to be allowed to give this for nothing.

journals.entry: There was a boy on the Baraque step this afternoon on his own — a lady brought him in a cab, put him out, said be good and she'd be back, and she didn't go in, and she never came back. Stage door shut, nobody in the yard but a man sat on a trunk who wouldn't shift off it and said fetch you and he couldn't leave his post. So I took the child to my room and gave him bread and he wouldn't eat it, and he said he was expected at the theatre tonight. Ansel's pasted their bills all over my half of the wall this week and I've read every one eleven times — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I went to the door I knew and knocked three times. It opened wide with a lamp low on the boards and the boy asked out loud if this was the finish and she said yes, and told us we were asked-for, not expected. Then she put me at her corner and I stood there with my mouth open for the rest of it and never said a word, and I could not tell you afterwards what I had seen. When it ended I found I was wiping my eyes with a paste-white cuff. She asked my name and I gave it — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her he wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, and he can read. She said I'd done every part of it right and called it three debts, and that I'd eat with them and be walked home by a man with a lantern. All I did was knock.
journals.state: At Harrow's prompt corner turned wing-side, paste dried white on his cuffs, hatless, being fed; dazed and wrung out and half proud, wanting to see the boy claimed and then his own bed.

journals.entry: The lady in the cab said I was expected and gave me a bun and put me out at a theatre and never came back, and Mam said go and be good and she'd fetch me after. The man with the paste took me to his room and gave me bread but I wasn't hungry. Then we went to a door round the dark side and he knocked three times and it opened and there was a lamp on the floor and warm coming out, and I asked if this was the finish, and the lady said yes and that I was in time for it, and that I was asked-for. A boy called Toby took my hand and gave me a programme and put me in row eleven, seat one, right by a lit door, and sat on the step next to me the whole time and never looked at the stage. There was a play about a house and a man who owed money, and a boy in a passage who asked a question, and this time somebody answered him. Then a bell rang and everybody stood up and made a noise that wasn't clapping. After, there was soup in the wing and a lady with a thimble made me a bed out of cloaks and didn't fuss, and I had two bowls, and Toby showed me the big black sheet that's the thunder and let me shake it low.
journals.state: On a nest of queen's cloaks in the O.P. wing with a programme on his knees and Toby beside him, fed and warm; not frightened any more, wanting to shake the thunder again and for Mam to come.

journals.entry: Sent round to that theatre again on the 3rd, and this time I got no further than the corridor door. Told the stage manager there was a gentleman at the front of house who would not come in and would not go away — small man in black — and that he said to say he was still in row four and would wait till she was free. She took it without a blink. Odd house. Cold soup smell in the wings and a child in it. Not my business.
journals.state: In the corridor doorway of the Theatre Royal, message delivered, already backing out; incurious and eager to be gone, wanting to be back at the Palace before eleven.

scenes.title: Given, Not Collected
scenes.summary:
In the emptied Theatre Royal, Harrow blocks the aisle before the pass door — a boy asleep behind it — and demands name and business. It is Ilse Bacher, arrived off the ten o'clock goods train in a horse-box, gloves stripped off and fisted; she has already moved Grelle off the door. She explains in a rush: a gloved lady came Tuesday, knew about the Rose and the door she'd opened, lied that a bill in Achterhalt carried her name, and said Fenner's only safety was to be seen and counted somewhere respectable — a theatre, the capital, a programme — so his name would sit in the right ledger. The lady left a five-pound note and vanished. Harrow's wire to Kessel had already put a constable at Ilse's gate. Harrow says "Unhurt. Fed twice," takes the note as "Exhibit, not money," and opens the pass door full width.

The reunion follows: Fenner runs to Ilse, who kneels; Krul boils water; Toby faces a rope; Prewick removes his hat; Falk comes only as far as the wardrobe cage, exchanging "Ilse of the Rose" / "Twenty years." Skarke, at Harrow's elbow, identifies the note as one of ten from a sealed Kanzelgasse hundred, sequentially numbered, and says he can name the family by noon. Harrow ends the night: beds found, Halloran walked home by Boyle, Grelle forgiven, a lamp sent to Wenzel.

Lenz, at the prompt desk, describes an unused procedure — retiring a proscribed work, sealed and Index-annotated — requiring certified performance, the company's consent, and every copy surrendered before the 6th. Harrow agrees on condition "each piece is given, not collected," producing the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight face-down, "surrendered unread." She books the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum for joy alone — "By command: ours" — and tells Vane the company is solvent; he admits why he hired her.

Next day, Skarke names Behn & Sonder, note six, the Vorn family, including Hessel Vorn, and delivers the thirty pages to Lenz. At the Baraque, Mirelle reveals to Harrow: Rupert Vorn, a child born the fifth year, an extortion summons, ten years' silence — "my son." She writes four rules in Harrow's book and signs her true name. On the 6th the lead case is soldered: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. On the stair, Lenz says there was never an eleventh part — the copyist struck the line because Harrow had already ruled nobody could volunteer: "You struck it, madam. Nine days before it was written."
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and a chalk-marked iron trunk tied to Katterau, an unfinished, prophetic play. Clerk Prewick, carpenter Falk, actress Mirelle Sorel, and manager Vane draw her into buried debts: Vane's unpaid loan from the dying Brandt, secured by "a play" rather than money, and creditor Skarke's inheritance of thirty lodged pages. Investigating registries, executors, and forged bills, Harrow uncovers Katterau's history—vanished bookkeeper Krug, wronged carpenter Grelle, Mirelle's hidden son Rupert Vorn, and Falk's guilt. She insists on honesty, certified copies, and paid debts throughout the tour (Vessendal, Achterhalt), while blank pages keep predicting real events. In the capital, Undersecretary Lenz reveals the play's Index history: fourteen partial "speakings," never completed. The company votes to perform it whole, under Office supervision, at the Theatre Royal. Harrow manages logistics, rules, and revelations—including abandoned boy Fenner Bacher, tied to a mysterious "Frau Dietz" and Kanzelgasse placements—while the performance proceeds successfully, certified by Lenz. Ilse Bacher's arrival resolves Fenner's crisis. Afterward, Lenz arranges the play's formal retirement, sealing all copies. Skarke identifies the note's origin family; Mirelle confesses her son's parentage. The case is closed, though Lenz notes Harrow unknowingly preempted the play's missing eleventh line before it was even written.

journals.entry: Footsteps down my aisle and I was in front of the pass door before I knew it, because a boy was asleep behind it. It was Ilse Bacher off a goods train in a horse-box, gloves in her fist, and she had shifted Grelle off my door and I don't blame her. A gloved woman had been in her kitchen Tuesday with the bolt on: a lie about a bill with her name near it, and the only safety being the boy seen and counted somewhere respectable with a programme, and five pounds left on the table. I told her unhurt, fed twice, laughing at my props boy; took the note by one corner as exhibit not money; held the door its whole width and warned her about the third board, which sang anyway. Then I stood out of the way of a mother on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal, and heard Falk say Ilse of the Rose from ten feet off and go no closer. Skarke read the note without touching it: a sealed Kanzelgasse hundred, numbered, ten to a wrapper — a family by noon. I struck the night: beds, Boyle's lantern for Halloran, Grelle stood down and forgiven twice over, a lamp across town to Wenzel. Lenz offered retirement: accounted closed, sealed under the Hall of Records, every copy in by the 6th. I gave him yes with one condition of manner — given, not collected, and me standing at each. I laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight face-down, unread and now never read; he underlined the word. Then I booked the 14th of Frost for nothing but joy — by command: ours — and put Vane in it, and he told the doorframe why he hired me. Noon at the bank: Behn & Sonder, note six, the Vorn family, and Hessel Vorn's stamp on Katterau. Skarke carried his own thirty to Room Fourteen. At the Baraque I sat on a hamper and took Mirelle's whole account, her name in ink once, Rupert Vorn, the lying-in house, the ward she was never told, the extortion summons, and my son said out loud. I gave her four steps; she took my pencil and ruled them in my own book and signed her true name. Thursday the paper died. On the 6th I watched the case soldered and stamped twice straight, and on the stair Lenz told me there is no eleventh part and never was — it wrote a line for one more maker, and I had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, so the copyist struck it. Nine days before it was written.
journals.state: Coming back up the Depository stair beside Lenz in her better coat, book under her arm, chalk long since washed off; hollowed out, level, and quietly appalled at what she has just been told, wanting to get to the 14th of Frost and hold the ladder for Mirelle.

journals.entry: Off the ten o'clock goods in a horse-box with the cows and walked in from the yards, and a man on the door said Fenner was inside and safe and then said I couldn't come in, so I moved him, and I am sorry for him. Then a woman standing across the pass door like a gate, asking my name and my business in that order, and I gave them and asked where my son was. She said unhurt, fed twice, laughing at her props boy, and I could hear him through the door. I told her the whole of Tuesday — the lady who knew about the Rose and the door I opened, the bill with my name near it that never existed, the being seen and counted at a theatre so his name went in the right ledger, and the five pounds left on my own table, which I have carried since and every hour of it wrong. She took it off me by one corner and called it evidence, and said it stops owning me now. Then she opened the door its whole width and told me to mind the third board. I went down on my knees on that stage floor and had the whole of him against my coat. Emeran Falk stood by the wardrobe cage and did not come nearer, and I said his name and he said mine, and twenty years. A little bald gentleman looked at my five-pound note as if it were a snake and said he could find the family by noon. They kept us in the nest of queen's cloaks, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper and our fares paid and the poster man walked us to the coach office. I have promised: the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, in at the front door, good seats, and Bacher with us.
journals.state: On the midday coach out of the capital with Fenner against her shoulder and Krul's hamper at her feet, fares paid; wrung out and fiercely grateful, wanting her own bolt on her own door and the 14th of Frost to come.

journals.entry: I was laughing at Toby when the board sang, and it was Mam. I ran and she got down on her knees on the stage and didn't let go for ages and cried into my hair. The lady with the thimble went and boiled water. Then we slept in the cloaks together, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper and the man with the paste on his hands walked us to the coach. Mam says we're going to the theatre again on the 14th, in at the front door, with Da.
journals.state: On the midday coach beside his mother with a programme still folded in his pocket; sleepy, happy and full of porridge, wanting to shake the thunder sheet again on the 14th.

journals.entry: I lost my door. A woman came at me out of the dark saying her son was inside and she went past me like weather, and I ran the aisle after her and stopped dead when Madam Harrow put her hand up. Then I stood at the top of the aisle and watched a mother get her boy back, and Madam Harrow told me the door I couldn't hold was a mother-shaped door, forgiven twice over, stand down. In the morning I asked to walk them to the coach office, because I have been on the wrong side of every departure in eleven years and wanted once to be on the right side of one. I carried the hamper. The boy waved from the step. Then back to the Baraque and a broom, and somewhere in the afternoon I heard myself laugh out loud in a theatre.
journals.state: In the Baraque with a broom and his coat brushed, back on the doors; hollow, light, and unaccountably cheerful, wanting to be given another door to hold.

journals.entry: Board sang, boy was off the nest like a hare, and there was his mother down on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal with the whole of him against her coat. I put down my thimble and went and boiled water, because there is nothing else to be done with a thing like that. Sat on a stool by the nest all night with the two of them asleep in the queen's cloaks and said sssh to nobody at least once. In the morning: porridge, and I packed them a hamper for the coach and made her promise to come the 14th and bring the butter man. Nobody in my cage, and that child claimed by his own mother. That's the whole of what I wanted and I got it.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the cloaks aired and the slippers mended, thimble on; tired and thoroughly satisfied, wanting a quiet week and a hamper packed for Vessendal.

journals.entry: I was making Fenner laugh and then the third board went and he was gone off the cot at a dead run, and it was his Mam. I went and stood at the pin rail and looked hard at a rope, because it wasn't my business any more and I wasn't going to be seen minding. She got down on the boards with him. Later Madam Harrow struck the night like a set and somebody was sent across town to fetch Wenzel in, and I'd have gone if my voice had been working. In the morning there was porridge and they went on the midday coach, and Herr Grelle carried the hamper. Herr Vane says I may hold the doors on the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum. So that's mine.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with his voice half back and a props list in his fist; a bit flattened by the departure and proud about the 14th, wanting a job to do this minute.

journals.entry: I was in the corridor doorway when the mother came through the pass door, and I took my hat off, which is not in any instruction I have ever been given. I wrote nothing while it happened. Afterwards I heard Assessment offer retirement of a proscribed work — accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck — and heard that my minute, signed by every hand including a cross and a smudge, is one of the three legs it stands on. Nineteen years in that Index and it goes out on a signature I drew at a props table. Harrow required that every page be given and not collected, and Lenz wrote unread and underlined it. My report will record all of it whole, including that Assessment overruled me and that I obeyed on purpose.
journals.state: At the props table in the Baraque with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, drafting the report; steadier than he has been since Merrow, wanting Kessel's answer and his own copy of Lenz's inventory.

journals.entry: I came as far as the wardrobe cage and no further, because a woman kneeling on the boards with her boy does not need me nearer. She looked up over his head and said my name — Emeran Falk — and I said Ilse of the Rose, and twenty years, and put my hand over my own mouth like a man at a graveside, and that was the whole of what I had. Then the settle from Ilsabet, the rug over my knees, my hands steady, eyes shut, and the house going out lamp by lamp. In the days after I took the lining to Room Fourteen myself with the rug on: ten leaves and some odd, unpicked out of my coat and put down on a government desk. Lenz stood up for it. Twenty years of ballast, and I walked out lighter than the arithmetic allows. The 14th of Frost at Loewe's, Ilsabet, doors wide, played for nothing. I told Krug our left, you see, and meant it.
journals.state: On the Baraque stage in his own coat with the lining empty and the rug over his arm, teaching Krug a crossing; spent, easy, twenty years lighter, wanting soup and the 14th.

journals.entry: Stood in the wing with my lamp when the mother came through and did not say a word, which was the right amount to say. Orders came quick: I was to walk the bill-poster home behind the lantern, so I did, all the way to the north side, and he talked the whole way about a lamp on the floor. Then across town with another lamp to fetch Wenzel off that trunk, and he argued about it, and lost, and slept against it in the yard till morning. Since then it's been ropes and hampers and the trunk still roped in the Baraque yard, empty as a bucket now, they tell me. And a booking: the 14th at Vessendal, front doors wide, and Wenzel on the horses and told to his face it's the best job in the building.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with his lamp hung up and the unlit pipe in his teeth, checking the ropes on an empty trunk; sober and content, wanting the wagons loaded early for Vessendal.

journals.entry: I followed her in where a man of my standing has no business standing, hat in my hands, and saw a mother get her son back on a stage floor. Then I asked to see the five-pound note without touching it and knew it at once: not out of a purse — out of a sealed hundred, ten to a wrapper, drawn by the Kanzelgasse for the families, numbered in sequence. I said I would have the family by noon and she let me want nothing for it, which cost her something. By noon I had it: drawn the 9th of Reap out of Behn & Sonder against fees for one client, note number six, and of their four clients the Vorn family — the house at the Bittersee, and a Hessel Vorn who stamped SEEN, NOT APPROVED at Katterau in the fifth year. The same family that has paid a placement out of this city since the fifth year and sent a gloved woman into two kitchens this week, and I do not yet know why, and I will in three days. Then I lifted my father's thirty pages out of the strongbox to give her — and took them back, because she had told Lenz given, not collected. I carried them to Room Fourteen myself and said over them that my father lodged them against seven pounds and a wool factor's kindness, that I had wanted them for twenty years, and that they were never mine. Lenz stood up for it and read the receipt aloud. She put her hand out to me across a government desk. Second time. I am to audit a nursery next, and report to Frau Sorel and not to them.
journals.state: Back in his own office in a plain black coat, wrapper and slip locked away, the strongbox empty for the first time in twenty years; frightened, useful and oddly light, wanting the Vorns' reason inside three days and to be allowed to want nothing.

journals.entry: I sat at the prompt desk squaring two hundred and eleven leaves while a woman came through the pass door for her child, and I did not intrude on it. When Harrow came to me I did not stand up, because I had a thing to say and wanted my hands on the folio while I said it. Two entries: what Assessment wants, and what Assessment can do. In law the folio goes back in the trunk and my office minds it another nineteen years — unless we are clever, and there is a procedure unused since the eleventh year: retirement. Certified as accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck. Three requirements, and I had two of them in my hands already: the certified performance with the audience noted, and Prewick's minute with every name. The third was the entire text, and I asked her at last about the leaf in her coat. She gave me yes with a condition I shall keep for the rest of my service: given, not collected, each holder surrendering by their own hand, herself standing at each. She laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and one leaf face-down — page the eighth, surrendered unread. I wrote unread and underlined it and shall forbid my successor to correct it. Then I walked home, which I have never once wanted to do. In the days after I sat from nine and stood up for each: Skarke's thirty, Falk's ten and some odd out of a coat lining, Frau Sorel's single page carried alone. On the 6th, three floors under the Hall of Records, I put the whole of it into a lead case, had the seam soldered, stamped twice straight, and labelled it: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. Shelf, row nine. On the stair I gave her my finding, having read every leaf twice, which nobody else alive can say: there is no eleventh part and never was. It wrote an eleventh line because it expected one more maker, and she had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, and the copyist strikes what is not needed. She struck it nine days before it was written.
journals.state: On the Depository stair with the keeper's lamp behind him, spectacles pushed up, hands empty of the folio for good; steady and inwardly shaken, wanting the annotation lodged in the Index today and never to be told he was wrong about the eleventh line.

journals.entry: Nobody touched my wheel but me, and I brought the whole of that enormous house down slow, lamp by lamp, till there was nothing but the pilot — one blue tooth of flame and the smell of nine hundred and forty people cooling. There was a mother and a child asleep in the cloaks in the wing and I gave them no glare to sleep in. Best gas I have ever done, twice over.
journals.state: At his board with the wheel shut off and the pilot burning, coat on to go; calm and quietly proud, wanting his bed and the same board on the 14th.

journals.entry: I stood at her corner with my hat in my hand like a man waiting to be told what he is in, and she told me: a solvent company, a certified miracle behind it, no man's debt on it. And a booking — the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, one night only, by command, because the bill exists and the words on it are ours now. Ilsabet, front doors standing wide, played for nothing but joy, Loewe's house, Perlmann on his daughter's arm, Ilse and the boy in through the front door in the good seats, and our dead toasted at the interval: Hessel, Anna, Frau Hentsch, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house. I opened my mouth to weep and decided not to, which I count as the best work I have done all tour. By command: ours — I shall have it printed in Hessler's own case with a note that the man was blameless. Loewe gets fifteen and not a penny rounded down. Then at the pass door I told the doorframe the thing I have not said: nineteen days, and I hired her in ten minutes because the last one left in the night at Katterau and I would rather have died than tell her why, and she may put in the book that I have said why. Next day I drove her to the bank, and the lift boy called me sir, and a young man listened to me on the acoustics of the Corn Exchange for a quarter of an hour.
journals.state: In the Baraque in the plum coat with his hat brushed, printer's copy for a new bill in his pocket; sober, useful and almost unbearably grateful, wanting the 14th of Frost done handsomely and nobody to thank him for it.

journals.entry: Sat on that trunk in the yard from the afternoon on, doing nothing, as arranged. Then a man came across town with a lamp very late and told me it was finished and the boy was safe, neither of which I knew, and said I was relieved. I argued. I lost. So I stopped where I was and slept against the thing, and it rained on the lid and there was nothing overhead but morning. They tell me the trunk is empty now and the papers gone under the Hall of Records. I have been told to my face that the horses on the 14th of Frost are the best job in the building, and I intend to go on believing it.
journals.state: Asleep and then waking against the roped trunk on the tailboard in the grey, damp and stiff, horses to see to; easy in himself and glad to have been outside the room, wanting breakfast and the horses fed.

journals.entry: I was still at her corner being fed when the boy's mother came through and got down on the floor with him, and I stood there with my mouth open the same as I had all night. Nobody needed me for that part. Then the stage manager said I was to be walked home behind a lantern, and I was — a big fellow with a lamp, all the way to the north side, and I talked the whole way like a fool. Three debts, she called it. All I did was knock on a door.
journals.state: At home in his own room on the north side with paste dried white on his cuffs, boots off; dazed, proud and half asleep, wanting to see the bill for the 14th and to tell somebody who'll believe him.

journals.entry: I was in the wardrobe cage with my sleeves rolled, mending the hem I tore in the second act of a play I had never read, when Harrow came and gave me a name. Behn & Sonder. Note number six. The Vorn family, of the house at the Bittersee — and a Hessel Vorn, district officer, who stamped a notice at Katterau in the fifth year. My needle stopped. Vorn. Well. Ten years I have carried two griefs, and they are one grief: the young man, the summons for a Tuesday, and the child of the fifth year. They have been paying since the fifth year, which means they kept him, which means the kind letter on good paper is not generosity — it is a family that has learned their placement is ten this winter and their name is about to be read out in a Palace by players. I told her to sit down and take out her book, and gave her the whole of it in order, no adjectives: my own name, which she wrote and will not repeat; Rupert Vorn, four nights in the second year, nineteen and charming; the lying-in house in the eighth ward; the papers I signed at twenty-three with no money and no advice; the ward I was promised and never told. The tenth year: Rupert dead in the mountains, the lawyers finding my two letters, and a charge of extortion for asking where my boy had gone. Over the mountains on a Monday night with a passport that spells a Kessarine town, and Odalric hiring me in a yard at Merrow without one question. Ten years of gloves. And then I said it out loud for the first time in my life: my son. She said this cage has good acoustics. Then she gave me four steps — the paper dies first, the keeping verified by my auditor reporting to me, the meeting only if the child is asked and says yes, on my ground, at his pace, and their name never spoken by this company — and handed me the pencil. I wrote them in her book in my own hand and signed my true name, on paper for the first time in ten years. Ruled. Then I put my face in my hands and let her sit there while I cried. Later I carried my one page to Room Fourteen alone, and came back with my gloves folded in my pocket.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the hem finished, gloves folded in her pocket and her name written once in Harrow's book; raw, upright and no longer alone with it, wanting the auditor's report and to be asked nothing until it comes.

journals.entry: Back at the Baraque, plotting nothing dangerous for once. Falk had me out on the stage going through a crossing — our left, you see, she said our left — and I let him teach me a thing I already knew because he wanted to teach it. They tell me the whole text went under the Hall of Records in a lead case, mine included, and that the trunk is a trunk. Two years of stone, and now a hamper to load and a house at Vessendal on the 14th.
journals.state: On the Baraque stage in shirtsleeves with a rope in his hand, taking Falk's crossing; steady and unburdened, wanting the 14th plotted properly and the exits walked twice as usual.

journals.entry: Took a gentleman in a plum coat and a lady with a book up to the top floor, and called him sir, and he went pink about it. Coming down again he stopped in the hall and talked to me for a quarter of an hour about the acoustics of the Corn Exchange, and I listened, because nobody in this building has ever explained anything to me before.
journals.state: Standing in his lift in the marble hall of the Skarke bank with the gate half open; pleased with himself, wanting the plum-coated gentleman to come back and finish about the Corn Exchange.

journals.entry: The Office man came down with a lady in a good coat, three floors under the Hall of Records, and had me solder a lead case: eleven minutes and a stink of hot metal. He would not touch the papers again once they were in. Stamped his seal twice, straight both times, wrote his label, and pasted a second slip beside it saying one leaf was lodged unread and was not to be corrected. I have never carried that instruction before. Shelf, row nine. My key, my iron door.
journals.state: In the Depository among a hundred yards of iron shelving with the key-ring on his hip and the soldering iron cooling; incurious and orderly, wanting the row nine ledger written up before he goes off.

scenes.title: Rain on the Trunk, and Row Four at Katterau
scenes.summary:
Harrow files her correction at the Depository, posts a notice rather than striking any line, and lets the copyist cut what's unneeded. She shakes Lenz's hand and invites him to tea; he agrees to come on the 9th, then goes up to the Hall of Records.

In the Baraque yard, the iron trunk is leaking rain. Boyle points it out; Harrow writes a notice, which Boyle pins to the wet iron on principle. She orders a bucket, then paint—Dessa picks vermilion, two coats, costing Toby his Thursday—and rules the trunk will carry the thunder sheet. Falk calls it "vulgar," approvingly. Skarke's standing invitation goes out in writing; his reply is four words: "Row four. Any night." Wenzel wakes gently and asks if the play was good; Krug says it was a great one.

On the 9th, Lenz drinks three cups of terrible tea over Prewick's fair copy. On the 11th, the wagons roll. Harrow closes the last open account by demanding her own wages; Vane counts out four pounds five and six—two shillings above his hiring rate—and weeps, driving off singing. At Achterhalt, Kessel waves them through and Hessler prints their bill free, keeping one copy for himself.

At Vessendal, Loewe lets the house for thirteen though Vane pays fifteen. Perlmann, walked onstage, says, "It is smaller than it sounds." The house is full and free; Vane toasts absent stage managers. Mirelle delivers Skarke's unopened audit minutes before beginners; Harrow refuses to read it yet, pocketing it, law unchanged.

Later, by the kettle, Mirelle reads it: her son, Anton, is twelve, safely placed with a steward's family, schooled, fed, unable to spell. Harrow rules no hurry—he'll be asked, in spring, on Mirelle's terms. Mirelle asks for time, privacy, and warns she'll one day ask something enormous. Harrow says yes.

Toby reports nine hundred and one paying bodies; Harrow records it, posts nothing. Falk, questioned on the standing page, calls it "a ledger with legs" and is folded into the repertory, tasked with teaching Fenner Bacher to stand.

Winter settles the company. In spring, on the Katterau road, Mirelle asks her enormous thing—a season's leave. Harrow says yes before she finishes. In Katterau, Falk gives away bread, laughs, repeats Perlmann's line. At the half, Krug hands over a slip: one seat sold, row four centre, paid at the door—Skarke, unannounced, "on the hour."
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the struggling Vermilion Players, inheriting a cursed, leaking iron trunk, a torn prophetic prompt page, and tangled debts to creditor Skarke tracing back to Katterau, a town where an unfinished, two-hundred-year-old "play" once nearly happened. She uncovers the histories of Odalric Vane's hidden debts, Falk's guilt, Mirelle Sorel's dead sister Anna and hidden son Rupert/Anton, vanished bookkeeper Anselm Krug, and clerk Prewick's Office files on thirty-one banned works. Through Perlmann, Loewe, Grelle, and Bacher, buried debts, lies, and abandoned children surface, all threading back to the same folio. Official Lenz reveals the play's rules: it must be performed whole, consented, witnessed, never interrupted. Harrow assembles the company, rules on debts and volunteers, and stages the complete play at the Theatre Royal under certification, filling the long-blank "eleventh line" role by ringing the bell herself. The performance succeeds without harm, retiring the work under seal. Aftermath ties loose ends: debts paid, Fenner Bacher reunited with his mother, Skarke identified and reconciled, the trunk repainted vermilion. The company becomes solvent under Harrow's stewardship. In spring, back at Katterau, Mirelle takes leave to see her hidden son, and Skarke quietly attends another performance, seated as always in row four.

journals.entry:
I gave Lenz my correction on the landing — no line struck, a notice posted, the copyist cutting what wasn't needed — and shook his hand and owed him tea. He said the 9th. Then home through the grey, and the trunk in the rain, doing nothing at all but leak, so I wrote it a notice and gave it a bucket and then paint: Dessa's vermilion, and the thunder sheet inside a box that has learned to hold its tongue. Skarke's invitation went in writing and came back four words. On the 11th I closed the last open account in my own book and made Vane count nineteen days into my palm in the arch — four and six, not three shillings, because he'd been paying me in his head since Achterhalt and could not say it without weeping. Four pounds five and six, unrounded, and he drove out singing.

Vessendal free and full, Vane toasting our dead and my whole trade. Mirelle brought me a sealed audit four minutes before beginners; I refused the hour and took the letter into my coat, and after the iron, with the kettle on, she read it standing: he's twelve, and his name is Anton, and he draws and cannot spell. The tens can retire. Spring, her ground, his pace, me present. Row four sold and paid at the door, one and six, no hat — entered exactly, posted nowhere.

Falk taught me how a bookkeeper closes what the world answered: transfer it. So I ruled him into the repertory and into the repertory's work — teaching a boy to stand — and struck the standing page clean across.

Winter, then Katterau by daylight. I stood where he could see me in the Rose and touched nothing, and kept his entry in pencil. Mirelle asked her enormous thing on the box and I said yes before she finished, as contracted. And at the half a slip came from the mayor's clerk: one seat, row four centre, paid at the door, not to be told until now. On the hour.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

journals.entry:
On the landing she entered her correction, and it was better than my finding: she posted a notice and the copyist cut what wasn't needed. I let it stand in the file that way. She put her hand out and called me the best colleague she never met and offered me the worst tea in the fourth ward, so I shook it once and said the 9th, and went up to the Hall of Records with my hat straight.

I went on the 9th and sat on a hamper in the O.P. wing while Prewick, humming with uprightness, read me his fair copy of the minute, and I drank two cups of genuinely terrible tea and then a third. I went twice again in the winter and did the same. Nobody has offered me anything since the eleventh year that I wanted so much.
journals.state: Back at his desk in the Office with the annotation lodged and a folder that no longer frightens him; steady, quietly warm, wanting his invitation to hold good next quarter.

journals.entry:
Oiling a hinge in the yard when she came back, and the rain came on, ordinary rain, and it lay on that trunk and ran off the corner and made a puddle like anything else in the world. I said out loud, Madam, that's leaking, and I have not enjoyed a sentence so much in twenty-two years. She wrote the notice on the spot and I pinned it to the wet iron, and it went to pulp in a minute and I left it, because that's the principle. Vermilion after, two coats, and it holds the thunder now.

Held the float purse while Vane counted her wages out in the arch, and marked the figure: four and six a day, not three shillings. Then first wagon out and a hundred and ten mile north, Achterhalt, Vessendal, and a house at nothing a head. Told the Bacher boy a lie about horses because he'd earned one. Rolled again in the spring for Katterau with the trunk on the tailboard and the props boy asleep against it, and argued a lashing with Krug for pleasure.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.

journals.entry: Asleep against the wheel, off duty, nobody having told me. They woke me gently and sat me down to tell me it was finished, which I said was fair enough — someone had to be off it. I asked was it a good play, and Krug said it was a great one, so that's settled and I went back to sleep. Horses to the capital gate and out again, the horses to Vessendal, the horses to Katterau in the spring. Best job in the building, and I go on believing it.
journals.state: At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.

journals.entry:
That trunk leaked in the rain like a coal scuttle, and I was asked to choose its paint, so I chose vermilion, being what we are, and the ironmonger had it honest. Two coats and Toby's whole Thursday, and Herr Falk stood over it drying and said it was vulgar in the voice men use for praise, and put the thunder in it and shut the lid, and it stayed shut like a box.

I sang the farrier's wife going out under the arch, since somebody had to, and Prewick pretended he didn't know the words. Vessendal for nothing a head and the slippers held. And that night when Vane got loud in the yard I shushed him, because there was a child asleep in the second wagon. In the spring, Katterau, by daylight, front doors wide, and I have my hamper packed and my cage to myself.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked, and I stood over the paint drying and told them it was vulgar, which it is, gloriously, and put my black sheet inside it and shut the lid, and it behaved.

Vessendal stood up before I opened my mouth, in the town where I once sat a night and a day with the gas down. I gave them nothing extra. Then in the dark house afterwards she came out with the standing page — my asking, in her hand, and no answer written — and I told her what I have been a fortnight working out: you don't close it, you transfer it. A company is a ledger with legs. Nine hundred and thirty-nine strangers paid it, and a boy in row eleven, and a man who does not drink, and I did not have to be brave once. Put it where the good notices go, I said, not the crowded page. Then I asked her to rule me something, because I did not know what I was without that question in my mouth, and she said: the repertory. In things, instead of carrying them. I said it twice out loud. Nine o'clock, the Bacher boy, weight on both feet, voice up out of the boots — and the rug is his; his hands will be cold on the cart.

Katterau in the spring is a town with washing out. I looked at the stone front from the box. In the afternoon I walked with her to the Rose, went in the front door, bought a loaf off a girl who has never heard of me, read the room, put my hand flat on the scullery door and did not open it, gave the bread to two children in the yard and laughed. It is smaller than it sounds. Perlmann's note, and mine now.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked. It leaked, and got a bucket and a notice and two coats of vermilion, like anything else that leaks in her house, and I did not say one word about signs and portents.

On the 11th I climbed up, took the reins, and asked her for a thing, and she asked me for money — her own wages, flat palm, in front of the company. So I paid the last account in my book: nineteen days at four and six, four pounds five and six, said twice on purpose, and told her I had been paying her at that figure in my head since Achterhalt and could not think how to say it without weeping, and then wept, and then sang going out the arch.

Achterhalt, Hessler's bill for nothing, a butter cart in my column. Vessendal: Loewe wanted thirteen and I paid fifteen and would not be argued down. Perlmann on my stage in a chair. At the interval I stood out front with my hat off and toasted Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel, Frau Hentsch of the Rasselgasse, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house, and nine hundred drovers drank to it. I counted a take of nothing afterwards and enjoyed it more than any money I ever had. Katterau in the spring, by daylight, front doors, and I drive where she points.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.

journals.entry:
Painted the trunk vermilion — two coats, my whole Thursday, and my hands were red to the wrist and I didn't mind. Ran the tea things on the 9th for the Undersecretary who isn't a relation. Hung off the tailboard out of the capital with the trunk beside me doing nothing at all.

On the 14th at Vessendal I laid a programme on row four centre same as always, though nobody had come, and then the box office slate said nine hundred and one bodies for nine hundred seats and Herr Grelle said the odd one came in late, paid at the door, sat in four centre and left before the calls. I carried it to her in the cage and she said enter it exactly and post nothing. Fenner came in the front door with his Mam and his Da and read the small print about the gas.

Doors at Katterau with Herr Grelle in the spring, and Herr Falk is to teach Fenner to stand at nine o'clock, and Herr Vane says I hold doors wherever we go now. I fell asleep against the trunk twice and it was just a box.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked. I wrote it down, because it is the only line in my notebook this month that required no seal.

On the 9th I read my fair copy of the minute aloud to an Undersecretary of Assessment seated on a laundry hamper in the O.P. wing, and he drank three cups of the worst tea in the capital, and I have never stood straighter in my life. I did not know the words to the song about the farrier's wife going out under the arch and shall continue not to.

My papers came through at midwinter: attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense. My mother now writes weekly to a theatre and is answered. I am comparing the Wolf King against the certified copy at winter quarters and expect to finish before Reap. At Katterau, by daylight, front doors, Hessler's bills ahead of us, nothing has occurred that is not in the book.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

journals.entry:
They woke Wenzel gently and told him sitting down, and he asked was it a good play, and I said it was a great one, because it was, and because he had earned a plain answer.

Second wagon out of the capital, up beside Falk, and we found we could talk for a hundred and ten miles. Vessendal ran itself. Over winter she gave me the second book and the advance work, which suits a man who likes arriving first, so Katterau was billed and papered before we came within sight of it. Load-in ran itself there too, which is what a company is when nothing is owed on it.

At the half in the prompt corner I brought her a folded slip from the stage door and said the first thing that mattered: not a page. Ordinary paper, mayor's clerk. One seat, row four centre, paid at the door, no programme, and not to be told until the half. He says: on the hour. I put my hand on the wood out of habit, and took it off again.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

journals.entry:
Skarke's audit came to me at ten in the morning and I carried it about unopened until I could not bear it, and then took it to Harrow four minutes before beginners and asked her to tell me when. She would not spend my instrument: after the iron, she said, the cage, the kettle, the two of us, and the ruling holds whichever way it reads. She put it in her coat, and I went on and lifted a house of drovers for nothing, which is harder than lifting them for money.

Then the cage, and I broke his seal with my thumb and read all four pages standing up. He is twelve. Twelve, and I have had ten in my head for a decade. Born the fifth year, eighth ward, placed that same month with a steward's brother's family in the Bittersee — not the Vorns — on a standing order that never varied in twelve years, school fees paid, a doctor's bills paid twice. His name is Anton. He draws and cannot spell. There is a schoolmaster's report, three lines, in some stranger's hand, and I sat down on a hamper with it. The pages were never counting his age.

Harrow poured tea and ruled no hurry: he gets asked, my ground, his pace, her present, in the spring. I took the cup and held it. I have never once been allowed to do a thing slowly. So I asked for a needle, my own light, six months and no questions, and warned her I would one day ask her for something enormous.

I asked it on the box on the Katterau road: leave from Reap to Frost, her hand on the letter to the schoolmaster because offices are believed and I write like a woman with something to hide, her standing where I can see her the first day and gone the second, and my place kept in the repertory because I mean to come back. She said yes before I finished, which was annoying, and which was also the contract.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

journals.entry:
Third wagon out of the capital, with the doors of the world in front of me instead of behind. Vessendal on the 14th, all eight open, free house, drovers and wool men, and I had my count and my aisle. Row four centre was sold and I saw the man: came in late by the front door, paid at the door, no hat, no programme, sat, and went before the calls. I told the boy for the slate.

On the gate at Katterau tonight, first watch, unasked. Doors with Toby in the spring, and a broom in between, and there is nothing wrong with any of it.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

journals.entry:
I counted their wagons twice off my own steps and then a third time on account of a butter cart, and told her plainly she had come back with more than she left with, which nobody does. I let them the house at thirteen and Vane paid me fifteen and would not be argued down, which was so offensive I had to go and stand in my box office a while.

Front doors wide, no bellman, no bills but the printer's, and half my market in my house for nothing. Perlmann was carried on to my stage and told where everything was. The storm came out of a painted box and the pit laughed and it did not matter. When Falk came through that door my town stood up before he spoke, and I was in my box office with the door shut, and I shall say nothing about it to anybody. The trough is sheeted. They were out clean.
journals.state: In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.

journals.entry:
They sent for me and Bettina walked me down at ten in the morning, and they put a chair in the middle of a stage I have never seen and told me where everything was — the doors, the corner, the trough, the box that holds the thunder. It is smaller than it sounds, I said, and they took that as though I had given them something.

At night I sat in the house and heard it whole, and when the storm came I said out loud that it was thunder and my daughter shushed me and half the pit laughed. Vane named Hessel at the interval, wool factor, and the woman's sister with him. The paper was enough. Nobody had to tell me.
journals.state: Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse in his chair under the shawl, stick against the arm; spent and lightened, wanting nothing but to be read the notices.

journals.entry: My arm down the steps and along the Kohlgasse and into a theatre, and my father set in a chair in the middle of the stage while they told him where the doors were. He said it was smaller than it sounded and they liked him for it. At night I sat beside him in the house and shushed him when he announced the thunder, and half the pit laughed, and I did not mind, because he was laughing too. Then home, and his chair, and the good kind of tired, which is twice now.
journals.state: In the rooms above the saddler's with the sewing back on her lap and her father asleep in his chair; quietly proud, wanting no more strangers on the stair and one more outing like that one.

journals.entry:
They came through on the second evening and I set the new bill myself, in my own case, with my own hands: the Vermilion Players, Ilsabet's Ransom, the Athenaeum, one night only, and under it BY COMMAND: OURS, which I liked so well I said it out loud twice. I re-set the old standing line off the broken forme from memory, because printers are magpies twice over, and the date, the 14th of Frost, at seven. Took no money for it. Asked to keep one for the shop wall, and it is up there now where the customers can see it, and I sleep.

Set their Katterau bills in the spring as well, ahead of them, daylight and front doors, and no crier and no coin under the stone this time.
journals.state: In his shop at Achterhalt with the case straight and one bill pasted on the wall; proud and sleeping nights, wanting his name on the next one too.

journals.entry: They came back through my square and I waved them on like old custom, which they are now. In the winter they played my town on the Thursday and I sat in the second row with the chain on, which is the whole point of a chain, and the leading man went off with nobody's wife.
journals.state: At home in Achterhalt with the chain in its box and his dinner waiting; pleased with himself and with them, wanting the Corn Exchange let again next season.

journals.entry:
We joined their column at Achterhalt at dawn — Bacher and the cart and the butter — and Fenner rode up beside the props boy the whole way. Vessendal, the 14th, in at the front door with my husband on the other side of him and good seats in the third row, and my boy read the programme down to the small print about the gas. At the interval Vane said the names of dead people out loud and I held Fenner's hand. Nobody looked at us sideways in that house, and nobody had to open a scullery door to let us in.

When they came to Katterau in the spring I sent word I'd rather not, being eleven miles off, and sent butter instead. I have been in that town's Rose and I do not need to go back. Falk knows why.
journals.state: In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.

journals.entry: We went in a butter cart with Da and I rode up with Toby, and at Vessendal we walked in the front door, all three of us, and had seats in the third row, and I read the whole programme even the bit about the gas. It was the same play but bigger and the thunder came out of a box painted red, which I know about, because I helped it dry. I clapped with my hands over my head at the end. Herr Falk is going to teach me how to stand at nine in the morning — both feet, and the voice out of the boots — and he says his rug is mine if I want it because my hands will be cold on the cart.
journals.state: Wrapped in a gentleman's rug in the second wagon or on the cart, programme folded in his pocket; sleepy, proud and impatient, wanting nine o'clock and the thunder sheet again.

journals.entry: Brought the cart up in their column from Achterhalt, and butter with it, and sat in a theatre on the 14th with my wife one side of the boy and me the other, in at the front door, which she made a great deal of and I have come to understand why. Good play. Very loud in the middle. My son knew what the storm was made of and told me so twice.
journals.state: Back at his own churns eleven miles out of Katterau, cart unloaded; plain and content, wanting the next invitation and his boy's boots mended.

journals.entry:
Her invitation came Tuesday, in writing, and I answered it in four words and a signature, because more would have been an imposition. Row four. Any night.

My audit of the Bittersee went where I said it would go — to Frau Sorel, not to them: four pages, the standing order unvaried twelve years, the steward's brother's household and not the Vorns, the fees, the doctor twice, and the schoolmaster's three lines, which cost me nothing and are the only thing in the folder worth having. Twelve, not ten. I did not soften it and I did not add a word of my own.

I went to Vessendal on the 14th and came in late by the front door and paid one and six at the door like anybody and took row four centre with no hat and no programme, and left before the calls, because the calls are theirs. The slate has it, I expect. I audit nothing quarterly now and send it in punctually with the stubs pinned on as receipts.

And at Katterau I bought the same seat off the mayor's clerk and asked that she not be told until the half, and sent word how it is to be read: on the hour.
journals.state: In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.

journals.entry: The players came back to us in daylight with their bills up ahead of them, and I went round to say what needed saying: the old mayor's favour died with him, but I have my own, and they might have the town's fire buckets. Twenty years this town has been waiting for somebody to be brave enough to come back, and we are not going to make a fuss about it. Then I sent my clerk over with a note about a seat.
journals.state: In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.

journals.entry: Big old gentleman in a good coat came in by the front door in the afternoon and bought a loaf and paid what it costs, and then stood in the middle of the taproom looking round the walls like he'd lost something, and put his hand on the scullery door without opening it. Took the bread out to the yard and gave it to the Mahl children, who ran off with it. Then laughed, out there, on his own. There was a woman with him who never touched a thing.
journals.state: Behind the counter of the Rose in Katterau with the dog under her feet and a cloth in her hand; mildly puzzled and already forgetting it, wanting the evening trade in.

scenes.title: Top of List
