scenes.summary:
At Katterau, Harrow's four-word message — "the house knows him" — clears Marius Skarke's seat, and the show plays whole: Mirelle opens, Falk enters through Boyle's door to a standing house, Krug runs gas for the absent Hebel, and the storm comes right. Three curtain calls; Skarke claps and leaves unremarked, owing nothing. Toby's count is full.

Vane rushes in with a letter: a fortnight in Vessendal during Reap, plus Merrow's paying fair — both accepted, and he tells Harrow "ask me for a thing." Harrow rules: Mirelle takes leave by contract, her reasons her own, unquestioned, her name still top-billed in Frost, bookings arranged never over her — and yes to Loewe's fortnight. Vane agrees, hat off. Mirelle asks that the letter to a schoolmaster be written formally, with a Clerk Third Class as reference. The schoolmaster replies that the boy, after two days' thought, asked if the lady was from the bills, and said yes.

In Reap, Harrow waits at the lane's turn while Mirelle walks alone to the boy on the wall, extending a hand she doesn't use; later they sit together over his paper. She leaves the next day, saying only "Frost." The fortnight plays without her and holds.

On the 14th of Frost, at Achterhalt, her letter arrives — she's returning as booked, and "he can spell 'vermilion.'" Harrow chalks her return atop the list; the company absorbs her wordlessly. In her cage: a pencil drawing of a wagon, one correctly spelled word. Ilse, Bacher, and Fenner arrive with butter; Fenner passes Falk's standing test. Privately, Mirelle tells Harrow the schoolmaster wrote to her. The show plays to four calls; Kessel calls it "a fine thing."

Over soup, Vane proposes a second wagon and carried fit-up — eighty-two pounds by Reap. All agree; Mirelle adds two Katterau spring nights. Toby asks to be second stage manager, claiming nineteen; Dessa says eighteen. Harrow approves the wagon, with Vane cutting Hessel Brandt's initials into the first plank, and sets Toby's terms: chalk, bucket rounds, plot tables from Krug, calling the spring storm clean by nineteen. Krug logs it, Falk tells him "weight on both feet." Harrow defines a call as "a promise with a signature on it." Toby writes his, crooked, in nine minutes, and signs it — legible, everyone's name included. Falk: "That's the trade, boy."
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players, inheriting a haunted prompt book, a leaking corner, and an iron trunk tied to Katterau, where a mysterious unfinished, centuries-old play once caused ruin. She uncovers debts, forgeries, and secrets: Vane's hidden loan history with Brandt, Skarke's inherited claim, Krug's guilt and hidden pages, Falk's authorship-by-memory, and Mirelle Sorel's true identity as Anna Sorel's sister and mother to a hidden son, Rupert/Anton. Through investigations, tribunals, and reconciliations—with clerk Prewick, Undersecretary Lenz, bailiffs, printers, and the returned "ghost" Grelle—Harrow assembles the company's tangled debts and histories into order. She rules the play must finally be performed whole, certified, and witnessed, refusing volunteers for its cursed "eleventh line." The performance at the Theatre Royal succeeds without harm, retiring the banned work formally. Aftermath brings restitution: debts paid, relationships mended, Fenner Bacher rescued and adopted into company life, Mirelle reunited with her son, and Skarke transformed from threat to devoted witness. The company gains solvency, a second wagon, and new stage manager Toby. The story closes with the troupe's cyclical touring restored, order maintained through Harrow's discipline, and Katterau's shadow finally settled—not erased, but lived through and closed with dignity.

journals.entry: Four words back with the mayor's clerk — the house knows him — and places, and Katterau got its play whole on the hour in the town that taught everyone the price of stopping early. Krug on the gas, Falk let the standing go on as long as it wanted, the storm came in low with a floor in it. Iron, three calls, row four out with the house, full count. Then Vane in the yard with a letter and two bookings and 'ask me for a thing', so I asked it and ruled it: Reap to Frost held open for Frau Sorel, her reasons hers, nobody to question her, her name at the top in Frost, book around her, never over her. Loewe's fortnight regardless. Mirelle told me how to write the schoolmaster — like a stage manager, not an office — so I did, and his answer said the boy was asked and asked back whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills. At the Bittersee I stood at the turn of the lane and no nearer, watched forty yards, then looked at the water for a quarter of an hour, and kept no entry, the first time in my working life. Coach at seven, 'Frost', 'Frost'. Then Vessendal without her, Merrow's actual money, and on the 14th her letter, and I chalked her onto the tailboard: TOP OF LIST. Took her hatbox at the gate. Left the boy's drawing exactly as propped. Ruled the eighty-two with Hessel Brandt's initials in the first plank, and gave Toby Lenz the book, with terms, and the storm at Katterau in the spring. Then I taught him what a call is, and let him write it himself. It was crooked and it was signed.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

journals.entry: I played the first scene in Katterau and the room forgot its own name, and when Falk came through that door his town stood up and I stood in it. Then Vane in the yard, and the whole cage heard him, and Harrow came in and said it was booked. Reap to Frost. I did not turn round. I told her one thing only: don't write like an office after all — write like a stage manager, tell him a woman is coming who does not perform for the people she cares about, and that she keeps her promises to the minute. Then the lane. He stood up on the wall to be nearer, and I put my hand out and did not touch him, and said something short, and afterwards we sat with his paper between us and he showed me. Two days he thought about it before he said yes; he asked whether I was from the theatre on the bills. At the coach I said Frost and she said Frost. And in Frost I came into that yard and the work stopped for a minute, which from them is an ovation, and nobody asked me one question, and Boyle handed me a hamper because there was a hamper. She had put my hatbox under my own light beside my needle, and against the mirror there was a drawing of a wagon with a red box on it and one word spelled right. I pinned it at eye height. At the half I called her in and told her, because I could not say it in the yard: his schoolmaster wrote to me. To me. Four calls tonight, and I took Falk's hand for the fourth. At the table I said in, and said the spring is Katterau, two nights.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

journals.entry: Katterau had its finish, whole, on the hour, and I shouted myself hoarse and nobody had to thank me. Afterwards I came into the yard with a letter and two bookings said yes to — Vessendal a fortnight in Reap, Merrow's fair paying actual money — and told Harrow to ask me for a thing, and she did, and it cost me my leading lady for a season. Held open, Reap to Frost. Nobody asks Frau Sorel anything, me first of all. Book around her, never over her. Thirty years and I have never managed a company that could afford it, and I find I can, and I took my hat off instead of making a speech, and I wrote to Loewe that night that her counterweights are missed. Then the road, and I rounded nothing at all, and on the fourteenth in Achterhalt I came at a run and read her call twice with both hands on the tailboard: SOREL, M., TOP OF LIST. Wept on the beat in act three, which is where it belongs. At soup I stood up and had to be told twice to sit, and gave the idea plain and without one rounded number: a proper second wagon and a fit-up we carry, Boyle's own door off its hinges, so that in a town with no theatre we are the theatre — eighty-two pounds, not eighty, by Reap if nobody buys a coat. Ruled yes, spent to the penny, and the first plank is to carry H.B. somewhere only we know. I shall cut them myself. I cut wood badly. It will look terrible and it will be right.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.

journals.entry: I came on stage left through Boyle's door and Katterau stood up, and I let it take as long as it liked, and then went on with the play. Whole, on the hour, in that town. Iron down, three calls, and out. Then the yard and Vane bellowing about bookings, and a ruling that keeps a place open for Mirelle from Reap to Frost, which is the correct way to spend money. On the fourteenth of Frost in Achterhalt I read the boy's chalk over his head and Harrow's before it — top of list — and said yes to it out loud. Fenner's mother sent butter again, the mayor's coming, and I am in things, which is what I asked to be ruled. The boy showed me his standing at four o'clock, weight on both feet and the voice out of the boots, and I inspected him like a soldier and passed him. Tonight the corn merchants went quiet by the third line, one faster than midsummer, and Mirelle took my hand for a call she hadn't asked for, which she has never done. At the table I said in, and did not propose a toast, because we have had enough of those; I said weight on both feet, all of you, and meant it as an instruction. Afterwards the boy wrote his first call crooked and went red about it, so I told him the trade: legible, everybody's name on it, signed. She'll tell him the rest for twenty years.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

journals.entry: Row four went out with the house at Katterau and I gave her the slate: full count, nobody late, nobody left, nobody empty, and I have never liked a sentence better. Then the winter road, Vessendal a fortnight, Merrow's fair, and on the fourteenth of Frost in the Achterhalt yard I read her chalk first and shouted, and started the whole yard off. Frau Sorel came in on the coach and everything stopped a minute. At soup she opened the floor youngest last, and my hands went cold, and I stood up with my ears burning and asked for it out loud: second stage manager, second on the book, not props, and I said I'm nineteen and I held the doors at the Palace and I never looked at the stage once. Krul said eighteen, in front of everybody. Madam Harrow ruled it — second on the book, with terms: I chalk tomorrow's call under her eye, the bucket rounds are mine alone from tonight, I learn the plot tables off Herr Krug, and in the spring at Katterau I call the storm to six hundred people with her standing behind me saying nothing. And I'm nineteen the day I call it clean. Herr Krug wrote me into the datebook himself and turned it round for her initials. Herr Grelle shook my hand like a man in a trade. Then she gave me the church of a call — legibly, where it can't be missed, beginners first and largest, names before numbers, nothing on the board you haven't checked with your own feet, your own name at the bottom, because a call is a promise with a signature on it. So I went out and put my hand on the wagon wheel in the cold first, and then wrote it. It took nine minutes and it's crooked and I spelled beginners with three n's. It's signed.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

journals.entry: Carried the slip to the prompt corner, then took the mayor's clerk his four words back — the house knows him — and Katterau had its play. I had the gas board with Hebel away and I know what warm means now, having been taught it. Nothing dangerous plotted, nothing owed, the exits walked twice. Then Vane bellowing for me and the datebook in the yard, and a place ruled open for Frau Sorel from Reap to Frost, which I entered without asking one question. Advance work all winter, so we arrived twice to find the roof already mended. On the fourteenth in Achterhalt she came off the coach and I asked her about act two, because there was act two to ask about. At soup Vane gave his figures and I said the honest thing: eighty-two is honest, and it is the first honest number he has ever handed me. Then the boy stood up and asked for the book, and she ruled it with terms and put the plot tables on me, which I take as the kindest sentence anybody has said to me in two years. I wrote him into the datebook myself — T. Lenz, 2nd on book, from 14 Frost — and turned it round for her initials, and watched him understand it had happened.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

journals.entry: Dressed Katterau and the slippers held, and the storm came out of my vermilion box with a floor in it and a farmer said God almighty and nobody shushed him. Then in Reap I dressed the girl who stepped up in Frau Sorel's place for a fortnight at Vessendal and she did not disgrace anybody. On the fourteenth I came out with pins in my mouth to check the spelling on that tailboard and took them out to say something I shan't write down. Let the hem down two inches and told her she'd want fitting before the half, and she did, and she sat. There's a drawing pinned to my mirror frame and nobody in that cage mentioned it, which is manners. At soup I said I'd want a proper hamper and no more than that. And when the props boy stood up and claimed nineteen I said eighteen, twice, with satisfaction, and put a second bowl in front of him, because he's had a night and a boy needs feeding when he's been made something.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

journals.entry: My door held for Falk's cue at Katterau and that town stood up, and I have never been prouder of a hinge. Iron down, trunk roped, quiet house, early load-out. In the yard Vane came out shouting about bookings and got told how the season's built: Frau Sorel's place held open Reap to Frost and nobody asks her anything, which is how it should be. Held the gate on the fourteenth of Frost, and when the boy's chalk went up I rang the gate bell with the flat of my hand for no reason on earth. Handed Frau Sorel a hamper when she came in off the coach because there was a hamper wanting carrying. At soup Vane wanted a fit-up and our own door carried in a wagon, and I said what wanted saying: that door's my door and I'll carry it. Then the trunk back on the tailboard at half eleven with the black sheet in it, roped, and Wenzel sat on it because he likes to.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.

journals.entry: Nothing occurred at Katterau that was not in the book. My hat came off and went back on twice on the fourteenth of Frost, once for the call on the tailboard and once for Frau Sorel coming in off the coach, which is the correct number. Counted fire buckets with Madam Harrow out of pure ceremony: nine of nine, no mice, entered. My mother sent a cake to a theatre in Reap and it was eaten by eleven people. At the table I was able to report that the Office allows a company its own portable proscenium, having looked it up already, twice, for pleasure. Wrote to her afterwards by the stove. I record also that a boy of nineteen — or eighteen — was made second on the book, and that the entry was made in the datebook and initialled, properly, in front of witnesses.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

journals.entry: Doors at Katterau, eight of them propped, count in my head, and row four went out with the drovers same as it came in. On the fourteenth at Achterhalt I had my doors and my aisle again and counted the hall in — Kessel's chain in the second row, the butter man's boy bolt upright with a programme. At soup I put in what I had: there's a fit-up firm in the fourth ward owes me a favour and a ladder, and they can have the favour called in. Then the props boy stood up scarlet and asked for the book, and she gave it him with terms, and I reached over and shook his hand as though we were two men in a trade, because that is what we are now, and it finished him off entirely. Twenty years on the wrong side of doors and now I hand a boy his start.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

journals.entry: Horses at Katterau, fed, and my supper was kept warm. Horses to Vessendal in Reap, horses to Merrow's fair, horses to Achterhalt in the cold. My name is on the boy's call, which I could not read but was told. Sat on the trunk at half eleven after Boyle roped it, because I like sitting on it, and it is only a box. Went to sleep at the table while they were still talking about eighty-two pounds and a door being carried about the country.
journals.state: At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.

journals.entry: One and six paid to the mayor's clerk, row four dead centre, no hat, no programme, and four words came back to me before the half: the house knows him. I sat in the town that stopped early and heard the finish given whole, on the hour, and when Frau Sorel took the first scene the room forgot itself. I stood with the rest of Katterau at the calls and clapped until the lights came up, and then went out with the drovers, paying nothing and owed nothing, and nobody looked at me, and I was gone before the calls had settled. That is the whole of what I wanted and it is more than I had any right to buy.
journals.state: In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.

journals.entry: They played my town on the fourteenth of Frost and I sat in the second row with the chain on, which is the whole point of a chain, and it went still in my hand by the third line. Afterwards I went backstage to say something official and said instead that it was a fine thing, and shook hands with the wrong people in the wrong order, and did not care. Nobody went off with anybody's wife. The Corn Exchange is let again next season if I have anything to do with it.
journals.state: At home in Achterhalt with the chain in its box and his dinner waiting; pleased with himself and with them, wanting the Corn Exchange let again next season.

journals.entry: Brought the cart in to Achterhalt at four with the butter and my husband and the boy, since Achterhalt is a town I can stand in. Fenner went straight to Herr Falk and showed him his standing and was inspected like a soldier and passed, and I watched from the cart. Then in at the front door and good seats, and my boy sat bolt upright with his programme waiting for the storm, and got it. Frau Sorel was back and they had her name chalked up on the wagon where anyone could read it. Nobody looked at us sideways. He would not admit he was tired and had to be carried out to the cart.
journals.state: In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.

journals.entry: Cart up to Achterhalt with the butter, boy beside me. Watched him show the old actor how to stand, and be passed, which he has been practising in the dairy since spring. In at the front door, good seats, good play. Very loud in the middle again. He told me twice what the storm was made of and then fell asleep on the way home saying he wasn't tired.
journals.state: Back at his own churns eleven miles out of Katterau, cart unloaded; plain and content, wanting the next invitation and his boy's boots mended.

journals.entry: We came in the cart to Achterhalt and I went straight to Herr Falk and showed him standing — weight on both feet and the voice up out of the boots — and he looked at me like a soldier and said I was passed. Then in the front door with Mam and Da, third row, programme read all through. Frau Sorel is back and her name was chalked on the wagon. I waited the whole way through for the storm and it came out of the red box and it was better than last time. I clapped over my head. I was not tired and they carried me out anyway.
journals.state: Wrapped in a gentleman's rug in the second wagon or on the cart, programme folded in his pocket; sleepy, proud and impatient, wanting nine o'clock and the thunder sheet again.

journals.entry: I sent my clerk over about the seat and he came back with four words for the gentleman in row four: the house knows him. Then I sat among my own townspeople with my chain at home in a drawer, and when the big man came through that door my town stood up, and it went on a good while, and he let it. The storm frightened a farmer in the third row into speech and nobody minded. No scandal, a full house, and twenty years ended quietly, which is how this town wanted it done.
journals.state: In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.

journals.entry: The schoolmaster asked me and I thought about it for two days, and then I asked whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills, and he said she was, so I said yes. She came up the lane on the first day and I stood up on the wall to be nearer, and she put out her hand and did not touch me, and said something short. Then we sat on the wall and I showed her my paper and she looked at all of it. There was another lady standing away at the turn of the lane who did not come nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion and I write it on things, and I drew the wagon with the red box on the back for her to have.

scenes.title: Harbor, and the Line Left Blank
scenes.summary:
Late in a wing, stove ticking, Bell Harrow finally asks Emeran Falk why "Harbor." Falk tells her of a bad season in a port, walking the mole at 4 a.m. watching boats come in shipping water — the harbour asked nothing, wasn't interested in bravery, just held still and let you tie up. He'd been drinking at nine every morning for eleven years when Vane hired Bell in ten minutes and she stepped over the third board unprompted, then posted a notice about a bucket. "So. Harbor." Bell keeps the name and gives her side: a harbor's pay is getting to be one — before this company no one ever tied up. She banks the stove; the tailboard reads T. LENZ, 2ND ON BOOK, FOR B. HARROW, S.M.

Winter: their own fit-up in Loewe's scene dock — Boyle's door carried in with H.B. cut into the first plank, Hebel's letters, Lenz at midwinter, Skarke's empty audit, Anton's drawings of theatres with every door open. Spring: Katterau twice, the mayor's favour being the town's carpenters and a barrel; both nights sell out. Night two is Toby's, ruled his two seasons back. Grey at the half says he can't remember what warm means; told warm was never in the pages, he's given Bell's own nail-worn watch to hold till the iron. He calls his performance clean despite being two seconds late on the act-two flat, covered by Krug's wheel; the storm lands on its one moment. Bell rules it publicly; Dessa Krul concedes: "He's nineteen."

Reap at the Athenaeum: Mirelle's schoolmaster's letter arrives. Anton comes to the door on the 20th with the schoolmaster's sister, says "It's smaller than it sounds," takes the yard, is told by Falk to stand on both feet, shakes his mother's hand, shouts "Vermilion!" from the street's top.

At Grevenholt the Corona's roof is mended; doorkeeper Krebs, the hinge-maker's brother, reports the bucket still under the prompt corner — Bell puts it on permanent duty. Ilsabet, then Prewick's certified Wolf King. Vane asks the company pass to the stage manager; Bell amends it to the keeper of the book, forever; Prewick writes it fair, all sign. Vane says, "Ask me for a thing" — she claims the first person answering a spring notice. Rosza Emmerich walks eleven miles in the wet, is hired in six minutes, signs, and plays.
scenes.history: Bell Harrow becomes stage manager of the Vermilion Players at the Corona, inheriting a mysterious prompt book, a leaking corner, and an unopened iron trunk tied to Vessendal's debts and a proscribed, unfinished two-hundred-year-old play from Katterau. Alongside Emeran Falk, Odalric Vane, Mirelle Sorel, and clerk Casimir Prewick, she uncovers cryptic pages, forged bills, and buried debts—Vane's hidden loan from Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel's sealed legacy, Mirelle's true parentage and hidden son Rupert/Anton, and copyist Anselm Krug's long guilt. Investigations lead through Achterhalt, the capital's Office of Public Morals (Lenz), and reclusive heir Marius Skarke, who secretly funds the play's revival. Harrow imposes strict rules—certified copies only, no wagers, no volunteering for the unfilled "eleventh line"—and orchestrates the play's full, certified performance at the Theatre Royal, breaking its centuries-old curse by finally answering its silent bell. Aftermath: debts settled, Grelle's long guilt resolved, Fenner Bacher rescued and adopted into the company, Mirelle reunited with her son, and the once-cursed script formally retired. The Players gain solvency, a new wagon, and stability. Seasons pass in performances, reconciliations, and quiet institutional rituals—chalk lists, certified books, Toby's promotion—cementing Harrow's harbor-like role holding the company together.

journals.entry: I sat up with Falk and his one thimble and finally asked for the word. A port, a bad season, four in the morning on a mole, boats coming in shipping water — and a harbour that asked nothing and let you tie up. He had been drinking at nine in the morning for eleven years so a play wouldn't surface in him, and I posted a notice about a bucket. So: Harbor. I said I'd keep it, and gave him the other side of the ledger — a harbour's pay is getting to be one; before this company nobody ever tied up. Then winter: our own proscenium, H.B. badly cut and varnished forever. Katterau in the spring, both nights out. The second was Toby's; he went grey at the half and couldn't remember what warm means, so I turned him to face the stage and told him you call what's happening, and put my watch in his fist until the iron. He called it clean — two seconds late on the act-two flat, covered by Krug — and held a pause nobody gave him. I ruled it out loud, and Krul conceded: he's nineteen. At the Athenaeum Mirelle brought me the schoolmaster's letter and I said doors are what we're for; on the 20th the front ones stood wide from four and Anton came as far as the door, said it was smaller than it sounds, took the yard, and shouted Vermilion from the top of the street. Season ruled off, one line blank. Then Grevenholt: Krebs's hinge held, his brother lowered the lamp, the bucket was where my first notice put it — permanent duty — and the third board sang the same note. Vane asked for the company to go to the stage manager; I had it written to the keeper of the book instead, in ink, Prewick fair, the wing witnessing, me countersigned. My thing in return: the first soul in out of the weather in spring is mine to hire. Rosza Emmerich, eleven miles, six minutes to spare. She signed, and then played us eleven miles at walking tempo, and Falk said we'd had thunder for a year and no music.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

journals.entry: She asked me for the word at last, over the stove, with my thimble on my knee, and I gave it her whole: the port, the bad season, the mole at four in the morning, boats coming in bad — shipping water, a man hurt, nothing in the hold — and the harbour taking every one of them the same, asking nothing, not even that you be interesting. It just held still and let you tie up. And I told her the rest: eleven years of drinking at nine in the morning so the play wouldn't surface, Anselm gone in the night, a coat full of pages, and then a stranger who stepped over the third board without being told twice and posted a notice about a bucket. She said she'd keep the name, and gave me her side, which was better than mine. I lifted the thimble to her the way I did in Grevenholt the night she came in out of the rain, drank it off, and went to my wagon on both feet. Katterau twice more; the boy called the second night and I told him weight on both feet, nineteen. At the Athenaeum a boy of thirteen stood in the doorway and said it was smaller than it sounds, and I had to put my hand over my mouth and turn away in the passage. Out in the yard I told him he was standing wrong and he corrected it instantly and looked pleased. At Grevenholt: the Corona with a mended roof, our own door, the initials at ankle height. And in the spring a woman played a cold dance tune at walking speed in an empty hall and I stood in the stalls with my head back and said it out loud: we've had thunder for a year and no music.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

journals.entry: Winter and a fit-up of our own; I cut H.B. into the first plank myself, badly, and had it varnished so it stays badly. Katterau in the spring, front doors first, and I said it aloud twice — it looks like a theatre. The boy called the second night and was clean, and I arrived from nowhere and wept, which is my function. Then Grevenholt, the Corona, the roof mended, the last curtain of the season, and the thing I have been carrying since Achterhalt: I put my hat down on the whole of the spring and asked her to have them. Fifty-four, a company that owes nothing, a second on the book who is nineteen — I want it minuted that the Vermilion Players go to whoever keeps the book, not to a creditor, not to a nephew. She said yes first, plainly, and then wrote it better than I asked it: not to Bell Harrow but to the book, keeper after keeper, forty years on to somebody neither of us will meet. To the book. That is much better than mine, and I sat down on a hamper and put my face in my hands and then hollered for Prewick, who wrote it fair on two sheets at eleven at night, and I signed unrounded and the whole wing witnessed. Then I could not help asking her for a thing, and her thing was my own trick back at me: the first soul who answers a spring notice is hers to hire, and I may watch from the wings and weep. I accepted on the spot. In the wet week of spring I stood in the shadow with my hat off and stopped breathing while a woman with a pulped notice and a fiddle got herself hired, and when it was done I came out with both arms and promised her a stove.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.

journals.entry: Winter was plot tables until Herr Krug said he dreamt in them. Then Katterau, and the second night was mine, ruled two seasons ago. I was up at five, walked the plot four times, checked a wagon I didn't need to check, and wrote the call so straight it looked printed, and at the half I went grey and told Madam Harrow the storm was on page nine and I couldn't remember what warm means. She turned me round to face the stage, not the book, and said warm was never in my pages — you call what's happening: Herr Falk's shoulders, Frau Sorel's hands, the house breathing. Then she put her own watch in my fist and closed my fingers on it, mine for tonight, to be given back at the iron. I stopped shaking all at once. Beginners, please, and my voice went where I sent it. I took the act-two flat two seconds late and Herr Krug covered it on the gas and nobody but the three of us will ever know. I held a pause nobody told me to hold and brought the light after Frau Sorel and not with her. In act four six hundred people leaned forward and I never looked at page nine: storm — go. It came in low with a floor in it and somebody in the gods laughed from fright. Iron down, three calls. I held the watch out on my palm and couldn't say one word. She weighed it, put it back on its nail, and ruled it in the wing out loud: clean. Krul said he's nineteen, and the whole wing went up. Later I went out with a lantern and stood with my hand on a wheel before I wrote a number down. At Grevenholt I called the load-in, and I signed the new minute last — T. Lenz, 2nd on book — and read it twice before I understood it. In the spring I wrote the new name on the call, spelled right, because I asked her twice.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

journals.entry: Watched the whole of the boy's act from the wardrobe doorway with pins in my mouth, and when she looked past his shoulder at me for the arithmetic I took the pins out one at a time and said it to the whole wing: he's nineteen. Then bedlam, as it should be — Boyle bellowing, Vane weeping on cue, Wenzel joining in without knowing why. At the Athenaeum I showed the schoolmaster's boy the queen's slippers and he didn't touch them, not being asked to, which is manners. He looked at the hamper properly. Later, a fiddle case steaming in my cage beside the slippers, which I have decided is acceptable and will not be discussing. Pins in the tin, and a new girl in the book who walked eleven miles.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

journals.entry: Went ahead on the Wednesday and pasted Katterau myself, so the bills were up before we came in sight of the town. Fit-up in five hours. First night ours; second night the boy's, and I had the gas board, so when he came two seconds late on the act-two flat I covered it and said nothing until she said it for me — and I told him from the board, without turning round, that he owed me a Katterau drink, which is the expensive kind. Advance work all winter, the datebook fattening. At the Corona at the end of the season the datebook lay open with eleven towns in it, and Vane put his hat over the whole spring and asked for something that wasn't a booking, and I signed my name to it in the wing with everybody else. In the spring I shut the datebook to listen to a woman play a dance tune at walking speed in a half-built house, and did not plot one dangerous thing all evening.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

journals.entry: My door taken off its hinges and carried about the country like a relic, with the initials cut in the plank badly, which is the right way to cut them. Katterau in the daylight, five hours to a fit-up, both nights out; the boy called the second and I bellowed as loud as anybody when the wardrobe woman said he was nineteen. Told the schoolmaster's lad in Loewe's yard what every rope was for, properly, with knots, and he listened. At Grevenholt I swore at the arch as usual and put my name to Vane's paper. In the spring I lost an argument with a beam, and was still holding it when the new woman played, and I stood in the O.P. entrance with the beam in my hands until she finished.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre yard at the half with his lamp lit and the unlit pipe in his teeth, wagons settled; sober and content, wanting a quiet house and an early load-out.

journals.entry: The winter fit-up I inspected as one inspects a text, and Undersecretary Lenz did the same at midwinter over three cups. At Katterau I applauded the boy at regulation volume with my hat off, and wrote to my mother about a second on the book who is nineteen. At the Corona my Wolf King comparison was finished, certified, stamped straight, my seal on the paper at last, and I stood at the back of the O.P. side through act one with my hat off and my mother's cake in the wing. Then, at eleven at night on the props table, I was hollered for and wrote the instrument fair in my own hand and read it aloud twice: the name, the wagons, the properties, the fit-up, the debts if any, and the goodwill pass upon death or retirement to the keeper of the company's book, and thereafter to each keeper in turn. Two sheets, numbered. Vane signed unrounded, Harrow countersigned, the wing witnessed, and I signed as scrivener. It goes in the book, which is where such things belong.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

journals.entry: Doors at Katterau both nights, and I had my hand on the boy's shoulder when the wing went up for him. At the Athenaeum in Reap I propped the pass door because that is what I do now instead of standing outside one. Signed Vane's paper in the wing at the Corona. In the spring, when the fiddle woman played, I held the pass door open with my shoulder although there was nobody to keep out, and did not mind at all.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

journals.entry: Horses through the winter and the spring, supper kept warm. Woke in the middle of the wing cheering the boy without knowing what for, which was fair enough. At the Athenaeum a lad of thirteen looked at the wagon and said the horse was too small, so I told him the horse is the right size and the wagon's too big, and he thought about it very seriously and said nothing, which I took as agreement. Put my cross to Vane's paper and Krul wrote my name after it. Fell asleep somewhere I shouldn't have while a woman played a fiddle in an empty hall.
journals.state: At the horse lines behind the Katterau theatre with a nosebag and a wisp of straw, coat wet at the shoulders; easy and unbothered, wanting the horses fed and his supper kept warm.

journals.entry: Katterau twice more, top of the list, and Falk gave me his fourth call and I gave it to the house. Mid-fortnight at the Athenaeum I came to the corner before the half with the schoolmaster's letter and no gloves at all: term ended, and the boy had asked in his own words, spelling his one word right, whether he might come as far as the door of the theatre where the wagon lives. She read it whole and said doors are what we're for, name the day, the front ones will stand wide. I named the 20th, Loewe's last Thursday, the coach, the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible and briefed. As far as the door — not a seat, not the house — and I said that was the wisest thing anybody in this business has said in ten years. I folded the letter in three and put it in my pocket, not my glove. He came at five, tall now, with a satchel, not wanting his hand held, and stood in the doorway and looked a long time and said it was smaller than it sounds. He took the wagon, the horse, the ropes, the hamper; Falk told him to stand on both feet and he looked pleased. Twenty-five minutes. I stood where I could see him and did not perform for him once. He thanked four people in the wrong order, and stopped in front of me and put out his hand, and I shook it. At the top of the street he turned and shouted Vermilion at the whole street. Then the yard was very quiet and I stood in it with my hands at my sides. I mended that night longer than anyone. Signed Vane's paper at the Corona, and in the spring stopped my needle to hear the new woman play.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

journals.entry: Their winter in my scene dock, building themselves a theatre out of my dust, and the counterweights sound and the gas tap mended and the brick in the passage scrubbed pale. In Reap the front doors stood wide from four o'clock on my last Thursday and nobody would tell me why, so I stopped asking, as I do. A woman in brown and a tall boy off the coach; he stood in my doorway and looked at my house and said it was smaller than it sounds, which is the truest thing said in it this year. They took him through to the yard and I kept out of it. When it was over and the yard went quiet I said doors open at half six and the gas tap is a disgrace, and went inside so as to be no trouble.
journals.state: In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.

journals.entry: The lady wrote back and I came on the coach with the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible, and I did not have my hand held. The theatre where the wagon lives had its front doors wide open and it was warm and dark inside, and I stood in the doorway and looked at the gas and the boxes and the empty stage, and I said it was smaller than it sounds. The stage manager said it was smaller than it sounds and bigger than it looks, and told me where the wagon lives, through the yard door, and that my pace was the law inside the walls. So I went as far as the wagon. The horse is too small, as I said in my drawing; the man on the bale said the horse is right and the wagon is too big, and I shall think about that. The big man told me what all the ropes are for, with knots. The lady with the pins showed me the queen's slippers and I did not touch them. Herr Falk came out with a rug on his arm and said I was standing wrong, weight on both feet, and I fixed it and he saw me fix it. Twenty-five minutes and then the six-forty. I said thank you to four people. I shook my mother's hand. At the top of the street I shouted Vermilion as loud as I could.

Brought the boy on the coach as arranged, set him down at the top of the street, and stood by while he went as far as the door and no further, which was the whole of the agreement. Twenty-five minutes in a theatre yard, ropes and a horse and an old actor telling him to stand up straight. I looked at my watch and said the six-forty, and we caught it.

Their bills were up before they were, pasted by their own man on the Wednesday. I met them in the square and gave them my favour, which was the loan of the town's carpenters and a barrel for the company, and they had a theatre standing inside five hours. Two nights, six hundred each, both out. The town went in at the front doors and came out satisfied, and nothing wanted a chain or a speech.
journals.state: In the Katterau house among her own townspeople, chain of office at home in a drawer; brisk and curious, wanting a quiet full house and no scandal in her town.

journals.entry: Three soft knocks, unhurried, and I came with the lamp and two bolts. A woman said she was Bell Harrow, stage manager of the Vermilion Players, so I lowered the lamp to the boards and not in her face, and told her she'd be the one that posted the notices, and that my brother did their hinge — which bites its frame still. Then I told her the thing I have been keeping: there's a bucket under her prompt corner, there since the other Katterau, the one before hers, and nobody has dared move it. She came in over the third board on purpose and let it sing, and then she ruled the bucket on permanent duty, dry or not, the oldest notice in their church. I set my lamp on the prompt shelf beside it and looked at the pair of them, and said I'd tell the gas boy, who has been trying to fill it with rags since June. Then she gave me the news like a present: two nights, Ilsabet first, and the second a debut — the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor.

Four days that notice sat on a board with a horse auction and two lost dogs, and I read it four times in the wet before I went in. Eleven miles, boots finished, fiddle under my coat. The stage door opened without a knock and I said so — it shouldn't have been open — and she said it was open on purpose, and turned her lamp down so the light was on the boards and not in my face. Bell Harrow, stage manager, and my ten minutes had started when I stepped on the singing board. She asked three things in any order I liked, so I thought about the order first: Rosza Emmerich; four years for a dancing school where you learn nobody is watching you and the tempo is the whole job; two years in a Kessarine pit band until it stopped being paid; a winter of weddings and a funeral a week, which teaches you to change a tune when a room changes. I can read, I transpose while playing, I don't drink at work, I can mend a bow and nothing else. And why they should carry me: because hers is the only bill I ever saw that said ask for the stage manager, which told me somebody in there keeps a book, and I have been paid out of hats for two years and would like to be in a book. She counted my three good signs back at me on three fingers, gave me terms — wages posted and unrounded, a line in the book, a bunk in the second wagon, and a church of four sentences — and I signed my whole name and asked what hour beginners were. Then a large weeping man in plum came out of the wing promising me a stove, and she ruled that harmless before supper. Then she told me to play, so I tuned badly and then properly and played a cold dance tune at the tempo of eleven miles, and the house gave it back bigger than me, and nobody clapped, and the old man in the stalls said they'd had thunder for a year and no music. Late, my case steaming beside the queen's slippers, I found the third board again in the dark and asked once more what hour beginners were.

characters.history:
I began this trade with a stage manager, Bell Harrow, hired the day she arrived with a notice and three references, and I steered her from a certain trunk while Prewick asked too much about it. That trunk held nine years of my life: a loan taken at Vessendal from a dying man, Hessel Brandt, who would not sign a receipt between friends and died before it was finished, leaving the debt to be bought up by a man named Skarke. I had told the company I had fourteen days when I had none, seduced by Katterau's six hundred seats, until Harrow made me lay it bare: names in ink, the notary Perlmann, Anna Sorel, a nun, Brandt's blind son Josias who remembered my sleeve after nine years. The truth was worse: Brandt had held the money for another party, never his to lend, and hidden the play itself, thirty pages, in a cupboard tagged unpaid.

Harrow ruled against Katterau, drove us to Vessendal, and there the debt was discharged, witnessed, not forgiven. I paid Achterhalt's bank myself, front door, hat on, and got my sky for the black plate scene. In the capital I broke and blamed Anselm for a theft I committed by silence, then unsaid it before the company and let Harrow rule again. That unearthed an older wound — Grelle, the landlord's seven pounds I'd claimed eleven years to have paid and never had. I found Hentsch's door at last, counted the coin out unrounded, and heard him say he'd always known.

Since then: certification, the bill by command at the Athenaeum, toasts to our dead, a second wagon built with H.B. cut crooked into the first plank, Sorel held open at any cost, and a testament written not to me nor mine but to whoever keeps the book. I asked for a last thing and was given the wettest, best gift: to watch, and weep, from the wings.

journals.entry: A stage manager walked in out of the weather with the notice in her fist — read, came, noticed the open door: three references on three fingers. Bell Harrow. I engaged her on the spot, promised plot tables, a bucket, a fair figure rounded kindly upward at Vessendal, and said of the book only that it is as honest as books are. Steered her wide of the trunk and would not be steered back; Prewick, curse his level lamp, held light over the lid and asked whether it was numbered. Showed her the thunder — the trough, the balls, the tin — while Falk told the story of the farmer at Merrow as he always does. Then the ladder's foot, and the trunk against it, and she asked me, without turning round, to shift it a hand's breadth left, and went off for her bucket like a good clock. Alone, I wiped the beading from the lid, pressed the chalk flat, said what I say. Lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox — light, wrong, answering — and I set it down and took my hands off it. Then I shoved it properly, a hand's breadth and a little more, and called out that the ladder was served and to note the repair to the credit of the management. After that I did not stay in the house.

Woke frightened and did what I do: coffee, the shutter up, and the Vessendal Advertiser on my Lear read aloud to nobody. Harrow came for three things while yes was cheap and had all three — Krebs for a shilling and let him feel he won, tin only because thirty-two feet is thirty-two feet, and ten minutes over the book, standing up. Then Emeran, sober and grey, told her it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town, and said she nailed the trough, so I laughed and went out the front doors for a carpenter I had no intention of finding. Found Skarke's man's card instead, or it found me: counted our seats from the street. Gave her her ten minutes at last, cornered by my own poster with my hat off. Told her the truth: the Palace said the 3rd, I have been telling the company the 17th since Merrow, because there is not money for four towns but there is time for three and Katterau, six hundred seats and a mayor who owes me. Fourteen days is what I have been selling myself, and I have run out of buyer. Asked her not for dishonesty but for books so clean a man learns nothing he is not owed. She wants the road laid against the 3rd tonight, and the company told if Katterau will not fit. Gave her the card; it went like handing over a bird. Called places in twenty and shut the pass door. After the curtain I counted the float twice, and the second count was smaller than the first, because the first was hopeful.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry: Came in wet and pleased with myself — a carpenter found, Krebs's brother-in-law and his cart bought at eleven shillings when I had offered twelve so the man might feel he lost — and there was my trunk dragged into the middle of the passage with the lid shut and Harrow's lamp on it, and Falk against the wall, and I put the chestnuts down on the flags like a fool. She made me stand and be looked at and put my hat in my hands with a torn playbill on top, pencil side up. Nine years. I read it twice. So I told her the thing I have not said aloud: the loan is two seasons old; nine years ago I borrowed in Vessendal from a man who was dying and my friend, and I paid him, and he signed nothing, and Skarke has bought his papers. What comes to the counting is a signature nobody gave. She did not weep at me or dismiss me — she gave me a task: every name that was in that room, in ink, in the wagon. There was a notary. There is always a notary. I gave the boy the chestnuts and a story. I slept four hours and called it seven, and answered present at her roll, and did not want to hear Boyle say there used to be a Krug on this list. Mirelle told me the company would hear the road tonight and I said yes. Harrow read the dates out unrounded, all of them, and everyone spoke, and Falk said Katterau and what it cost me. I stood up with my hat in my hands and asked her to rule it. I shall drive where she points.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry:
She ruled, standing, and did not spare me: Katterau no, the 3rd stands, and drive for Vessendal. I wept — I am not ashamed of it — quoted my Lear notice at nobody, and slept in my coat. At the toll gate I paid eight shillings to the penny because she was standing there. Vessendal came up out of the flat and the Athenaeum knows what it has; I went straight to the box office to learn the number of seats sold, which is the only prayer I have.

At breakfast I gave her the names in ink as promised: Hessel Brandt on the Kohlgasse; the notary, Perl or Perlmann, inky fingers and a cold; Anna Sorel; a doctor whose name I never had; a nun; myself; and the one in the passage I never saw and have thought of for nine years. Writing it down was worse than saying it.

Then she took me up a stair that smelled of leather with her clerk behind, set me at the door and said: no performance. Three knocks — the smallest sound I have made in my life. Bettina opened it, and then Josias in the doorway with his white eyes past me, finding my sleeve and rubbing the worn place on my cuff: nine years, and I have not changed my coat. He told them what I have never been able to prove: I came at eleven at night with the whole of it and said God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and he would not sign, between friends, and died on the Tuesday. The receipt was never finished. It is the only unfinished instrument of the old man's life. I stood in the doorway and could not speak.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry:
Perlmann said it all again in front of them, and then said the bag had a bank's mark, and my mouth answered before my head: the Farriers' and Merchants' — and then no, no branch here in the fifth year, I drew it at Achterhalt and carried it two days on my knees, and I remember that coach seat as I remember my mother. Three items: the loft lease, the certificate, and a packet with my company's name on it that has sat in a tin box for nine years because we never came back. He gave it to Harrow. He told me to change my coat, and he was right, and I did not answer.

On the stair I shook. In the yard she opened it and made me read the letter standing, silently, twice, and I did — and it is worse than being owed. Hessel refused the receipt because the money was never his to lend. He held it out of a fund for another party whose name he never told me, and he took that party's marker as security, and put it in the green-room cupboard, and tagged the key unpaid, and left it for us, and asked God to have mercy. Four hundred and twelve marks, the whole of it, and nine years of me saying so, and all the time the thing behind the debt was not paper. It was the play.

I went into the green room with Harrow and Emeran and saw her lift out thirty pages, which is not a folio. Then the day put its boots on: load-in at ten, and a matinee, and a take so good I came through the pass door shouting about it with the bag in my fist, and stopped when I saw their two faces.
journals.state: Gone from the house — hat face down and one glove on the passage flags, the plum coat hung on the box office peg, the iron trunk open behind him; unaccounted for, and owed a reckoning at midnight he may not keep.

journals.entry: She sent me to bank the bag with Boyle at the half and kept the word for the counting, which I obeyed without asking, being a man who has learned that much. Then the house, and Falk through that door on the hour, and the applause coming up out of the stalls over him, and I stood at the back of the wings and wept and told nobody that the Advertiser would not have been generous. Three calls, and a third for Emeran alone that he did not ask for. In the box office with the shutter down I sat with my hat off and my hands flat while the assignment was read out and the second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in Skarke's own hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe, who insisted. Every figure initialled against her book. Discharged tonight, said the agent, not forgiven. And then it was nine o'clock on a Wednesday and I owed no man anything, and I sat on a stool too small for me and could not name what I was feeling, and asked her what in God's name we do now. She said: learn to be solvent, two more nights, Perlmann's oath banked Thursday all the same, then Achterhalt, then the capital early. In the green room I stood with the jug and the wrong hat and toasted Hessel Brandt, wool factor of this parish, who would not sign and would not tell and would not open a parcel for nine years, and I did not round the number. Thursday the oath was sworn before Braun and the bank confirmed the draw at Achterhalt in my name. Friday full, Saturday the strongbox gone. At load-out I gave Harrow the float bag without being asked, and asked her to ask me for a thing.
journals.state: In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.

journals.entry: She asked for a thing I did not expect and it cost me more than money: the Farriers' and Merchants' at Achterhalt, front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed. I told her about the four hours in the back room and the boy on the horse and the drainage pamphlet nineteen times, and then I said yes, and promised her a sky and to round the price down aloud in front of her. Loewe raised a hand and Falk raised the rug and we were out of Vessendal. On the road I talked about kettles versus a hung sheet to nobody at all. At the crest she read a page and put it in her coat and Falk got down off his box and asked her a question; then a crier in Achterhalt with our name in the printer's biggest type and by command under it, and I stood three feet behind her with my hat off and said nothing, which is new for me and cost something. Bailiff came, and she divided us like a woman dealing cards, and gave the man the Office's shilling and my name only for dull certified things. Then he said his brother-in-law asks eighteen and takes twelve, and I heard myself say twelve like a lover. Bank, ironmonger, haggle. The happiest day of my life.
journals.state: In the Athenaeum square at load-out in his coat, hatless of the plum one, empty-handed now that the float bag is hers; solvent, bewildered by being unafraid, and dreading and wanting Achterhalt where he drew the bag nine years ago.

journals.entry: She walked me in the front door with my hat on and a boy of nineteen called me sir and had never heard of me, and I have not been so kindly used in ten years. Eleven minutes. Paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H. I put the receipt over the notice in my breast pocket and could not speak on the steps. Then she asked me for her sky and I found it — the black plate with a floor in it, and I did not round the price, and I made her watch me not round it. Hall for thirteen, which is a defeat, and I was happy. Achterhalt stood and the storm came in low and I wept in the wing. Then the capital, and Anselm on a mounting block in my own yard, and everything I have carried since Katterau came up my throat at once: I told the company he took the Wednesday take. Seven pounds. I made him a thief to save myself the explaining, and I have known his address two years. I sat down in the wet and said it, and Mirelle said I should unsay it at supper, and I asked Harrow for a thing because I always do, and she gave me three letters to write in ink with my name large enough to hurt. I wrote them. At supper I said it whole and laid the seven pounds on the table and he would not take it. He wanted her instead, and gave her nine pages, and I sat with my hat off and let the stage manager rule.
journals.state: In the Baraque's O.P. wing after a short night, coat rumpled, seven pounds still lying refused on the hamper; hollowed out, unexpectedly light, wanting Krug to stay and wanting to be told what to carry next.

journals.entry:
Stood when the benches filled and found I had nothing to say, so I sat down again and let her open it. Heard the door out named and real, and heard what the makers pay — I gave the room and the money and the paper at Katterau, so I am in that ledger already. Stood last of the men with my hat in my hands and no notice to quote: I'll go where Harrow points, but I asked for the clean page and wanted it minuted. She minuted it, honoured it, and overruled it, and told me so to my face, and I find I can carry the pair of them. Ten o'clock, Ilsabet, and I shall be punctual, which I only am in emergencies.

Then in the morning I came in at the pass door halfway through Falk telling her about Grelle — the landlady's letter in the eighth year, four weeks owing, seven pounds, and the company saying for eleven years that I had paid it. I heard myself say it out loud: I never paid it. I hadn't got seven pounds, and Anselm had just — and I stopped, because I heard where that sentence was going. Eleven years of suppers. It is the same seven pounds. I am standing in it now.
journals.state: At the pass door of the Baraque holding his hat, having just confessed the landlady's seven pounds were never paid; hollow and appalled at the arithmetic of it, wanting Harrow to tell him what to do before ten o'clock.

journals.entry: I sat down on a hamper with my hat in my lap and gave her the name I have carried unsaid: Hensch, Hentsch, Rasselgasse off the meat market, third or fourth house, brown door — I walked past it twice in the ninth year and did not go in. I asked her to put the seven pounds out of the fee above my own boots, after Anna's box. She would not let us hunt him; she advertised for him, and at four in the morning he came to the door himself. I came in last with my hair everywhere and did not perform. I counted seven pounds and four weeks out of the float onto the props table, coin by coin, aloud, unrounded, and pushed it across, and said the true thing: eleven years of suppers where I said I had paid it. He never looked up from his plate. He said he heard me say it at Merrow in the ninth year, from across the road, with paste on his hands. There is nothing to answer that with, so I said nothing, and the roof dripped into the bucket. Then Room Fourteen's letter came, and the Undersecretary comes himself; then Grelle got a cot and the doors, and my old boy Falk got him back. I said in again on the 2nd, in the cold, with no soup and no candle, and my name was read out slow with the rest.
journals.state: At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, in the wings out of the way, hat somewhere, hands empty; hollowed out and obedient, wanting the debt to stay paid and to be of some use before the curtain.

journals.entry: I wept at the top of act three on cue and meant every drop of it, which has not happened to me in years. At the interval I came to her corner with my hat off and said nothing while she went out and told them the truth instead of selling it, and no one clapped, and I found I was glad. In Part the Second I discovered I had an entrance in the matter following; nobody told me; I took it, hat in hand, and said my one line, which is a number, and I did not round it. Then we three stood still and let nine hundred people look at us, and Lenz said Certified, and the iron came down. Afterwards there was soup in the wing and a strange boy in it, and a gloved woman in a cab somewhere in the city, and Mirelle going the colour of paper at the word Tuesday.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing in the plum coat with his hat in his hand, hollow and unusually quiet; wanting to be of use to whoever asks and not to be thanked.

journals.entry: I stood at her corner with my hat in my hand like a man waiting to be told what he is in, and she told me: a solvent company, a certified miracle behind it, no man's debt on it. And a booking — the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, one night only, by command, because the bill exists and the words on it are ours now. Ilsabet, front doors standing wide, played for nothing but joy, Loewe's house, Perlmann on his daughter's arm, Ilse and the boy in through the front door in the good seats, and our dead toasted at the interval: Hessel, Anna, Frau Hentsch, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house. I opened my mouth to weep and decided not to, which I count as the best work I have done all tour. By command: ours — I shall have it printed in Hessler's own case with a note that the man was blameless. Loewe gets fifteen and not a penny rounded down. Then at the pass door I told the doorframe the thing I have not said: nineteen days, and I hired her in ten minutes because the last one left in the night at Katterau and I would rather have died than tell her why, and she may put in the book that I have said why. Next day I drove her to the bank, and the lift boy called me sir, and a young man listened to me on the acoustics of the Corn Exchange for a quarter of an hour.
journals.state: In the Baraque in the plum coat with his hat brushed, printer's copy for a new bill in his pocket; sober, useful and almost unbearably grateful, wanting the 14th of Frost done handsomely and nobody to thank him for it.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked. It leaked, and got a bucket and a notice and two coats of vermilion, like anything else that leaks in her house, and I did not say one word about signs and portents.

On the 11th I climbed up, took the reins, and asked her for a thing, and she asked me for money — her own wages, flat palm, in front of the company. So I paid the last account in my book: nineteen days at four and six, four pounds five and six, said twice on purpose, and told her I had been paying her at that figure in my head since Achterhalt and could not think how to say it without weeping, and then wept, and then sang going out the arch.

Achterhalt, Hessler's bill for nothing, a butter cart in my column. Vessendal: Loewe wanted thirteen and I paid fifteen and would not be argued down. Perlmann on my stage in a chair. At the interval I stood out front with my hat off and toasted Hessel Brandt, Anna Sorel, Frau Hentsch of the Rasselgasse, and every stage manager who ever rang a bell to an empty house, and nine hundred drovers drank to it. I counted a take of nothing afterwards and enjoyed it more than any money I ever had. Katterau in the spring, by daylight, front doors, and I drive where she points.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.

journals.entry: Katterau had its finish, whole, on the hour, and I shouted myself hoarse and nobody had to thank me. Afterwards I came into the yard with a letter and two bookings said yes to — Vessendal a fortnight in Reap, Merrow's fair paying actual money — and told Harrow to ask me for a thing, and she did, and it cost me my leading lady for a season. Held open, Reap to Frost. Nobody asks Frau Sorel anything, me first of all. Book around her, never over her. Thirty years and I have never managed a company that could afford it, and I find I can, and I took my hat off instead of making a speech, and I wrote to Loewe that night that her counterweights are missed. Then the road, and I rounded nothing at all, and on the fourteenth in Achterhalt I came at a run and read her call twice with both hands on the tailboard: SOREL, M., TOP OF LIST. Wept on the beat in act three, which is where it belongs. At soup I stood up and had to be told twice to sit, and gave the idea plain and without one rounded number: a proper second wagon and a fit-up we carry, Boyle's own door off its hinges, so that in a town with no theatre we are the theatre — eighty-two pounds, not eighty, by Reap if nobody buys a coat. Ruled yes, spent to the penny, and the first plank is to carry H.B. somewhere only we know. I shall cut them myself. I cut wood badly. It will look terrible and it will be right.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.

journals.entry: Winter and a fit-up of our own; I cut H.B. into the first plank myself, badly, and had it varnished so it stays badly. Katterau in the spring, front doors first, and I said it aloud twice — it looks like a theatre. The boy called the second night and was clean, and I arrived from nowhere and wept, which is my function. Then Grevenholt, the Corona, the roof mended, the last curtain of the season, and the thing I have been carrying since Achterhalt: I put my hat down on the whole of the spring and asked her to have them. Fifty-four, a company that owes nothing, a second on the book who is nineteen — I want it minuted that the Vermilion Players go to whoever keeps the book, not to a creditor, not to a nephew. She said yes first, plainly, and then wrote it better than I asked it: not to Bell Harrow but to the book, keeper after keeper, forty years on to somebody neither of us will meet. To the book. That is much better than mine, and I sat down on a hamper and put my face in my hands and then hollered for Prewick, who wrote it fair on two sheets at eleven at night, and I signed unrounded and the whole wing witnessed. Then I could not help asking her for a thing, and her thing was my own trick back at me: the first soul who answers a spring notice is hers to hire, and I may watch from the wings and weep. I accepted on the spot. In the wet week of spring I stood in the shadow with my hat off and stopped breathing while a woman with a pulped notice and a fiddle got herself hired, and when it was done I came out with both arms and promised her a stove.
journals.state: In the Katterau theatre at the half in the plum coat, hat brushed, dressed for Ilsabet and hoarse from shouting in the yard; sober, hugely happy, wanting the town to have its finish and nobody to thank him.
