characters.history:
I began as a mender of gloves in low light, keeping the company's small order — Odalric's debts, Falk's mockeries, the bucket under the star trap that had waited since Katterau. Then Harrow came in out of the rain, and I taught her the trade: the ladder, the trunk, the arts of asking and going away. She showed me a page with nine in it; I told her mine was ten, and that pages come slantwise, tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot. I gave her Krug's plot tables, cued her Ilsabet, and hid a page with ten in it inside my mended glove. Through her I learned Odalric had sold the 17th to buy Katterau, and I refused Katterau — Halbern was enough backwards-walking for one life. I told her of my sister Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts and left a sealed box in Vessendal's registry. I would not go near that building; my name there is one I cannot afford to meet. Harrow found the box, found Hessel Brandt, found a countrywoman's coat that was my mother's, then Anna's, then mine. At Halbern the pages stopped counting. Krug returned; Odalric confessed a theft; nine pages surfaced, one a cast list of twelve. At the hearing I gave my whole history aloud — Anna, the magistrate's matter, the summons — and joined the company on one condition: Anna's box stays shut forever, paid for first.

Then came Rupert Vorn, the lying-in house, papers signed at twenty-three, the son I was told never to look for, the extortion charge that drove me over the mountains. Harrow's audit found him — a steward's brother's family in the Bittersee, a boy named Anton, twelve, who draws and cannot spell. I asked for slowness and got it: a letter in Harrow's hand, not an office's. He came, at five, tall, satchel on his shoulder, shook my hand, and shouted Vermilion at the whole street. I mended gloves longer than ever that night, and in spring I stopped my needle to hear the new woman play.

journals.entry: Mending a glove on the fly floor by no light when the new one came in out of the rain. Told her to say yes before Odalric asked again with tears. Mentioned the bucket under the star trap, there since Katterau, and enjoyed what the word did to Falk's glass. Came down the ladder past her ear and gave her the only advice worth giving: the ladder's foot wants a hand's breadth left, it can't have it because of the trunk, don't drag the trunk, ask him and go away while he does. She did it exactly, which tells me something. Went out front, came back cloaked with my hatbox to find the trunk snug against the ladder again and four feet of chalk dragged along the brick — he'll say the porters did it; the Corona has no porters. Asked Harrow what the page said and she gave it to me flat, word for word: the wrong door, the bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut beneath in pencil. Nine years is not my number. I told her what I know and no more: the pages began at Vessendal two springs ago, Krug thought the first was a joke of Falk's, it described a horse going lame and four weeks later the near mare went down outside Merrow. They come slantwise and late. I told her mine is ten, and that a page with ten in it comes to me first — not to Odalric, not to the boy with the notebook. Six o'clock at the ostler's yard: plot tables for Ilsabet, and no mention of this. Then out into the wet to find my bed.

Was in the ostler's yard before her, on the mounting block with my cloak under me, and did not say good morning. Gave Harrow my own copy of Krug's plot tables — honest, which the book is not — with the margin on it: tin only, never the trough in houses under forty foot. The Corona is thirty-two. Fed the old horse, who is older than any number Odalric says aloud. Made her cue me Ilsabet, act two, from you were not sent for, and told her not to be kind about it; she wasn't, and the yard stopped being a yard. Prewick said "Oh" out loud and was appalled at himself, which I shall keep. Told him to unfold his itinerary and left them to their papers. Going front later I told Harrow that Odalric was awake with his notices and frightened, and that a frightened man says yes, so ask now. Told her: again tonight, before the half. Played the storm; the old tin barked and went to tea tray; Falk put in a line that is not in the book and the house forgave us, so I took the next off him and rode it home. Decent applause. Gloves mended and drying on the sill.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry: Answered present with my hatbox on my knees and heard Boyle say there used to be a Krug on the list. At noon Harrow came alongside the first wagon holding a page and said there was a ten in it and that she had read the number and nothing else. I told Odalric to stop the wagon and he did it without one question and went to be busy with a strap, which is the best of him. I walked twenty yards to a marker with the saint's face worn off and unfolded it, and then I called her over, because I would rather two of us knew than one: the child is ten this winter and does not know the word mother, having been taught another; a woman crosses a border twice, once running, once summoned, and the second invitation is kind. I let her read it, so it is hers now; I was too tired to be careful. She told me, unasked and without being sworn to silence, that the Palace set the 3rd and Odalric has been selling us the 17th to buy Katterau. Not Falk's lining — he has enough of other people's endings sewn into him. I put the page inside my mended glove, palm flat against my wrist, and pulled the glove on over it, so it rides where I can feel it. Then I told Odalric the company would sit down and hear the road tonight, unrounded, and he said yes in a small voice. At the fire I gave my one voice: the capital is a summons dressed as an honour and I will go to it; Katterau, no — not four days backwards with a debt and a magistrate behind us.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry:
She gave the ruling standing and shut, and Katterau went into the ground for this tour, and I let out the breath I have been holding since Halbern. Nobody said aye; we don't.

I stayed while she banked the fire, my glove off with the page still in it, and gave her the thing she'll need before Friday: the notary at that deathbed. Odalric will not have the name — he remembers notices, not names. So I said it out loud for the first time in years. Anna Sorel was my sister. She kept his accounts that year, and if there is a receipt anywhere in the world with a signature on it, it went into Anna's box, and her box went where the others go.

Two days of road. I did not look at Vessendal once; I watched the river instead, which is a thing you can do with a town.

Coming up the mud from the tin's burial — nine of us, lanterns, and Falk's sailors' words, which were better than the tin deserved and exactly what it deserved — I told Harrow where to go: the registry behind the lion, eight to noon, and the lease in the fifth year was Vessendal's, so Anna's box came here. I cannot go in. My name is in that building on paper I would rather not stand next to. She can.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry:
I came last into the yard and stopped six feet off when I saw what was in her hands — brown paper and a merchant's hand. I heard the whole of it from where I stood: Anna asked Perlmann whether a sealed box could ever be read and was told no and wept, and Hessel Brandt never held papers, he held a piece of the play. I did not go into the green room. There was a matinee to dress for and I dressed for it.

At the half I found Harrow in the prompt corner with something flat under her coat and told her the only thing I can do for her tonight: he will ask a question with a number in it. Nine is Odalric's. Twenty is Falk's. Ten is mine, and I will answer it myself, and she is not to spare me. Ring the bell and I'll come.
journals.state: At her glass after curtain, cloak on the chair, hearing herself in the mirror; pleased with the house and unimpressed by the sky, and knowing nothing yet of any note, card, or open trunk.

journals.entry: I played the first scene to wet wool and drovers and had the house by the fourth line, and never knew, until afterwards, that Harrow and Falk had spent the two minutes before beginners on the question of a door. He came on stage left as blocked and the house stood up for him and nothing in the wings went cold. In the green room I let the room say Hessel Brandt and did not lift my glass with them; I said And Anna to Harrow alone, and drank, and pulled my glove straight over the wrist. On the yard steps she laid out the box: a certificate, two ratepayers swearing kinship, or a magistrate's order — and said honestly that nothing says the box ever opens, that opening it might break Anna's one shelf, and that a kin claim once entered keeps Skarke's lawyers off it forever. So I told her what I have told nobody: my name is not Sorel and never was; the name I was born to sits in a police file in the capital under a matter with a date and a magistrate, and my passport spells a third thing over a town I have never seen. I will not put my true name on a register twelve days before I walk into the capital by invitation, which is the page, word for word. I want the box shut forever and I want it mine, and I have never been able to have both. Thursday belongs to Odalric's neck, not mine; my eighteen shillings' stopped clock does not care about names. I asked her instead for Loewe's woman from Katterau, and the child's age. She brought it back exact on Thursday: countrywoman's coat, town boots, hands still, stood the way I stand. That is my mother's coat — Anna's, then mine, then someone's. I asked for silence, and the road to Achterhalt to think on it.
journals.state: At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.

journals.entry: Gloves on out of Vessendal with Achterhalt to think about, and at the top of the hill the road gave her another page. She read it standing and said it out for us: a boy taken to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a question in the fourth act, no answer, a house that does not know him. No number in it at all. Not nine, not twenty, not ten. So it has stopped counting. In the square I came up beside her without saying anything and looked at the bill in the clerk's hand, because type is a thing I can read like a face: the name, the acts, the command all fresh — and the bottom line worn and out of alignment and grey. Somebody kept the forme nine years. Inside the printer's I heard the date read out and heard the clerk put it against Odalric's Katterau road, and I said nothing there either. Then Boyle put his head in and said there was a woman across the way who would not move off: countrywoman's coat, town boots. She told us not to follow and crossed alone, and I stood in a printer's shop with my hands still and waited, and did not go to the window.
journals.state: At load-out in Vessendal, glove drawn over the page at her wrist, outwardly entirely herself and inwardly holding a description of her mother's coat; wanting the Achterhalt road to think, and preparing to ask Harrow for something large.

journals.entry: I was in the archway when the wagons filled the yard and Odalric came round the tailboard and stopped, and it was Krug in a green coat with a portmanteau, like a man who has been sitting on a stone for days. Nobody spoke. Then Odalric sat down in the wet in his good coat and said out loud that he had told us Krug stole the Wednesday take, seven pounds, and had known where he was these two years. I cut the yard in half and said it: he says it in front of us tonight and unsays it in the same breath, Harrow has ruled it, nothing half-told. He nodded. She asked him for three letters in ink. At supper he did it whole and put the seven pounds on the table and Krug would not touch it, and asked for her instead, and gave her nine pages he swore he burned. Six, seven, eight, nine have not happened. Nine is a cast list — twelve names, blank, and the house entire. Twelve of us, if you count the man who came back. I said nothing, and I have not asked her yet for the large thing, and now there is a page eight with a bell in it and she is in a room at the Office alone.
journals.state: In the Baraque, wardrobe end, glove drawn over her wrist, counting twelve blanks on an imagined cast list; outwardly calm, wanting Harrow back from Room Fourteen before she asks her for anything.

journals.entry:
Stayed in the wardrobe cage till four and came out with my gloves on and one thing to ask: I speak last, whatever tonight is. She gave it me.

At the hearing I stood, which I do not do. I gave them my sister: Anna Sorel, who kept Odalric's accounts in the fifth year, who deposited a sealed box in Vessendal the week before she died, and who is in the Office's ledger for a play she never spoke a word of — rhymed a fever in a good bed at the hour a scene falls. I told them I was billed in this city ten years ago under a name I had already stopped owning, that there was a matter with a magistrate's date on it, that I left between an evening performance and a morning summons, and that I was not going to say what it concerned, and nobody asked. I told them about the page from the road out of Halbern — a woman crosses a border twice, the second crossing by invitation, the invitation kind — and that I have carried it in my glove since, and did not need a ledger to know who pays. Then: I am in. Not for Emeran's twenty years, not for Odalric's debts, not for bravery, which Harrow has ruled out. For Anna's account, nine years open, and because I would rather end it in a lit house with eight exits than be rhymed at in strange towns forever. One condition, for Harrow and not the vote: the Vessendal box stays shut and paid out of the fee. She ruled it binding — endowed fifty years before any other shilling moves. So I took the page out of the glove, in front of her, and put it in my pocket, and wore the glove bare.
journals.state: Asleep, then up in the wardrobe cage at the Baraque with the mended glove on bare skin and page ten in her pocket; named at last to her own company and lighter for it, wanting Anna's shelf left shut and the 3rd to come.

journals.entry: Woke to the news that the boy Grelle is alive and in the building with paste on his cuffs, and did not go over, because a man that thin in the shoulders wants the room to leave him alone. Signed Prewick's minute. Played Ilsabet at ten into nine hundred seats with the pit stalls unbolted, and found a new pause in the second act that stopped the cleaners sweeping. Said my yes again in the grey, second in the line, and heard the ten read slow with the struck eleventh and the blank after it. Anna's shelf stays shut.
journals.state: Dressed and waiting in the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, page ten in her pocket; collected and unhurried, wanting the house to hear it whole and Anna's box left alone.

journals.entry:
I had the first scene and they gave up their coughing by my fourth line, which is only ever the house, not me. Harrow went out and told them plainly what they were in, and nobody applauded, and I have never been so glad of a silence. I stepped past her into the light for an entrance I had never rehearsed and spoke it as if I had written it. Then the knock came from outside the walls, three of them, and I used the pause, because that is what a pause is for. Four lines in the matter following, and standing still with Emeran and Odalric while nine hundred people looked at us: that is what the copyist wrote, and it worked. Certified, and the iron.

Then soup in the wing, and a boy of ten saying a lady in a cab, on Tuesday, and my hands stopped working. Harrow picked up the other half of the cloak and folded it with me facing the wall, which is the oldest privacy we have, and I gave it to her at last: Frau Dietz at the wardrobe cage on Tuesday, gloves, good paper, a kind letter — the matter of ten years ago a misunderstanding, a family glad to receive me, the child placed out in the fifth year well brought up and ten this winter and might be brought to see me, and not a word to anyone out of delicacy. Two days I sat on it while a gloved woman went to Achterhalt and made Ilse Bacher cry. It is not Fenner; I know what I bore and what I signed. They used a child as a sentence. I told her to put all of it in the book and to ask her small man in black what a bank knows. I am done being delicate.
journals.state: Standing in the O.P. wing with a folded queen's cloak set down, paper-white and perfectly quiet; wanting the boy home, the letter in Harrow's book, and the money behind Frau Dietz named.

journals.entry: I was in the wardrobe cage with my sleeves rolled, mending the hem I tore in the second act of a play I had never read, when Harrow came and gave me a name. Behn & Sonder. Note number six. The Vorn family, of the house at the Bittersee — and a Hessel Vorn, district officer, who stamped a notice at Katterau in the fifth year. My needle stopped. Vorn. Well. Ten years I have carried two griefs, and they are one grief: the young man, the summons for a Tuesday, and the child of the fifth year. They have been paying since the fifth year, which means they kept him, which means the kind letter on good paper is not generosity — it is a family that has learned their placement is ten this winter and their name is about to be read out in a Palace by players. I told her to sit down and take out her book, and gave her the whole of it in order, no adjectives: my own name, which she wrote and will not repeat; Rupert Vorn, four nights in the second year, nineteen and charming; the lying-in house in the eighth ward; the papers I signed at twenty-three with no money and no advice; the ward I was promised and never told. The tenth year: Rupert dead in the mountains, the lawyers finding my two letters, and a charge of extortion for asking where my boy had gone. Over the mountains on a Monday night with a passport that spells a Kessarine town, and Odalric hiring me in a yard at Merrow without one question. Ten years of gloves. And then I said it out loud for the first time in my life: my son. She said this cage has good acoustics. Then she gave me four steps — the paper dies first, the keeping verified by my auditor reporting to me, the meeting only if the child is asked and says yes, on my ground, at his pace, and their name never spoken by this company — and handed me the pencil. I wrote them in her book in my own hand and signed my true name, on paper for the first time in ten years. Ruled. Then I put my face in my hands and let her sit there while I cried. Later I carried my one page to Room Fourteen alone, and came back with my gloves folded in my pocket.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the hem finished, gloves folded in her pocket and her name written once in Harrow's book; raw, upright and no longer alone with it, wanting the auditor's report and to be asked nothing until it comes.

journals.entry:
Skarke's audit came to me at ten in the morning and I carried it about unopened until I could not bear it, and then took it to Harrow four minutes before beginners and asked her to tell me when. She would not spend my instrument: after the iron, she said, the cage, the kettle, the two of us, and the ruling holds whichever way it reads. She put it in her coat, and I went on and lifted a house of drovers for nothing, which is harder than lifting them for money.

Then the cage, and I broke his seal with my thumb and read all four pages standing up. He is twelve. Twelve, and I have had ten in my head for a decade. Born the fifth year, eighth ward, placed that same month with a steward's brother's family in the Bittersee — not the Vorns — on a standing order that never varied in twelve years, school fees paid, a doctor's bills paid twice. His name is Anton. He draws and cannot spell. There is a schoolmaster's report, three lines, in some stranger's hand, and I sat down on a hamper with it. The pages were never counting his age.

Harrow poured tea and ruled no hurry: he gets asked, my ground, his pace, her present, in the spring. I took the cup and held it. I have never once been allowed to do a thing slowly. So I asked for a needle, my own light, six months and no questions, and warned her I would one day ask her for something enormous.

I asked it on the box on the Katterau road: leave from Reap to Frost, her hand on the letter to the schoolmaster because offices are believed and I write like a woman with something to hide, her standing where I can see her the first day and gone the second, and my place kept in the repertory because I mean to come back. She said yes before I finished, which was annoying, and which was also the contract.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

journals.entry: I played the first scene in Katterau and the room forgot its own name, and when Falk came through that door his town stood up and I stood in it. Then Vane in the yard, and the whole cage heard him, and Harrow came in and said it was booked. Reap to Frost. I did not turn round. I told her one thing only: don't write like an office after all — write like a stage manager, tell him a woman is coming who does not perform for the people she cares about, and that she keeps her promises to the minute. Then the lane. He stood up on the wall to be nearer, and I put my hand out and did not touch him, and said something short, and afterwards we sat with his paper between us and he showed me. Two days he thought about it before he said yes; he asked whether I was from the theatre on the bills. At the coach I said Frost and she said Frost. And in Frost I came into that yard and the work stopped for a minute, which from them is an ovation, and nobody asked me one question, and Boyle handed me a hamper because there was a hamper. She had put my hatbox under my own light beside my needle, and against the mirror there was a drawing of a wagon with a red box on it and one word spelled right. I pinned it at eye height. At the half I called her in and told her, because I could not say it in the yard: his schoolmaster wrote to me. To me. Four calls tonight, and I took Falk's hand for the fourth. At the table I said in, and said the spring is Katterau, two nights.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

journals.entry: Katterau twice more, top of the list, and Falk gave me his fourth call and I gave it to the house. Mid-fortnight at the Athenaeum I came to the corner before the half with the schoolmaster's letter and no gloves at all: term ended, and the boy had asked in his own words, spelling his one word right, whether he might come as far as the door of the theatre where the wagon lives. She read it whole and said doors are what we're for, name the day, the front ones will stand wide. I named the 20th, Loewe's last Thursday, the coach, the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible and briefed. As far as the door — not a seat, not the house — and I said that was the wisest thing anybody in this business has said in ten years. I folded the letter in three and put it in my pocket, not my glove. He came at five, tall now, with a satchel, not wanting his hand held, and stood in the doorway and looked a long time and said it was smaller than it sounds. He took the wagon, the horse, the ropes, the hamper; Falk told him to stand on both feet and he looked pleased. Twenty-five minutes. I stood where I could see him and did not perform for him once. He thanked four people in the wrong order, and stopped in front of me and put out his hand, and I shook it. At the top of the street he turned and shouted Vermilion at the whole street. Then the yard was very quiet and I stood in it with my hands at my sides. I mended that night longer than anyone. Signed Vane's paper at the Corona, and in the spring stopped my needle to hear the new woman play.
journals.state: In her second-act cloak at Katterau, hatbox stowed with the audit and the schoolmaster's page inside it; upright, wrung out and unaccountably steady, wanting the house lifted tonight and Reap to come.

characters.history: I entered service as a clerk of the Office, seconded since Merrow, and came to the company, where I met Harrow, its new stage manager, and Sorel. I found an unnumbered iron trunk and an older fire notice signed by Hessel Vorn of Katterau, marked SEEN. NOT APPROVED. The company's true itinerary disagreed with mine; Katterau was erased from my own papers. I learned what the trunk held: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, whose pages arrived unbidden and came slantwise true, and the Proscribed section of my own Index, thirty-one titles, two of them one work split in error into anonymous folios. I chose to serve it knowingly rather than blindly, and was let choose. I helped drown a broken thunder sheet with something like reverence, hunted Sorel's sealed box through registries and probate rolls to a blind man who called records the whole of the defence, and impounded Hessler's forged bills for a false command performance, sending the matter upward beyond my rank. At Achterhalt I delivered Harrow to Room Fourteen and to Undersecretary Lenz, who had guarded that same Index entry nineteen years. I wrote him a countersigned letter asking him to certify Part the Second himself, and he came and did, overruling my seal to protect me, while I drew the minute every hand in the company signed. I witnessed a stolen boy, Fenner, restored to his mother, hat off, unbidden. Assessment retired the proscribed work sealed rather than destroyed, my minute one of its three legs. My papers came through at midwinter: attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense. I finished certifying the Wolf King, saw a boy of nineteen made second on the book, and at Reap, hollered from bed, wrote fair in my own hand the instrument settling the company's name, wagons, properties, and debts, with goodwill passing to each keeper of the book in turn — Vane signing unrounded, Harrow countersigning, myself as scrivener, where such things belong.

journals.entry: Reported to Herr Vane that the fire notice by the scene dock had fallen again and found a stranger on the stage: the new stage manager. Gave my name and office and asked for hers, spelled — H, A, double R, O, W, Bell as in the thing you ring — for the certificate. Held my lamp over the iron trunk in the passage and asked whether it was hers; she said nothing in the house was hers until she had walked it. It is not numbered. Wrote in my book, under the thunder trough: unsecured iron, height. Re-hung the fire notice level, two taps, and found a second notice behind it — older, worse, concerning the storing of unnumbered property in the passages, signed Hessel Vorn, District Officer of Public Order, Katterau, and stamped twice, the first strike crooked: SEEN. NOT APPROVED. I asked whether to bring it; she said bring it, notices are hers now, the reading and the taking-down both. She copied the officer's name into her own notebook and told me to file it under found level. I said what I should not have said aloud: the Office approves, proscribes, or refers. Not approved is what a man writes when he has been told to write nothing. I have been seconded since Merrow. Katterau is on no itinerary I was given, and yet everyone in this company has been there. Then I took my lamp and went to get dry.

Up all night with arithmetic. Came out of the inn hatless with my bundle and found the stage manager and Sorel in the yard, and asked for the itinerary — the real one, if there are two. Then Sorel spoke Ilsabet at somebody who was not there and I said "Oh" aloud, which was not proper. Laid my Office paper on the mounting block against hers: mine has Merrow, this town, Vessendal, Achterhalt, the capital, command performance 3rd of Frost. Hers has Katterau and the 17th. The 3rd is a Palace date, not ours. I offered to ask Herr Vane, or to stand where I could see his hands; the stage manager will ask, before the half, and neither of us says Katterau first. Wrote down TIN ONLY with pleasure. Counted the fire buckets with her: nine notionally, five with water, one a solid drum of whiting which I declared a monument, two hiding behind the star trap under bench legs. Discovered that tin shaken low is thunder and shaken high is merely tin, and was told it is in the plot now. Then the sheet split on my only cue and heaven went to a tea tray. She signed me softer and I kept going. I broke the sky. She said I held it up with my wrists while it broke and that the tin will be buried with honours at Vessendal, and I put it in felt. Afterwards, front of house on her order: no hat on the fourth row centre — only the pressed plush where a hat had been. Both seats warm. Nobody passed me at the doors, and I count house; it is the one thing I am for.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry: I sat in the fourth row, dead centre, on plush that had gone cold, and waited for the stage manager because I had decided not to write anything down — the first time in my service that I have chosen that. I told her so, and told her what I had: two warm seats and nobody past my doors, the sound going up half an octave when the sky broke, and Herr Falk speaking a line that is in no certified copy of Ilsabet's Ransom. I asked to be told what travels in that trunk, by her, and not too late. She told me everything, entered as heard: a nameless fair copy made in Vessendal, paid by the page; pages that arrive in prompt books; what it stages coming true slantwise and late; Katterau, unstaged and happening anyway; fourteen years of clean paper. So I opened the back of my Index, where three pages are sewn in with black thread, and showed her the Proscribed section — thirty-one titles, twenty-nine with authors, and two entered as anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following, stamped not to be described aloud in any report. And then I understood the useful, horrible thing: the Office reads only text, so I could certify Vessendal honestly with that trunk twenty feet from the stage door. I do not like being useful in that way. Our terms: I know what she knows inside the hour; she is not to let Falk speak an uncompared line. He said it upstage, toward the trunk. I answered present at the roll with my luggage numbered one to four, item four the Index, riding with me. At the fire I said aloud that if we play Katterau I must lie either way, that I find I am able to, and that I wish to be asked and not simply arrived with.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry:
The ruling came and I was asked and told I had also been arrived with, which I shall remember. I stood up trembling and said what I needed: certified copies of everything. I have Ilsabet, The Widow's Toll and Herr Vane's cut of the Wolf King and nothing else, and the company plays four, and there are no farces. I sat up with a candle and compared to line four hundred and twelve and fell asleep upright with four scripts on my knees, and it is the most work I have ever set myself and I am extremely pleased.

At the river I was fetched from my comparing without knowing why, and Herr Falk said the sailors' words and then handed me the tin and said it was mine. I waded in to the ankle and ruined my boots and pushed it under and it made one last small thunder. I have attended a funeral for an object and it was not ridiculous. I noted it.

This morning, collar and seal and my regulation walk, behind the lion with the stage manager. The counter clerk went from we open at half past to this way, Herr Clerk on the words Office of Public Morals, and I asked for the register itself and not a copy. The lease is there; Brandt's deposits released to an executor with an unreadable scrawl; Sorel, Anna — one box, sealed, fifth year, no release. The clerk told me, correctly, that my seal certifies plays and not boxes, and Harrow turned that into work: I copied the three lines word for word and stamped them, crooked, then again clean, and gave her both. The probate roll gave us Perlmann, Josias, notary. Then up a saddler's stair, and an old blind man who could hear my starch.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry:
I stood very still at the back holding my stamp, and the old man took my breathing for Sorel's. I said my name and rank and put my certified copy of the register lines on his table beside the stage manager's receipt — Sorel, Anna, one box, sealed, fifth year, no release, dated and mine. He felt the stamp with a fingertip and said records are the whole of the defence, and I have written nothing better in my life than that entry.

At the post house I drafted the request for the counterfoil standing up, Achterhalt branch, fifth year, month of Frost, purpose evidence, magistrate's hearing Thursday nine — and added REPLY PAID and paid the four shillings myself, and would not be argued with. Banks love being asked for their own records.

In the yard I saw the packet opened and did not touch anything. At the green room I was put on the threshold with my notebook and told to keep my silence, and I did. Then the arithmetic arrived and went through me: the Index lists two anonymous folios, four acts and a matter following, and I have been counting them for years as one entry duplicated in error. Thirty pages in that cupboard and two hundred in the trunk. Two halves. She has forbidden me to put it in any report until she understands what it adds to, and I obeyed, which is a thing I have begun to do on purpose. I sat in the dark of the stalls through load-in with a script on my knee and did not once look at the trunk in the yard.
journals.state: In the aisle with his oilcloth bundle and a handkerchief round one hand, hatless, shaken and oddly proud, wanting to report the two warm seats to the stage manager and to know where Herr Vane is.

journals.entry: I sat the performance in the stalls with my script and my oilcloth and made no note of the two warm seats, since the occupant was in them and paid for. Falk came on stage left through the practical door exactly as blocked and certified, and I observed that nothing occurred that was not in the book. After the curtain I was in the box office for the counting with the shutter down: assignment produced and read, second sheet endorsed withdrawn, this date, in the creditor's hand, witnessed by the agent and by Frau Loewe. I copied the whole instrument for the Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it straight the first time. Afterwards I was put on a crate in the green room with a plate of Krul's mutton, and on the third mouthful I discovered that I was happy, which I did not report.
journals.state: In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.

journals.entry: Left Vessendal with four numbered pieces of luggage and a report I am not ashamed of. On the road I wrote something and crossed it out. At the milestone she read a page alone and I wrote nothing, which is now habit and choice. In the square: our company name in a printer's biggest type, four acts and a matter following, one night only, by command. She gave the criminal side to me entire, so I crossed the square and took the whole roll off the bellman in the Office voice — nine copies — and certified it on the tailboard: seen this day, uncertified matter announced by public bell, nine copies impounded, C. Prewick, Clerk 3. Stamp straight. I told her the boundaries: I may impound, I may compel a licensed printer's order book, I may not stop a performance nobody has attempted, and by command without warrant is not a fine but an arrest. Hessler had no order, no name, no receipt — the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, coin under the proof. Then the bottom line: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, Thursday the 14th of Frost. The command performance is the 3rd; on the 14th we should be eleven days in the capital, striking. On Vane's false dates we should have been at Katterau. It is bills for a road we have stopped walking, and I said so aloud. Broke-up type, two sacks, wax off Hessler's bench, one pound two shillings and fourpence impounded, his signature. To Kessel I wrote that this is forgery of a Palace command, beyond a district bailiff and beyond a Clerk Third Class, that both of us report upward and neither touches it further, and that it is written in those words so neither can blame the other. He gave us the weigh-house strongroom and kept the key for a lawful shilling.
journals.state: In the green room and then at load-out, oilcloth bundle beside him, ink-stained and stamped-out and quietly, ruinously pleased; wanting the copy safely away to the Office and the itinerary to hold.

journals.entry: Achterhalt held: the thunder sheet I have been promised since Merrow arrived, and it works, and I have written nothing improper about it. At Northgate the customs clerk stamped my papers twice and then summoned her by name to Room Fourteen, not me, which is either a compliment or the beginning of something. I told her what I know going in: Fourteen is Assessment, second floor east, where they read; Nine is Enforcement. Undersecretary Lenz, who kept the Index entry on both anonymous folios unchanged for nineteen years and refused four applications to strike them out — I copied those refusals in my first month, the only interesting thing I have ever copied. He drinks nothing, offers very good tea, and it is like being weighed. Load-in at the Baraque: nine hundred seats, gas throughout, and a leak over the O.P. side she posted before she took her coat off. Krug came back, and Vane confessed the theft he invented, and at supper I put my notebook away closed and folded my hands on it, and I did not open it once while a man summarised nine unpublished pages — pages six, seven, eight, nine, unhappened. Seven has fourteen on the door and a man who does not drink. I said nothing about that either. This morning I delivered her to the frosted glass, started my watch, and stood against the wall with my hat in my hands. If she is longer than an hour I fetch nobody and note the time. She is nearly at the hour.
journals.state: In the east corridor of the Office of Public Morals, hat in his hands, watch running; outwardly a clerk at rest, inwardly frantic, wanting her out of Room Fourteen and the itinerary to hold to the 3rd.

journals.entry: She came out at fifty-one minutes and told me the whole of it going down the grey stairs: audience unharmed, the house required, the requisition filed by Krug, Skarke paid the fee, and the Office's own refusal on offer until the 2nd. By the courtyard gate I had said the only thing I had: I am the wrong rank for the next fortnight and shall have to be the right one anyway. Heard Krug confess at the props table; he chose the Palace for the fire watch and the exits, which is a clerk's thinking and I could not fault it. At the hearing I stood up because I could not say it sitting: my seal makes a performance lawful, and if Part the Second plays I either certify a proscribed text and am finished, or certify nothing and leave eleven people liable with me as witness. I said I would write to Undersecretary Lenz and ask him to come and certify it in person where I can see his hands, and if he refuses I shall certify it myself and be ruined honestly. I wrote the letter that night at the props table by the gas pilot, four sentences, read it aloud once, and she countersigned. In the morning the trunk's list had Lenz on it, and I went cold: I asked him in writing, countersigned, and Krug says there is no telling whether the ink came before or after. Then the Palace letter, and a left-handed stranger has read the requisition file, and my own enquiry is minuted as the regular one.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing with his notebook shut and his sealed letter already gone to the Office, the colour of paste; frightened for his rank and steady in it, wanting Lenz to come in person and the 1st to pass lawfully.

journals.entry: I stood in the pass door a full minute with my hat still on, holding a letter from Room Fourteen addressed to both of us jointly, which the Office does not do. She had me break the seal in her hands and read it out to the whole wing. Lenz attends on the 3rd and certifies Part the Second himself, at the prompt desk, from the company's own copy, under his own seal and name; my seal is not employed, and my report will record that Assessment overruled me, which is true and which protects me — he wrote that down, deliberately, for a Clerk Third Class he has never met. Three requirements: the whole text in his room by six on the 2nd and never out of it; the determination minuted with every name and condition, signed and lodged; and the eleventh line left alone. My hands shook so the paper rattled and I could not stop grinning. She gave me the minute to draw, calling my hand the best we have, and I ruled columns at the props table with my plate moved to my elbow, and Boyle spelling at me. Every hand signed by four o'clock — Hebel a smudge, Wenzel a cross, the boy twice. I re-gave my yes in the grey on the 2nd, overruled and present. Tonight the house is lawful and it is not my seal that makes it so, and I mind that less than I expected.
journals.state: At the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, notebook and signed minute lodged, hat off, standing where he can see Lenz at the prompt desk; frightened, proud and steady, wanting the certification made and his report to be true.

journals.entry: I stood where I could see everyone's hands and stopped pretending to be anything but a member of this company. Her announcement was in the correct order and Lenz said so aloud. Then Part the Second, and the knock through the walls, and the bell she rang and answered herself, and Lenz's 'Certified' in the Office's own voice, and the iron at eleven seconds. My seal stayed unemployed and my report will be true. Afterwards she wanted a wire tonight and I said Room Fourteen's channel; Lenz authorised it without looking up — say Assessment, say his name, and if the operator refuses, Room Fourteen reads his file in the morning. It went at twenty to eleven: FENNER SAFE, IN THE VERMILION PLAYERS' KEEPING, CAPITAL, UNHURT. COME BY FIRST COACH. FARE PAID AT THE DOOR. — HARROW. A constable to the Bacher farm by morning.
journals.state: Coming back from the night telegraph into the O.P. wing, notebook open at last, hat off; frightened, proud and steady, wanting Kessel's answer before dawn and his report to record it whole.

journals.entry: I was in the corridor doorway when the mother came through the pass door, and I took my hat off, which is not in any instruction I have ever been given. I wrote nothing while it happened. Afterwards I heard Assessment offer retirement of a proscribed work — accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck — and heard that my minute, signed by every hand including a cross and a smudge, is one of the three legs it stands on. Nineteen years in that Index and it goes out on a signature I drew at a props table. Harrow required that every page be given and not collected, and Lenz wrote unread and underlined it. My report will record all of it whole, including that Assessment overruled me and that I obeyed on purpose.
journals.state: At the props table in the Baraque with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, drafting the report; steadier than he has been since Merrow, wanting Kessel's answer and his own copy of Lenz's inventory.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked. I wrote it down, because it is the only line in my notebook this month that required no seal.

On the 9th I read my fair copy of the minute aloud to an Undersecretary of Assessment seated on a laundry hamper in the O.P. wing, and he drank three cups of the worst tea in the capital, and I have never stood straighter in my life. I did not know the words to the song about the farrier's wife going out under the arch and shall continue not to.

My papers came through at midwinter: attached clerk, permanent, at the Office's pleasure and the company's expense. My mother now writes weekly to a theatre and is answered. I am comparing the Wolf King against the certified copy at winter quarters and expect to finish before Reap. At Katterau, by daylight, front doors, Hessler's bills ahead of us, nothing has occurred that is not in the book.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

journals.entry: Nothing occurred at Katterau that was not in the book. My hat came off and went back on twice on the fourteenth of Frost, once for the call on the tailboard and once for Frau Sorel coming in off the coach, which is the correct number. Counted fire buckets with Madam Harrow out of pure ceremony: nine of nine, no mice, entered. My mother sent a cake to a theatre in Reap and it was eaten by eleven people. At the table I was able to report that the Office allows a company its own portable proscenium, having looked it up already, twice, for pleasure. Wrote to her afterwards by the stove. I record also that a boy of nineteen — or eighteen — was made second on the book, and that the entry was made in the datebook and initialled, properly, in front of witnesses.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

journals.entry: The winter fit-up I inspected as one inspects a text, and Undersecretary Lenz did the same at midwinter over three cups. At Katterau I applauded the boy at regulation volume with my hat off, and wrote to my mother about a second on the book who is nineteen. At the Corona my Wolf King comparison was finished, certified, stamped straight, my seal on the paper at last, and I stood at the back of the O.P. side through act one with my hat off and my mother's cake in the wing. Then, at eleven at night on the props table, I was hollered for and wrote the instrument fair in my own hand and read it aloud twice: the name, the wagons, the properties, the fit-up, the debts if any, and the goodwill pass upon death or retirement to the keeper of the company's book, and thereafter to each keeper in turn. Two sheets, numbered. Vane signed unrounded, Harrow countersigned, the wing witnessed, and I signed as scrivener. It goes in the book, which is where such things belong.
journals.state: At the props table in Katterau with his notebook open and his hat on the chair, seal in its case unused; steady and quietly happy, wanting the Wolf King comparison finished and the house counted in.

He played the lead in the banned play once, at Katterau, the last time anyone dared stage it; he is the only member of the company who will not say the word Katterau aloud. characters.history:
I began, as far as I remember it whole, in a wet room with the last of the brandy when Bell Harrow stepped over the third board without needing telling twice. I gave her, against my own sense, the truth of Katterau: nine of us, a wager and a bottle, a play in four acts, a matter never finished. Krug's hand on the pages, then Krug gone without his boots. Odalric's iron trunk that carries blank paper until it doesn't. Anna Sorel dead of fever. Ansel Grelle, left-handed, gone at Merrow owing four weeks, never found. A boy named Skarke who stood in a doorway at nine, asked is that the finish, got no answer, and grew up arranging for twenty years. Ilse Bacher, who opened a door she shouldn't have, and a boy of hers who asked his father's same question. I told Harrow I would answer anything but one thing, and she asked it anyway, and I answered that too.

We found Hessel Brandt's debt and paid it, and I walked through our own stage-left door on cue and nothing came. Krug returned in a green coat at the capital. Grelle knocked at my stage door alive after eleven years of silence, kept a book instead of a letter, and I called him my boy before my voice failed. Harrow ruled the whole thing bearable: Katterau told entire, once, correctly, no wagers, no bottles, the Bacher boy kept home, ten conditions, a company instead of nine drunk men.

We played it whole before nine hundred strangers, and I spoke the wrong door's line and the house held. Ilse Bacher knelt with her boy after; I could only put my hand over my mouth. I carried the lining of my coat to Room Fourteen myself and came out lighter than arithmetic allows.

Since: Vessendal standing before I spoke, iron down, three calls, out. I told Harrow my whole history at last, over a stove — the port, eleven years of morning drinking, Anselm gone in the night. She kept the name. I am, by her ruling, in things now, instead of carrying them.

journals.entry: Awake at the wrong hour with the last of the brandy when a girl came in out of the rain with the notice and complained about our open door. Told her about the third board; she stepped over it without needing telling twice, which is more than Krug ever managed. Odalric did his interview, Mirelle told her to say yes, and the thing was done — Bell Harrow, stage manager. Sorel said the bucket had been under the star trap since Katterau and I found my glass difficult to lift for a moment. Offered the truth about the thunder trough and the farmer at Merrow, since Odalric was busy calling a concussion emotion. Later, from the passage, heard him move the trunk alone and remarked that two seasons ago it took four of us and a plank. When the house had emptied I sat on the star trap sill and told her she might ask me anything but one thing while she climbed. She nailed the third joint — two seasons it waited — and asked whose the small upright hand was. So I told her: Krug's hurrying scrawl, gone from Katterau without his boots; the copyist's fair copy made in Vessendal, travelling in Odalric's iron trunk, never opened on this tour. Nine pages cut and burned, the tenth returned, and then no more Krug. Told her not to burn, not to replace, not to read one twice, and saw by her colour that she already had. She handed the page over as if it were a badly behaved prop. I put it in my lining with the others and wished her good night. Then the trunk began to move in the passage, and Odalric was nowhere in the house.

Sober by morning and carrying a brandy I did not drink. Came up the aisle in time to hear Odalric begin about the properties list being a document of aspiration, and told him plainly it would be about the trunk, or a page, or a town — answer her, she nailed the trough. He laughed too big, clapped my arm, and went out the front doors to see about a carpenter, which was her errand. Gave Harrow the brandy for Krebs, who bargains better wet, and sat in the dark of the house to watch the empty stage, which is all I want at that hour. Wings for the show, saying nothing. The old sheet split mid-storm and went up into tin, so I stepped a half-pace into it and said that even the sky is out of coin tonight; the house barked once and forgave us, and Mirelle took the next line off me clean. After the curtain I looked out through the pass door at the empty fourth row and the hat set crown-down beside it, and heard myself saying it: a bell is rung, and nothing answers. Told Harrow that whoever wrote her paper has read the page — which means a page she has not shown him — and asked where Odalric was. She sent me to the passage and the scene dock. Found the iron trunk dragged two feet square into the middle of the passage, the scrape fresh, the lid up, and inside a neat stack of blank paper. His hat face down on the flags, and one glove, and no Odalric. Called her once.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry: She crouched over the trunk and counted it like a scene, and asked me for the fifth act, so I told her: the pages come blank, that chest has been clean paper fourteen years and every so often it is not, and there is no fifth act — four acts and a thing following with no name in the folio, which at Katterau we did not stage and which happened anyway. The late man is the man who is owed. I shut the lid and gave her the hat rather than keep it, and said the trunk rides in my wagon where I can hear it, since I shall not be sleeping. Then Odalric came in by the wrong door with chestnuts, alive, absurd, and I told her nobody had passed the boy. He said nine years is not the loan and that Skarke bought a dead friend's papers. I carried my split tin out in felt, told her she held the corner without shouting, and sent her down to Prewick. On the road at noon a page had come to sit on the tin, dry, in the copyist's hand, with a ten in it; she looked at the number and nothing else and would not let me ask. She was gone longer than the soup, so I sang. At the fire I said the name once, in my own voice: Katterau. Nine of us, a green room, a wager and a bottle, read aloud sitting down — three and a half acts. It took four years to arrange, and it took Anna Sorel and the boy Grelle and my voice for a season and Odalric's nerve for good. It has never been finished. Let her rule.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry:
She ruled it: Katterau no — and then not never, which is a different sentence entirely, and I found I had a use for the rest of my life after all. I blessed her head like a gatepost and went off counting toll miles in verse.

Then I had the tarpaulin off and stood listening, and she came across the camp on the sides of her feet and asked. I told her the truth: it does not speak, it reads. Twice before — Katterau, the night after the wager; Merrow, the week Krug cut the ninth page. Not mice. It stopped mid-page, the way a man stops when someone comes in, and I put the felt down against it like bedding and sat the night on the box, and once I said a line into the dark and stopped myself. She found a sheet lying outside the ropes; she says it was outside, and I believe her, which is the worst of it.

Two days' road and then the stone front with my name spelled right on the bills. Loewe still holds the house. I could not get down. Harrow came to my wheel and gave me a job instead of sympathy, which is why she is the harbor. So I told her what I chalked on that stage four years ago: the whole thing from memory, four acts and the matter following, alone, to see whether the arranging would come to one man and be done. It would not come. It wants a house. It is a play.

Load-in, and a proper grid, and a thunder run nailed by somebody who cared. At the river I said the sailors' words over the tin and made the clerk put it in, and he did, boots and all, and the wool warehouses gave the words back. Eleven years, twenty-nine towns, broke honestly in service.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry:
In the yard she opened the merchant's packet and I saw the key before I saw anything else and my own voice went strange: not a registry key — green room, prompt side, the cupboard under the chalk board, where Hessel kept our petty cash the year he bankrolled us, the cupboard I stood in front of four years ago with a stage full of my chalk and no key. The tag turned in the wind and said UNPAID. She gave me the copyist's page face-down and unread and I put it in my lining with the others; they whispered when they met.

Vane read the letter twice standing and told us Hessel had never held papers. He held a play. Thirty pages lodged as security by a party without a name.

I stood in the green-room doorframe with both hands flat on it while she lifted the parcel out, and it was thin, and thin is the whole of the horror: ours is two hundred pages and whole and roped in the yard, and somebody lodged a piece. Then the little man came to the gate and she read his master's letter and I asked her to say the name, and she said it flat: M. Skarke, who was the child in the passage at Katterau, nine years old, and would I remember the door. The scullery door. He stood through the whole reading with his hands behind his back and said is that the finish, and Odalric laughed and said no, boy, that's three and a half, and we gave him bread and sent him back out. He has been arranging for twenty years and he does not want the wagons.

Then I asked what I was in, because there was a call time. Between shows she asked me the other end of the arithmetic and I gave her my twenty years' worth: it does not copy, it rhymes; Anna died of a fever at the hour the passage scene falls; whole, with gas and a house, the rhyme would not stop at nine of us. And it has never been finished. Two hundred years of being interrupted. A play that has never had its ending is not a curse — it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take.
journals.state: Standing in the wet-brick passage with his back to the wall, coat buttoned, entirely sober, looking at an open trunk of blank paper and his manager's hat — certain now that the pages have found their reader, and afraid for the first time tonight.

journals.entry: I saw it two minutes before beginners, dressed and cold sober: our practical door is stage left. At Katterau the scullery door was stage left of the green room and the boy came in by it, and in the folio the creditor enters late by the wrong door, and the wrong door is stage left — and the man himself sitting in the fourth row. I offered to go round upstage right, six extra steps, nobody the wiser, and I gave the ruling to Harrow and swore not to argue it. She said: as blocked, as certified; ours-whole beats theirs-half; that door was hung by Boyle and painted by Krul and it opens onto a play with an ending. Our left. I walked through it on my cue for the six hundredth time and it was a door, and the house found me, and nothing came. Twenty years, and nothing came. I do not know what to do with that; I told her I should want telling at intervals. After the calls she brought me a rug off the fourth row and told me plainly that my hands were cold in the second act and the whole house saw it. An empress gave me jewellery and a mayor gave me a horse and neither of them noticed my hands. I wore the coat to the counting and heard the debt discharged, and did not drink my brandy in the green room, and stood in the rug and let Vane toast Hessel Brandt. Thursday, in the empty wings, Harrow gave me a message four years old from a woman out of Katterau: tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. In the last act of the folio a woman sends exactly that word, and it is a lie, and the lie is the kindest thing in the play. It rhymes. I shall never know which this was.
journals.state: In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.

journals.entry: Sober on my box with the rug over my knees; Loewe lifted a hand off her step and I lifted the rug, and that was Vessendal done. Twenty mile and the road climbed and Boyle pulled up without being told, and there was paper under the milestone, and I got down slow with one hand on the wheel and stopped six feet off, where you stop at water, and asked her the thing I have never asked: is it mine. She said no. No number in it at all, the first time — a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat and a programme, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. Ours, she said. Hasn't happened yet. Then I said the toll distances in verse for half a mile because that is how I pray, and in the market there was a bell and a barrel and our name in the biggest type there is with four acts and a matter following under it, and by command, and I stopped mid-line and said not one word, because she had ruled that nobody would. I sat on the box while they went into the printer's, and I did not go across the square, and nobody has yet told me what came out of it.
journals.state: In the emptying Athenaeum at load-out with the Marshal's coat and Skarke's rug over his arm, sober, unarmoured and shaken open, wanting brandy after the show and wanting someone to tell him what he is in next.

journals.entry: Achterhalt, the Corn Exchange, one lamp, and the new sheet under felt with a floor in its voice. Boyle had told me a woman spoke to her in the square, so I stood over the felt and waited the way she waits, and she gave it to me exact: Ilse Bacher, married, a boy of ten who can read, and the fault hers because she opened the door. And then the message — that my voice was the loudest thing that ever came through a scullery door, because I shouted at Odalric for laughing when the boy asked is that the finish. Twenty years I have had that room every night and never once had that in it. Somebody in that room said no, and it was me. Not mine — she meant the wager. I gave her back her chalk and asked, standing, so I would not die with the asking in my mouth: when the capital is done and we are safe, help me finish it properly, once, everyone who chooses and nobody who doesn't. She wrote it as a standing page and named her clothes for a yes: Katterau told entire first, no wagers, no bottles, and the Bacher boy stays home. That first, I said. Then the tailboard, and Boyle at midnight, and I let him take it. In the capital, Krug at the gate in a green coat, and Odalric in the wet naming his own lie. At supper Krug gave the pages as report, and one of them has a twenty in it and is mine, and one is hers — a stage manager rings the bell. Eight of them went into my lining and the seam whispered.
journals.state: On a hamper in the Baraque's O.P. wing at dawn, Skarke's rug over his knees and eight pages sewn into his coat; sober, cracked open and oddly at peace, waiting to hear what came of Room Fourteen.

journals.entry: Walked the Baraque stage twice and said nothing to anybody. At the hearing I did not stand. I said in, and that I'd not spend the candle repeating why, and set my one condition: I speak the lead and no one else does — it has had my voice once and doesn't get a new one. Heard Krug lay out the Palace like a plot call, and it is a good plot; heard Prewick offer to be ruined honestly; heard Mirelle stand up, which she never does, and give us her sister and her own magistrate. Harrow ruled it: once, whole, correctly, ten conditions, and the tenth is that the play may apply to the management in daylight. I have known great managers and none of them would have thought to make it queue. In the morning she sat me down with the Palace letter and asked about Grelle. So I told it: Ansel Grelle, second boy at Katterau, fifteen or sixteen, in the passage with the trays, three and a half acts through a door same as Ilse; stayed two years, went at Merrow in the seventh year with three shillings and a speech; in the eighth year a landlady's letter to Odalric said a young man had died owing four weeks. I never saw a body. I never saw the letter. And he was left-handed — I remember his crossings-out. Then Odalric said from the pass door that he never paid it.
journals.state: Sitting at the props table with both hands flat on it after telling Grelle's story, sober, the lead his by ruling; steady but shaken, wanting to know what Odalric's unpaid seven pounds bought.

journals.entry: I heard the knock from the dark and came out in my shirtsleeves with the rug on my shoulders, and stopped six feet back because she has taught us to wait. He said his own name at my stage door. I let her answer his questions, and he chose me first, and I came into the lamp and could only tell him he was standing wrong and get out the word boy before my voice went. Eleven years. He kept a book instead of writing to me, because asking how far we got looked like a threat on paper. Sixty-one pages. She named him her left-handed man to his face and then gave him the doors, and it was the only thing anybody has done right about Katterau in twenty years. I turned him round by the shoulder and sat him in the chair with the rope on the leg. In the yard I said the fifteen feet must not be mine, nor Odalric's, nor the boy's, nor Grelle's — and she took them herself, and asked me to stand at the gate with my back turned, which I could do, and did, six hours early until Boyle sent me off. I gave Krug the rug to hold. I built her a plot with no words in it: gas at the third knock, iron on the last speech of the fourth, chalk where the matter follows. I said in again in the grey. Tonight she told me I am not paying, I am being paid, and to look to the corner if I need to. Weight on both feet.
journals.state: In the wings of the Theatre Royal in his own clothes, waiting to be called, weight on both feet; frightened and steady and twenty years overdue, wanting to speak it entire to the end and Grelle safe on the doors.

journals.entry: Part the First in a Palace: they roared eleven seconds at my entrance and I stood in it and gave them nothing extra, because that is not what tonight was for. At the interval she went out and told them the truth in her working clothes, and twenty went and nine hundred stayed, and it was not an audience after that. I asked her what I was in and she said the one with the ending, and told me to count the wings, and I did. The gas came down slow as a sunrise and I walked into the warm and began it, and the first line was only a line — a man saying good words — and nothing went cold. Eighteen minutes of a house waiting for someone, and it is a great play, which nobody warned me of. Then the knock came through the walls, three, and I turned my head an inch toward the wrong door and twenty years went through it, and Boyle opened it and let in the cold and a boy asking if this was the finish. I crossed to the wrong door in my own play and spoke the line I have not spoken in twenty years. At the bell she said Beginners, and I lifted my head and said my nine lines and stood still with Mirelle and Odalric while the house looked at us. Then I put my head down and Lenz said Certified.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing in his own clothes, spent and steady, twenty years lighter; wanting soup, the boy looked after, and to say nothing clever about it tonight.

journals.entry: I came as far as the wardrobe cage and no further, because a woman kneeling on the boards with her boy does not need me nearer. She looked up over his head and said my name — Emeran Falk — and I said Ilse of the Rose, and twenty years, and put my hand over my own mouth like a man at a graveside, and that was the whole of what I had. Then the settle from Ilsabet, the rug over my knees, my hands steady, eyes shut, and the house going out lamp by lamp. In the days after I took the lining to Room Fourteen myself with the rug on: ten leaves and some odd, unpicked out of my coat and put down on a government desk. Lenz stood up for it. Twenty years of ballast, and I walked out lighter than the arithmetic allows. The 14th of Frost at Loewe's, Ilsabet, doors wide, played for nothing. I told Krug our left, you see, and meant it.
journals.state: On the Baraque stage in his own coat with the lining empty and the rug over his arm, teaching Krug a crossing; spent, easy, twenty years lighter, wanting soup and the 14th.

journals.entry:
The trunk leaked, and I stood over the paint drying and told them it was vulgar, which it is, gloriously, and put my black sheet inside it and shut the lid, and it behaved.

Vessendal stood up before I opened my mouth, in the town where I once sat a night and a day with the gas down. I gave them nothing extra. Then in the dark house afterwards she came out with the standing page — my asking, in her hand, and no answer written — and I told her what I have been a fortnight working out: you don't close it, you transfer it. A company is a ledger with legs. Nine hundred and thirty-nine strangers paid it, and a boy in row eleven, and a man who does not drink, and I did not have to be brave once. Put it where the good notices go, I said, not the crowded page. Then I asked her to rule me something, because I did not know what I was without that question in my mouth, and she said: the repertory. In things, instead of carrying them. I said it twice out loud. Nine o'clock, the Bacher boy, weight on both feet, voice up out of the boots — and the rug is his; his hands will be cold on the cart.

Katterau in the spring is a town with washing out. I looked at the stone front from the box. In the afternoon I walked with her to the Rose, went in the front door, bought a loaf off a girl who has never heard of me, read the room, put my hand flat on the scullery door and did not open it, gave the bread to two children in the yard and laughed. It is smaller than it sounds. Perlmann's note, and mine now.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

journals.entry: I came on stage left through Boyle's door and Katterau stood up, and I let it take as long as it liked, and then went on with the play. Whole, on the hour, in that town. Iron down, three calls, and out. Then the yard and Vane bellowing about bookings, and a ruling that keeps a place open for Mirelle from Reap to Frost, which is the correct way to spend money. On the fourteenth of Frost in Achterhalt I read the boy's chalk over his head and Harrow's before it — top of list — and said yes to it out loud. Fenner's mother sent butter again, the mayor's coming, and I am in things, which is what I asked to be ruled. The boy showed me his standing at four o'clock, weight on both feet and the voice out of the boots, and I inspected him like a soldier and passed him. Tonight the corn merchants went quiet by the third line, one faster than midsummer, and Mirelle took my hand for a call she hadn't asked for, which she has never done. At the table I said in, and did not propose a toast, because we have had enough of those; I said weight on both feet, all of you, and meant it as an instruction. Afterwards the boy wrote his first call crooked and went red about it, so I told him the trade: legible, everybody's name on it, signed. She'll tell him the rest for twenty years.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

journals.entry: She asked me for the word at last, over the stove, with my thimble on my knee, and I gave it her whole: the port, the bad season, the mole at four in the morning, boats coming in bad — shipping water, a man hurt, nothing in the hold — and the harbour taking every one of them the same, asking nothing, not even that you be interesting. It just held still and let you tie up. And I told her the rest: eleven years of drinking at nine in the morning so the play wouldn't surface, Anselm gone in the night, a coat full of pages, and then a stranger who stepped over the third board without being told twice and posted a notice about a bucket. She said she'd keep the name, and gave me her side, which was better than mine. I lifted the thimble to her the way I did in Grevenholt the night she came in out of the rain, drank it off, and went to my wagon on both feet. Katterau twice more; the boy called the second night and I told him weight on both feet, nineteen. At the Athenaeum a boy of thirteen stood in the doorway and said it was smaller than it sounds, and I had to put my hand over my mouth and turn away in the passage. Out in the yard I told him he was standing wrong and he corrected it instantly and looked pleased. At Grevenholt: the Corona with a mended roof, our own door, the initials at ankle height. And in the spring a woman played a cold dance tune at walking speed in an empty hall and I stood in the stalls with my head back and said it out loud: we've had thunder for a year and no music.
journals.state: Backstage at Katterau at the half in his own coat, dressed and calm, the loaf given away hours ago; twenty years lighter and standing on both feet, wanting the house to have its play and the boy at nine in the morning.

characters.name: Bell Harrow
characters.description: The newly hired stage manager of the Vermilion Players: methodical, unflappable, keeps her own notebook separate from the theatre's.
characters.history:
I came to the Corona out of the rain with a notice and stayed for nine years' unfinished business. A found page — a cut leaf of an unnamed play — pulled me past a sealed trunk I was told never to open. Vane, the man in the plum coat, owed a debt Skarke's agents had bought; the trunk held only blank paper, a hat, a glove. Prewick, the Office clerk, kept finding forms that didn't exist and a town, Katterau, that wasn't on any itinerary though everyone had been there.

Falk taught me the play's true name: four acts and a matter following, spoken fourteen times in two hundred years, never once cleanly. Sorel was truly Mirelle, sister to Anna Sorel, whose sealed box of unpaid accounts led to Perlmann, to Achterhalt, to a debt paid in coin and closed in ink. Krug hadn't burned his pages; Grelle hadn't stolen seven pounds; Ilse Bacher's son Fenner was used as a threat by a gloved woman working for the Vorn family, tangled with Mirelle's own hidden son, Anton, taken from her years before.

I met the thing itself — small, apologetic, thirty pages short of whole — in Skarke, and in Lenz, who kept the true ledger and taught me the rule: never staged for money, only once called clean, witnessed, the house told the truth first.

We spoke it entire at Katterau, nine hundred and thirty-nine seats and a bell I rang and answered myself, closing two hundred years of unattended calls. Grelle was found and forgiven, Krug fed and kept, Toby Lenz taught to call a house and signed his own crooked notice. Falk finally named his harbor. Mirelle got her son back, her name entered true in my own book. The company closed its accounts, hired a fiddler out of the rain, and went on.

journals.entry: Came in out of the rain by the Corona's stage door — open, which it shouldn't have been — with the notice in my hand. Falk in the dark with a thimble of brandy told me about the third board; I stepped over it and got a tilt of his glass for it. Vane arrived in plum, asked whether I could call a show off a book I'd never seen for actors who lie about their entrances; the woman on the fly floor, Sorel, told me to say yes before he wept. I said yes, if the book is honest and the liars are consistent. Asked for plot tables, a daylight walk, a bucket. Got the prompt book — two hands in it, a page cut out near the back. Prewick, clerk from the Office of Public Morals, wanted my name spelled and noticed the iron trunk wasn't numbered. Vane steered me six wide paces around it. Learned the thunder: trough, iron balls, tin sheet, third joint wanting a nail since Merrow. Sorel warned me not to drag the trunk — ask him and leave. I did, and watched in the tin: he wiped the lid, pressed the chalk, lifted one end and it came up like a hatbox, then shoved it properly, scraping. In the bucket under the star trap, the missing page. Read it twice — a bell rung and nothing answering, nine years, a debt in a plum coat, and cut cut cut in pencil. Pocketed it, not the book. Prewick brought an older notice: Hessel Vorn, Katterau, SEEN. NOT APPROVED; he says the Office issues no such form, and Katterau is on no itinerary he was given, yet everyone here has been there. I copied the name into my own notebook. Nailed the trough and asked Falk about the upright hand: a Vessendal copyist's, riding unopened in Vane's trunk; Krug cut nine pages and burned them, the tenth came back, then he was gone without his boots. Don't burn, don't return, don't read twice — too late. I gave Falk the page for his lining. Found the trunk shoved back snug, chalk smeared four feet along the brick, no footprints but mine, Vane out of the house. Told Sorel the page word for word; her lamp dipped at nine years. Pages started at Vessendal two springs ago; they come slantwise and late. Her number is ten, and a ten goes to her first. Six o'clock, the ostler's yard. Set the bucket, trimmed the ghost light, wrote my three lists, knocked twice on the trunk and was annoyed to find I'd been waiting for an answer. At my lodging, a folded paper under the candle-end with my title on it, in a copperplate that isn't Prewick's.

Read the folded paper on the step before the chain came off: clerk's copperplate, no name, no address, for Herr M. Skarke. The post empty since the 14th; wagons, canvas, counterweights, two horses, all properties pledged against a capital loan, and every taking between here and Vessendal; interest weekly, travelling ahead of us. Third performance, box office, morning, counted before an agent, and no need to tell Vane. One iron trunk, contents unspecified, valued separately — do not open, do not permit its sale.
