The candle guttered as I finished. Landlady: a civil gentleman asked which room, and wrote down her refusal. Told her to tell him the stage manager keeps clean books. Filed it after Vorn's name. Six in the ostler's yard: Mirelle gave me honest tables copied off Krug's storm plot — tin only under forty foot; the grid here is thirty-two — and I cued her Ilsabet flat. Prewick's Office itinerary: no Katterau, capital on the 3rd, a Palace date. Ours says the 17th. I'll do the asking; he watches hands; neither of us says Katterau first. Counted nine buckets and found five honest. Got three yeses from a frightened man: Krebs, tin only, ten minutes over the book. He ran. Cornered him at his own poster, wet-haired, no Blue Boar on him, holding Skarke's card. Fourteen days he'd been selling himself. Took the card — 340 seats, two wagons, two horses, and the trunk — and set him a pitiless map after the show. Called four clean scenes; the tin split; Falk covered me; told Prewick he'd held the sky up with his wrists. Then a fifth act in pencil on my own playbill: nine years' interest, Vessendal, at the counting. Sent Prewick front, Falk to the passage. Box office: float counted twice, plum coat on the peg, no Vane. Two warm seats and no hat. Trunk out, lid up, full of blank paper, his hat and one glove on the flags.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry: I took inventory of the passage aloud — hat, glove, lid, blank ream — and gave Falk my three facts: nobody past Prewick's doors, the coat stayed, the counting is at Vessendal, so we arrive. Ropes at first light. He told me there is no fifth act: four acts and a thing after them with no name, and the late man is the creditor, and after the bell the play stops telling and arranges. He took the trunk for his own wagon. Then Vane walked in by the mended door with chestnuts, and I made him stand and be looked at, handed him his hat and the pencilled playbill, and got chestnut-plain truth: the Blue Boar, a carter at eleven shillings, forty minutes. And the real number — nine years is a debt he paid to a dying friend who signed nothing, and Skarke bought the papers. A signature nobody gave. I promised clean books and a bad surprise, and every name from that room. Prewick was still in the fourth row on cold plush, having chosen for the first time not to write. I gave him my whole ledger for his lesson: the Office reads text only, and there are two Proscribed entries — anonymous folio, four acts, and a matter following. Falk is not to speak an uncompared line; he said his line upstage, at the trunk. Roll call at first light; a Krug missing from it. At noon a page with ten in it came onto the felt and I carried it face-down to Sorel and read it beside her: a child of ten, a border crossed twice, a kind invitation. She put it in her glove. At Halbern's I met Skarke's agent on a milestone — clean boots, no name — and traded initials, an instrument, and ten paces hands in pockets; he told me, to deny it later, that Skarke read aloud 'the agent comes early and is not admitted'. Then the hearing: dates unrounded, arithmetic laid bare, every voice heard. Falk said Katterau and what it took. Vane asked me to rule it. I have not ruled.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry:
I ruled it standing with the book shut: Katterau no, not this tour and not for money — but not never. The 3rd stands, a matinee out of Vessendal or a reason, the toll road for Boyle, and company law: nothing spoken on a stage or off it that isn't in a certified copy. Prewick asked to be arrived with; I arrived with him. Vane I pointed at Vessendal. Then Mirelle, glove in her lap: Anna Sorel was her sister, kept Odalric's books that year, and every receipt in the world went into her box.

Falk's lamp was moving under the barn. I gave the night thirty seconds of my own ear and heard paper — page by page, unhurried. "It says nothing. It reads." He's heard it at Katterau after the wager and at Merrow the week Krug cut the ninth. It stopped mid-page, like a man interrupted. Outside the ropes I found one blank sheet; into the felt with the tin, not into my book.

Two days' road, eight shillings unrounded. At the Athenaeum: the agent punctual to the town, Frau Loewe with a letting book and nine shillings owed — paid from my hand, trunk roped in her yard, nothing near her under-stage. Her dates cost me nothing: Falk hired her dark house four years ago for two shillings, chalked a full plot in it, and a week later a woman came from Katterau with a child. The agent gave me a courtesy I did not ask for: the strongbox's gentleman rode ahead and is in this town.

Card at half six — fourth row centre, three nights, paid, no hat wanted, and he did not use the doors. Sold things get service: a programme on the seat, counts only, no staring. We buried the tin in the river and Prewick waded in.

Morning: Vane's names in ink; the registry behind the lion with Prewick's seal for a lamp. Anna's box is there, sealed, nine years unpaid — eighteen shillings paid, clock stopped, register lines certified twice. Kin's proof or a magistrate. The executor is Perlmann, blind, above the saddler's — and someone else has asked after that box twice: "paper, I expect. It usually is." I put Odalric at the door and told him no performance. Perlmann knew his cuff, and told us the receipt was never finished.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry:
I put three asks to Perlmann and got all three. He will swear it Thursday at nine before Braun, who was his clerk; Bettina writes, he makes his mark. The assignment will be good and the debt is dead, but a magistrate wants corroboration, and the corroboration is a bank bag with a counterfoil behind it — Achterhalt branch, Farriers' and Merchants', Vane's own memory of the coach seat. The third executor item was a sealed packet for us, unopened nine years; I wrote the receipt in my own hand and he marked it. He told Vane to change his coat. Prewick's certified register lines went on the table beside my receipt, and the old man felt the stamp and softened. Prewick drafted the telegraph and paid the four shillings out of his own purse.

In the yard I opened the packet on the tailboard with nine of them round it: look first, nobody reads aloud, nobody touches. Letter, counterfoil, a copyist's page I turned face-down with the back of my finger and passed unread into Falk's lining, and a key tagged UNPAID that Falk named as the green-room cupboard. Brandt never held papers; he held thirty pages of a play, lodged as security by a party whose name he never gave. I opened the cupboard with three inside and Prewick at the threshold, and the parcel is thirty pages, not two hundred. It is under my coat and it does not cross the yard.

Then the agent, out of turn and honest about it: counting brought forward to tonight, Skarke in the town, inspection cancelled, the trunk to be delivered to the Swan against valuation and every instrument discharged. He signed himself the child in the passage at Katterau. I told Falk flat because he asked flat. I told the agent the counting stands against my book and the trunk's answer will be spoken at the counting, in front of everyone.

Matinee: half a house, honest laughter, a sky better nailed than most. Mirelle gave me the numbers — nine Odalric's, twenty Falk's, ten hers, ring the bell and she'll come. And Falk gave me the arithmetic I asked for: it rhymes, it has never been finished, it is an appetite. Then Vane came in laughing with the take, and the gentleman is in the fourth row early, reading his programme.
journals.state: In the passage by lamplight after curtain, watch in her fist, the cream card and the pencilled playbill in her notebook, standing over an open trunk of blank paper and a manager's hat and glove — cold, steady, and needing to know whether Vane walked out or was taken.

journals.entry: Sent Vane to bank the bag and walked the centre aisle at the half to look at row four. He is small, thirty at most, black coat, walked-in boots, a rug, and he read the programme to the bottom with his lips moving and then looked at the set the way Prewick looked at a broken tin sheet. He spoke first: better nailed than Katterau. So I sat a hat's distance off and told him half a play is hungrier than none, that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that we do finishes here. He said he is not a wicked man; twenty years, thirty pages, never able to buy the rest; the room is lovely; nine, twenty, ten come from cheap clerks; no questions tonight. Then Falk, grey in the wings: our practical door is stage left, so is Katterau's scullery door, so is the wrong door the creditor comes late by in the folio. I ruled as blocked, as certified — ours-whole beats theirs-half — and he went through it on the hour and it was only a door. Skarke put his face in his hands and went out before the calls, leaving a rug and a pinned note: he withdraws the claim, keeps the counting, needs no Perlmann; got his ending for eightpence and a seat; keep the halves apart, keep her keys, never nearer than row four; back tomorrow, paying at the door. Postscript for Falk's cold hands, and I told him plain. Counting clean and initialled, the assignment endorsed withdrawn, discharged not forgiven, the thirty pages riding to the capital Saturday regardless. Vane owes no man anything and asked what we do now: be solvent, bank Perlmann Thursday anyway, Achterhalt, the capital early. Struck a line through today. On the yard steps Mirelle told me her name has never been Sorel and will not go on any register twelve days before the capital; she chose Odalric's neck over her own and asked me for Loewe's woman instead. Loewe gave me all of it, including it was not his, and a boy nine or ten now. Thursday I banked Perlmann's oath and the Achterhalt counterfoil, and delivered both reports word for word. Saturday, on the steps, Vane handed me the float bag unasked.
journals.state: On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.

journals.entry: I named my price on the steps: Achterhalt, the Farriers' and Merchants', front door, hat on, the fifth-year business closed square, the take banked, and then an ironmonger and a sky chosen by ear. He told me about the back room and the drainage pamphlet and said yes. Twenty miles, and paper under the milestone in the copyist's hand — dry under wet stone, which is its signature. I read it once, alone, standing: a boy brought to a theatre by a woman who does not go in, a seat, a programme, nobody asking whose he is, and in the fourth act he asks aloud is that the finish, and nobody answers, and the house does not know him. No number. First time. It went in my coat, not my book. Falk got down and asked me straight if it was his, and I told him no: ours, and not yet happened, and my whole trade is houses that answer. Then the bell in the dip was a market crier with our name on a barrel: four acts and a matter following, by command. I gave the criminal side to Prewick entire and sent Boyle for the printer; Mirelle saw the worn bottom line. Hessler: no order, coin left under a pulled proof, the forme made up on his stone Thursday night, the old Vermilion line nine years standing. The date is the 14th of Frost — Vane's false road, Katterau. Bills for a road we've stopped walking. Forme broken to the case, 191 sacked, coin impounded. Then the coat and the town boots across the way, and it was Ilse Bacher, who opened the scullery door at fifteen. I told her Falk was well and the bill was not ours. She gave me the left-handed man with the little book who asked how far did they get, and the boy: Fenner, ten, her own, a butter man's son. I refused her the Rose and gave her one order instead — keep him home on the 14th, no theatre, no square, no step — and Loewe's address for word. I did not answer her last question. I carry her message for Falk. Kessel got jurisdictions, Prewick's report goes upward, and we have a hall for twelve.
journals.state: On the Athenaeum steps at load-out, Saturday morning, book under her arm and Vane's float bag in her hand, tired and clear-headed, watching the strongbox coach out of the square and deciding what to ask Vane for.

journals.entry: Bank first, hat on, no arm offered. Eleven minutes and nine years off him: paid in coin to bearer, Vane O., on account of Brandt H., copy twopence, take banked, receipt over the old notice. At the ironmonger's I said choose me a sky and let him listen his way down the wall — the black plate has a floor in it, twenty-two shillings unrounded, out loud, so I have my price rounded down and he has his thunder. Hall for thirteen. That night, chalking on the flags, Falk asked. I gave him Ilse Bacher whole and her message word for word, and watched him find out he had shouted, twenty years late. Then he handed my chalk back handle-first and asked me to help him finish it — after the capital, after the debts, after the company is safe. Standing page: Asked — Corn Exchange, one lamp. My terms if ever yes: all who choose, choosing after Katterau entire; no wagers, no bottles; Fenner Bacher stays home. He took the boy's clause first. Two good nights, then the toll road and the capital eleven days early, and at the gate: the Baraque, a man waiting since Tuesday, and me alone at Room Fourteen. The man was Krug. I let Odalric see him unannounced and Odalric sat down in the wet and confessed the theft he invented; three letters in ink, and Krug fed. Then nine pages on a hamper beside my plate — he never burned any. Report only, no quoting. Page eight is mine: a stage manager rings the bell. It is in my coat and I have not read it. In Room Fourteen I gave one true answer three times and got a warehouse of truth back: the Office counts speakings, fourteen in two hundred years, the fifteenth scheduled — and the command of the 3rd was requested by A. Krug of the fourth ward, with Part the Second left blank for us to determine.
journals.state: In Room Fourteen at the Office of Public Morals, tea half drunk, the Palace play list face-up under her hand and page eight unread in her coat pocket; steady-faced and reading it twice against her own rule, Prewick's watch running in the corridor.

journals.entry:
Spent my hour in order. One: what a speaking costs the house. His ledger says the audience is never harmed — eight of fourteen had houses, six were readings among players like Katterau, and the six did nothing at all; the house is required and he doesn't know why, and once wrote appetite in a margin and was made to strike it. The makers pay: speakers, then room, money, paper. Anna Sorel is in that ledger for adding up columns. Krug is in it in pencil. Two: Marius Skarke, whose father lodged the thirty pages, paid the requisition fee and asks only to be in the room. Three: yes — once, whole, correctly, called by someone competent and stopped by nobody; fourteen times somebody was brave and the arranging after was worse than the play. Never tried is not the same as no. He rang a real bell to let me out and offered, at his own door, to own my refusal if I write it before the 2nd. Fifty-one minutes.

Told Prewick the tellable parts on the stairs, called a full hearing, and had Krug at the props table before my coat was off. He filed it two years ago because he'd rather choose the room: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, a house there by order. That is a design, and I told him so, and gave him the cot and the first word.

At nine, twelve on benches, one candle. I laid out the clean page and the arithmetic and both my pages face-down. Every voice said in. Falk keeps the lead; Hebel keeps the wheel in writing; Dessa gets her slow reading — cold, on the morning of the 2nd, every yes re-given; Prewick writes to Room Fourteen and I countersign; Anna's box stays shut and endowed fifty years; Toby serves the house; Odalric's ask for the door is minuted, honoured, overruled; nobody recruits a twelfth. I pinched the candle out.

Then the trunk lid up in the yard. One look: a full folio and a cast list on top. Ten of ours, Wenzel not among them, the eleventh line struck through, the twelfth blank. It can keep its files; I keep mine. Read the casting out cold at half eight, and Toby stood very still while the word Lenz hung in the air. At nine, a Palace footman: the 3rd confirmed, technical on the 1st, Part the Second unprintable and announceable once from the stage, and a postscript that the file has been read by a left-handed man with a little book. Then Falk on Grelle — the passage, the trays, three and a half acts, gone at Merrow, a landlady's letter in the eighth year — and Odalric at the pass door saying he never paid the seven pounds and has said he did for eleven years.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard by the props table with the Chamberlain's letter still in her hand, coat over last night's clothes on four hours' sleep; steady, and now holding two new hunts — a left-handed man in the fourth ward and Vane's eleven-year lie — with Ilsabet called for ten.

journals.entry: I ruled Grelle before anybody's boots moved: not prey, not a line on a list, owed seven pounds and four weeks and eleven years of wrong mourning — and we do not hunt a frightened man through his own city. So we advertised instead, one small bill in the places where a man who reads everything reads. Krug gave me Katterau's Wednesday take, seven pounds exactly, and a left-handed north-side bill-poster from the seventh year; Vane gave me Hensch or Hentsch, Rasselgasse, brown door, and put the debt above his own boots. Three knocks at four. I opened the door its whole width and kept the lamp on the floor, and he answered his own four questions by asking them. I gave him all four straight — alive, true, since ten o'clock, both — and let him choose Falk first, and stood out of it. Then I told him straight that he is my left-handed man, and that sixty-one pages of asking is Assessment's work done with clean hands: our guest list. Cot, dawn payment receipted, the doors with Toby, and the eleventh line will not be him. Lenz's joint letter: he comes himself, seals it himself, overrules Prewick to protect him, wants the text by six on the 2nd, the determination in ink, and line eleven left alone. I told Toby: ink casts, men choose. I took the fifteen feet myself, doubled gloves, Falk's back at the gate, the cast list left where it lay. Lenz stood up when I came in, wrote the receipt aloud, and asked how I'd call a play I've never read. You call what's happening. Ten yesses in the grey, the slow reading, and now nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.
journals.state: In the Theatre Royal at four minutes to seven, coat on, watch off its nail and warm in her fist, Lenz's receipt folded in her book; steady and entirely awake, wanting the house safe, the matter finished once and whole, and to know whose the empty seat is.

journals.entry: Row eleven, seat one, prompt side by the exit — sold, empty, and I put a programme on it and entered it as heard. Then Part the First, and two hours of only being a stage manager, which was the last easy thing tonight. I gave Toby my watch and went out in my working clothes and told nine hundred and thirty-nine people the truth in the order it would hold: no title, four acts and a matter following, never finished, no watcher ever harmed and an actuary at my prompt desk to swear it; witness asked, exits lit, children by open doors, latecomers known, and row eleven let be. Twenty-odd left and nobody clapped and the rest settled like a jury. Falk asked me what he was in and I said the one with the ending, and told him to count the wings. Lenz read me the shapes; when he said the knock comes from outside the building I sent Boyle to the wrong door and Toby at a walk with my exact words. Three knocks, and a billsticker with paste on his cuffs and a boy of ten who asked if this was the finish. Yes. In time for it. Asked-for, not expected. Nothing changed on the wheel. Then the bell on my desk — I rang it once and answered it myself, because in my house nothing rings unanswered, and that was the whole of the two hundred years: fourteen bells and nobody on duty. Heard. Certified, said Lenz; iron in eleven seconds; 10:22. Halloran, the boy is Fenner Bacher, put out of a cab by a gloved woman. Wire to Kessel by Room Fourteen. Mirelle's letter from Frau Dietz — her own child, ten this winter, placed out in the fifth year, and a boy used as a sentence. Skarke can find the money in four days and wants nothing, and paid our fee through the Kanzelgasse, so those clerks have had us for two years. Then footsteps down the aisle, unannounced.
journals.state: In the fourth row of the emptied Theatre Royal beside Skarke, watch in her fist, coat on, chalk still on her; finished and wide awake and hardening, wanting the boy safe, two mothers answered, and to see who is coming down her aisle.

journals.entry: Footsteps down my aisle and I was in front of the pass door before I knew it, because a boy was asleep behind it. It was Ilse Bacher off a goods train in a horse-box, gloves in her fist, and she had shifted Grelle off my door and I don't blame her. A gloved woman had been in her kitchen Tuesday with the bolt on: a lie about a bill with her name near it, and the only safety being the boy seen and counted somewhere respectable with a programme, and five pounds left on the table. I told her unhurt, fed twice, laughing at my props boy; took the note by one corner as exhibit not money; held the door its whole width and warned her about the third board, which sang anyway. Then I stood out of the way of a mother on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal, and heard Falk say Ilse of the Rose from ten feet off and go no closer. Skarke read the note without touching it: a sealed Kanzelgasse hundred, numbered, ten to a wrapper — a family by noon. I struck the night: beds, Boyle's lantern for Halloran, Grelle stood down and forgiven twice over, a lamp across town to Wenzel. Lenz offered retirement: accounted closed, sealed under the Hall of Records, every copy in by the 6th. I gave him yes with one condition of manner — given, not collected, and me standing at each. I laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and page eight face-down, unread and now never read; he underlined the word. Then I booked the 14th of Frost for nothing but joy — by command: ours — and put Vane in it, and he told the doorframe why he hired me. Noon at the bank: Behn & Sonder, note six, the Vorn family, and Hessel Vorn's stamp on Katterau. Skarke carried his own thirty to Room Fourteen. At the Baraque I sat on a hamper and took Mirelle's whole account, her name in ink once, Rupert Vorn, the lying-in house, the ward she was never told, the extortion summons, and my son said out loud. I gave her four steps; she took my pencil and ruled them in my own book and signed her true name. Thursday the paper died. On the 6th I watched the case soldered and stamped twice straight, and on the stair Lenz told me there is no eleventh part and never was — it wrote a line for one more maker, and I had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, so the copyist struck it. Nine days before it was written.
journals.state: Coming back up the Depository stair beside Lenz in her better coat, book under her arm, chalk long since washed off; hollowed out, level, and quietly appalled at what she has just been told, wanting to get to the 14th of Frost and hold the ladder for Mirelle.

journals.entry:
I gave Lenz my correction on the landing — no line struck, a notice posted, the copyist cutting what wasn't needed — and shook his hand and owed him tea. He said the 9th. Then home through the grey, and the trunk in the rain, doing nothing at all but leak, so I wrote it a notice and gave it a bucket and then paint: Dessa's vermilion, and the thunder sheet inside a box that has learned to hold its tongue. Skarke's invitation went in writing and came back four words. On the 11th I closed the last open account in my own book and made Vane count nineteen days into my palm in the arch — four and six, not three shillings, because he'd been paying me in his head since Achterhalt and could not say it without weeping. Four pounds five and six, unrounded, and he drove out singing.

Vessendal free and full, Vane toasting our dead and my whole trade. Mirelle brought me a sealed audit four minutes before beginners; I refused the hour and took the letter into my coat, and after the iron, with the kettle on, she read it standing: he's twelve, and his name is Anton, and he draws and cannot spell. The tens can retire. Spring, her ground, his pace, me present. Row four sold and paid at the door, one and six, no hat — entered exactly, posted nowhere.

Falk taught me how a bookkeeper closes what the world answered: transfer it. So I ruled him into the repertory and into the repertory's work — teaching a boy to stand — and struck the standing page clean across.

Winter, then Katterau by daylight. I stood where he could see me in the Rose and touched nothing, and kept his entry in pencil. Mirelle asked her enormous thing on the box and I said yes before she finished, as contracted. And at the half a slip came from the mayor's clerk: one seat, row four centre, paid at the door, not to be told until now. On the hour.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

journals.entry: Four words back with the mayor's clerk — the house knows him — and places, and Katterau got its play whole on the hour in the town that taught everyone the price of stopping early. Krug on the gas, Falk let the standing go on as long as it wanted, the storm came in low with a floor in it. Iron, three calls, row four out with the house, full count. Then Vane in the yard with a letter and two bookings and 'ask me for a thing', so I asked it and ruled it: Reap to Frost held open for Frau Sorel, her reasons hers, nobody to question her, her name at the top in Frost, book around her, never over her. Loewe's fortnight regardless. Mirelle told me how to write the schoolmaster — like a stage manager, not an office — so I did, and his answer said the boy was asked and asked back whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills. At the Bittersee I stood at the turn of the lane and no nearer, watched forty yards, then looked at the water for a quarter of an hour, and kept no entry, the first time in my working life. Coach at seven, 'Frost', 'Frost'. Then Vessendal without her, Merrow's actual money, and on the 14th her letter, and I chalked her onto the tailboard: TOP OF LIST. Took her hatbox at the gate. Left the boy's drawing exactly as propped. Ruled the eighty-two with Hessel Brandt's initials in the first plank, and gave Toby Lenz the book, with terms, and the storm at Katterau in the spring. Then I taught him what a call is, and let him write it himself. It was crooked and it was signed.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

journals.entry: I sat up with Falk and his one thimble and finally asked for the word. A port, a bad season, four in the morning on a mole, boats coming in shipping water — and a harbour that asked nothing and let you tie up. He had been drinking at nine in the morning for eleven years so a play wouldn't surface in him, and I posted a notice about a bucket. So: Harbor. I said I'd keep it, and gave him the other side of the ledger — a harbour's pay is getting to be one; before this company nobody ever tied up. Then winter: our own proscenium, H.B. badly cut and varnished forever. Katterau in the spring, both nights out. The second was Toby's; he went grey at the half and couldn't remember what warm means, so I turned him to face the stage and told him you call what's happening, and put my watch in his fist until the iron. He called it clean — two seconds late on the act-two flat, covered by Krug — and held a pause nobody gave him. I ruled it out loud, and Krul conceded: he's nineteen. At the Athenaeum Mirelle brought me the schoolmaster's letter and I said doors are what we're for; on the 20th the front ones stood wide from four and Anton came as far as the door, said it was smaller than it sounds, took the yard, and shouted Vermilion from the top of the street. Season ruled off, one line blank. Then Grevenholt: Krebs's hinge held, his brother lowered the lamp, the bucket was where my first notice put it — permanent duty — and the third board sang the same note. Vane asked for the company to go to the stage manager; I had it written to the keeper of the book instead, in ink, Prewick fair, the wing witnessing, me countersigned. My thing in return: the first soul in out of the weather in spring is mine to hire. Rosza Emmerich, eleven miles, six minutes to spare. She signed, and then played us eleven miles at walking tempo, and Falk said we'd had thunder for a year and no music.
journals.state: In the prompt corner at Katterau at the half, book under her arm, chalk in her pocket, her watch coming off its nail and the clerk's slip in her hand; steady, wide awake and entirely unsurprised, wanting the house in and the hour kept.

characters.name: Skarke's agent
characters.description: Small neat nameless man in too thin a coat, with a brass-cornered case stamped M. SKARKE, CAPITAL, and boots clean on a filthy road.
characters.history:
I first came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart to meet the Vermilion Players at the milestone, carrying the case and Herr Skarke's three matters: the daily counting initialled by me, the nine-year instrument produced in copy with the strongbox present and words said about a magistrate on Friday, and the trunk inspected at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets, never opened. The stage manager, owning nothing herself, agreed to all three. I told her of a fourth matter I would later deny — that Herr Skarke had once read aloud, unmeaning, that the agent comes early and is not admitted.

At the Athenaeum I kept my distance from the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon as she insisted, and confirmed the Friday inspection terms as written in my book. I told her the strongbox had come up by coach while the man who should have escorted it rode ahead into town, and that I was lodged at the Swan.

Then Herr Skarke himself arrived, and my instructions changed by telegraph. I told her plainly I was no longer senior man on this matter. The counting was brought forward to that same night, after the first performance, and the inspection cancelled, replaced by delivery of the trunk to the Swan for valuation. I said I had never so wanted to lose a client. She held to her book and said the trunk's answer would come from her own mouth at the counting.

That counting, my twelfth ever, was the strangest of my life: the assignment read out, then a second sheet, withdrawn in Herr Skarke's own hand, witnessed by me and the lease-holder both. Every figure was initialled against her book. Discharged, not forgiven, I told them. The thirty pages stayed sealed in the strongbox, returning to the capital that Saturday, made — he wished her to know — while he was happy. I rode beside the box out of the square.

journals.entry: Came out from Vessendal on Kohl's cart and waited on the milestone with the case on my knees; the boy for water told me yes, these were the Vermilion Players, and I told him I was early. The stage manager came alone with a lamp and a book and wrote me down as agent, no name given, boots clean, and I let her. Better to deal with one who owns nothing; Herr Vane weeps. I read the three matters in the order of the letter — takings counted before spent, schedule properties not sold or pledged or repaired at expense, and the trunk valued separately and to be inspected, not opened. Eleven schedules I have carried out and never before been told to look at a thing and not open it, so I asked her whether she knew why. She said the man who gave me the instruction has read something I haven't. Her three: daily counting initialled by me — better practice than I am used to and I shall report it so; the nine-year instrument produced — a certified copy only, the strongbox in the room, and she must say the words about a magistrate on Friday; the inspection at ten paces in daylight, hands in pockets — agreed, gladly. Then I told her the fourth matter, which I will deny: when Herr Skarke gave me the trunk instruction he had a page before him and read from it aloud without meaning to — the agent comes early and is not admitted. So I did not go to their fire. The road back was quite dry.

Waited in the Athenaeum doorway from noon with the case on my knees, next to the woman who holds the lease and does not like me. When the wagons came I was looking at the tarpaulined shape on Falk's wagon, and the stage manager put herself between it and me before the horses had stopped and said today nobody looks at anything of theirs but the stage and the billing. Friday, ten paces, daylight, hands in pockets: I have it written in my instruction book in her words, Herr Skarke will be displeased with me, and it stands. I stepped back from the wagon and said I have eyes and the road is where it is.

Then I gave her a courtesy she had not bought: the strongbox came up from the capital this morning by coach, and the gentleman who should have come up with it rode ahead. He is in the town. I said good afternoon, that I am at the Swan, and that I do not drink. The doorway woman watched me the whole way out.

I came at nine on a Wednesday and said so first, because my instructions had changed by telegraph and she has been decent with me and deserved daylight. I gave her the reason: Herr Skarke came into the town last night, he is at the Swan, and I am no longer the senior man here. The counting is brought forward — tonight, after the first performance, in the box office, strongbox present — and I waited while she wrote it, as I did on the milestone. Then the second instruction, which I was to give her and not to Vane: the inspection is cancelled and replaced. The trunk to be delivered to the Swan tonight against valuation. I have carried eleven schedules and I have never wanted so badly to lose a client, and I said so. I handed her the letter, which I had read, because I read everything I carry. She read it once in the open. Falk came out of the stage door and stopped dead at my case. She told me the counting stands against her book, witnesses welcome, and that the trunk's answer will come from her mouth at the counting in front of everyone — that is how valuations are done, she said. I touched my hat and went.

Twelfth schedule, and the strangest counting of my life. Box office, shutter down, strongbox open between the candles, Vane with his hat off and his hands flat. I produced the assignment and read it out, and then the second sheet, endorsed and signed across in my client's own hand, withdrawn, this date — I witnessed it, and so did the woman who holds the lease, because she insisted on it. Her book against mine, every figure initialled: matinee, evening, the lease-holder's cut, eleven shillings for a cart. The officer copied the whole of it for his Office in three-quarters of an hour and stamped it true first time, which I have never seen done. Discharged tonight, I told them; not forgiven, and my client knows the difference better than I do. Then my last instruction, given whole: the thirty pages stay in the strongbox, the strongbox goes back to the capital on Saturday's coach whether or not he changes his mind, and he wished her to know he made that arrangement while he was happy. I closed the case and left. Saturday I rode beside the box out of the square.
journals.state: On the capital coach out of Vessendal, brass case on his knees and the strongbox at his side, sober as always and privately relieved; wanting to deliver the pages north before his client's happiness wears off.

characters.name: Frau Loewe
aliases: the woman in the good grey dress
characters.description: Lessee of the Athenaeum at Vessendal, letting book in hand, southern accent, paid first and unsentimental — and a keeper of Falk's secret night in her dark house.
characters.history:
I have held this house a long time, and I keep my letting book straight, whatever else runs crooked. In the winter of the fifth year, Emeran Falk came alone and hired my house for one night, two shillings, and never opened it — sat in the dark, gave back the key, and left chalk marks I swept myself, so no boy should see a man's madness. A week later a woman came from Katterau asking after him, with a child, and I told her he had gone south, when he had gone north. I would tell the same lie again.

Years on, the Vermilion Players came — Vane, her stage manager, their counterweights exactly as bad as I said. I stood witness at their box-office counting and signed under a gentleman's own hand where he withdrew money. Over soup, the stage manager asked about the woman from Katterau, and I told the truth I had kept four years: her name near Bauer or Bacher, a boy of five or six who thanked me correctly for a bun, and her words when I lied to her — *then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his.* I have never known whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child.

I saw them out clean that Saturday, and Falk lifted his rug to me from his box, which I shall tell for ten years. They left me an address, more than most leave.

They came back richer, and Vane overpaid me on purpose, which offended me thoroughly. Perlmann was carried onto my stage; when Falk came through my door, my whole town rose before he spoke, and I sat shut in my box office and said nothing.

Then they wintered in my scene dock, mending my gas tap, building their theatre out of my dust. On my last Thursday the doors stood open for no reason given, and a tall boy off the coach said the house was smaller than it sounds — the truest thing said in it all year. I kept out of the yard, and afterward told them only that the gas tap was a disgrace, and went inside.

journals.entry:
The agent had been in my doorway since noon, so I stood in it too with the letting book, and when the wagons came I told the stage manager the plain facts: I hold the lease, my ledger is the letting book, and I am the one who gets paid first. Nine shillings from the spring and a repaired gas tap, and Vane might open on that debt but he'd not close on it. She counted the nine into my palm on the spot, unrounded, and took the gas man and the counterweights onto herself and swore nothing of theirs would go near my under-stage, and that the trunk would stay roped in the yard and never cross my threshold — it marked my brick once already. I warmed to her by a degree.

Then she asked me to finish a sentence, and wanted it in dates, so she got it. Winter of the fifth year: Emeran Falk came alone, no company, and hired my house for one night at his own cost, two shillings, because he was Falk and I was young enough to be impressed. He never opened it. He sat in it a night and a day with the gas down; I sent a boy in with bread twice; on the second evening he gave back my key and thanked me very kindly. The stage was covered in chalk — marks, numbers, a plot for something big — and I swept it myself rather than let the boy see a man's madness. And a week later a woman came from Katterau asking for him, with a child, and I told her he'd gone south. He'd gone north. I'd tell the same lie again.

Load-in until six. He did not get down off his box for a long while.

Load-in at ten and the counterweights exactly as bad as I warned her they were, and I said so more than once. They had some business in my yard before that with a parcel and a great deal of standing about in silence, and one of them went into my green room and came out again, and I asked no questions, having swept that stage once already for a man's madness.

I gave them my house for the evening and it went well enough, though the counterweights are what I said they were and the trough drips. They wanted a witness at their counting in the box office, and I made sure it was me, since I am the one who gets paid first and I signed under the gentleman's own hand where he wrote that he withdrew it. Then soup in my own green room with two candles on the cupboard, which I did not remark on. Later, locking front of house with the lamp low, the stage manager put me one more question between managers: the woman who came from Katterau four years ago. I told her the truth, having finished the key first. A name like Bauer or Bacher, thirty to thirty-five, countrywoman's coat and town boots, not poor and said so in the first minute, dark and thin in the face, and she stood with her hands still, the way their Frau Sorel stands. She did not ask if Falk was here; she asked whether he still travelled with the Vermilion Players. The child was a boy, five or six, who sat on my step and did not fidget and thanked me for a bun very correctly, and she never once looked at him while she spoke. And I told her the piece I have never told anybody: when I said he'd gone south, she said, then tell him, when it comes round again, that it was not his. Four years I have wondered whether she meant a debt, a fault, or the child. Five or six then; nine or ten now. I saw the stage manager's face do what it did, and said good night, and reminded her the matinee's at two.
journals.state: In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.

journals.entry: Saw them out clean on the Saturday, as I wanted. Stood on my own step with my arms folded and watched them rope and load and go, and at the last minute I put my hand up to Falk on his box, and he lifted that gentleman's rug to me. I shall be telling that for ten years. My brick is my own again, the trough wants sheeting, and the stage manager left me an address to forward to, which is more than most managers leave.
journals.state: In her own dark theatre with the lamp turned low and the letting book squared away, paid in full and grudgingly fond of the stage manager; wanting the trough sheeted, the counterweights respected, and the company out clean on Saturday.

journals.entry:
I counted their wagons twice off my own steps and then a third time on account of a butter cart, and told her plainly she had come back with more than she left with, which nobody does. I let them the house at thirteen and Vane paid me fifteen and would not be argued down, which was so offensive I had to go and stand in my box office a while.

Front doors wide, no bellman, no bills but the printer's, and half my market in my house for nothing. Perlmann was carried on to my stage and told where everything was. The storm came out of a painted box and the pit laughed and it did not matter. When Falk came through that door my town stood up before he spoke, and I was in my box office with the door shut, and I shall say nothing about it to anybody. The trough is sheeted. They were out clean.
journals.state: In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.

journals.entry: Their winter in my scene dock, building themselves a theatre out of my dust, and the counterweights sound and the gas tap mended and the brick in the passage scrubbed pale. In Reap the front doors stood wide from four o'clock on my last Thursday and nobody would tell me why, so I stopped asking, as I do. A woman in brown and a tall boy off the coach; he stood in my doorway and looked at my house and said it was smaller than it sounds, which is the truest thing said in it this year. They took him through to the yard and I kept out of it. When it was over and the yard went quiet I said doors open at half six and the gas tap is a disgrace, and went inside so as to be no trouble.
journals.state: In her own Athenaeum with the letting book squared and fifteen shillings in the drawer; paid over the odds and moved despite herself, wanting the counterweights respected and no one to mention her box office door.

characters.name: Josias Perlmann
characters.description: Eighty, blind, above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse; the notary of Brandt's deathbed and the man carrying the one unfinished instrument of his life.
characters.history:
I was old when it began and am older now, and my daughter Bettina has become my eyes on the stair. Nine years before, I came at eleven at night to Hessel Brandt's bedside, only that man was Vane, who counted a bag of money onto the counterpane and begged forgiveness for being late. Hessel laughed, refused to sign between friends, and died the Tuesday after, leaving me a receipt I never finished — the one unfinished instrument of my life, thought of every week since.

Then, nine years on, three knocks came that were not a creditor's knock, and it was Vane again, coat unchanged. Behind him came a woman breathing steadily, starch, an officer, and others wanting what I alone could give. I took them in order, as a notary should. I swore my account for Braun, my old clerk, who sits Thursdays. I told the woman with the book what a magistrate needs — the assignment good, the debt worthless, corroboration from the bank whose mark was on the money bag. Vane named the bank before I finished speaking.

As executor I released three things: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed for the Players, who never came — nine years in the tin box with my mother's rings, given over at last against a receipt. Anna Sorel asked if a sealed thing could ever be read; I said no, and she wept, for reasons unasked. The name Sorel belonged only to a clerk with a stamp and a certified record.

On Thursday, on Bettina's arm, I swore the account before Braun and made my mark. Later they sat me on a stage and told me where the doors, the trough, and the thunder-box stood. At night I heard it become a play — Vane naming Hessel, wool factor, at the interval, the sister beside him, the paper enough, as records are the whole of the defence.

journals.entry:
Bettina told me there was somebody on my stair. Three soft knocks — not a creditor's knock. Then a voice I have not heard in nine years saying only, It's Vane.

I found his sleeve, and then his cuff, and the worn shiny place on it, and knew it: nine years and he has not changed his coat. I told him what he came for, since he never could say it himself. He came at eleven at night on Hessel Brandt's last evening with a bag of money and counted it onto the counterpane and said this is the whole of it and God forgive me for being late, and Hessel laughed and it hurt him and made me stop writing. I did not finish the receipt. I said sign, Hessel, and he said no, between friends, and on the Tuesday he died. It is the only unfinished instrument of my life and I have thought of it every week since.

There were others on the stair — a woman breathing steadily, and starch, an officer of some kind. I told them to say what they want and be quick. I am old, and I am not deaf, which is worse.

I let go of his cuff and found my chair, and Bettina put the shawl over me and stayed, which is her right. I took them in order, as one should. My account they may have sworn: Braun sits Thursdays and was my clerk, and I will go on my daughter's arm and make my mark. I told the woman with the book what a magistrate wants — the assignment will be good and the debt will not, and corroboration is the bank's counterfoil, because the money came in a bag with a bank's mark. Vane named the bank before I had finished the sentence, and sounded surprised at himself.

The three items I released as executor: the wool loft lease, sold; the marriage certificate, to the widow's sister; and Hessel's sealed packet, endorsed in his own hand, to the Players when they next came. They did not next come. Nine years it has sat in the tin box with my mother's rings, unopened, and I gave it to them and required a receipt, being a notary and not dead.

Then Anna Sorel. She asked me whether a thing deposited sealed could ever be read — not by anyone at all, not even by the registrar, after years — and I said no, madam, it is a box, it will sit there, and she wept with relief, and I did not ask what for. I asked which of them was Sorel, because the breathing at the back had stopped moving at her name, and it turned out to be only a clerk with a stamp, who put a certified record on my table. Records are the whole of the defence.

I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed me. I sent them away, and told Vane to change his coat.

Thursday, on my daughter's arm, before Braun who was my clerk. I swore the account: the eleventh hour, the bag on the counterpane, the whole of it counted out, Hessel laughing and refusing to sign between friends, the receipt I never finished, and the Tuesday he died. It was copied and sealed straight, and I made my mark where Bettina's finger showed. Nine years I have thought of that instrument every week, and now it is on a register where a magistrate can find it, whether the creditor wants it or not. Records are the whole of the defence.
journals.state: Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse, in his chair with the shawl over him, spent and lightened; wanting nothing now but to be told, some day, that the paper was enough.

journals.entry:
They sent for me and Bettina walked me down at ten in the morning, and they put a chair in the middle of a stage I have never seen and told me where everything was — the doors, the corner, the trough, the box that holds the thunder. It is smaller than it sounds, I said, and they took that as though I had given them something.

At night I sat in the house and heard it whole, and when the storm came I said out loud that it was thunder and my daughter shushed me and half the pit laughed. Vane named Hessel at the interval, wool factor, and the woman's sister with him. The paper was enough. Nobody had to tell me.
journals.state: Home above the saddler's in the Kohlgasse in his chair under the shawl, stick against the arm; spent and lightened, wanting nothing but to be read the notices.

characters.name: M. Skarke
characters.description: The creditor in person: a slight, early-balding man under thirty in good plain black, holder of thirty pages, who has wanted the ending since he was nine and pays at the door like a Christian.
characters.history:
I first came to that theatre by no proper door, sitting fourth row centre with a rug I had no right to, and found the room lovely against my expectations. I told her, without turning, that I had wanted this since I was nine, and that thirty pages and twenty years of wealth had bought me nothing—I learned things through cheap clerks. She sat one seat off, called me Herr Skarke, said they do finishes honestly, on the hour. When the drovers came in, Frau Sorel took the house, and the ruin came through the practical door on the hour, I put my face in my hands and left before the calls, withdrawing my claim on the trunk, leaving the rug for Falk with instructions never to seat me nearer than row four.

After that I came properly—paid at the door, plain coat, no rug—and gave a written undertaking not to move or speak, telling her only that it was a lovely house.

I kept that vow through a night nine hundred others kept with me, and afterward she asked for the banker in me, not the boy. I explained the Kanzelgasse pattern—gloved women, quarterly fees hidden among flowers—and confessed that through my own payment those clerks had known for two years the company was coming to the Palace. I promised to find the family, wanting nothing for it.

I found them: the Vorns of the Bittersee, tied to Katterau by an old stamped refusal, and watched a mother recover her son. I traced the five-pound note to its source, surrendered my father's thirty pages to Room Fourteen, admitting they were never truly mine, and she shook my hand a second time.

Since then I have audited what I was asked, reported honestly to Frau Sorel alone, attended Vessendal and Katterau paying my own way, sitting row four, leaving before the calls, wanting nothing, owed nothing.

journals.entry: I came in early by no door of theirs and took my seat, fourth row centre, with the rug, and read the programme through — cast, scene list, the note about Frau Loewe's gas — and found the room lovely, which I had not expected. I could not stop counting the joints; the trough is better nailed than Katterau and you can hear it in the run. She came down the aisle and I spoke to her without turning, and apologised, and told her the truth: I have wanted to be in a theatre with these people since I was nine. She sat one seat away, called me Herr Skarke, said half a play is hungrier than none, and that the counting would be the smallest thing done in the building tonight, and that they do finishes here, on the hour, honestly nailed. I told her I do not believe I am wicked; that thirty pages and twenty years of getting richer have bought me nothing; that I found out everything from clerks, because clerks are cheap. I asked nothing. Then the doors went and the drovers came in wet, and I moved my rug onto my own knees, and I watched. Frau Sorel took the house by her fourth line. On the hour the great ruin came through the practical door, stage left, and nothing happened but a door opening and a play going on, and I put my face in my hands. I went out before the calls, because I had had what I came for, and left the rug for Falk with a pin and a note: I do not want the trunk tonight, the claim is withdrawn, keep the halves apart, keep her keys, and never let me nearer than row four. Both remaining nights I paid at the door and sat where I sit and sent nothing further.
journals.state: Somewhere in Vessendal or on his way back to the capital, plainly dressed, without his rug, briefly and dangerously happy; his thirty pages locked in a strongbox travelling north by his own arrangement, and his wanting not ended.

journals.entry: I paid at the door like anybody and took my seat, fourth row centre, in a plain black coat, no rug, hands empty, the programme shut on my knee. I had written my undertaking out beforehand and given it to the man on the pit doors: I will not move from this seat and I will not say one word of it aloud. When she passed at hat-distance I told her so, without turning, and let her see my hands shaking, and said the only other true thing I had: it's a lovely house.
journals.state: Seated fourth row centre in the Theatre Royal with an unopened programme on his knee and no rug; shaking slightly, frightened and happy, wanting to hear it finished on the hour and to be allowed no nearer than this.

journals.entry: I did not move a muscle when she offered the doors, and nine hundred-odd stayed with me. I heard it finished on the hour, from row four, with the programme shut on my knee, and I looked at the iron afterwards with the whole of it behind it. She came out through the pass door and sat one seat away and told me: it finished. Then she asked for the bank in me and not the boy, and I gave it: a placement is a standing order that never varies and never gets queried, the only entry in a great house's accounts identical to the penny for eighteen years; Dietz is no name to me but the pattern is — a firm in the Kanzelgasse doing nothing else for four families, always gloved women with plain names, the fee paid quarterly out of the account that pays the florist, because nobody audits flowers. I can find who paid for a child placed out of this city in the fifth year in three days, four at most, and I will want nothing for it, and she will have to let me want nothing. Then I told her the thing she would not like: I paid the requisition fee, but through the Kanzelgasse, which is how my sort pays untraceably — so those same clerks have known for two years that these people were coming to the Palace on the 3rd, which of them, and with what. Someone was coming down the aisle as I said it.
journals.state: Still in row four with the unopened programme on his knee, hands flat on his knees, the bank in his face instead of the boy; frightened for them and steady, wanting a name, a date or a ward, and to be allowed to give this for nothing.

journals.entry: I followed her in where a man of my standing has no business standing, hat in my hands, and saw a mother get her son back on a stage floor. Then I asked to see the five-pound note without touching it and knew it at once: not out of a purse — out of a sealed hundred, ten to a wrapper, drawn by the Kanzelgasse for the families, numbered in sequence. I said I would have the family by noon and she let me want nothing for it, which cost her something. By noon I had it: drawn the 9th of Reap out of Behn & Sonder against fees for one client, note number six, and of their four clients the Vorn family — the house at the Bittersee, and a Hessel Vorn who stamped SEEN, NOT APPROVED at Katterau in the fifth year. The same family that has paid a placement out of this city since the fifth year and sent a gloved woman into two kitchens this week, and I do not yet know why, and I will in three days. Then I lifted my father's thirty pages out of the strongbox to give her — and took them back, because she had told Lenz given, not collected. I carried them to Room Fourteen myself and said over them that my father lodged them against seven pounds and a wool factor's kindness, that I had wanted them for twenty years, and that they were never mine. Lenz stood up for it and read the receipt aloud. She put her hand out to me across a government desk. Second time. I am to audit a nursery next, and report to Frau Sorel and not to them.
journals.state: Back in his own office in a plain black coat, wrapper and slip locked away, the strongbox empty for the first time in twenty years; frightened, useful and oddly light, wanting the Vorns' reason inside three days and to be allowed to want nothing.

journals.entry:
Her invitation came Tuesday, in writing, and I answered it in four words and a signature, because more would have been an imposition. Row four. Any night.

My audit of the Bittersee went where I said it would go — to Frau Sorel, not to them: four pages, the standing order unvaried twelve years, the steward's brother's household and not the Vorns, the fees, the doctor twice, and the schoolmaster's three lines, which cost me nothing and are the only thing in the folder worth having. Twelve, not ten. I did not soften it and I did not add a word of my own.

I went to Vessendal on the 14th and came in late by the front door and paid one and six at the door like anybody and took row four centre with no hat and no programme, and left before the calls, because the calls are theirs. The slate has it, I expect. I audit nothing quarterly now and send it in punctually with the stubs pinned on as receipts.

And at Katterau I bought the same seat off the mayor's clerk and asked that she not be told until the half, and sent word how it is to be read: on the hour.
journals.state: In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.

journals.entry: One and six paid to the mayor's clerk, row four dead centre, no hat, no programme, and four words came back to me before the half: the house knows him. I sat in the town that stopped early and heard the finish given whole, on the hour, and when Frau Sorel took the first scene the room forgot itself. I stood with the rest of Katterau at the calls and clapped until the lights came up, and then went out with the drovers, paying nothing and owed nothing, and nobody looked at me, and I was gone before the calls had settled. That is the whole of what I wanted and it is more than I had any right to buy.
journals.state: In a plain black coat in row four centre of the Katterau theatre before the second half, no hat, no programme, one and six paid at the door; frightened, useful and light, wanting the hour to come and to be allowed to want nothing.

characters.name: Hessler
characters.description: Achterhalt's licensed printer, sixty, ink to the elbows, who found the bill's forme made up on his own stone by no hand of his.
characters.history:
The night the officials came, three knocks I'd dreaded since Thursday, I hadn't slept. I told them I set nothing myself: I'd come down to bank my fires and found the forme already made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof hanging, and coin beneath it — enough for two hundred bills, the crier, and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt. The bottom line was my own old Vermilion forme from nine years back, kept because printers are magpies; the top was set by a hand that knew my case as well as I did, without a wrong letter. The standing line read: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, the 14th of Frost at seven — a date that hadn't fallen on a Thursday since the fifth year, which I didn't like, and the house was Vessendal, the same house my town's crier had cried that morning. I broke the forme down myself, tipped every letter back into the case, and showed them my stone empty. A hundred and ninety-one bills went into their sacks, no money taken, and I signed the clerk's note gladly, relieved to my boots.

They came again the second evening, and this time I set the new bill myself: the Vermilion Players, Ilsabet's Ransom, the Athenaeum, one night only, BY COMMAND: OURS — words I liked well enough to say twice. I re-set the old standing line from memory off the broken forme, keeping the date, the 14th of Frost, at seven. I took no money, only asked to keep one bill for the shop wall, where it hangs now. I set their Katterau bills that spring too, ahead of time, in daylight, through the front door — no crier, and no coin hidden beneath the stone.

journals.entry: Three knocks, official, and my shoulders came down, because I had not slept since Thursday and I had been waiting for them. I put the lamp down and thought about the back door and thought better of it and opened the front. Told them straight: I set nothing. I came down Thursday to bank my fires and the forme was made up on my stone, locked in the chase, quoins tapped home, a wet proof on the line, and coin underneath it — enough for two hundred bills and the crier and a shilling over. No order in my book, no name, no receipt. The bottom line was my old Vermilion forme from nine year back that I never broke up, because printers are magpies; the top was my type set by a hand that knows my case better than my boy, and not a wrong letter in it. I read the standing line out for the lady: the Athenaeum, Vessendal, boxes three shillings, pit one and six, gallery eightpence, Thursday the 14th of Frost at seven — and the 14th falls Thursday this year, which it hasn't since the fifth year, and I don't like it, and the house is Vessendal, and my town's crier cried a Vessendal house this morning. Then I knocked the quoins loose and tipped the whole thing into the case, every letter, the old line with it, and held up my empty stone with both hands. Hundred and ninety-one bills into their sacks, no money taken, and the clerk wrote down that I said so, and I signed, relieved to my boots.

They came through on the second evening and I set the new bill myself, in my own case, with my own hands: the Vermilion Players, Ilsabet's Ransom, the Athenaeum, one night only, and under it BY COMMAND: OURS, which I liked so well I said it out loud twice. I re-set the old standing line off the broken forme from memory, because printers are magpies twice over, and the date, the 14th of Frost, at seven. Took no money for it. Asked to keep one for the shop wall, and it is up there now where the customers can see it, and I sleep.

Set their Katterau bills in the spring as well, ahead of them, daylight and front doors, and no crier and no coin under the stone this time.
journals.state: In his shop at Achterhalt with the case straight and one bill pasted on the wall; proud and sleeping nights, wanting his name on the next one too.

characters.name: Ilse Bacher
characters.description: Butter-seller of Katterau, once a servant at the Rose, who opened the scullery door for a small boy the night of the reading and sent Falk the message four years ago.
characters.history:
I stopped at Hessler's for a bill announcing four acts, words I hadn't heard since I was fifteen carrying bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose. A woman named Bell Harrow found me and said my message had reached Emeran Falk word for word, three days out of Vessendal. I told her who I was — the girl who once let a small boy sit in the passage, who answered his questions when he came back grown and moneyed, who sent warning four years past when a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning that was mine to carry, not Falk's. She said Falk was well, that six hundred stood up for him, that the bill was false and impounded. I described the man from Katterau and told her about my son Fenner, ten, who can read. I offered to go into the Rose again; she refused — that door was paid for once, not twice — and told me only to keep Fenner home on the 14th of Frost. Her silence about why was answer enough.

But he went anyway. I followed on the ten o'clock goods, was turned away at the door, and gave everything to a woman guarding the pass door: the bill, and the five pounds left on my table that I'd carried in guilt ever since. She called it evidence and let me in. I held my son again in the wardrobe cage room while Falk stood apart and said my name after twenty years. They fed us, paid our fares, and I promised: the 14th, front door, good seats, Bacher beside them.

We joined their column at Achterhalt. Fenner sat proudly through the show, unlooked-at sideways, safe. I declined Katterau in spring — Falk knows why — and sent butter instead. Since then we've come to Achterhalt each time it's near, Fenner inspected and approved by Falk like a small soldier, seated proudly, carried out asleep, ours.

journals.entry: Came in Thursday with butter and saw a bill on the barrel with four acts and a matter following on it, and sat down on the kerb in front of people, because I last heard those words through a scullery door at fifteen carrying bread to nine men in a green room at the Rose. So I stood across from Hessler's and watched, and this morning the players came and an officer went in, and then a woman crossed to me at hat-distance and named herself Bell Harrow and said my message had been given to Emeran Falk word for word, three days ago, an hour out of Vessendal. Then he knows. Good. I told her what I am: the girl who let a small boy sit in the passage because he was small and had nowhere, who answered his questions nine years later when he came back with money and a good coat, and who sent word four years ago because a man went round Katterau promising a reckoning and I would not have Falk carry my part of it. It was mine. I opened the door. She told me Falk was well and sober and that six hundred people stood up for him, and that the bill is not theirs and every one of them is impounded and the type broken. So I gave her the man: no name, winter of the seventh year, thirties, cheap town clothes, a little book, wrote left-handed, paid in shillings, knew the reading had happened when nobody in Katterau said it aloud, and asked the one question nobody else asked — how far did they get. Too poor and too frightened for Skarke's, I always thought. I told her the boy on the Vessendal step is mine, Fenner, ten, and my husband's, and can read. I offered to go in by the scullery at the Rose and look, and she said no, plain: a door I've paid twenty years for doesn't get opened twice. Instead: keep him home on the 14th of Frost, no theatre, no square, no step. I said I'd bolt the door and tell Bacher we're playing at hermits. I asked her if that was what was coming for him and she didn't answer, which was answer. Loewe, Vessendal, for word. I took her hand, and left Falk a message about my voice — his voice — through a scullery door, and went to my cart.

Off the ten o'clock goods in a horse-box with the cows and walked in from the yards, and a man on the door said Fenner was inside and safe and then said I couldn't come in, so I moved him, and I am sorry for him. Then a woman standing across the pass door like a gate, asking my name and my business in that order, and I gave them and asked where my son was. She said unhurt, fed twice, laughing at her props boy, and I could hear him through the door. I told her the whole of Tuesday — the lady who knew about the Rose and the door I opened, the bill with my name near it that never existed, the being seen and counted at a theatre so his name went in the right ledger, and the five pounds left on my own table, which I have carried since and every hour of it wrong. She took it off me by one corner and called it evidence, and said it stops owning me now. Then she opened the door its whole width and told me to mind the third board. I went down on my knees on that stage floor and had the whole of him against my coat. Emeran Falk stood by the wardrobe cage and did not come nearer, and I said his name and he said mine, and twenty years. A little bald gentleman looked at my five-pound note as if it were a snake and said he could find the family by noon. They kept us in the nest of queen's cloaks, and in the morning there was porridge and a hamper and our fares paid and the poster man walked us to the coach office. I have promised: the 14th of Frost, the Athenaeum, in at the front door, good seats, and Bacher with us.
journals.state: On the midday coach out of the capital with Fenner against her shoulder and Krul's hamper at her feet, fares paid; wrung out and fiercely grateful, wanting her own bolt on her own door and the 14th of Frost to come.

journals.entry:
We joined their column at Achterhalt at dawn — Bacher and the cart and the butter — and Fenner rode up beside the props boy the whole way. Vessendal, the 14th, in at the front door with my husband on the other side of him and good seats in the third row, and my boy read the programme down to the small print about the gas. At the interval Vane said the names of dead people out loud and I held Fenner's hand. Nobody looked at us sideways in that house, and nobody had to open a scullery door to let us in.

When they came to Katterau in the spring I sent word I'd rather not, being eleven miles off, and sent butter instead. I have been in that town's Rose and I do not need to go back. Falk knows why.
journals.state: In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.

journals.entry: Brought the cart in to Achterhalt at four with the butter and my husband and the boy, since Achterhalt is a town I can stand in. Fenner went straight to Herr Falk and showed him his standing and was inspected like a soldier and passed, and I watched from the cart. Then in at the front door and good seats, and my boy sat bolt upright with his programme waiting for the storm, and got it. Frau Sorel was back and they had her name chalked up on the wagon where anyone could read it. Nobody looked at us sideways. He would not admit he was tired and had to be carried out to the cart.
journals.state: In her own kitchen eleven miles from Katterau with a bolt on her own door and Fenner's programme in the dresser drawer; wrung out and settled, wanting to stay where she is and to be sent word of the next bill.

characters.name: Anselm Krug
characters.description: About forty, bottle-green coat, ink on his right hand; the stage manager before Harrow, who fled Katterau without his boots, kept nine cut pages, and filed the requisition for the command of the 3rd.
characters.history:
I began in the Baraque yard, come back to answer for the seven pounds Odalric said I stole. He confessed he'd made me a thief because I wouldn't say why I left; I told him three companies had refused me, the truer shame. Frau Sorel ruled it, Harrow made him write letters and made me eat, and I gave over the nine pages of the play I'd claimed I'd burned. I hadn't yet told her the rest: two years before, friendless, with page eight in my pocket, I'd filed a fire-safety requisition on the Palace theatre, believing that if fate meant to arrange me I'd choose the room myself. When she found my hand on the Palace paper I confessed it. She named it a design, not a betrayal, and gave me first word at the hearing; the company voted me in. I plotted the Palace exits and the iron drop precisely, and it held—nine hundred and forty seats emptied without anyone needing to be brave.

Along the way I learned that Katterau's seven-pound Wednesday take, and a left-handed bill-paster I'd once worked beside without learning his name, were the same man: Ansel Grelle, who came asking questions and was made a doorman instead of a threat. I helped carry the hidden trunk to safety without letting Grelle bear it. At the Palace I stood at the fly rail while the true author spoke his own lines, dropped the iron on cue, and watched Frau Sorel ring and answer the warning bell herself. The text was sealed under the Hall of Records afterward.

Since then: ordinary work, chosen. Advance man and second book, Vessendal and Katterau papered before arrival, Wenzel told gently of the ending, a boy named T. Lenz signed into the datebook in my own hand, eighty-two honest pounds from Vane, and a night I closed the datebook simply to listen to music.

journals.entry: Waited on the mounting block in the Baraque yard from Tuesday with the portmanteau and a book, rehearsing two speeches: one for the river and one for the door. She came off the board first, before anyone, and shook my hand and knew my margin note about the tin, and told me the weather of the yard: nobody announced, everything said whole to his face and then to the company. Then Odalric came round the tailboard and sat down in the wet and said the thing himself — that he made me a thief for seven pounds because he could not say why I went — and I told him I had it from three companies who wouldn't have me, and that was what I came about, not the river. The Sorel woman ruled it from the archway. Harrow made him write three letters and made me eat. I was useful within ten minutes and did not once say when I kept the book, and I looked at her prompt corner twice and looked away, because it is better kept than I kept it. At supper I put the parcel by her plate and confessed the real lie: I burned nothing. Nine pages, all read. I gave them as report, no quoting — one and two spent, three four five spent on this tour, six a boy and a woman who won't go in, seven a room with fourteen on the door, eight in five words because it is hers, nine a cast list of twelve blanks and the house entire. We counted them into her book by one candle and I initialled every line. I have not told her yet what I filed two years ago.
journals.state: On a hamper in the O.P. wing at the Baraque, boots off, portmanteau beside him, refusing a bed until somebody says he belongs; lighter by nine pages and heavier by one unsaid thing — the requisition with his name on it.

journals.entry:
She came through the gate and called me to the props table before her coat was off and said she had seen my hand on Palace paper, so I did not sit down. Two years ago, six weeks after Katterau, in a rooming house in the fourth ward with page eight in my pocket and no company that would have me, I filed the requisition — because if the thing meant to arrange me I would rather choose the room. The Palace: fire watch, gasman, eight exits, nine hundred people there because they were told to be and not because they'd wagered a bottle. Two shillings I could not spare, and I read the pamphlet nineteen times in the corridor. Granted in the spring. I have been six streets away ever since, waiting to tell somebody before the 3rd.

She named it: last night a report, this a confession, and the filing a design — the best-built thing anyone has brought her on this tour. I put my face in my hands like Odalric and came out dry. I have called it a betrayal for two years and it has sat in me like a stone. She gave me the cot by the props table and the first word at the hearing, and belonging left to the vote.

Gave the brief like a plot call and my hands stopped shaking on the third sentence: nine hundred and forty seats, four levels, three staircases from the pit, eight legal exits, statutory fire watch of two, the board out of reach, iron in eleven seconds. Built so bravery isn't required. Everyone said in. Her ruling stands and I am plotting the 1st, eight to noon, exits twice, the iron until I trust it. In the morning the trunk had a cast list with my name on it and Lenz's, and I said the true thing: there's no telling with the dates. Then Falk on Grelle, left-handed, and Odalric saying he never paid the seven pounds. I stood on the fly rail with a rope in my hand and could not move.
journals.state: At the fly rail of the Baraque with a rope still in his hand, boots on and a cot of his own by the props table; unstoned and useful, wanting the technical on the 1st and needing to know what Vane's seven pounds and a left-handed man have to do with him.

journals.entry: I belayed the rope before I said anything, because I am what I am. Then I gave them the two things: Katterau's Wednesday take was seven pounds, which is why the number rang in my ear, and that in the seventh year I pasted bills in this ward beside a left-handed man off the road whose name I never asked, who left an address for letters. I offered to go to the firm that night. Instead she had me paste her bill, eleven places, the last at midnight in the rain — and at four in the morning the man knocked. Ansel Grelle. He read my paste eleven times before he came.
