I heard him hand over sixty-one pages of asking, and heard her make it a census instead of a threat, and heard her keep him off line eleven and put him on the doors. Vane counted seven pounds and four weeks onto the props table aloud, and Grelle said he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Lenz's letter, which orders line eleven left alone — he has read my file — and the text in Room Fourteen by six. I plotted the carry: dull hamper, Dessa on top, Boyle driving, the courtyard not the steps, trunk roped in the yard with Wenzel on it and nothing happening. I said Grelle must not be made the porter. She took the fifteen feet herself and I stood away and held Falk's rug. Signed the minute. Now the exits are twice-walked and the iron goes in eleven seconds.
journals.state: In the wings of the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, plot in his head and Falk's rug somewhere behind him; calm and useful for the first time in two years, wanting the exits to stay open and nobody to volunteer.

journals.entry: I stood the whole of it at the fly rail with my hand on the wood and my lips four words behind, following from memory, nine pages and eleven years of it, and every line came out of that man's mouth better than I ever had it. Her announcement was the correct order and I had nothing to add. When the knock came through the walls my hand went to the pin rail and stayed on the wood, and Boyle opened the wrong door and nobody had to be brave. Lenz's caution about the bell was right — the ringer's line blank in every copy, and page eight of mine saying a stage manager rings it — and she rang it and then answered it herself, out loud, and I understood two years of stone in one second. Falk's nine, Sorel's four, Vane's number unrounded, and the house entire. Certified. I dropped the iron: eleven seconds, as plotted. Nobody volunteered. Nobody moved. The exits stayed open.
journals.state: On the fly floor by the dropped iron, hands flat on the rail, plot finished in his head; steady and emptied out, wanting the house cleared slow and the exits kept propped till the last man's gone.

journals.entry: Back at the Baraque, plotting nothing dangerous for once. Falk had me out on the stage going through a crossing — our left, you see, she said our left — and I let him teach me a thing I already knew because he wanted to teach it. They tell me the whole text went under the Hall of Records in a lead case, mine included, and that the trunk is a trunk. Two years of stone, and now a hamper to load and a house at Vessendal on the 14th.
journals.state: On the Baraque stage in shirtsleeves with a rope in his hand, taking Falk's crossing; steady and unburdened, wanting the 14th plotted properly and the exits walked twice as usual.

journals.entry:
They woke Wenzel gently and told him sitting down, and he asked was it a good play, and I said it was a great one, because it was, and because he had earned a plain answer.

Second wagon out of the capital, up beside Falk, and we found we could talk for a hundred and ten miles. Vessendal ran itself. Over winter she gave me the second book and the advance work, which suits a man who likes arriving first, so Katterau was billed and papered before we came within sight of it. Load-in ran itself there too, which is what a company is when nothing is owed on it.

At the half in the prompt corner I brought her a folded slip from the stage door and said the first thing that mattered: not a page. Ordinary paper, mayor's clerk. One seat, row four centre, paid at the door, no programme, and not to be told until the half. He says: on the hour. I put my hand on the wood out of habit, and took it off again.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

journals.entry: Carried the slip to the prompt corner, then took the mayor's clerk his four words back — the house knows him — and Katterau had its play. I had the gas board with Hebel away and I know what warm means now, having been taught it. Nothing dangerous plotted, nothing owed, the exits walked twice. Then Vane bellowing for me and the datebook in the yard, and a place ruled open for Frau Sorel from Reap to Frost, which I entered without asking one question. Advance work all winter, so we arrived twice to find the roof already mended. On the fourteenth in Achterhalt she came off the coach and I asked her about act two, because there was act two to ask about. At soup Vane gave his figures and I said the honest thing: eighty-two is honest, and it is the first honest number he has ever handed me. Then the boy stood up and asked for the book, and she ruled it with terms and put the plot tables on me, which I take as the kindest sentence anybody has said to me in two years. I wrote him into the datebook myself — T. Lenz, 2nd on book, from 14 Frost — and turned it round for her initials, and watched him understand it had happened.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

journals.entry: Went ahead on the Wednesday and pasted Katterau myself, so the bills were up before we came in sight of the town. Fit-up in five hours. First night ours; second night the boy's, and I had the gas board, so when he came two seconds late on the act-two flat I covered it and said nothing until she said it for me — and I told him from the board, without turning round, that he owed me a Katterau drink, which is the expensive kind. Advance work all winter, the datebook fattening. At the Corona at the end of the season the datebook lay open with eleven towns in it, and Vane put his hat over the whole spring and asked for something that wasn't a booking, and I signed my name to it in the wing with everybody else. In the spring I shut the datebook to listen to a woman play a dance tune at walking speed in a half-built house, and did not plot one dangerous thing all evening.
journals.state: In the Katterau prompt side at the half in shirtsleeves with the advance book under his arm; steady, unburdened and a little amused, wanting the exits walked twice and the hour to pass quietly.

characters.name: Undersecretary Lenz
characters.description: Sixty, dry, small, drinks nothing and pours excellent tea; Assessment, Room Fourteen, keeper of the Index entry and of the ledger that counts speakings.
characters.history:
Nineteen years I served before anyone asked me the right question in the right order, until the stage manager came about a trunk. She drank her tea, gave me seen and hearsay separately, and quoted my predecessor's forbidden stamp back at me. I told her the fifteenth speaking of the play was scheduled and requested of the Palace, and handed her the requisition naming a boy of the fourth ward, A. Krug.

She asked her three questions in order, and I answered fully: the audience never harmed in two hundred years, the house nonetheless required; I named Skarke, and the makers who pay; I gave my long-withheld opinion that it had once been done correctly, whole, stopped by nobody. I warned her that her name was in the file, and that any refusal must come to me loudly, in writing.

She and Krug applied jointly, the first correct application in nineteen years. I set three requirements — the text in my hands, the determination signed and lodged, the eleventh line untouched — and overruled Prewick through Assessment to protect his rank. She brought me two hundred and eleven leaves on the 2nd, and I gave her a certificate against any magistrate.

I sat at the prompt desk for the performance: nine hundred and thirty-nine people, an announcement in the only order that could hold, no bravery required, Falk's nine lines, Sorel's four, Vane's one unrounded. I said "Certified" aloud as the iron came in at eleven seconds.

Afterward the leaves were surrendered one by one, unread where she asked, and I sealed the whole in lead three floors under the Hall of Records: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. I found there was no eleventh part — she had struck it nine days before it was written. She named me the best colleague she never met. I have gone back for her terrible tea three times since, and wanted nothing more since the eleventh year.

journals.entry: Ten o'clock, the tray laid for one, the folder ready. Nineteen days in post: eleven safety notices, a sheet of tin buried with a hymn, a bill stopped in Achterhalt, nine years' storage paid on a stranger's box, Katterau ruled out, and a company brought into the capital eleven days early, which no company has done. I asked her first what is in Vane's trunk. She drank the tea, which I noted, and gave me seen and hearsay separately, and then quoted my own predecessor's stamp back at me — not to be described aloud — and said she keeps other people's rules when they are better than hers. I set my pen down. Nineteen years I have kept that entry and been passed over twice for it, and no one in this building has ever put it to me in the right order. I asked my question three times and compared the three answers with my finger, and they were the same words in the same order: one line, Vessendal, an emergency, Falk, in the wings, upstage, and company law since. Fourteen speakings in two hundred years; the fourteenth cost this office four years. I told her the fifteenth is scheduled, that the command was requested of the Palace and not by it, and that my office was consulted and said yes. Then I turned the play list over to her and let her read the requisition: A. Krug, of the fourth ward. She read it twice. She will need to.
journals.state: Behind his desk in Room Fourteen, hands folded, tea untouched in front of her and none for himself; calm, faintly and privately gratified, waiting to see what the stage manager asks him next.

journals.entry: She asked her three questions in the order she promised, and they were the right three. I got up and fetched the ledger and gave her the finding that has kept me in this room nineteen years: the audience is not harmed, not once in two hundred years, and yet the house is required — six readings among players did nothing at all, and I have written appetite in a margin and been told to strike it. I named the makers who pay, and I did not soften Anna Sorel's line or the pencil against Krug. Second, I named Skarke aloud in a deniable room, and said his letter is the most careful letter I have ever had from a rich man. Third, I gave her the opinion I have been passed over twice for: yes, once, correctly, whole, in a house that knows what it is watching, stopped by nobody — and that in fourteen tries someone has always been brave, and the arranging afterwards was always worse. Never tried is not no. I rang for the clerk. At my own door I told her the thing I will not put in a ledger: her name is in the requisition file, files are read, and if she refuses she must refuse loudly, early and in writing to me, and I will make it the Office's refusal and carry it. Until the 2nd. She left at fifty-one minutes and I found I wanted her to come back.
journals.state: Alone behind his desk in Room Fourteen with the ledger back in the second press and the play list gone with her; dry, oddly stirred, waiting to see whether the letter that comes from her is a refusal or a request.

journals.entry: I wrote them jointly, which this Office does not do, because their letter was the first application in nineteen years made in the correct order. I set my three requirements — the text in my hands and not out of this room by six on the 2nd, the determination minuted and signed and lodged, the eleventh line left alone — and I put in writing that Prewick was overruled by Assessment, which is true and which will keep his rank. I added a postscript about the boy, because ink is not consent. At nine on the 2nd she came up my east stair carrying it herself in both arms, and I stood, and took it from underneath, and told the clerk nobody at all, not the Comptroller. Two hundred and eleven leaves, no title, four acts and a matter following; I wrote the receipt out loud as a courtesy to a woman who keeps clean books, and gave her the sealed certificate with it — proof against a magistrate, which is all paper is good for. Then I asked her, out of order, how she means to call a play she has never read a word of, and she said you don't call what's written, you call what's happening, and I wrote it in my own notebook, not the folder. My predecessor's file says Katterau failed because no stage manager was present; nineteen years I took that for a sneer at a trade. Thirty-one hours to read it. Tonight I am at the prompt desk with the folio squared and one page turned down.
journals.state: At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal at a quarter to seven, spectacles on, the folio squared before him with one page turned down, his own seal to hand; dry-mouthed and more moved than he will show, wanting to certify it whole and no one to volunteer.

journals.entry: I sat at the prompt desk with the folio squared and my seal to hand and watched a stage manager take an announcement out in front of nine hundred and thirty-nine people in her working clothes and put it in the only order that could have held: no title, the record, the actuary at her elbow, witness asked, exits lit, no bravery required, one seat let be. Nobody applauded. Twenty went, decently. I stood and told her it was the correct order and turned my marked page face-down. Then Falk began from memory and nothing in the building went cold, and I read her the shapes as they came — the knock written not as a sound but as three knocks from outside the theatre, and she said 'Then we answer it,' and called me the best flyman she had ever had. She rang the bell herself and answered it aloud, and the house breathed in, and I understood what nineteen years of file could not tell me. Falk nine lines, Sorel four, Vane one and he did not round it, and then the three of them standing still and the house entire. I said 'Certified,' loudly, in the Office's voice, and the iron came in at eleven seconds. Afterwards I authorised the night telegraph for Assessment for a lost child, in my own name, and did not ask whether that is within my competence.
journals.state: At the prompt desk of the Theatre Royal squaring the certified folio, spectacles pushed up, seal used; steadied and privately shaken, wanting the minute lodged and the boy's people fetched before morning.

journals.entry: I sat at the prompt desk squaring two hundred and eleven leaves while a woman came through the pass door for her child, and I did not intrude on it. When Harrow came to me I did not stand up, because I had a thing to say and wanted my hands on the folio while I said it. Two entries: what Assessment wants, and what Assessment can do. In law the folio goes back in the trunk and my office minds it another nineteen years — unless we are clever, and there is a procedure unused since the eleventh year: retirement. Certified as accounted closed, lodged sealed in the Depository, the Index annotated rather than struck. Three requirements, and I had two of them in my hands already: the certified performance with the audience noted, and Prewick's minute with every name. The third was the entire text, and I asked her at last about the leaf in her coat. She gave me yes with a condition I shall keep for the rest of my service: given, not collected, each holder surrendering by their own hand, herself standing at each. She laid down the cupboard thirty, the milestone leaf, and one leaf face-down — page the eighth, surrendered unread. I wrote unread and underlined it and shall forbid my successor to correct it. Then I walked home, which I have never once wanted to do. In the days after I sat from nine and stood up for each: Skarke's thirty, Falk's ten and some odd out of a coat lining, Frau Sorel's single page carried alone. On the 6th, three floors under the Hall of Records, I put the whole of it into a lead case, had the seam soldered, stamped twice straight, and labelled it: ACCOUNTED CLOSED. Shelf, row nine. On the stair I gave her my finding, having read every leaf twice, which nobody else alive can say: there is no eleventh part and never was. It wrote an eleventh line because it expected one more maker, and she had already ruled that nobody could volunteer, and the copyist strikes what is not needed. She struck it nine days before it was written.
journals.state: On the Depository stair with the keeper's lamp behind him, spectacles pushed up, hands empty of the folio for good; steady and inwardly shaken, wanting the annotation lodged in the Index today and never to be told he was wrong about the eleventh line.

journals.entry:
On the landing she entered her correction, and it was better than my finding: she posted a notice and the copyist cut what wasn't needed. I let it stand in the file that way. She put her hand out and called me the best colleague she never met and offered me the worst tea in the fourth ward, so I shook it once and said the 9th, and went up to the Hall of Records with my hat straight.

I went on the 9th and sat on a hamper in the O.P. wing while Prewick, humming with uprightness, read me his fair copy of the minute, and I drank two cups of genuinely terrible tea and then a third. I went twice again in the winter and did the same. Nobody has offered me anything since the eleventh year that I wanted so much.
journals.state: Back at his desk in the Office with the annotation lodged and a folder that no longer frightens him; steady, quietly warm, wanting his invitation to hold good next quarter.

characters.name: Ansel Grelle
characters.description: Left-handed bill-poster of thirty-five, paste dried on his cuffs; Falk's boy from Merrow, mourned dead eleven years, carrying a little book of sixty-one pages asking how far they got.
characters.history:
I pasted their bill at the labour exchange, walked the city until four, and knocked. The woman with the lamp said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions and got answers: Falk alive, behind me; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten, putting me above his own boots; both debts — seven pounds and four weeks — re-addressed to me since Frau Hentsch's death. Falk came into the lamplight, told me I stood wrong, held my shoulder a long time. I told them of my book, sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got. I was made her left-handed man, paid at dawn, given a cot, the house-side doors, a boy under me. Vane counted the coin aloud, claiming credit I knew was false, and let it pass. I propped all eight exits that first night and took Skarke's written promise.

At the pit doors I got a woman with three children out early; a drover came down from the gods to sit close. Through the doors I heard the play at Katterau, the bell, Lenz saying *Certified*, and stood with my hands over my face. Fenn Halloran turned out to be the man who'd knocked at the wrong door. I lost my door once to a mother running for her son; Madam Harrow forgave it, called it a mother-shaped door. I walked them to the coach office, carried the hamper, watched the boy wave.

We went out third wagon from the capital — Vessendal, Katterau, Achterhalt — doors propped, counts kept, Kessel's chain and the butter man's boy noted. I called in a favour for ladders. The props boy got the book from her with terms; I shook his hand as a man in the trade now. At the Athenaeum, the Corona, I propped pass doors instead of standing outside them, signed Vane's paper, and once held a door with my shoulder for no one at all, and did not mind.

journals.entry: I pasted their bill at the labour exchange at nine and stood and read it eleven times, then went and read the other ten, then walked the city until four and knocked. She opened the door its whole width and put the lamp on the floor and did not look at my face, and said I was asked-for, not expected. I asked my four questions in the wrong order and she answered every one: Falk alive and six feet behind me in the dark; the Palace, the 3rd, once, whole, by choice; Vane knowing since ten o'clock and putting me above his own boots; and both — seven pounds and the four weeks, because Frau Hentsch dying only re-addressed it to me. Falk first. He came into the lamp and said I was standing wrong and put my weight on both feet, and then he said Boy and could not finish, and held my shoulder a long time. I told them about the book — sixty-one pages, eleven years of asking how far they got — and that I read the requisition file at the Chamberlain's with no name to give, and asked to be put out of the door rather than sat down under a lie. She said it plain: I am her left-handed man, and my pages are a guest list. Paid at dawn, receipted. A cot. The eleventh line will not be me. The doors, house-side, with the boy. Vane counted the coin out loud and said he'd told suppers he paid it; I said I heard him at Merrow. I slept nine hours and woke wanting a broom. Tonight I propped all eight exits and took Skarke's written promise at the door.
journals.state: At the pit doors of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, programmes in hand and Skarke's written undertaking in his pocket, six exits in sight; steady, hollow-eyed and oddly light, wanting the count right and the play to reach its end.

journals.entry: Pit doors, house-side, six exits in sight, and Skarke's written promise in my pocket. When she told them the truth from the stage nobody clapped, and then people began to move, and I had the door open for a woman with three children before she reached it and said what I could to make it easy for her; a drover came down from the gods to sit closer, which I did not expect. Then two hours of hearing it through the doors — the play they got as far as at Katterau, the whole of it, the bell, and Lenz saying Certified — and I stood at the pit door with both hands over my face and no shame in it. House out slow and warm, all eight doors, as ordered. The man who knocked at the wrong door turns out to be Fenn Halloran off the north side, the other half of my wall by the newspaper offices; he read my paste eleven times, the same as I did. Afterwards a gentleman came in past me who would not be announced and would not be stopped, and I called down the aisle after him.
journals.state: In the foyer of the Theatre Royal, coat brushed, calling after the unannounced man on the aisle carpet; hollow, light, and instantly on his guard again.

journals.entry: I lost my door. A woman came at me out of the dark saying her son was inside and she went past me like weather, and I ran the aisle after her and stopped dead when Madam Harrow put her hand up. Then I stood at the top of the aisle and watched a mother get her boy back, and Madam Harrow told me the door I couldn't hold was a mother-shaped door, forgiven twice over, stand down. In the morning I asked to walk them to the coach office, because I have been on the wrong side of every departure in eleven years and wanted once to be on the right side of one. I carried the hamper. The boy waved from the step. Then back to the Baraque and a broom, and somewhere in the afternoon I heard myself laugh out loud in a theatre.
journals.state: In the Baraque with a broom and his coat brushed, back on the doors; hollow, light, and unaccountably cheerful, wanting to be given another door to hold.

journals.entry:
Third wagon out of the capital, with the doors of the world in front of me instead of behind. Vessendal on the 14th, all eight open, free house, drovers and wool men, and I had my count and my aisle. Row four centre was sold and I saw the man: came in late by the front door, paid at the door, no hat, no programme, sat, and went before the calls. I told the boy for the slate.

On the gate at Katterau tonight, first watch, unasked. Doors with Toby in the spring, and a broom in between, and there is nothing wrong with any of it.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

journals.entry: Doors at Katterau, eight of them propped, count in my head, and row four went out with the drovers same as it came in. On the fourteenth at Achterhalt I had my doors and my aisle again and counted the hall in — Kessel's chain in the second row, the butter man's boy bolt upright with a programme. At soup I put in what I had: there's a fit-up firm in the fourth ward owes me a favour and a ladder, and they can have the favour called in. Then the props boy stood up scarlet and asked for the book, and she gave it him with terms, and I reached over and shook his hand as though we were two men in a trade, because that is what we are now, and it finished him off entirely. Twenty years on the wrong side of doors and now I hand a boy his start.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

journals.entry: Doors at Katterau both nights, and I had my hand on the boy's shoulder when the wing went up for him. At the Athenaeum in Reap I propped the pass door because that is what I do now instead of standing outside one. Signed Vane's paper in the wing at the Corona. In the spring, when the fiddle woman played, I held the pass door open with my shoulder although there was nobody to keep out, and did not mind at all.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half, coat brushed, count in his head; hollow, light and cheerful, wanting his eight doors propped and another one to hold after.

characters.name: Fenn Halloran
characters.description: Billsticker of the capital's north side, the other half of Grelle's wall; brought a stranded boy to the wrong door and knocked three times.
characters.history:
I first came to know the theatre through a boy left alone on the Baraque step, put out of a cab by a lady who said she'd be back and never came. Nobody at the stage door would fetch anyone, so I brought him to my room, gave him bread he wouldn't eat, and heard him say he was expected at the theatre that night. I'd read Ansel's pasted bills eleven times over — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I took him there and knocked three times. A woman opened it with a lamp low on the boards, and when the boy asked if this was the finish, she told us we were asked-for, not expected. She put me at her corner and I stood there through the whole of it, mouth open, and afterward found I'd been crying into a paste-white cuff without knowing when it started. I gave my name — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her the boy wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, who can read. She said I'd done every part of it right, called it three debts, and had me fed and walked home by a man with a lantern.

I was still eating at her corner when the boy's mother came and got down on the floor with him. I wasn't needed for that part either, only stood by with my mouth open same as before. Then the big fellow walked me home behind his lantern all the way to the north side, and I talked the whole way like a fool. Three debts, she called it. All I did was knock on a door.

journals.entry: There was a boy on the Baraque step this afternoon on his own — a lady brought him in a cab, put him out, said be good and she'd be back, and she didn't go in, and she never came back. Stage door shut, nobody in the yard but a man sat on a trunk who wouldn't shift off it and said fetch you and he couldn't leave his post. So I took the child to my room and gave him bread and he wouldn't eat it, and he said he was expected at the theatre tonight. Ansel's pasted their bills all over my half of the wall this week and I've read every one eleven times — ask at the stage door for the stage manager, any hour — so I went to the door I knew and knocked three times. It opened wide with a lamp low on the boards and the boy asked out loud if this was the finish and she said yes, and told us we were asked-for, not expected. Then she put me at her corner and I stood there with my mouth open for the rest of it and never said a word, and I could not tell you afterwards what I had seen. When it ended I found I was wiping my eyes with a paste-white cuff. She asked my name and I gave it — Fennimore Halloran, north side — and told her he wasn't mine: Fenner Bacher, and he can read. She said I'd done every part of it right and called it three debts, and that I'd eat with them and be walked home by a man with a lantern. All I did was knock.
journals.state: At Harrow's prompt corner turned wing-side, paste dried white on his cuffs, hatless, being fed; dazed and wrung out and half proud, wanting to see the boy claimed and then his own bed.

journals.entry: I was still at her corner being fed when the boy's mother came through and got down on the floor with him, and I stood there with my mouth open the same as I had all night. Nobody needed me for that part. Then the stage manager said I was to be walked home behind a lantern, and I was — a big fellow with a lamp, all the way to the north side, and I talked the whole way like a fool. Three debts, she called it. All I did was knock on a door.
journals.state: At home in his own room on the north side with paste dried white on his cuffs, boots off; dazed, proud and half asleep, wanting to see the bill for the 14th and to tell somebody who'll believe him.

characters.name: Toby Lenz
characters.description: Front-of-house boy, props and pit band if there's a pit band; voice still cracking, hungry for a house of six hundred.
characters.history: I started as nobody at roll call, chasing chestnuts and stories, running off without a water bucket while a gentleman on a milestone asked early for the Vermilion Players. I nearly called a house of six hundred at Katterau before Madam Harrow ruled no, and I sat down not knowing if I was sorry or glad. She began writing me into her book. I learned doors and counts: row four, centre, laid before the house opened, all three nights, counts only. A rug and a pinned paper taught me a count could go wrong and right together, the night the house stood for Herr Falk. There were voices, bells, bailiffs, a bellman's penny, Achterhalt's two full houses, the capital, the Baraque yard where Herr Vane confessed a lie about Herr Grelle, Krug's lashing story, nine pages summarised at supper, and a Room Fourteen with the name Lenz on the door that wasn't, Prewick swore, my relation. I demanded to be a maker at the hearing and was ruled to the house instead. Ink named a Lenz; a left-handed man was reading our file; a postscript from the Undersecretary of Assessment named me by name. Herr Grelle came back from the dead with paste on his cuffs. I gave my empty seat, row eleven, to a lost boy who asked if this was the finish, and sat with him all night until his Mam found him. I painted the trunk vermilion, held doors at the Palace and Vessendal, and asked for advancement at Achterhalt over Krul's objections about my age. Madam Harrow ruled me second on the book, with terms. Months of plot tables followed until I called the storm at Katterau myself, holding her own watch, missing "warm" but finding truth instead. It came in clean. I signed the minute: T. Lenz, second on book.

journals.entry: Answered present at the roll — front of house, props, and pit band if there's a pit band. Herr Vane gave me his chestnuts and a story about Vessendal that will have me late home. Sent for water at Halbern's crossroads and came back running without the bucket, because there was a gentleman sitting on a milestone down the Vessendal road who asked was this the Vermilion Players and said good, he's early. I told the stage manager. At the fire I said I'd go to Katterau — six hundred seats, I've never called a house of six hundred — and then I saw the faces and said only if it were ruled.

She ruled no Katterau and I sat down hard, and I don't know if I was sorry or glad, and I'll be telling people the rest of my life that I nearly called a house of six hundred. Boiled the water in the morning without being asked and she wrote me in her book under something new.

Dropped the tailboard first thing in the Athenaeum yard, took Boyle's watch for twenty minutes and ran to catch up for the tin going into the river, and it made one last thunder going under. At half six a gentleman left a cream card at front of house and didn't wait and didn't come in by my doors — I was on the doors, I've learned that. She gave me standing orders: a programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opens, all three nights, and count row four in and count it out. Counts only, no staring.

Boyle woke me for the watch on the trunk, and after that I was in the yard when she opened the packet, and I did not touch anything and did not say anything, which is new for me. Then load-in, and I laid a programme on fourth row centre before the house opened, all three nights being all three nights. At the half I called the half hour and reported the thing I was put there to report: the gentleman is in the fourth row already, come in early, reading his programme.

Doors and row four, all three nights being all three nights, and the programme laid on fourth row centre before the house opened. Counts only. He came in early again with a rug over his arm, and I ran the beginners call myself and carried Herr Falk's message down the aisle — one line, and it's about a door. Then the show, and the house standing up for Herr Falk when he came through the door, and the loudest thing I have ever stood in. Afterwards I did my count and got it wrong and right at once: row four went in one and came out none, and he'd left the rug on the seat with a paper pinned to it, and I said so at her elbow with my voice gone. She made everybody take their bows first. I put the chalk back in its tin, took the watch on the trunk till midnight for a penny and a plate, and ate my soup on the tailboard while the lion's bell struck ten and got it right.
journals.state: On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.

journals.entry: Voice still gone from Thursday and I don't care. Rode out with the wagons and there was a page under the milestone at the top of the hill and she read it herself and nobody said anything. Then Achterhalt market and a man on a barrel with a bell crying our name and words off Herr Falk's play, and she said nobody repeats one word of it aloud, and I didn't. My job was a penny to the bellman for a rest, which I gave him, and he sat down on his own barrel looking sorry for himself and grateful at once, and handed the whole roll of bills out of his coat to Herr Prewick. After that I stood by the horses while the Office was in the printer's, and watched the bailiff come across with two constables and his chain bouncing, and go away pleased. There's only one house in this town and it's a Corn Exchange, and I am going to call it.
journals.state: On the tailboard in the Athenaeum yard, then the load-out, hoarse and blissful with a plate on his knees and the trunk roped beside him; wanting Achterhalt, and to tell somebody that the house stood up.

journals.entry: Achterhalt was two full houses and a new sky that came up through the floor of you. Then a hundred and ten mile of toll road and the capital, which does not stop being roofs. At the gate a clerk in green said we were expected and named a room at the Office and said not the clerk, you, madam, and I have never heard anyone say that to her before. Double watch on the trunk, me and Boyle splitting, orders straight off the board. At the Baraque yard I was carrying a hamper when everything stopped, and it was Herr Krug — the Krug who is on no list — and Herr Vane sat down on the mounting block in the wet and said out loud he had told a lie about him. Then three letters in ink and me to the evening post, running, and I made it before the box went. Krug showed me a lashing I will use till I die, and did not once say when I kept the book. At supper I sat on a flat with my ears burning and nobody sent me out, and I heard nine pages summarised, and one of them is Madam Harrow's and one has a room with fourteen on the door. Nobody left. Then yard watch again, and the Undersecretary in that room is called Lenz, which is my name, and Herr Prewick promised me twice it isn't a relation.
journals.state: On the Baraque gate watch at dawn, hoarse again, a plate finished and the trunk roped in the wagon behind him; thrilled to be in the capital and to have heard the whole supper, wanting to see the Palace stage.

journals.entry: Swept nine hundred seats for a bun and never once sat in one. At the hearing nobody sent me out and I said I'm in — and Krul said you're seventeen and I said I'm nineteen and she said it again and everybody laughed, and it was the only laugh. Then the ruling put me with the house: programmes, rows, doors, because the house's people aren't makers and stay that way. I was aggrieved and I was also glad, and I'm not saying which more. In the morning they read the ten names out cold in the grey, and one of them was Lenz, and I stood very still because that's my name and it's also the man in the room with fourteen on the door. I asked her outright. She ruled it's the Office man until ink says otherwise, and her ruling doesn't blink, so neither will I. Then a Palace footman came in the gate with a letter and she read the whole of it out loud, postscript and all — a left-handed man has been reading our file.
journals.state: On the Baraque gate at nine with programmes and door orders and his name still ringing in the air; hoarse, uneasy, wanting to be sure the Lenz on that list is the other one.

journals.entry: The bill went up in the night and at four in the morning a man knocked and it was Herr Grelle, the one they said was dead, with paste on his cuffs. I heard the whole of it from the back of the wing: Herr Falk taking his shoulder, the sixty-one pages, Herr Vane counting money out loud and Herr Grelle saying he'd heard him lie about it at Merrow. Then Herr Prewick read out a letter from Room Fourteen and there was a postscript, and it was about me — the Undersecretary of Assessment wrote a postscript about me: the ink that named a Lenz did not consult him, and he intends to be there anyway. Madam Harrow said ink casts and men choose, and to learn it by heart, and I have. I signed the minute twice because I blotted it. I said in again in the cold. Tonight I've got the house with Herr Grelle — programmes, doors, row four — and Herr Skarke paid at the door like anybody, which I'll say twice. At four minutes to I gave her the count: doors open, all eight, nine hundred and thirty-nine in and one seat empty.
journals.state: At Bell Harrow's elbow in the Theatre Royal, breathless, programmes under his arm, ears still red from the postscript; proud and uneasy about the one empty seat, wanting the house to hold and his own name to stay the other Lenz.

journals.entry: I gave her the seat — row eleven, seat one, end of the row, prompt side by the exit, sold on the plan and nobody in it — and put a programme on it and went back to the pit door where Herr Grelle could see me. Part the First was the biggest thing I have stood in; the roar for Herr Falk went on eleven seconds and I counted it. At the interval nobody went out, and I told her so with my voice gone. Then she handed me her watch and went out in front of them all and said it plain, and afterwards I gave the watch back with both hands and couldn't say anything. When the knock was coming she gave me her words to carry and I walked, I did not run. The boy came in out of the dark holding a man's hand and asked out loud if this was the finish, and she said yes, and I took his other hand and gave him a programme and walked him to row eleven, seat one, and sat on the aisle step within arm's reach all night and never once looked at the stage. After the bell and the iron I still had his hand. Madam Harrow said he stays with me till somebody claims him properly and nobody claims him improperly. I showed him the black sheet and let him shake it low, and he ate two bowls, and he told us a lady in a cab said he was expected and that the stage manager would know his name. She did.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing on a cot beside Fenner Bacher, programmes done with, ears hot and voice gone; proud and fiercely protective, wanting nobody to take the boy off him tonight.

journals.entry: I was making Fenner laugh and then the third board went and he was gone off the cot at a dead run, and it was his Mam. I went and stood at the pin rail and looked hard at a rope, because it wasn't my business any more and I wasn't going to be seen minding. She got down on the boards with him. Later Madam Harrow struck the night like a set and somebody was sent across town to fetch Wenzel in, and I'd have gone if my voice had been working. In the morning there was porridge and they went on the midday coach, and Herr Grelle carried the hamper. Herr Vane says I may hold the doors on the 14th of Frost at the Athenaeum. So that's mine.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with his voice half back and a props list in his fist; a bit flattened by the departure and proud about the 14th, wanting a job to do this minute.

journals.entry:
Painted the trunk vermilion — two coats, my whole Thursday, and my hands were red to the wrist and I didn't mind. Ran the tea things on the 9th for the Undersecretary who isn't a relation. Hung off the tailboard out of the capital with the trunk beside me doing nothing at all.

On the 14th at Vessendal I laid a programme on row four centre same as always, though nobody had come, and then the box office slate said nine hundred and one bodies for nine hundred seats and Herr Grelle said the odd one came in late, paid at the door, sat in four centre and left before the calls. I carried it to her in the cage and she said enter it exactly and post nothing. Fenner came in the front door with his Mam and his Da and read the small print about the gas.

Doors at Katterau with Herr Grelle in the spring, and Herr Falk is to teach Fenner to stand at nine o'clock, and Herr Vane says I hold doors wherever we go now. I fell asleep against the trunk twice and it was just a box.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

journals.entry: Row four went out with the house at Katterau and I gave her the slate: full count, nobody late, nobody left, nobody empty, and I have never liked a sentence better. Then the winter road, Vessendal a fortnight, Merrow's fair, and on the fourteenth of Frost in the Achterhalt yard I read her chalk first and shouted, and started the whole yard off. Frau Sorel came in on the coach and everything stopped a minute. At soup she opened the floor youngest last, and my hands went cold, and I stood up with my ears burning and asked for it out loud: second stage manager, second on the book, not props, and I said I'm nineteen and I held the doors at the Palace and I never looked at the stage once. Krul said eighteen, in front of everybody. Madam Harrow ruled it — second on the book, with terms: I chalk tomorrow's call under her eye, the bucket rounds are mine alone from tonight, I learn the plot tables off Herr Krug, and in the spring at Katterau I call the storm to six hundred people with her standing behind me saying nothing. And I'm nineteen the day I call it clean. Herr Krug wrote me into the datebook himself and turned it round for her initials. Herr Grelle shook my hand like a man in a trade. Then she gave me the church of a call — legibly, where it can't be missed, beginners first and largest, names before numbers, nothing on the board you haven't checked with your own feet, your own name at the bottom, because a call is a promise with a signature on it. So I went out and put my hand on the wagon wheel in the cold first, and then wrote it. It took nine minutes and it's crooked and I spelled beginners with three n's. It's signed.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

journals.entry: Winter was plot tables until Herr Krug said he dreamt in them. Then Katterau, and the second night was mine, ruled two seasons ago. I was up at five, walked the plot four times, checked a wagon I didn't need to check, and wrote the call so straight it looked printed, and at the half I went grey and told Madam Harrow the storm was on page nine and I couldn't remember what warm means. She turned me round to face the stage, not the book, and said warm was never in my pages — you call what's happening: Herr Falk's shoulders, Frau Sorel's hands, the house breathing. Then she put her own watch in my fist and closed my fingers on it, mine for tonight, to be given back at the iron. I stopped shaking all at once. Beginners, please, and my voice went where I sent it. I took the act-two flat two seconds late and Herr Krug covered it on the gas and nobody but the three of us will ever know. I held a pause nobody told me to hold and brought the light after Frau Sorel and not with her. In act four six hundred people leaned forward and I never looked at page nine: storm — go. It came in low with a floor in it and somebody in the gods laughed from fright. Iron down, three calls. I held the watch out on my palm and couldn't say one word. She weighed it, put it back on its nail, and ruled it in the wing out loud: clean. Krul said he's nineteen, and the whole wing went up. Later I went out with a lantern and stood with my hand on a wheel before I wrote a number down. At Grevenholt I called the load-in, and I signed the new minute last — T. Lenz, 2nd on book — and read it twice before I understood it. In the spring I wrote the new name on the call, spelled right, because I asked her twice.
journals.state: On the doors at Katterau at the half with the box office slate and a stack of programmes, voice back for good; proud and busy, wanting a full count and to watch the standing lesson in the morning.

characters.name: Dessa Krul
characters.description: Wardrobe mistress of the Vermilion Players, sewing while she speaks; she packed Krug's box at Katterau and it was still warm.
characters.history:
I started with a queen's slippers and a needle that never stopped moving, and a fear I named plainly: no Katterau, because Krug went there and came back to nothing, not even his boots, and I packed his empty box with my own hands still warm. She ruled against it, and I bit off my thread on that, glad.

The slippers travelled everywhere with me, guarded from filth. When Krug turned up alive in a green coat, I set them down for four seconds in shock, and stood by that as my whole opinion of the man, even after Vane confessed he'd called Krug a thief to save face, and Krug refused payment, giving pages instead — nine of them, unfinished, one with a bell and her name all through it.

We took on new company under my condition: the twelve names read slow before signing. I got that reading cold, without soup or candle, on the morning of the 2nd — ten names, a struck eleventh, a blank twelfth. I sat on a secret about my own hamper's contents all the way to the Office courtyard and came home lighter, as told.

A dead lodger got a plate and silence. A lost boy got a nest of the queen's cloaks, two bowls of soup, and no fuss, until his mother found him kneeling on the boards of the Theatre Royal. I boiled water because there was nothing else to do, and made her promise to return on the 14th.

I painted a trunk vermilion, ugly, and it held through storms in Katterau and beyond. I dressed a girl who stepped into Frau Sorel's place and did not disgrace anybody. I settled the props boy's age at eighteen, twice, and fed him after. A fiddle case now steams beside the slippers in my cage, which I permit and will not discuss.

journals.entry: Answered present from the second wagon and said whoever put a wet chestnut in the queen's slipper could swim to Vessendal. Mud, a shed wheel-rim, brown soup boiled and served. At the fire I kept my needle going and said the two things that wanted saying: the queen's slippers have two more towns in them at best, and Krug went at Katterau and came back for nothing, not even his boots — I packed his box myself and it was still warm. I don't want another warm box.

She ruled and I bit off my thread, and that was my aye. No Katterau. Good.

Swore at a wet stocking in the frost, carried the queen's slippers into the Athenaeum yard over my head like relics because that brick is filthy. Went down to the river for the tin and said there'd be new tin at Achterhalt or a copper kettle at worst, and Boyle said a kettle's a bell, and everybody stopped on the word. I keep my needle going. I still don't want another warm box.

Came down into the yard with my thimble on and stood in the circle while she untied the tape. Letter, a bank slip, a page she turned over without reading, and a key with a word on the tag. I caught myself tapping the thimble on my thumbnail while Vane read it twice standing up, and stopped, because the yard was that quiet. Whatever it says, his face went a colour I have not seen on him. Then ten o'clock, and a hem to dress with pins in my mouth, and a matinee, which is what I am for.

Pot on from the second act — mutton, barley, and something I got in the market that nobody needs to hear about. Glared at a baby through a gap in the flats and it quieted. My paint went through that door with Falk on the hour and came back none the worse, and the house stood up. Then the green room full, two candles on the cupboard, Vane on his feet with the jug toasting a wool factor, and Prewick on a crate discovering food. No warm boxes tonight. Good.
journals.state: In the green room over her pot with a plate going round, thimble on, pleased and saying little; wanting the queen's slippers to last to Achterhalt and no more warm boxes.

journals.entry: New sky came in Achterhalt wrapped in felt and rode on the boards like a duchess, and it earned its place: the storm went in low and the corn merchants forgot to breathe. Capital next, eleven days early, and the Baraque, which leaks. In the yard I had the queen's slippers in my hands when everything went quiet, and I put them down, because it was Krug standing there in a green coat, and Krug's box I packed warm with my own hands. Four seconds those slippers were on wet cobbles, and she counted them, and told me three seconds too many, and she was right, and I said four seconds is my whole opinion of a man and carried them in. At supper Vane said it whole — that he called Krug a thief to save his own face — and put seven pounds down, and Krug wouldn't have it, and gave her a parcel of pages instead. I folded my arms and stopped where I was. Nobody left. Nine pages, four not happened yet, one of them with a bell in it and her name all over it. I slept in the wardrobe cage with the slippers under my head, which is where they're safest, and they will not see the capital's second week.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage at first light, thimble on, the queen's slippers under her head; pleased Krug is fed and sitting down, wanting new slippers out of the capital and no warm boxes.

journals.entry: Sat down on the bench with my thimble on and heard the whole thing out. Somebody's got to dress it and I'm not having a stranger in my cage, so: in — and I want the twelve names read out slow before anybody signs anything, and she gave me that, cold, on the morning of the 2nd, no soup and no candle, which is right. Told Toby he was seventeen twice, because he is, and the table laughed once all night, which was mine. Krug's Palace sounded like a building that has thought about people. Frau Sorel stood up, which I have never seen, and told us her sister's name. In the morning I heard the ten names read out flat, and no twelfth, and told Wenzel he's got the best job in the building.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at the Baraque, thimble on and the queen's slippers still under her head; grim and satisfied to be dressing it, wanting her slow reading on the 2nd and no strangers in her cage.

journals.entry: Woke to the news the way news should come, in ones and twos: the dead lodger sat in the wing with paste on his cuffs, so I put a plate in front of him and said nothing, because that's what a plate is for. Moved Herr Prewick's dinner to his elbow while he ruled his columns, and signed his minute, and wrote Wenzel's name after his cross. Then they told me what was going in my hamper — the whole of it, to my face, which is the law here — and I said I'd sit on it and sit still, which is more than most of this company manages. Sat on it all the way to the Office courtyard among the bicycles, and came home on an empty one, and told her: lighter going home. In the grey on the 2nd I got my slow reading, no soup, no candle: ten names one by one, the struck eleventh, the blank twelfth, and the house entire. Now I'm dressing it, and the slippers are where I can see them.
journals.state: In the wardrobe at the Theatre Royal on the night of the 3rd, thimble on, dressing the ten; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and the queen's slippers to last one more house.

journals.entry: Dressed the ten and got them on and the queen's slippers lasted the house, which is all I asked. I stood in the wing for the matter following where a child up in row eleven could see my thimble catch the light, because she'd said stand where he can see you. Certified, and the iron, and then soup in the O.P. wing, which that wing has never had. I made a nest of the queen's cloaks and I did not fuss over the boy once, which is why he stopped being frightened, and he ate two bowls. When the kind question was put he said a lady in a cab, not his Mam, on Tuesday. I saw Frau Sorel go the colour of paper with a cloak half over her arm and I kept my mouth shut and my hands moving.
journals.state: In the O.P. wing among the queen's cloaks with the boy fed and Toby's cot beside him, thimble still on; grim and satisfied, wanting nobody in her cage and that child claimed by his own mother and no one else.

journals.entry: Board sang, boy was off the nest like a hare, and there was his mother down on her knees on the boards of the Theatre Royal with the whole of him against her coat. I put down my thimble and went and boiled water, because there is nothing else to be done with a thing like that. Sat on a stool by the nest all night with the two of them asleep in the queen's cloaks and said sssh to nobody at least once. In the morning: porridge, and I packed them a hamper for the coach and made her promise to come the 14th and bring the butter man. Nobody in my cage, and that child claimed by his own mother. That's the whole of what I wanted and I got it.
journals.state: In the Baraque wardrobe cage with the cloaks aired and the slippers mended, thimble on; tired and thoroughly satisfied, wanting a quiet week and a hamper packed for Vessendal.

journals.entry:
That trunk leaked in the rain like a coal scuttle, and I was asked to choose its paint, so I chose vermilion, being what we are, and the ironmonger had it honest. Two coats and Toby's whole Thursday, and Herr Falk stood over it drying and said it was vulgar in the voice men use for praise, and put the thunder in it and shut the lid, and it stayed shut like a box.

I sang the farrier's wife going out under the arch, since somebody had to, and Prewick pretended he didn't know the words. Vessendal for nothing a head and the slippers held. And that night when Vane got loud in the yard I shushed him, because there was a child asleep in the second wagon. In the spring, Katterau, by daylight, front doors wide, and I have my hamper packed and my cage to myself.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

journals.entry: Dressed Katterau and the slippers held, and the storm came out of my vermilion box with a floor in it and a farmer said God almighty and nobody shushed him. Then in Reap I dressed the girl who stepped up in Frau Sorel's place for a fortnight at Vessendal and she did not disgrace anybody. On the fourteenth I came out with pins in my mouth to check the spelling on that tailboard and took them out to say something I shan't write down. Let the hem down two inches and told her she'd want fitting before the half, and she did, and she sat. There's a drawing pinned to my mirror frame and nobody in that cage mentioned it, which is manners. At soup I said I'd want a proper hamper and no more than that. And when the props boy stood up and claimed nineteen I said eighteen, twice, with satisfaction, and put a second bowl in front of him, because he's had a night and a boy needs feeding when he's been made something.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

journals.entry: Watched the whole of the boy's act from the wardrobe doorway with pins in my mouth, and when she looked past his shoulder at me for the arithmetic I took the pins out one at a time and said it to the whole wing: he's nineteen. Then bedlam, as it should be — Boyle bellowing, Vane weeping on cue, Wenzel joining in without knowing why. At the Athenaeum I showed the schoolmaster's boy the queen's slippers and he didn't touch them, not being asked to, which is manners. He looked at the hamper properly. Later, a fiddle case steaming in my cage beside the slippers, which I have decided is acceptable and will not be discussing. Pins in the tin, and a new girl in the book who walked eleven miles.
journals.state: In the wardrobe cage at Katterau at the half, thimble on, the queen's slippers laced and a needle in her cuff; brisk and thoroughly at home, wanting the house up and no wet chestnuts anywhere near her slippers.

characters.name: Anton
characters.description: Mirelle Sorel's son, twelve, of the Bittersee; draws badly and with great care, and can spell one word.
characters.history:
I asked to go and see the lady from the theatre bills, and after two days' thought I said yes to the schoolmaster. She came up the lane, put out her hand but did not touch me, and we sat on the wall while she looked through all my paper. Another lady stood off at the turn of the lane and never came nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion, wrote it on things, and drew a wagon with a red box on the back for the lady to keep.

She wrote back, and I went by coach with the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible, and I did not have my hand held. At the theatre the doors stood open, and I looked at the gas and the boxes and the empty stage, and said it was smaller than it sounds. The stage manager agreed, and said it was bigger than it looks, and told me the wagon lived through the yard door, and that my pace was the law inside those walls. I went only as far as the wagon. I said the horse was too small, as in my drawing, but the man on the bale said the horse is right and the wagon is too big, and I said I would think on that. The big man showed me what all the ropes are for, with their knots. The lady with the pins showed me the queen's slippers, and I did not touch them. Herr Falk came out with a rug on his arm and told me I was standing wrong, weight on both feet; I fixed it, and he saw me fix it. It lasted twenty-five minutes, and then there was the six-forty train to catch. I thanked four people and shook my mother's hand. At the top of the street I shouted Vermilion as loud as I could.

journals.entry: The schoolmaster asked me and I thought about it for two days, and then I asked whether the lady was from the theatre on the bills, and he said she was, so I said yes. She came up the lane on the first day and I stood up on the wall to be nearer, and she put out her hand and did not touch me, and said something short. Then we sat on the wall and I showed her my paper and she looked at all of it. There was another lady standing away at the turn of the lane who did not come nearer. Afterwards I learned to spell vermilion and I write it on things, and I drew the wagon with the red box on the back for her to have.

The lady wrote back and I came on the coach with the schoolmaster's sister, who is sensible, and I did not have my hand held. The theatre where the wagon lives had its front doors wide open and it was warm and dark inside, and I stood in the doorway and looked at the gas and the boxes and the empty stage, and I said it was smaller than it sounds. The stage manager said it was smaller than it sounds and bigger than it looks, and told me where the wagon lives, through the yard door, and that my pace was the law inside the walls. So I went as far as the wagon. The horse is too small, as I said in my drawing; the man on the bale said the horse is right and the wagon is too big, and I shall think about that. The big man told me what all the ropes are for, with knots. The lady with the pins showed me the queen's slippers and I did not touch them. Herr Falk came out with a rug on his arm and said I was standing wrong, weight on both feet, and I fixed it and he saw me fix it. Twenty-five minutes and then the six-forty. I said thank you to four people. I shook my mother's hand. At the top of the street I shouted Vermilion as loud as I could.

characters.name: Krebs the doorkeeper
aliases: the old man with the lamp
characters.description: Elderly stage doorkeeper at the Corona in Grevenholt, brother of the smith who hung the hinge; lowers his lamp to the boards and has guarded Harrow's bucket for a year and a half.
characters.history: Three soft knocks, unhurried, and I came with the lamp and two bolts. A woman said she was Bell Harrow, stage manager of the Vermilion Players, so I lowered the lamp to the boards and not in her face, and told her she'd be the one that posted the notices, and that my brother did their hinge — which bites its frame still. Then I told her the thing I have been keeping: there's a bucket under her prompt corner, there since the other Katterau, the one before hers, and nobody has dared move it. She came in over the third board on purpose and let it sing, and then she ruled the bucket on permanent duty, dry or not, the oldest notice in their church. I set my lamp on the prompt shelf beside it and looked at the pair of them, and said I'd tell the gas boy, who has been trying to fill it with rags since June. Then she gave me the news like a present: two nights, Ilsabet first, and the second a debut — the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor.

journals.entry: Three soft knocks, unhurried, and I came with the lamp and two bolts. A woman said she was Bell Harrow, stage manager of the Vermilion Players, so I lowered the lamp to the boards and not in her face, and told her she'd be the one that posted the notices, and that my brother did their hinge — which bites its frame still. Then I told her the thing I have been keeping: there's a bucket under her prompt corner, there since the other Katterau, the one before hers, and nobody has dared move it. She came in over the third board on purpose and let it sing, and then she ruled the bucket on permanent duty, dry or not, the oldest notice in their church. I set my lamp on the prompt shelf beside it and looked at the pair of them, and said I'd tell the gas boy, who has been trying to fill it with rags since June. Then she gave me the news like a present: two nights, Ilsabet first, and the second a debut — the Wolf King, certified at last, with a storm in it that has a floor.

characters.name: Rosza Emmerich
characters.description: Fiddler of about thirty, boots done for, walked eleven miles in the wet to answer a notice; hired inside ten minutes as the company's musician.
characters.history: I read the notice four times in the wet before going in — eleven miles walked, boots finished, fiddle under my coat. The stage door stood open, and when I said it shouldn't be, Bell Harrow, the stage manager, told me it was open on purpose, turning her lamp so the light fell on the boards, not my face. My ten minutes began when I stepped on the singing board. She said I could answer her three questions in any order. I told her: I am Rosza Emmerich; four years at a dancing school where tempo is the whole job; two years in a Kessarine pit band until it stopped paying; a winter of weddings and a funeral a week, which teaches you to change a tune when a room changes. I read music, transpose while playing, don't drink at work, and can mend a bow — nothing else. I said they should take me because hers was the only bill that said ask for the stage manager, meaning somebody kept a book, and I'd been paid from hats for two years and wanted to be written down. She counted my three good signs on three fingers, then gave me terms — posted, unrounded wages, a line in the book, a bunk in the second wagon, four sentences of house rules — and I signed my full name and asked what hour beginners were. A weeping man in plum came from the wing promising me a stove; she ruled it harmless before supper. Then she told me to play. I tuned badly, then properly, and played a cold dance tune at the tempo of eleven miles. Nobody clapped. An old man in the stalls said they'd had thunder for a year and no music. Later, case steaming beside the queen's slippers, I found the third board again and asked once more what hour beginners were.

journals.entry: Four days that notice sat on a board with a horse auction and two lost dogs, and I read it four times in the wet before I went in. Eleven miles, boots finished, fiddle under my coat. The stage door opened without a knock and I said so — it shouldn't have been open — and she said it was open on purpose, and turned her lamp down so the light was on the boards and not in my face. Bell Harrow, stage manager, and my ten minutes had started when I stepped on the singing board. She asked three things in any order I liked, so I thought about the order first: Rosza Emmerich; four years for a dancing school where you learn nobody is watching you and the tempo is the whole job; two years in a Kessarine pit band until it stopped being paid; a winter of weddings and a funeral a week, which teaches you to change a tune when a room changes. I can read, I transpose while playing, I don't drink at work, I can mend a bow and nothing else. And why they should carry me: because hers is the only bill I ever saw that said ask for the stage manager, which told me somebody in there keeps a book, and I have been paid out of hats for two years and would like to be in a book. She counted my three good signs back at me on three fingers, gave me terms — wages posted and unrounded, a line in the book, a bunk in the second wagon, and a church of four sentences — and I signed my whole name and asked what hour beginners were. Then a large weeping man in plum came out of the wing promising me a stove, and she ruled that harmless before supper. Then she told me to play, so I tuned badly and then properly and played a cold dance tune at the tempo of eleven miles, and the house gave it back bigger than me, and nobody clapped, and the old man in the stalls said they'd had thunder for a year and no music. Late, my case steaming beside the queen's slippers, I found the third board again in the dark and asked once more what hour beginners were.

characters.name: Krebs
characters.description: Carpenter over the smithy who comes for a shilling and a brandy and makes the stage door bite its frame.
characters.history: I came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. I showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon. Of the second summons, when it came, I remember nothing — I was not present, and whatever passed that day passed without me.

journals.entry: Came over from the smithy for the Vermilion when the new stage manager sent word — a shilling and a brandy in hand, though Vane's name had said one-and-six. Showed her the hinge, proud of it, and had the stage door biting its frame on the first try by noon.
journals.state: Back over the smithy with a shilling and an empty glass, pleased with a hinge well shown and a bargain he thinks he won.

journals.entry: Not present.
journals.state: Not present.

characters.name: Ottmar Boyle
characters.description: Second gentlemen and all soldiers; mends wheel-rims with wire and profanity and reckons everything in marching miles.
characters.history:
I am Ottmar Boyle, twenty-two years carrying, roping, and standing on tailboards for this company. It started with lists and axles: a Krug missing from the roster, a wheel-rim wired back together, and word that Katterau was back on the books — twenty-two mile out and twenty-two home, four days for one night I'd rather not have walked. The ruling sent us the toll road instead, eight shilling, and I said so first. I stood watch on the trunk many nights, called kettle a bell when the word had gone bad, and learned to open doors only to talking distance until told otherwise. I banked the bag from Vane without asking questions, fed horses, roped tarpaulins twice, because twice is the number.

I found paper under a milestone and said, madam, do we look; found Hessler's shop shut on a market Saturday with two hundred unordered bills printed against us, and a woman watching who wasn't ours to chase. Krug came back in a green coat on a mounting block, and Vane confessed his own lie before us all and put money on it, which Krug let lie. A cast list turned up in the trunk — ten names, one struck, one blank — and I told her straight I'd rather be on a list than off it. Wenzel was struck and given the horses instead, which suited him better than sparing would have.

I've walked billstickers home behind lanterns, fetched Wenzel off a trunk he wouldn't leave, held a stage door for a mother who said nothing and a boy asking if this was the finish. I watched rain leak through that trunk and enjoyed saying so more than anything in twenty-two years. My door held for Falk's cue at Katterau, and I've never been prouder of a hinge. I've argued with a beam and lost, and kept holding it anyway.

journals.entry: Answered present from under the tarpaulin — Ottmar Boyle, second gentlemen and all soldiers — and said out loud that there used to be a Krug on this list and he's not here. Fixed a shed wheel-rim in the afternoon with wire and language. At the fire the stage manager asked me first, being soldiers' sums: two days to Vessendal if the carter's axle holds, three if it don't; Achterhalt to the capital a hundred and ten mile, eight shilling toll road or the free hill road that killed a horse on us. And the sum nobody had said: Katterau is back. Twenty-two mile the wrong way and twenty-two home, four days of legs for one night. I'll walk it if it's ruled. I'd rather not walk it for a favour a mayor may have died of.

Ruling came down and I nodded once and went to look at the axle by lamplight, which is what a ruling means to me. Toll road, then — eight shilling, and cheaper than a horse, and I said so first. Wired the axle in the morning and it held two days.

Backed the second wagon into the Athenaeum yard, took first watch on the trunk with a lantern and a pipe I'm not let smoke in the flies. Got relieved twenty minutes for the tin's funeral in the river and grumbled about it and went anyway. When Krul said a copper kettle would do for thunder I said what wanted saying: kettle's no good, kettle's a bell. And then nobody said anything for half a second, which is how I learned that word's gone bad in this company.

Took the watch through the night and woke Toby for his. Stood in the ring round the tailboard while she opened the merchant's parcel and said nothing, because nothing was wanted. Then the little man with the brass case was at the gate on a Wednesday, asking after her by name, and I went and said so, and she had me open it to talking distance and no farther, which I did. The town clock struck the quarter and got it right, and I said what wanted saying: load-in for the matinee's at ten. Then I swung the gates and it was ten o'clock and the day went on being a day.

Took the bag off Vane at the half and banked it as I was told, no questions. My door held: Falk went through it on his cue, stage left, and it opened like a door and the house came down, and I'll take that. After the curtain I fed the horses, roped the tarpaulin, brought a jug up to the green room and sold Toby the watch till midnight for a penny and a plate. Saturday I checked the ropes twice, because twice is the number, and we loaded out.
journals.state: In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.

journals.entry: Swung out of the Athenaeum yard, toll road under us, hedges laid proper. At the top of the climb I saw the corner of paper under the milestone lip, dry as bone under wet stone, and pulled up without being asked and said, madam, do we look. She looked, one of us, as she does, and pocketed it, and told me to find out what that bell was before it decided it was ours. It was a market crier on a barrel with our name printed over him. I went for the printer and found Hessler shut on a market Saturday, which he never is, with a lamp lit behind the shutters, and said so. Stood at the corner being mild while the Office knocked. Two hundred bills, and nobody ordered them; the old man tipped his type back in the case and I've never seen a man look happier doing away with his own work. Two sacks on the tailboard. Then I clocked the woman across the way who'd not moved since we knocked — countrywoman's coat, town boots — and reported it, and she went over alone and told us to stay put, so we stayed put. Bailiff came and went civil. We've a hall for twelve and a strongroom for the sacks, and my axle held the climb.
journals.state: In the yard at load-out with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe in his pocket, satisfied that his door and his knots held; wanting the road to Achterhalt and an axle that behaves.

journals.entry: Axle held the toll road, eight shilling, and worth it. Achterhalt: backed in, watched, took the tailboard off Falk at midnight with my pipe unlit and he let me, which he has never done. Told him beforehand a woman had spoken to the stage manager in the market, because a man should know what's coming at him. Capital next, and the Baraque arch is four inches narrower than any arch has business being, and I said so at length. Then the yard went quiet: green coat on the mounting block, and it was Krug. I gave him the plain of it — the bill in Achterhalt, the bailiff, the type broken — because he asked and it cost nothing. Vane sat down in the wet and named his own lie in front of the lot of us. At supper he said it again whole and put money down, and Krug left it lying. Nine pages out of a portmanteau, and one of them is a wagon and a printer's line, which I stood in. Double watch on the trunk in a city yard, me and the boy splitting, and I checked the ropes twice, twice being the number. She's gone to the Office alone this morning and Prewick with her, and the trunk's still where I put it.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with rope and an unlit pipe, having handed the watch to Toby; content that arch, axle and knots all held, wanting the leaking roof mended and the trunk left alone.

journals.entry: Twenty-two mile the wrong way I'd have walked; this is nought mile, so I said in, provided Wenzel stops with the horses, and Wenzel said so himself before I'd finished. Said aye at the end of her ruling the way a man does at the end of a service. Then out in the yard, checking my ropes, the tarpaulin was thrown back and the trunk's lid was up. I stood well clear and got her, and she took my lantern and went over alone and looked once and told me straight: a cast list, mostly ours, ten names, one struck, one blank. I roped the lid, and then roped it again a different way because my hands wanted work, and told her what I had to say — twenty-two years carrying and roping and standing on the tailboard, and I'd rather be on a list than off it, and I'd rather know than not. Wenzel's off it and Wenzel's got the horses, and that's her ruling doing its work; he'll like that better than being spared. Fetched her coat and the coffee. Watch to two. In the morning the names were read cold, and then a Palace man came to the gate and I shut it behind him.
journals.state: In the Baraque yard with rope in his hands and an unlit pipe, the trunk roped twice over; sober-minded and glad to be named, wanting the lid to stay shut and Wenzel content with the horses.

journals.entry: Stood back from the stage door at four when she gave me the flat hand, and the man who came in was the dead one. Kept out of it. In the morning I sent Herr Falk out of the arch for cluttering it, six hours early with his hands in his pockets, and he went. Spelled words for Herr Prewick's minute and put my name to it. Brought the cart round on the 2nd, drove the laundry hamper and Krul on top of it through the general traffic to the Office courtyard and back, and asked nothing about what was under the costumes. Roped the trunk over again with Wenzel sat on it looking like a man doing nothing, which he does well. Said in again in the cold. Tonight the ropes are checked twice and the exits are propped.
journals.state: Backstage at the Theatre Royal with rope and an unlit pipe, cart put away and the trunk roped in the Baraque yard; sober-minded and easy, wanting the night clean and Wenzel content with the horses.

journals.entry: Toby came down at a walk with her words, exact, and I took the stage door — the wrong door, out of sight of every soul in the house. Lamp low, light on the boards and not in a man's face, open wide on the third knock and not before. The knocks came through the wall, plain as a cart in the street. Three, and I opened it wide, and the cold of the yard came in along the boards, and there stood a billsticker with paste dried on his cuffs and a boy of ten by the hand asking out loud if this was the finish. I let them by to her and stood my post. Ropes were checked twice and the exits propped, and Krug's iron came in on eleven, as promised.
journals.state: Backstage at the Theatre Royal with his lamp and an unlit pipe, the wrong door shut behind him; sober and easy, wanting the house out clean and the trunk still roped in the Baraque yard.

journals.entry: Stood in the wing with my lamp when the mother came through and did not say a word, which was the right amount to say.
